66186276B31593004124297.blindSummary:
The state/province restricts restroom and locker-room use by sex assigned at birth in public schools and government-owned buildings. A law introduced on 11 January 2024 and signed by the state/province governor on 30 January 2024 gives effect to that rule. It does not reach private businesses, so hotels, gyms and commercial venues fall outside it. New government buildings must include single-occupant facilities. A person facing a complaint may answer it with documentation: a birth certificate and, where the marker on that certificate has been changed, proof of gender-affirming surgery. The defence rests on records a visitor will generally not carry, and the law provides no alternative route for someone whose documents were issued outside the state/province.

Enforcement runs through complaints rather than police action. A reporting form allows residents to report transgender people in privacy spaces such as changing rooms and restrooms, and complainants may choose whether their own names are included while the state/province investigates each reported violation. A procedure adopted in May 2024 allows officials and individuals to file formal complaints about suspected incorrect bathroom use in schools and government buildings. A civil-liberties organisation opposed the law on the ground that it invites discriminatory enforcement.

In March 2025 the state/province enacted a ban on LGBTQ pride flags in public schools and government buildings. A May 2025 account places the signing on 7 May and describes the state/province as the first to prohibit such flags explicitly, with fines of $500 a day. A major city in the state/province adopted a flag modelled on the transgender pride flag as an official city flag in May 2025. A state/province advocacy organisation's executive director said the state/province leads the country in anti-LGBTQ legislation.

Gender-affirming care for minors is banned. The ban passed the lower chamber on 26 January 2023 and the upper chamber 20-8 the following day, and was signed on 28 January 2023 with immediate effect; treatment already under way in January 2023 could continue. Clinicians may provide care to patients under 25, but those patients hold a retroactive right to disaffirm consent and sue. A legislative legal review found the ban potentially unconstitutional for targeting transgender people. A two-year systematic review commissioned under the ban and released in May 2025 concluded that the treatments are effective for mental health and psychosocial outcomes and for body changes consistent with an affirmed gender, and safe with respect to bone density, cardiovascular risk, metabolic change and cancer; the legislature dismissed the findings and kept the ban in force.

State/province-issued identity documents remain amendable. A transgender person may change the gender marker on a birth certificate on submission of a certified court order changing name and gender; surgery is not required, and an X descriptor is available subject to judicial approval. In May 2021 the highest court held 4-1 that judges must grant sex and name changes when the clinical requirements are met.

Nondiscrimination protection is partial. A 2015 statute bans discrimination based on gender identity in employment and housing but not in public accommodations, and exempts religious organisations and their affiliates, including schools and hospitals. The hate-crime statute amended in 2019 covers gender identity, carries enhanced penalties and requires the collection and publication of hate-crime statistics; those amendments passed the upper chamber 18-11 and the lower chamber 64-9, with concurrence 22-3, and were signed on 2 April 2019.

Sports participation has been contested for several years. A 2022 law barring transgender athletes from sports, athletics and the Olympics was vetoed by the governor on 22 March 2022 and enacted over the veto to take effect on 1 July; on 19 August a judge partly reversed it and allowed transgender girls to be considered case by case for girls' sports in 2022-2023. On 3 October 2024 two public universities forfeited matches against another university during litigation over a transgender player's eligibility. In 2024 the state/province also barred transgender students from dormitories matching their gender identity, after a transgender woman was assigned to a women's dormitory at a public university.

Marriage equality reached the state/province on 6 October 2014, after a national appellate court affirmed a lower court ruling of 20 December 2013 striking the ban; that ruling displaced a 1995 non-recognition statute and a 2004 constitutional amendment defining marriage as the union of a man and a woman, which voters approved 65.8 per cent to 33.2 per cent. Adoption follows from the recognition of the marriage. Foster care and adoption are otherwise limited to married or single persons, with cohabiting unmarried couples barred and priority given to married couples under a 1998 statute. For couples using in vitro fertilisation, parental recognition of the non-genetic, non-gestational parent follows only from marriage. In August 2019 the highest court held the bar on same-sex surrogacy agreements unconstitutional.

Private consensual sexual conduct is not criminalised. The sodomy statute was invalidated by a national court ruling in 2003 and repealed by the legislature in 2019, following lower-chamber approval 74-0 with one abstention on 29 January, upper-chamber approval 25-2 with two abstentions on 22 February, and the governor's signature on 25 March 2019. Earlier changes had reduced the offence from a felony to a misdemeanour in 1969 and created an exemption for married couples in 1973.

66186276B22881275445497.summary:
North Dakota stands under the United States national framework for passports, entry screening and federal identity documents; the findings below are specific to the state.

A national anti-trans legal-risk assessment dated July 2026, built from five years of daily legislative tracking and a rubric scoring the most severe bills, lists North Dakota among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults, and among the states that prohibit any change to birth certificates. The assessment states that this prohibition forces transgender people to disclose their status when presenting documents.

Birth-certificate gender markers are effectively closed. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document tracker records that North Dakota's 2023 law bans all gender-marker changes on birth certificates with a narrow exception for individuals who have had genital surgery, a stricter and more explicit surgical requirement than in many other states, and marks North Dakota a negative-law state. The regulations accompanying the 2023 statute were rejected, leaving in place a 2008 regulation restricting changes to those who have undergone a sex conversion operation.

Driver's licences and state ID cards follow a separate and lower threshold: the Department of Transportation updates the gender marker on receipt of a physician or therapist letter stating that the applicant has completed a permanent gender role transition.

North Dakota statutes do not explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity. Employment discrimination is addressed federally under Bostock v. Clayton County (15 June 2020), and city-level protections exist in Grand Forks for city employees and applicants and in rental housing from 2013. An April 2021 state law allows student groups at colleges, universities and high schools to discriminate against LGBT students.

Providing gender-affirming care to minors is illegal under a bill passed by a veto-proof majority on 5 April 2023.

Two bills signed into law in April 2023 ban individuals assigned male at birth from female sports and athletics in schools and in higher education respectively. A 2021 bill to the same effect passed the House 69 to 25 and the Senate 27 to 20 but was vetoed by Governor Doug Burgum on 21 April 2021.

An April 2023 law, effective 1 July, explicitly allows restriction of transgender individuals' public bathroom usage in many state-run facilities.

HB 1522 (2023), an act relating to preferred pronouns and accommodations to a transgender student, carried a penalty provision and an emergency clause, was signed by the governor, and had its last official action filed with the Secretary of State on 9 May 2023. The corresponding May 2023 law, effective 1 July, forbids schools and government entities from requiring or prohibiting preferred pronoun use and requires disclosure of transgender students to parents in state-run schools. A March 2023 bill requiring parental and administrative approval for preferred pronoun use in state-run schools and classrooms had been vetoed.

North Dakota's hate-crime law does not cover gender identity, while federal prosecution for crimes motivated by gender identity has been available since the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act of 2009. A June 2021 committee regulation bans conversion therapy by social workers, psychologists and counsellors.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 26 June 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges, following prior constitutional and statutory restriction to one man and one woman; proceedings in Ramsay v. Dalrymple were suspended in January 2015. The Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians legalised same-sex marriage on its reservation by 6 to 2 in August 2020.

Private adult consensual homosexual relations were legalized in 1973 as part of a Criminal Code revision setting universal age of consent at eighteen, after prior sodomy prohibitions dating to 1862 and expansions in 1885, 1903 and State v. Nelson in 1917 and a forced sterilization law expanded in 1927 to habitual criminals, moral degenerates and sexual perverts and repealed in 1965. Same-sex marriage has been legal since June 26 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges after prior constitutional and statutory restriction to one man and one woman, with proceedings in Ramsay v. Dalrymple suspended in January 2015 and the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians legalizing same-sex marriage on its reservation by 6 to 2 in August 2020. Adoption by individuals is permitted with no express ban on LGBTQ people or same-sex couples, though a 1980s Supreme Court ruling made parental sexual orientation decisive in custody because of societal prejudices before reversal in 2003, while state law expressly allows private adoption agencies to discriminate based on sincerely held religious belief. Lesbian couples have access to in vitro fertilization with state law recognizing the non-genetic, non-gestational mother as legal parent after donor insemination irrespective of marital status, with gestational surrogacy expressly permitted for intended parents whether same-sex or different-sex and traditional surrogacy prohibited. State statutes do not explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, though Title VII protects employees after Bostock v. Clayton County on June 15 2020, with Fargo since 2001 and Jamestown protecting city employees on sexual orientation and Grand Forks from 2013 protecting city employees and applicants and rental housing, while a February 17 2015 Senate bill banning sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations passed 25 to 22 but failed in the House. An April 2021 law allows student groups at colleges, universities and high schools to discriminate against LGBT students despite institutional non-discrimination policies upheld in Christian Legal Society v. Martinez in 2010, and a March 2023 bill passed to allow businesses to refuse service on any grounds based on religious objective alone awaited gubernatorial action. State hate crime law does not cover sexual orientation, though federal law since 2009 allows federal prosecution for crimes based on sexual orientation. In July 2020 North Dakota Republican delegates voted for the party 2020 election platform opposing absolutely any civil rights protections for LGBTQ people while accusing transgender people "of preying on women" and LGBTQ people of "recruiting children". Many Republican delegates condemned the platform. Governor Doug Burgum opposed the platform calling it "divisive and divisional" and stating "As I've long said, all North Dakotans deserve to be treated equally and live free of discrimination". A 2022 Public Religion Research Institute poll found 78 percent of residents supported an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity while 22 percent were opposed. Residents have no state statutory protection against gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing or public accommodations; the practical floor is federal Title VII under Bostock v. Clayton County, supplemented by municipal rules for city employees and applicants and rental housing in Grand Forks from 2013.

Adoption is permitted with no express statutory ban on LGBTQ people or same-sex couples, but state law expressly allows private adoption agencies to discriminate on the basis of sincerely held religious belief. A 1980s supreme court ruling had made parental sexual orientation decisive in custody cases because of societal prejudices; that precedent was reversed in 2003.

Family-law provisions available to residents include recognition of the non-genetic, non-gestational mother as legal parent after donor insemination irrespective of marital status, express permission for gestational surrogacy for intended parents whether same-sex or different-sex, and prohibition of traditional surrogacy.

Conversion therapy is banned for social workers, psychologists and counsellors under a June 2021 committee regulation, while the state hate-crime statute still excludes gender-identity-motivated violence.

Several tribal nations within North Dakota maintain distinct traditions of gender-nonconforming roles, including third-gender people also called two-spirit, recorded as skuxát among the Arikara, miati and mihdeke among the Hidatsa and Mandan, and wįktą, winkta and wíŋkte among the Assiniboine, Dakota and Lakota. The sources state that perceptions of gender and sexuality within these communities differ from those of residents of European descent, both historically and at present.

66186276B22881275445497.displaySummary: North Dakota stands under the United States national framework for passports, entry screening and federal identity documents. The national record for United States covers the federal layer in detail. A national anti-trans legal-risk assessment dated July 2026, built from five years of daily legislative tracking and a rubric scoring the most severe bills, lists North Dakota among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults, and among the states that prohibit any change to birth certificates. The assessment states that this prohibition forces transgender people to disclose their status when presenting documents. Birth-certificate gender markers are effectively closed. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document tracker records that North Dakota's 2023 law bans all gender-marker changes on birth certificates with a narrow exception for individuals who have had genital surgery, a stricter and more explicit surgical requirement than in many other states, and marks North Dakota a negative-law state. The regulations accompanying the 2023 statute were rejected, leaving in place a 2008 regulation restricting changes to those who have undergone a sex conversion operation. Driver's licences and state ID cards follow a separate and lower threshold: the Department of Transportation updates the gender marker on receipt of a physician or therapist letter stating that the applicant has completed a permanent gender role transition. North Dakota statutes do not explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity. City-level protections exist in Grand Forks for city employees and applicants and in rental housing from 2013. An April 2021 state law allows student groups at colleges, universities and high schools to discriminate against LGBT students. Providing gender-affirming care to minors is illegal under a bill passed by a veto-proof majority on 5 April 2023. Two bills signed into law in April 2023 ban individuals assigned male at birth from female sports and athletics in schools and in higher education respectively. A 2021 bill to the same effect passed the House 69 to 25 and the Senate 27 to 20 but was vetoed by Governor Doug Burgum on 21 April 2021. An April 2023 law, effective 1 July, explicitly allows restriction of transgender individuals' public bathroom usage in many state-run facilities. HB 1522 (2023), an act relating to preferred pronouns and accommodations to a transgender student, carried a penalty provision and an emergency clause, was signed by the governor, and had its last official action filed with the Secretary of State on 9 May 2023. The corresponding May 2023 law, effective 1 July, forbids schools and government entities from requiring or prohibiting preferred pronoun use and requires disclosure of transgender students to parents in state-run schools. A March 2023 bill requiring parental and administrative approval for preferred pronoun use in state-run schools and classrooms had been vetoed. North Dakota's hate-crime law does not cover gender identity. A June 2021 committee regulation bans conversion therapy by social workers, psychologists and counsellors. Prior state constitutional and statutory restriction limited marriage to one man and one woman, and proceedings in Ramsay v. Dalrymple were suspended in January 2015. The Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians legalised same-sex marriage on its reservation by 6 to 2 in August 2020.

66186276B38006515706420.name: South Dakota
66186276B38006515706420.summary:
South Dakota restricts transgender people from using bathrooms, locker rooms and changing areas matching their gender identity in public schools and state-owned buildings under House Bill 1259, signed by Governor Larry Rhoden on 20 March 2025 and announced the following day. The law took effect on 1 July 2025 and passed the state House 49-21. Its scope covers state-run facilities, primarily K-12 schools and state colleges, including off-campus activities. It is the first facilities restriction of its kind to be enacted in the state, after comparable bills failed in 2016, 2017, twice in 2018 and in 2022.

The law's "reasonable accommodation" clause and the floor debate around it raised the prospect that incarcerated transgender people would be placed in solitary confinement in order to comply.

No South Dakota statute explicitly prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations, and the state hate-crime law does not cover gender identity. Federal law supplies the only backstop: Title VII employment protection as construed in Bostock v. Clayton County (2020) and federal hate-crime prosecution under the 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Act.

Identity documents are closed to gender-marker change. On 5 March 2026 the South Dakota Supreme Court ruled that a transgender person cannot amend the sex designation on a South Dakota birth certificate to reflect gender identity, affirming the denial of Sigrid Nielsen's September 2024 petition to change the marker from male to female and holding that a change is permitted only to correct an error made at birth. A legal gender change on a driver's licence or state ID remains available by court order or a physician affidavit confirming sex reassignment surgery, and on a birth certificate by court order, photo ID, application and fee.

Gender-affirming care for people under 18 is banned under House Bill 1080, passed in February 2023 and signed on 13 February 2023. The law required prior puberty-blocker or hormone treatment to be systematically reduced, ending no later than 31 December 2023, and authorises affected people to sue until age 25 or within three years of discovering an injury.

An advocacy legal-risk assessment published in July 2026 lists South Dakota among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults, drawing on five years of daily legislative tracking and a rubric for the most severe bills.

State institutions have also acted against transgender health provision directly. On 16 December 2022 South Dakota terminated The Transformation Project's $136,000 federally funded Community Health Worker contract for LGBTQ+ and transgender community health in Sioux Falls. To settle the organisation's discrimination lawsuit, Health Secretary Melissa Magstadt issued an apology letter on 17 January 2024 acknowledging the termination and differential treatment compared with other Community Health Worker contractors, affirming equal treatment under law regardless of race, colour, national origin, religion, disability, age or sex; the state paid $300,000 covering attorney fees, committed not to discriminate against the Project in violation of state or federal law in any services, programmes or activities, and allowed the retention of community health worker Jack Fonder.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in South Dakota (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: South Dakota law contains no explicit prohibition of discrimination on the basis of gender identity, though federal Title VII protection was established by Bostock v. Clayton County on June 15, 2020, and Oglala Lakota County and the cities of Sioux Falls, Vermillion and Brookings provide limited public-employee or comprehensive employment, housing and public-accommodations protections, with Brookings acting in March 2018. A March 2021 law signed by Governor Kristi Noem allows businesses to deny goods or services to LGBTQ people based on owners' purported religious beliefs, and in 2024 the Transformation Project won a discrimination lawsuit against the state. South Dakota hate-crime law does not cover gender identity, but federal prosecution has been available since the 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Act, and in September 2019 the Oglala Sioux Tribal Council passed hate-crime legislation protecting LGBT and two-spirit individuals by 14-2-1. For identity documents, the article states both a March 2026 Supreme Court of South Dakota ruling banning change of sex on a birth certificate unless an error was made at birth and a procedure allowing legal gender change via court order, photo ID, application and fee for birth certificates and via court order or physician affidavit confirming sex reassignment surgery for driver's licenses and state IDs. Gender-affirming healthcare for persons under 18 was banned by House Bill 1080 passed in February 2023 and signed February 13, 2023, requiring prior puberty-blocker or hormone treatment to be systematically reduced ending no later than December 31, 2023, and authorizing suits by affected persons until age 25 or within three years of discovering injury. A March 2016 bill requiring transgender students to use bathrooms and locker rooms matching birth sex was vetoed by Governor Dennis Daugaard, while House Bill 1108 barring K-7 instruction on gender identity and expression passed the House February 12, 2019 but failed in the Senate on March 29, 2019 adjournment. Transgender participation in female school sports was restricted by executive order in March 2021 after Governor Noem declined to sign a broader legislative ban over college-sports concerns, followed by a statutory ban signed February 4, 2022 effective July 1, 2022, with ACLU federal litigation threatened. Private adult consensual non-commercial same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1976 after prior Dakota Territory criminal bans dating to 1862 with penalties up to life imprisonment, later ten years, expanded in 1910 in State v. Whitmarsh to include fellatio, with current age of consent at fifteen after initial thirteen. Same-sex marriage has been recognized since June 26, 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges, superseding a November 2006 constitutional amendment and statutes defining marriage as man-woman and barring other recognition, following Rosenbrahn v. Daugaard filed May 22, 2014 where Judge Karen Schreier ruled for plaintiffs January 12, 2015 but stayed pending appeal. Adoption law does not specify rules for single individuals or married same-sex couples, lesbian couples have access to in vitro fertilization with non-genetic married mothers recognized after donor insemination, gay male couples may use surrogacy with pre-birth orders, but S.J. 746 enacted May 2017 permits agencies to refuse placements violating religious or moral convictions. No state provision explicitly bars sexual-orientation discrimination in employment, housing or public accommodations, though Oglala Lakota County, Sioux Falls, Vermillion, Minnehaha County, Spearfish, Watertown and Brookings provide limited public-employee or, in Brookings' March 2018 ordinance, comprehensive protections, while federal Bostock protection applies from June 15, 2020 and a March 2021 law permits religious-based denial of goods or services. State hate-crime law does not cover sexual orientation, but federal coverage has existed since 2009 allowing federal prosecution. A 2022 PRRI poll found 63% support for same-sex marriage, 67% support for anti-discrimination laws covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and 62% opposition to religious-based refusal to serve gay and lesbian people.

66186276B10933057601622.name: Wyoming
66186276B10933057601622.summary:
Wyoming's facilities law is the most immediate exposure for a trans visitor. House Bill 72, the "Protecting privacy in public spaces act," was signed by Governor Mark Gordon on 3 March 2025 after passing the House 52-8 on 7 February 2025 and the Senate 25-6, and took effect 1 July 2025. It defines male and female by biological sex and requires public facilities to reserve multi-occupancy restrooms, changing areas and sleeping quarters exclusively for males or exclusively for females, prohibiting entry into a facility that does not match biological sex. Accommodations are permitted only where they do not include opposite-sex multi-occupancy access. The law creates a cause of action for a person who encounters an opposite-sex person in a sex-designated restroom or changing area where the facility permitted it or failed to prohibit it, and for a person required by a correctional or educational facility to share sleeping quarters with the opposite sex.

A second measure signed the same day, Senate File 62, "Sex-designated facilities and public schools," requires public school children from pre-kindergarten up, including charter school students, to use restrooms aligned with sex assigned at birth, with districts required to provide a "reasonable accommodation" to any student who does not wish to use a multiple-occupancy restroom or locker room matching the gender at that student's birth.

Wyoming has no state nondiscrimination protection on the basis of gender identity in public accommodations, housing, employment, or credit and lending. As of 12 October 2026 the Movement Advancement Project rates Wyoming's gender-identity policy score at -9 out of 25 and its overall score at -6.5 out of 47, a Negative rating, with the sole noted protection being federal recourse for employment discrimination under Bostock v. Clayton County (June 2020), available through the EEOC and federal courts. 66186276B64762166704956.summary:
West Virginia's controlling statute on sex and facilities is Senate Bill 456, the Riley Gaines Act, signed by Governor Patrick Morrisey on 12 March 2025 after passing the state Senate on 3 March and the House of Delegates on 6 March. It defines "woman" as an adult human of the female sex and "man" as an adult human of the male sex, and the law recognises no category beyond male and female; language requiring genital examination was struck before signing. At the ceremony the Governor said bathrooms, locker rooms, domestic violence shelters and rape crisis centres "should be kept private for women only."

The statute's stated reach covers locker rooms, bathrooms, rape crisis centres, dormitories and prisons, so exposure runs from a rest stop restroom to any shelter or correctional setting a visitor might enter. West Virginia's facility restrictions are catalogued in the Movement Advancement Project's equality map of state bans on transgender people's use of public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity.

An independent anti-trans legal risk assessment published 27 August 2026 places West Virginia in its "Worst States" group, one tier below the four states it rates "Do Not Travel," within a national frame it describes as "Worst Policies In Effect."

State identity documents remain changeable but the route is narrow. A gender marker on a West Virginia birth certificate requires a Birth Certificate Request Form with a court order for gender change and fees paid to Vital Registration; a driver's licence or state ID requires a Gender Designation Form signed by a licensed physician, with no surgery or sterilisation required. In July 2020 the West Virginia Supreme Court upheld a circuit court's refusal to allow a marker change even after reassignment surgery, so a court order does not guarantee approval.

House Bill 3293, passed in March 2021 and effective 1 July 2021, restricts transgender athletes from teams aligned with their gender identity by defining male and female solely on reproductive biology and genetics at birth. The Fourth Circuit held the ban unconstitutional in West Virginia v. B.P.J. in April 2024, and in July 2025 the Supreme Court agreed to hear the case, leaving the operative position unsettled.

Gender-affirming care for minors is restricted by a March 2023 law effective 1 January 2024 banning puberty blockers, hormone therapy and surgery except for severe dysphoria diagnosed by at least two physicians. For adults, a 1997 Medicaid ban on sexual reassignment surgery was ruled unconstitutional in August 2022 and coverage was required, but the Fourth Circuit overturned that ruling in 2026, holding that refusing funding is not irrational; Anderson v. Crouch, challenging the adult Medicaid exclusion, was argued on 9 December 2025 and remains unresolved.

An April 2025 bill passed both houses and awaited gubernatorial action that would require teachers and principals to immediately out transgender, non-binary and intersex students to parents and guardians.

West Virginia statutes provide no discrimination protection on gender identity, and the only statewide employment protection comes from Bostock v. Clayton County under federal Title VII. Fifteen cities bar gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations, with further protections for county and city employees in Kanawha County, Buckhannon and Elkins. House Bill 3042, passed 27 and 28 February 2023, is a Religious Freedom Restoration Act letting a person or corporation claim that a state or local law or government policy burdens religious belief and claim exemption from compliance, which permits denial of business service, housing and government service on grounds of gender identity, and it carries qualified immunity. On 26 March 2025 the state Senate approved by 25 to 8 a bill to nullify all city and county LGBTQ anti-discrimination ordinances, which awaited a House vote.

Marriage for couples the state would class as same-sex has been recognised since 9 October 2014, when Attorney General Patrick Morrisey ceased defending the ban and Governor Earl Ray Tomblin directed agencies to comply with federal rulings, despite a statute defining marriage as between a man and a woman that was never repealed.

66186276B86295910312663.summary:
Arkansas stands under the United States national framework on travel documents, and adds its own state-level restrictions. A bathroom bill became law on 11 April 2023 as Act 619, making Arkansas the fourth state to restrict transgender students' use of school bathrooms matching their gender identity; the law was amended and extended in 2025, and the Movement Advancement Project's equality-map citations record HB 1156 as a 2023 K-12 facility ban extended in 2025. Act 619 of 11 April 2023 separately creates a misdemeanour for transgender use of public bathrooms, locker rooms or changing facilities where a minor is present, dependent on intent of arousing or gratifying sexual desire.

Erin In The Morning's Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map of July 2026 places Arkansas in 'The Worst States' group, one tier below the 'Do Not Travel' designation given to Florida, Idaho, Kansas and Texas. The grading reflects the state's own body of anti-trans law rather than any federal measure.

Arkansas was the first state, in 2021, to ban gender-affirming healthcare for trans minors, after the legislature overrode the governor's veto. HB 1570, banning puberty blockers, hormone therapy and surgery for under-18s, was vetoed on 5 April 2021 as overbroad and extreme but overridden on 6 April 2021; it was blocked and then struck down on 20 June 2023 by Judge James M. Moody Jr. for discrimination and constitutional violations, before the Eighth Circuit overturned that ruling on 12 August 2025 and allowed enforcement, citing United States v. Skrmetti. Litigation over the 2021 care ban continues, and a federal judge enjoined it for 'irreparable harm' to minors while litigation was ongoing.

Identity documents at state level have narrowed. Arkansas has permitted transgender people to amend birth certificates since 1981, when Senate Bill 256, the Arkansas Vital Statistics Act, passed 34-0 in the Senate and 92-0 in the House on 19 February 1981, codifying a surgery-based pathway requiring court order verifying sex reassignment surgery and a name change. Identity documents with an X sex descriptor were available from December 2010, but in March 2024 the Department of Finance and Administration rescinded X descriptors for driver's licences.

Arkansas law does not address discrimination based on gender identity, leaving protection only through the 2020 Bostock v. Clayton County nationwide ban. Little Rock, Conway, Hot Springs, North Little Rock and Pulaski County bar gender-identity discrimination in public employment, while the comprehensive ordinances in Eureka Springs and Fayetteville are unenforced under the Intrastate Commerce Improvement Act; the Arkansas Supreme Court struck down Fayetteville's ordinance in February 2017.

Arkansas has no hate-crime penalty-enhancement statute, and its civil remedy for intimidation, harassment, violence or property damage covers only racial, religious or ethnic animosity, not gender identity. The April 2021 state hate-crimes law, signed effective immediately, excludes sexual orientation or gender identity explicitly or implicitly. Federal law has covered gender identity since October 2009 under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Act.

SB 289, signed 26 March by Governor Asa Hutchinson and effective immediately, allows medical practitioners to cite religious beliefs to deny healthcare to LGBT patients. In March 2021 the Legislature passed a ban on transgender athletes in sports, signed 25 March and effective immediately; ESPN records it as enacted 25 March 2021, prohibiting transgender women and girls from competing on school sports teams consistent with their gender identity across K-12 and collegiate sports, and allowing a student or school claiming harm to sue a school for violation.

In March 2023 the Legislature passed a gender-affirming litigation bill, signed 13 March 2023 by Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders, allowing those who received such care as minors to sue providers 15 years after turning 18, versus two years for other care. On 21 March 2023 a law prohibiting trans people from using public school bathrooms matching gender was signed, making Arkansas the fourth such state.

66186276B76680759932915.summary:
Ohio is a state within the United States; federal law and the federal document regime apply here and are carried at national level. What follows covers Ohio's own statutes, courts and agencies.

Erin In The Morning's Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map of July 2026 places Ohio in "The Worst States," a group of sixteen states forming the second-highest tier beneath the four states graded "Do Not Travel," under the map's national frame of "Worst Policies In Effect."

Ohio's facility law, Senate Bill 104, the "Protect All Students Act," was signed by Governor Mike DeWine on 27 November 2024 and took effect 25 February 2025. It requires every K-12 school and every college and university, public and private, to designate bathrooms, locker rooms, changing and shower rooms and overnight accommodations for the exclusive use of males or females on the basis of sex assigned at or near birth, and requires students to use the facilities matching their birth certificate. Single-occupancy restrooms with controlled use are exempt. The bill was signed out of public view over the objections of Democrats, teachers' unions and civil rights groups; its sponsor was Republican state Senator Jerry Cirino. The statute contains no enforcement mechanism.

State identity documents are being narrowed. Amendment of the gender marker on an Ohio birth certificate was barred under the 1987 precedent In re Ladrach, challenged by four transgender Ohioans in March 2018 and invalidated as unconstitutional by federal Judge Michael H. Watson in Ray v. McCloud in December 2020; corrections have been officially permitted since 1 June 2021, although some counties continue to refuse them. Transgender people can change name and gender on Ohio driver's licences by court order together with a Declaration of Gender Change signed by a physician, nurse practitioner, social worker, therapist or psychologist, and an X marker has been available since April 2022. In August 2026 the Bureau of Motor Vehicles announced rules allowing only male or female markers and requiring an exact-matching birth certificate or passport.

Care and sport are governed by HB68, the Saving Adolescents from Experimentation Act, which bans puberty blockers, hormones and surgery for under-18s and bars transgender girls and women from women's high-school and college sports. It passed on 13 December 2023, was vetoed by Governor DeWine on 29 December 2023, and was enacted by House override on 10 January 2024 and Senate override on 24 January 2024. A court blocked it in April 2024, allowed it to take effect in August 2024 after finding the regulation of transgender individuals a legitimate state interest, and the Ohio 10th District Court of Appeals re-enjoined it on 18 March 2025, with Attorney General Dave Yost vowing to appeal. The operative position on any given provision should be checked before relying on it.

Protection is patchy. Ohio statutes do not address discrimination on account of gender identity, but gender-identity discrimination in state employment has been barred by executive order since 19 December 2018, and the Sixth Circuit held on 7 March 2018 that discrimination on the basis of transgender status is sex discrimination under Title VII. Thirty-three Ohio cities and counties have ordinances barring gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations.

66186276B63937528568220.summary: Iowa law operates alongside United States federal law, which applies in the state. Gender identity has been removed from Iowa's civil rights statutes. The state had prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations since 2007; in February 2025 the Legislature passed a veto-proof bill removing that category, and Governor Kim Reynolds signed it with effect from 1 July 2025. Iowa became the first state to withdraw anti-discrimination protection from a group that already held it. A 2026 law then barred localities from maintaining civil rights protections stronger or broader than the state's, after several cities passed their own ordinances, with the capital city's protections dating to 1991. A transgender visitor who is refused service, denied housing or dismissed from a job in Iowa has no state-law remedy on the ground of gender identity.

sources.summary: Since 2007 Iowa prohibited discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations, but in February 2025 the Legislature passed a veto-proof bill removing gender identity from anti-discrimination laws, signed by Governor Kim Reynolds and effective July 1, making Iowa the first state to remove anti-discrimination protections for any class and the first to take a protected group away from civil rights protections. In 2025 Iowa stripped nondiscrimination protections from trans people and in 2026 passed a bill banning localities from maintaining civil rights protections stronger or broader than the state government, after several cities passed their own protections. As of July 1, 2025 under Senate File 418 transgender people may not alter legal gender on government IDs or documents or be legally recognized differently from assigned sex, stripping 2007 gender-transition language and imposing an unchangeable binary legal definition of sex determined at birth based on gametes expected to be produced later in life. Iowa hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes based on sexual orientation but not gender identity; a March 8, 2016 Senate bill to add gender identity passed 27-21 but died in the Republican-controlled House, though federal law has covered gender identity since October 2009. In March 2019 the Iowa Supreme Court required Medicaid coverage of sex reassignment surgery, but the General Assembly passed and Reynolds signed a ban on state funding a month later, a Polk County District Court ruled that ban unconstitutional in November 2021, and in June 2025 Reynolds signed another law banning Medicaid coverage for transgender surgeries and hormone treatments effective July 1, 2025. In March 2022 Iowa limited women's sports to cisgender females based on sex at birth, effectively barring transgender girls and women at all accredited public or private educational institutions including colleges and universities effective July 1, 2022, with civil lawsuit cause for any direct or indirect harm from violation. In March 2023 Senate File 538 banned provision of any gender-affirming healthcare to transgender minors effective immediately with 180-day wind-down for existing patients, and a separate March 2023 bill required written parental permission for students to use a single-person restroom at school. In May 2023 Iowa banned sexual orientation and gender identity lessons in Kindergarten through grade 6 classrooms, and only Davenport has banned conversion therapy on minors by 8-2 council vote April 22, 2020 after statewide Senate and medical and psychology board efforts failed. Iowa Territory adopted Wisconsin anti-sodomy law in 1838 punishable by up to three years, omitted sodomy in its 1843 code making it legal as noted in 1860 Estes v. Carter, re-criminalized sodomy in 1892 with one to ten years for heterosexual or homosexual consensual activity with first conviction in 1900 State v. Todd and fellatio criminalized in 1902, limited prosecution of heterosexual sodomy in a divided 5-4 1976 Supreme Court ruling requiring compelling state interest for private consensual adult opposite-sex conduct, and repealed same-sex criminalization in a 1978 comprehensive code with no mention of sodomy and age of consent 16 regardless of gender and sexual orientation. Iowa provided benefits to same-sex partners of state employees since 2003, recognized same-sex marriages since April 3, 2009 after unanimous Iowa Supreme Court affirmance in Varnum v. Brien, issued licenses from April 27, 2009 as fourth U.S. state to legalize same-sex marriage, defeated constitutional amendment and convention attempts to ban it, and removed three participating justices in November 2010 retention elections while retaining a fourth in November 2012. Joint adoption by married same-sex couples has been legal since a 2008 Supreme Court ruling with individuals and married couples allowed to adopt regardless of sexual orientation, state courts ordered listing of married lesbian non-birthing mothers on death certificates in December 12, 2012 Buntemeyer v. Iowa DPH and on birth certificates in Gartner v. Newton unanimously affirmed May 3, 2013 to ensure support and fundamental legal rights at birth, lesbian couples have IVF access with non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognized if married, and courts are generally favorable to gestational or traditional surrogacy despite no defined surrogacy laws. Since 2007 Iowa has outlawed discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, housing and public accommodations with Des Moines protected since 1991, and hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes based on sexual orientation. On March 17, 2015 the Senate voted 26-24 to ban sexual orientation change efforts on LGBT minors but the bill died in the Republican-controlled House, the Board of Medicine and Board of Psychology declined in 2016 to ban conversion therapy by rule, and Davenport became the first city to ban conversion therapy on minors by 8-2 vote April 22, 2020. In March 2020 the House unanimously passed 95-0 a bill to abolish the gay panic defence twice, but the Republican-controlled Senate twice refused to take it up.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in South Carolina (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Changing legal gender on the birth certificate does not require sex reassignment surgery. State anti-discrimination law contains no explicit prohibition of discrimination on the basis of gender identity, but 2020 federal workplace protections against LGBT discrimination apply in South Carolina, with additional local employment protections for gender identity in Mount Pleasant, Myrtle Beach and Richland County and for city employees only in Columbia, Charleston and Latta. South Carolina has no state hate crime law, while hate crimes motivated by gender identity are prohibited federally under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. In April 2016 Governor Nikki Haley said she opposed a transgender bathroom-restriction bill introduced in the Legislature and viewed it as "unnecessary". On May 17, 2022 the governor signed a transgender sports ban. In May 2024 legislation signed into law and effective immediately banned gender-affirming healthcare for individuals under 18 and banned federal funding going directly or indirectly toward gender-affirming care for adults, after which providers including the Medical University of South Carolina stopped providing such care regardless of age. The 2024-25 and 2025-26 budget appropriations bills require students to use bathrooms based on sex "at the time of birth", though on September 10, 2025 the U.S. Supreme Court allowed trans student plaintiff John Doe to continue using the boys' bathroom while his challenge proceeds, with all other trans students required to follow state law. Same-sex sexual activity is legal under the 2003 U.S. Supreme Court decision in Lawrence v. Texas, which invalidated South Carolina's sodomy law making "buggery" a felony punishable by five years in prison or a $500 fine, though the legislature has not repealed it. Voters adopted a November 2006 constitutional amendment defining marriage as the union of a man and a woman, which was overturned in Condon v. Haley on November 12, 2014, with stay denials by the Fourth Circuit on November 18 and by the U.S. Supreme Court on November 20, the first same-sex marriage on November 19, 2014 and general recognition and performance from the next day. South Carolina permits adoption by individuals with no explicit prohibition on adoption by same-sex couples or on stepchild adoptions, and since a February 15, 2017 federal order the state must list both same-sex parents on children's birth certificates without the adoption or Family Court order previously required only of same-sex couples. No state anti-discrimination provision explicitly covers sexual orientation, though 2020 federal workplace protections apply, supplemented by local employment protections in Mount Pleasant, Myrtle Beach and Richland County and for city employees in Columbia, Charleston and Latta. South Carolina is the only state not to include same-sex couples in domestic violence statutes, which explicitly cover only opposite-sex couples, and it has no state hate crime law, though crimes motivated by sexual orientation are covered federally under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. In March 2020 a federal judge declared unconstitutional the 1988 law "banning homosexual or gay topics within school classrooms".

66186276B65591139260314.name: Florida
66186276B65591139260314.summary:
Florida stands under the United States national framework and adds a state layer a trans visitor meets directly on the ground, most sharply in public facilities. Under the Facility Requirements Based on Sex Act (Fla. Stat. 553.865), in force since 1 July 2023, a trans person may not use a restroom or changing facility consistent with their gender identity in buildings owned or leased by the state or local government: state offices, courthouses, legislative offices, prisons and jails, local immigration detention facilities, state parks, toll-road plazas, state schools, state universities, beaches and airports. The statute purports to cover all schools, public and private. Private businesses are outside its scope.

The statute's mechanics put the decision with an authority figure on site. Gender labels are required, an internal disciplinary procedure applies, and an authority figure may order a person to depart; a non-member who does not leave can be charged with criminal trespass. The ACLU of Florida advises that refusing to leave a sex-segregated restroom or changing facility can amount to criminal trespass and that each situation calls for fact-specific judgment and legal counsel.

There is one documented arrest. Marcy Rheintgen, a 20-year-old trans college student, was charged on 19 March 2025 after police, alerted in advance, arrested her washing her hands in a women's restroom at the Florida State Capitol, where she had declared "I am here to break the law" on entering. The misdemeanor trespass charge carried up to 60 days in jail and was described as the first arrest under Florida's transgender bathroom restrictions. On 20 June 2025 Leon County Judge Lashawn Riggans threw the case out: as a defendant charged under the statute she had no standing to argue that the law itself was illegitimate, so the statute was never substantively tested. No later arrest under the law is documented in this record.

The restriction reaches higher education through administrative rulings. On 23 August 2023 the Board of Education approved firing employees of 28 public community and state colleges who enter the forbidden bathroom, and on 18 October 2023 it voted to apply a similar restriction to private college and university buildings including student housing, with compliance proof due by 1 April 2024. The federal appellate rule moved the other way first: an August 2020 Eleventh Circuit ruling that a Ponte Vedra Beach high school violated the law by refusing a transgender student consistent restroom use was reversed in January 2023 when the court sided with the district to uphold the ban, which was codified on 17 May 2023.

State identity documents diverge from what many visitors hold. In January 2024 the Department of Highway Services and Motor Vehicles stopped issuing any driver's licence bearing a gender marker different from sex assigned at birth, treating holders, users and applicants as criminally guilty of fraud, with suspension and revocation of the document. In July 2024 transgender people born in Florida could not update or change sex on birth certificates despite explicit legislation permitting it. Before that closure, an amended birth certificate required an application to amend a Florida birth record, a notarized affidavit and a physician letter confirming appropriate clinical treatment, without requiring surgery or sterilisation; after 2011 a driver's licence or ID name change required a court order alongside a physician statement.

Gender-affirming care is restricted in state law, and the restrictions reach adults as well as minors. On 31 October 2022 the Medical Board required a 24-hour waiting period for adults before sexual reassignment surgery; on 4 November 2022 it approved a ban on gender-affirming healthcare for minors, effective 16 March 2023 and codified 17 May 2023, which prohibits hormone replacement therapy for transgender minors and adds adult barriers including a bar on insurance coverage and a requirement that treatment be administered by a physician rather than a nurse practitioner. Minors under 18 cannot receive puberty blockers, hormone therapy or confirming surgeries unless intersex, and a board memo stated that social transition should not be a treatment option. Senate Bill 254's Physicians Only provision prohibited nurse practitioners and physician assistants from providing gender-affirming care to transgender adults, which the Human Rights Campaign reported disrupted care for an estimated 80 percent or more of transgender clinic patients, with temporary or permanent suspensions after signing. A May 2023 law allows medical practitioners to refuse treatment on grounds of conscience, religion or belief. Litigation has partly checked these rules: three plaintiffs obtained a preliminary injunction on 6 June 2023 limited to themselves, the Eleventh Circuit stayed it on 26 August 2024, and a federal judge permanently blocked provisions banning care for minors and adults in June 2024.

Protection machinery at state level is thin. Florida's statutes do not address discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing or other areas, and nursing home and hospital protections in force since 2000, amended in 2007, cover sexual orientation but not gender identity. The state hate-crime law provides harsher penalties for crimes based on sexual orientation but does not cover gender identity. Since February 2021 the Florida Commission on Human Relations has announced enforcement of Bostock v. Clayton County (15 June 2020) to investigate employment, housing and public accommodations claims. Counties and cities comprising about 55 percent of the population, among them Jacksonville, Miami, Tampa, Orlando, St. Petersburg, Tallahassee and West Palm Beach, prohibit discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity in private and public employment, housing and public accommodations.

Two advocacy organisations have warned travellers directly. On 12 April 2023 Equality Florida took what it called the unprecedented step of issuing a travel advisory on risks to the health, safety and freedom of those considering short or long-term travel or relocation to Florida, citing laws hostile to LGBTQ people alongside reproductive-health restrictions, gun-safety rollbacks and book bans and curriculum censorship; the organisation reports events and conferences cancelling. The Human Rights Campaign joined with an updated Florida travel advisory in May 2023, citing recently signed legislation, stopping short of a boycott. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Florida since 6 January 2015, when Brenner v. Scott held the state's ban unconstitutional.

Since July 1, 2023 under the Facility Requirements Based on Sex Act it is illegal for a trans person at any state school, state university, or government building e.g. beach or airport to use a bathroom or changing facility consistent with gender identity, requiring gender labels and internal disciplinary procedures where an authority figure may order departure and a non-member who does not depart can be charged with criminal trespass; on August 23 the Board of Education approved firing employees of 28 public community and state colleges who enter the forbidden bathroom, and on October 18, 2023 voted to apply similar restriction to private college and university buildings including student housing with compliance proof by April 1, 2024, after an August 2020 Eleventh Circuit ruling that Ponte Vedra Beach high school violated the law by refusing transgender student Andrew Adams consistent restroom use was reversed in January 2023 when the Eleventh Circuit sided with the district to uphold the ban, codified May 17, 2023. For identity documents, in January 2024 the Department of Highway Services and Motor Vehicles unilaterally banned issuing any driver's license with a gender marker different from assigned sex at birth, treating holders/users or applicants as criminally guilty of fraud with suspension and revocation, and in July 2024 transgender individuals born in Florida could not update or change sex on birth certificates despite explicit legislation permitting it; previously an amended birth certificate required an Application to Amend a Florida Birth Record, notarized Affidavit, physician letter confirming appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition without requiring surgery or sterilization, and after 2011 driver's license/ID changes required a court order for name and physician statement of appropriate clinical treatment, while in January 2022 the first sex-unknown birth certificate was reported. For healthcare, after August 2022 rule-change citing state guidance against gender-affirming care, on October 31, 2022 the Medical Board required a 24-hour waiting period for adults before sexual reassignment surgery and banned minors from gender-affirming healthcare approved November 4, 2022 and effective March 16, 2023, codified May 17, 2023 to prohibit hormone replacement therapy for transgender minors and create adult barriers including banning insurance coverage and requiring a physician rather than nurse practitioner to administer treatment; minors under 18 cannot receive puberty blockers, hormone therapy, or confirming surgeries unless intersex and a memo stated social transition should not be a treatment option, opposed by HHS, the Endocrine Society and other major medical organizations. On custody, May 17, 2023 Senate Bill 254 allows child custody modifications on the basis the child received or might receive gender-affirming care, and April 2023 legislation allowed modifying or nullifying out-of-state parental custody agreements if the child is allowed or threatened with access, described by opponents as allowing kidnapping across state lines amid protests where trans children were detained and one arrested for disturbing the peace; three plaintiffs obtained a June 6 preliminary injunction limited to them, stayed August 26, 2024 by the 11th Circuit, before a federal judge in June 2024 permanently blocked provisions banning care for minors and adults. On discrimination and protection, statutes do not address gender identity discrimination in employment, housing or other areas and nursing home/hospital protections since 2000 amended 2007 cover sexual orientation but not gender identity, but counties and cities comprising about 55 percent of population prohibit private and public employment, housing and public accommodations discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity, the February 2021 Commission on Human Relations announced enforcement of Bostock v. Clayton County June 15, 2020 holding workplace discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity is sex discrimination under Title VII to investigate employment, housing and public accommodations, and Glenn v. Brumby December 2011 held employment discrimination based on transgender status is sex discrimination, while hate-crime law provides harsher penalties based on sexual orientation but not gender identity. In May 2023 a medical practitioner law allows discrimination in doctors surgery, medicine and hospitals on conscience, religion or belief effective immediately by emergency clause criticized as preventing PrEP, gender-affirming care and abortion access, a May 2023 law bans adult live performances anywhere a minor might view under criminal penalty which DeSantis said was about drag shows but was preliminarily enjoined June 23 as not all drag is obscene, and on April 23, 2026 HB 1001/SB 1134 effective January 2027 prohibits state and local funding or promoting diversity, equity and inclusion defined to include gender identity with suits and removal of officials, interpreted as banning government support to LGBTQ organizations/events as in Palm Beach County denying a HUD grant to repair Compass headquarters air conditioning; in April 2023 Equality Florida issued a travel advisory to avoid visiting or moving to the state joined in May by the Human Rights Campaign citing DeSantis-signed legislation. Same-sex sexual activity became legal after Lawrence v. Texas June 26, 2003 striking all sodomy laws, though the 1868 felony crime against nature law punishable up to 20 years and 1917 misdemeanor unnatural and lascivious act law punishable by up to $500 or 6 months remained unenforced and unrepealed as of 2020, with the 1955 psychopathic offender law labeling sodomy convicts criminal sexual psychopathic persons for periodic examination repealed in 1979; in 2026 the legislature passed CS/CS/HB 1525 repealing §800.02, House 108-0 March 3, 2026 and Senate 38-0 March 10, 2026, signed June 16, 2026 effective October 1, 2026, and in October 2018 during a gay sex sting a judge ruled gay sex is not illegal in a public space so long as within a room. On enforcement, in September 2020 Hillsborough County arrested 11 men on misdemeanor non-sex charges after agreeing to consensual sex in a park and published names and mugshots, with critics accusing deliberate targeting of gay men and asking if a man and woman meeting similarly would have been arrested. Same-sex marriage has been legal since January 6, 2015 after Brenner v. Scott August 21, 2014 held Florida's ban violated the U.S. Constitution as marriage is a fundamental right under Fourteenth Amendment Due Process and Equal Protection subject to strict scrutiny, superseding the 1977 same-sex marriage ban law and November 2008 Amendment 2 adding Article I Section 27 banning same-sex marriage, civil unions and substantial equivalents; nine counties, thirty cities and one town offer domestic partnership benefits, and a 2016 repeal of the 1868 unmarried cohabitation ban passed House 112-5 and Senate 38-0, signed April 6, 2016 effective July 1, 2016. On protection, Bostock v. Clayton County June 15, 2020 outlawed workplace discrimination on sexual orientation as sex discrimination under Title VII, which the Florida Commission on Human Relations announced in February 2021 it will enforce for employment, housing and public accommodations, though statutes otherwise do not address sexual orientation discrimination; counties and cities comprising about 55 percent of population including Jacksonville, Miami, Tampa, Orlando, St. Petersburg, Tallahassee and West Palm Beach prohibit private and public employment, housing and public accommodations discrimination on sexual orientation, nursing homes and hospitals since 2000 amended 2007 cannot discriminate on sexual orientation, the Department of Agriculture added sexual orientation to workplace policy in January 2019, and hate-crime law provides harsher penalties for crimes based on sexual orientation. 66186276B65591139260314.blindSummary:
The state/province stands under the national framework and adds a layer a trans visitor meets directly on the ground, most sharply in public facilities. Under the state's 2023 public-facility statute, in force since 1 July 2023, a trans person may not use a restroom or changing facility consistent with their gender identity in buildings owned or leased by state/province or local government: state/province offices, courthouses, legislative offices, prisons and jails, local immigration detention facilities, state/province parks, toll-road plazas, state/province schools, state/province universities, beaches and airports. The statute purports to cover all schools, public and private. Private businesses are outside its scope.

The statute's mechanics put the decision with an authority figure on site. Gender labels are required, an internal disciplinary procedure applies, and an authority figure may order a person to depart; a non-member who does not leave can be charged with criminal trespass. A state/province civil-liberties organisation advises that refusing to leave a sex-segregated restroom or changing facility can amount to criminal trespass and that each situation calls for fact-specific judgment and legal counsel.

There is one documented arrest. A 20-year-old trans college student was charged on 19 March 2025 after police, alerted in advance, arrested her washing her hands in a women's restroom at the state capitol, where she had declared "I am here to break the law" on entering. The misdemeanor trespass charge carried up to 60 days in jail and was described as the first arrest under the state's transgender bathroom restrictions. On 20 June 2025 a county judge threw the case out: as a defendant charged under the statute she had no standing to argue that the law itself was illegitimate, so the statute was never substantively tested. No later arrest under the law is documented in this record.

The restriction reaches higher education through administrative rulings. On 23 August 2023 the state board of education approved firing employees of 28 public community and state colleges who enter the forbidden bathroom, and on 18 October 2023 it voted to apply a similar restriction to private college and university buildings including student housing, with compliance proof due by 1 April 2024. The national appellate rule moved the other way first: an August 2020 ruling by a national appeals court that a high school violated the law by refusing a transgender student consistent restroom use was reversed in January 2023 when the court sided with the district to uphold the ban, which was codified on 17 May 2023.

State/province identity documents diverge from what many visitors hold. In January 2024 the state motor-vehicle agency stopped issuing any driver's licence bearing a gender marker different from sex assigned at birth, treating holders, users and applicants as criminally guilty of fraud, with suspension and revocation of the document. In July 2024 transgender people born in the state/province could not update or change sex on birth certificates despite explicit legislation permitting it. Before that closure, an amended birth certificate required an application, a notarized affidavit and a physician letter confirming appropriate clinical treatment, without requiring surgery or sterilisation; after 2011 a driver's licence or ID name change required a court order alongside a physician statement.

Gender-affirming care is restricted in state law, and the restrictions reach adults as well as minors. On 31 October 2022 the state medical board required a 24-hour waiting period for adults before sexual reassignment surgery; on 4 November 2022 it approved a ban on gender-affirming healthcare for minors, effective 16 March 2023 and codified 17 May 2023, which prohibits hormone replacement therapy for transgender minors and adds adult barriers including a bar on insurance coverage and a requirement that treatment be administered by a physician rather than a nurse practitioner. Minors under 18 cannot receive puberty blockers, hormone therapy or confirming surgeries unless intersex, and a board memo stated that social transition should not be a treatment option. A 2023 state/province bill's Physicians Only provision prohibited nurse practitioners and physician assistants from providing gender-affirming care to transgender adults, which a national LGBTQ advocacy group reported disrupted care for an estimated 80 percent or more of transgender clinic patients, with temporary or permanent suspensions after signing. A May 2023 law allows medical practitioners to refuse treatment on grounds of conscience, religion or belief. Litigation has partly checked these rules: three plaintiffs obtained a preliminary injunction on 6 June 2023 limited to themselves, a national appeals court stayed it on 26 August 2024, and a national judge permanently blocked provisions banning care for minors and adults in June 2024.

Protection machinery at state level is thin. The state's statutes do not address discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing or other areas, and nursing home and hospital protections in force since 2000, amended in 2007, cover sexual orientation but not gender identity. The state hate-crime law provides harsher penalties for crimes based on sexual orientation but does not cover gender identity. Since February 2021 the state human-relations commission has announced enforcement of a June 2020 national supreme court holding that employment discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity is sex discrimination, to investigate employment, housing and public accommodations claims. Counties and cities comprising about 55 percent of the population prohibit discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity in private and public employment, housing and public accommodations.

Two advocacy organisations have warned travellers directly. On 12 April 2023 a national LGBTQ advocacy organisation took what it called the unprecedented step of issuing a travel advisory on risks to the health, safety and freedom of those considering short or long-term travel or relocation to the state/province, citing laws hostile to LGBTQ people alongside reproductive-health restrictions, gun-safety rollbacks and book bans and curriculum censorship; it reports events and conferences cancelling. A national LGBTQ advocacy group joined with an updated travel advisory in May 2023, citing recently signed legislation, stopping short of a boycott. Same-sex marriage has been legal in the state/province since 6 January 2015, when a state court ruling held the state's ban unconstitutional.

The inventory records a preliminary injunction of 6 June 2023 limited to three plaintiffs, a stay by the Eleventh Circuit on 26 August 2024, and a federal judge permanently blocking provisions banning care for minors and adults in June 2024, without documenting what happened on appeal after that.

Whether the January 2024 driver's licence marker rule or the July 2024 birth certificate practice has been litigated is not sourced here. The Equality Florida travel advisory is dated 12 April 2023 and the Human Rights Campaign's update May 2023. No later reissuance or withdrawal by either organisation appears in this inventory, so their current status is unresolved.

66186276B73402293045483.name: Nebraska
66186276B73402293045483.summary:
Nebraska's state-level framework for trans visitors is set by Executive Order No. 23-16, signed by Governor Jim Pillen on 30 August 2023. The order establishes a Women's Bill of Rights and defines sex, female, male, woman, girl, man, boy, mother and father for use by state agencies, stating that biological sex is determined at birth and that biological differences between males and females in athletic ability and safety warrant sex-based segregation in some athletic, social and educational spaces. The order backs single-sex spaces for women's sports, bathrooms and changing rooms. Pillen was the second U.S. governor to sign such an order. Opponents questioned the order's scope and legality.

State documents are correspondingly restrictive. A legal gender marker change on a Nebraska birth certificate requires a notarized affidavit from the physician who performed sex reassignment surgery together with a certified copy of a court order changing the applicant's name. A driver's licence or state ID change requires a court order certifying the change and/or a physician-signed form confirming sex reassignment surgery. A name change requires district court paperwork, a court date, and publication for four consecutive weeks, or two weeks for minors. These requirements apply to state-issued documents; a visitor holding an out-of-state or foreign passport is not directly governed by them, but a trans person resident in Nebraska or seeking Nebraska-issued identification faces them.

Participation rules for trans students in Nebraska athletics have tightened in stages. The Nebraska School Activities Association requires transgender students to show evidence of hormone replacement therapy and/or sex reassignment surgery. In June 2025 Legislative Bill 89, banning transgender athletes from any sports, passed the unicameral legislature by a two-thirds majority and was signed by Governor Pillen; ten transgender athletes were identified as affected.

Gender-affirming healthcare for people under 19 is barred in Nebraska. The legislature passed the ban 33-15 in May 2023 and Governor Pillen signed it effective immediately. The Nebraska Supreme Court upheld it 6-1 in July 2024. A trans visitor under 19 cannot obtain this care in the state, and a visitor of any age cannot obtain it for a minor in their care.

Custody is a documented site of harm specific to Nebraska. A transgender woman diagnosed with gender dysphoria and transitioning while held in Nebraska's men's prison sued prison officials and workers; on 10 August 2022 U.S. District Judge Brian C. Buescher ruled for the defendants, dismissing her claims of failure to treat her dysphoria, denial of gender-conforming surgery, and failure to protect her. Nebraska had housed her by assigned sex at birth among male prisoners and placed her in a cell with a convicted male sex offender who sexually assaulted her. The judge had earlier dismissed the failure-to-protect claim over that placement, wrote that without medical evidence no reasonable jury could conclude the providers were deliberately indifferent to her serious medical need, and said she had not plausibly alleged more than de minimis injuries from the assault. He found no support for inferring a substantial risk from a prospective cellmate's sexual-offence conviction coupled with the alleged vulnerability of a transgender inmate transitioning to a woman in a men's prison. The placement followed her within the system.

Protection machinery is uneven. Nebraska's 1997 hate crime law guarantees the right to live free from violence or intimidation by threat of violence and enhances sentences for manslaughter, assault, terroristic threats, stalking, kidnapping and false imprisonment, rape and sexual assault, arson, criminal mischief and trespassing. It does not address gender identity. Federal law has covered gender identity under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act since 2009. The state Supreme Court upheld the hate crime law in April 2016, in a case protecting even a straight victim in the company of gay friends.

Discrimination protection for trans people in Nebraska rests on federal rulings and municipal ordinances rather than statewide statute. Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity became illegal under Bostock v. Clayton County, decided 15 June 2020. In August 2020 the Nebraska Equal Opportunity Commission announced it would investigate and resolve housing discrimination claims on account of sexual orientation or gender identity, applying the same ruling to housing. Federal enforcement followed: from 11 February 2021 the Fair Housing Act prohibition on discrimination because of sex was enforced to include sexual orientation and gender identity, with HUD accepting, investigating and enforcing complaints of anti-trans housing discrimination covering sale, rental, terms, conditions and services. Omaha has prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment and public accommodations in both the public and private sectors since 2012, when the City Council voted 4-3 on 13 March to amend the city's anti-discrimination laws to add sexual orientation and gender identity as protected classes, with an exemption for religious institutions. Lincoln passed a 5-0 ordinance in February 2022 covering employment, accommodation and housing, but the protections were removed in June 2022 after a petition drive. In November 2021 the Nebraska State College System voted 4-2 to include gender identity in its policy.

Conversion therapy aimed at changing gender identity is outlawed in Lincoln under a 2021 ordinance and remains lawful in the rest of Nebraska. Statewide ban bills were reintroduced in 2021 and 2025 but have not passed.

Marriage and family recognition are settled in Nebraska as a matter of federal law. Same-sex marriage has been legal since Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015, with then Attorney General Doug Peterson directing compliance and non-enforcement of contrary Nebraska laws. That replaced a constitutional ban adopted in November 2000 by 70 per cent to 30 per cent defining marriage as the union of a man and a woman. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can marry and have that marriage recognised. Nebraska permits adoption by same-sex couples and single LGBT individuals: the Lancaster County District Court ruled for the plaintiffs in Stewart v. Heineman on 5 August 2015, the Nebraska Supreme Court upheld that ruling in April 2017 striking down the ban on same-sex foster parents, and in March 2021 it held that state adoption law clearly allows a same-sex married couple to adopt.

Sodomy prohibitions in Nebraska were repealed by a revised criminal code enacted in June 1977, effective 1 July 1978, by a veto override of 32-15 against Governor J. James Exon.

Initiative Measure 442, approved by voters on 3 November 2026 with 68% support, requires schools to designate sports teams as male, female, or co-ed and prohibits male participation on female sports teams.
