sources.summary: In August 2022 a federal judge in Nebraska ruled against a transgender woman who had been denied gender-affirming care in prison and placed in a cell with a male sex offender who sexually assaulted her, holding there was insufficient evidence of deliberate indifference to her gender dysphoria and that she had not proven more than minimal injuries from the assault, and finding no support that a substantial risk could be inferred from a prospective cellmate's sexual-offence conviction 'coupled with the alleged vulnerability of a transgender inmate transitioning to a woman in a men's prison.' Nebraska housed her by assigned sex at birth in a men's prison, and the placement followed her there. Federal Bureau of Prisons policy permitted transfer to facilities of the gender prisoners identify with under January 2017 Obama-era guidelines until May 11 2018, when the BOP rescinded them so that assigned sex at birth determines where trans prisoners are jailed.

sources.title: Transgender inmate loses lawsuit over prison's treatment for her gender dysphoria — Lori Pilger, Lincoln Journal Star (via Norfolk Daily News, archived)
sources.summary: The Lincoln Journal Star reported that on Aug. 10, 2022 U.S. District Judge Brian C. Buescher ruled for Nebraska prison officials and workers sued by a transgender inmate identified only as 'Jane Doe', who was diagnosed with gender dysphoria and transitioning to be a woman while held in Nebraska's men's prison. The judge dismissed her claims of failure to treat her dysphoria, denial of gender-conforming surgery, and failure to protect her: he had previously dismissed the claim that guards failed to protect her after she was placed in a cell with a convicted sex offender who victimized her, wrote that 'without medical evidence, no reasonable jury could conclude that the providers were deliberately indifferent to Doe's serious medical need', and said she had not plausibly alleged more than de minimis injuries from the assault. Nebraska housed her by assigned birth sex among male prisoners and celled her with a male sex offender.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Nebraska (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: On August 30, 2023 Governor Jim Pillen signed an executive order defining sex by biological reproductive system, female as system designed to produce ova and male as system designed to fertilize the ova of a female, to provide single-sex spaces for women's sports, bathrooms, and changing rooms. Legal gender marker change on a birth certificate requires a notarized affidavit from the physician that performed sex reassignment surgery and a certified copy of a court order changing name, while driver's licenses/IDs require a court order certifying the change and/or a physician-signed form confirming sex reassignment surgery, and name change requires district court paperwork, a court date, and publication for four consecutive weeks (two weeks for minors). The Nebraska School Activities Association requires transgender students for athletics to show evidence of hormone replacement therapy and/or sex reassignment surgery, and in June 2025 Legislative Bill 89 banning transgender athletes from any sports passed the unicameral legislature by two-thirds majority and was signed by Governor Pillen, affecting 10 transgender athletes identified. In May 2023 the legislature passed 33-15 a ban on gender-affirming healthcare for individuals under age 19, signed by Governor Pillen effective immediately, which the Nebraska Supreme Court upheld 6-1 in July 2024. Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity became illegal under Bostock v. Clayton County decided June 15, 2020, and in August 2020 the Nebraska Equal Opportunity Commission announced it will investigate and resolve housing discrimination claims on account of sexual orientation or gender identity. Omaha has since 2012 prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment and public accommodations in public and private sectors, while Lincoln passed a 5-0 ordinance in February 2022 covering employment, accommodation and housing but protections were removed in June 2022 after a petition drive, and in November 2021 the Nebraska State College System voted 4-2 to include gender identity in policy. The 1997 hate crime law guarantees the right to live free from violence or intimidation by threat of violence and enhances sentences for manslaughter, assault, terroristic threats, stalking, kidnapping and false imprisonment, rape and sexual assault, arson, criminal mischief and trespassing but does not address gender identity, though federal law has covered gender identity since 2009 under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. Attempting to change gender identity through conversion therapy has been outlawed in Lincoln since 2021 and remains lawful in the rest of the state, with statewide ban bills reintroduced in 2021 and 2025. Same-sex sexual activity is legal, after sodomy prohibitions were repealed by a revised criminal code enacted in June 1977 effective July 1, 1978 via veto override 32-15 over Governor J. James Exon. Same-sex marriage has been legal since June 26, 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges, with Attorney General Doug Peterson directing compliance and non-enforcement of contrary Nebraska laws, replacing a constitutional ban adopted November 2000 by 70% to 30% defining marriage as union of a man and a woman. Nebraska permits adoption by same-sex couples and single LGBT individuals, with Lancaster County District Court ruling in Stewart v. Heineman on August 5, 2015 for plaintiffs, the Nebraska Supreme Court upholding in April 2017 striking down the ban on same-sex foster parents, and holding in March 2021 that state adoption law clearly allows a same-sex married couple to adopt. Employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation became illegal under Bostock v. Clayton County on June 15, 2020, with a Nebraska Legislature resolution supporting the decision 28-8 in early August 2020 and the Nebraska Equal Opportunity Commission investigating housing claims, plus an Omaha ordinance since 2012 prohibiting sexual orientation discrimination in employment and public accommodations. The 1997 hate crime law provides the right to live free from violence or intimidation and enhances penalties for manslaughter, assault, terroristic threats, stalking, kidnapping and false imprisonment, rape and sexual assault, arson, criminal mischief and trespassing based on sexual orientation, upheld by the state Supreme Court in April 2016 to protect even a straight victim in the company of gay friends. Attempting to change sexual orientation through conversion therapy is outlawed in Lincoln since 2021 and lawful elsewhere in the state.

66186276B73402293045483.blindSummary:
This division's state-level framework for trans visitors is set by an executive order, signed by the governor on 30 August 2023. The order establishes a Women's Bill of Rights and defines sex, female, male, woman, girl, man, boy, mother and father for use by state agencies, stating that biological sex is determined at birth and that biological differences between males and females in athletic ability and safety warrant sex-based segregation in some athletic, social and educational spaces. The order backs single-sex spaces for women's sports, bathrooms and changing rooms. The governor was the second governor in this country to sign such an order. Opponents questioned the order's scope and legality.

State documents are correspondingly restrictive. A legal gender marker change on a birth certificate issued in this division requires a notarized affidavit from the physician who performed sex reassignment surgery together with a certified copy of a court order changing the applicant's name. A driver's licence or state ID change requires a court order certifying the change and/or a physician-signed form confirming sex reassignment surgery. A name change requires district court paperwork, a court date, and publication for four consecutive weeks, or two weeks for minors. These requirements apply to state-issued documents; a visitor holding an out-of-state or foreign passport is not directly governed by them, but a trans person resident in this division or seeking identification issued here faces them.

Participation rules for trans students in this division's athletics have tightened in stages. The state schools sports association requires transgender students to show evidence of hormone replacement therapy and/or sex reassignment surgery. In June 2025 a bill banning transgender athletes from any sports passed the legislature by a two-thirds majority and was signed by the governor; ten transgender athletes were identified as affected.

Gender-affirming healthcare for people under 19 is barred in this division. The legislature passed the ban 33-15 in May 2023 and the governor signed it effective immediately. The highest civil court upheld it 6-1 in July 2024. A trans visitor under 19 cannot obtain this care in this division, and a visitor of any age cannot obtain it for a minor in their care.

Custody is a documented site of harm specific to this division. A transgender woman diagnosed with gender dysphoria and transitioning while held in this division's men's prison sued prison officials and workers; on 10 August 2022 a federal district judge ruled for the defendants, dismissing her claims of failure to treat her dysphoria, denial of gender-conforming surgery, and failure to protect her. The prison service had housed her by assigned sex at birth among male prisoners and placed her in a cell with a convicted male sex offender who sexually assaulted her. The judge had earlier dismissed the failure-to-protect claim over that placement, wrote that without medical evidence no reasonable jury could conclude the providers were deliberately indifferent to her serious medical need, and said she had not plausibly alleged more than de minimis injuries from the assault. He found no support for inferring a substantial risk from a prospective cellmate's sexual-offence conviction coupled with the alleged vulnerability of a transgender inmate transitioning to a woman in a men's prison. The placement followed her within the system.

Protection machinery is uneven. This division's 1997 hate crime law guarantees the right to live free from violence or intimidation by threat of violence and enhances sentences for manslaughter, assault, terroristic threats, stalking, kidnapping and false imprisonment, rape and sexual assault, arson, criminal mischief and trespassing. It does not address gender identity. Federal law has covered gender identity under this country's federal hate crimes prevention act since 2009. The highest civil court upheld the hate crime law in April 2016, in a case protecting even a straight victim in the company of gay friends.

Discrimination protection for trans people in this division rests on federal rulings and municipal ordinances rather than statewide statute. Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity became illegal under a national supreme court ruling decided 15 June 2020. In August 2020 the state equal opportunity agency announced it would investigate and resolve housing discrimination claims on account of sexual orientation or gender identity, applying the same ruling to housing. Federal enforcement followed: from 11 February 2021 the federal Fair Housing Act prohibition on discrimination because of sex was enforced to include sexual orientation and gender identity, with the federal housing agency accepting, investigating and enforcing complaints of anti-trans housing discrimination covering sale, rental, terms, conditions and services. One municipality has prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment and public accommodations in both the public and private sectors since 2012, when its municipal council voted 4-3 on 13 March to amend the local anti-discrimination laws to add sexual orientation and gender identity as protected classes, with an exemption for religious institutions. A second municipality passed a 5-0 ordinance in February 2022 covering employment, accommodation and housing, but the protections were removed in June 2022 after a petition drive. In November 2021 the state college system voted 4-2 to include gender identity in its policy.

Conversion therapy aimed at changing gender identity is outlawed in that first municipality under a 2021 ordinance and remains lawful in the rest of this division. Statewide ban bills were reintroduced in 2021 and 2025 but have not passed.

Marriage and family recognition are settled in this division as a matter of federal law. Same-sex marriage has been legal since a national supreme court ruling on 26 June 2015, with the attorney general directing compliance and non-enforcement of contrary state laws. That replaced a constitutional ban adopted in November 2000 by 70 per cent to 30 per cent defining marriage as the union of a man and a woman. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can marry and have that marriage recognised. This division permits adoption by same-sex couples and single LGBT individuals: a district court ruled for the plaintiffs in a named case on 5 August 2015, the highest civil court upheld that ruling in April 2017 striking down the ban on same-sex foster parents, and in March 2021 it held that state adoption law clearly allows a same-sex married couple to adopt.

Sodomy prohibitions in this division were repealed by a revised criminal code enacted in June 1977, effective 1 July 1978, by a veto override of 32-15 against the governor.

A ballot measure approved by voters on 3 November 2026 with 68% support requires schools to designate sports teams as male, female, or co-ed and prohibits male participation on female sports teams.

66186276B73402293045483.tangentialFactors:
The practical weight of Nebraska's state measures depends on how long a visitor stays and what they need from state institutions. A short-stay visitor using only federal documents and private accommodation encounters the state framework mainly through facilities practice and the absence of a statewide gender-identity discrimination statute. A trans person resident in Nebraska, or a visitor needing Nebraska-issued identification or care, meets the marker requirements, the under-19 care ban and the athletics rules directly.

A trans visitor in a relationship that Nebraska authorities would read as same-sex under birth-sex status has full marriage and adoption recognition, so the usual concern about partner recognition in hostile jurisdictions does not arise here. The exposure lies elsewhere: in facilities, in custody if arrested and held in state or county detention, and in the absence of a statewide hate-crime or anti-discrimination provision naming gender identity.

Enforcement of the 1997 hate crime law is documented in a case the state Supreme Court decided in April 2016 protecting a straight victim in the company of gay friends, which indicates the statute is applied to perceived-association bias, but nothing in the state's own law extends that to gender identity. Federal protection under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act covers gender identity, so a bias-motivated offence against a trans person can be charged federally even where state law is silent.

66186276B22971435435932.summary:
Senate Bill 150, enacted on 29 March 2023 after the General Assembly overrode Governor Andy Beshear's veto, carries Kentucky's restriction on which bathrooms transgender students may use in public schools alongside its ban on gender-affirming medical care for transgender minors. It is the single 2023 statute containing the K-12 facility restriction, and the Movement Advancement Project's equality map lists it among state-level bans on transgender people using public facilities according to gender identity. The facility provision is written for public school students; the sources reviewed identify no statewide rule governing adult use of bathrooms or other sex-segregated facilities.

Responsibility for carrying out the school restriction sits with local districts. The Kentucky Department of Education issued guidance in April 2023 for districts implementing the state's 2023 rules, advising them to remove sex education from the fifth-grade curriculum and to proceed cautiously with the bathroom provisions.

The care ban took effect on 14 July 2023, when U.S. District Judge David Hale lifted the injunction he had issued the previous month, barring transgender minors from puberty blockers and hormone therapy. Seven transgender children and their parents had sued to block the law, and the ACLU of Kentucky described the ruling as a temporary setback. On 28 September 2023 a federal appeals panel allowed the ban to remain in force while challenges proceed. Minors already receiving care were given no phase-out.

Birth certificates can be amended only for post-operative applicants: a doctor's letter stating that gender-affirming surgery has been performed goes directly to the Department of Vital Statistics in Frankfort. A court order was previously required for a Kentucky-born person.

School sport is closed to transgender girls under Senate Bill 83, which passed the General Assembly in March 2022, was vetoed by Governor Beshear in April 2022 on constitutionality and vagueness grounds, and was enacted over that veto the same month with immediate effect. House Bill 470, carrying the minors' care ban among other provisions, advanced on 2 March 2023 and passed on 17 March 2023, was vetoed, and was overridden on 29 March 2023 by simple majority votes; police arrested 19 capitol protesters for criminal trespassing that day.

Employment protection derives from federal appellate and executive sources rather than from statute. On 7 March 2018 the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, which covers Kentucky, held in EEOC v. R.G. & G.R. Harris Funeral Homes that Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 bars firing an employee for being transgender or for transitioning, because it penalises failure to conform to birth-assigned sex stereotypes, and that the Religious Freedom Restoration Act does not permit a private employer to dismiss a transgender worker on religious grounds. The case arose from funeral director Aimee Stephens, dismissed in 2013 after disclosing her planned transition. A June 2008 executive order barred hiring or firing state employees on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, restoring protections first issued in 2003 and removed in 2006. Nineteen cities maintain Fairness Ordinances covering gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations.

Kentucky's hate-crime statutes cover sexual orientation and expressly exclude gender identity, so bias-motivated violence against a transgender person falls outside the state's hate-crime enhancement. The sexual-orientation provision was used in the April 2011 beating of Kevin Pennington at Kingdom Come State Park near Cumberland, which produced arrests on 15 March 2012 by Kentucky State Police working with the FBI and guilty pleas from two defendants after advocacy by the Kentucky Equality Federation.

Conversion therapy on minors has been illegal statewide since Governor Beshear's executive order of 18 September 2024, following city bans in Covington (March 2020, 5-0), Louisville (September 2020, 24-1) and Lexington (May 2021, unanimous).

Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since the Kentucky Supreme Court struck down KRS 510.100 in Kentucky v. Wasson in 1992 on state constitutional grounds, a result reinforced by Lawrence v. Texas in 2003. The unenforceable statute remains on the books; it formerly punished specified sexual acts as a misdemeanour carrying up to 12 months in jail and a $500 fine, with solicitation punishable by up to 90 days and $250.

Religious-exemption and service-access rules cut against those protections. The 2013 Religious Freedom Act requires the state to show clear and convincing evidence before burdening a sincerely held religious belief; Governor Beshear vetoed it over vagueness and the risk of overriding local non-discrimination ordinances, and the General Assembly overrode him 79-15 in the House and 32-6 in the Senate. Senate Bill 17, signed by Governor Matt Bevin in March 2017, allows religious student organisations use of school facilities and control of their internal affairs. In August 2020 a district court held that a Christian photographer, as a public business, could not be compelled to photograph same-sex weddings because the photographs are art and speech protected against compulsion.

66186276B6801956407400.name: North Carolina
66186276B6801956407400.summary:
North Carolina stands under the United States framework, and national rules on passports, entry screening, federal custody and federal health funding apply in the state as they do elsewhere in the country. The state layer is where the facility, identification, care and bias-crime questions are decided.

Facility rules are the subject of live legislative conflict rather than settled prohibition. House Bill 2, passed in an emergency 2016 session after the Charlotte city council allowed transgender people to use facilities matching their gender identity, required public bathroom use according to the sex listed on a birth certificate and barred cities from enacting anti-discrimination ordinances covering gay and transgender people. The birth-certificate bathroom provision was repealed by the General Assembly on 30 March 2017, and no state statute now bars a trans person from using the facility matching their gender identity, nor criminalises facility use. Republican legislators revived a bathroom bill in the 2025 session, so the position remains open and could change within a legislative term.

Identification documents are narrowing. A federal ruling of 26 June 2022 removed the undefined sex-reassignment-surgery requirement from the state's birth-certificate amendment process after Lambda Legal's November 2021 suit. House Bill 805, enacted over veto on 29 July 2025 and effective 1 January 2026, recognises only male and female sexes and requires an amended certificate to keep displaying the sex originally assigned alongside any change, which means a corrected state document still carries the original marker.

Care for minors is closed. Three veto-overridden laws effective 16 August 2023 ended the prescription of puberty blockers and hormone therapy and the provision of gender-affirming surgery to people under 18, and House Bill 574 barred individuals assigned male at birth from female sports and athletic teams. House Bill 805 additionally bars state funds for gender-transition care for minors and for people in prison, so a trans visitor held in state custody would not obtain transition care at state expense. A trans athlete visiting or competing in the state falls under the sports restriction.

Recourse after violence is limited. The state hate-crime statute covers neither gender identity nor sexual orientation, so an assault on a trans visitor may not be charged as a bias crime under state law even where bias is evident.

Non-discrimination coverage outside public employment is municipal and county-level. A state prohibition on local ordinances covering gender identity expired on 1 December 2020; Charlotte and Wake County ordinances explicitly covering gender identity took effect 1 January 2022, and roughly 30 per cent of the state's population lives under a local ordinance covering sexual orientation and gender identity. A trans visitor therefore has no statewide protection in private employment, housing or public accommodations, and the answer depends on the particular city or county.

sources.summary: In March 2016 the Public Facilities Privacy & Security Act (HB2) barred local governments from enacting contrary hiring and bathroom-facility policies and required bathroom use according to gender listed on birth certificate, with the birth-certificate bathroom-use portion repealed by the legislature March 30, 2017. A prior state ban on local non-public-employment ordinances prohibiting discrimination based on gender identity expired December 1, 2020, and Charlotte (August 2021) and Wake County (October 2021) ordinances explicitly covering gender identity took effect January 1, 2022, with the article reporting about 30% of the state population covered by local sexual-orientation and gender-identity ordinances. For public employment, an April 12, 2016 executive order barred LGBT discrimination including gender identity and an October 2017 extension applied protection to state contractors, while the University of North Carolina system and most listed campuses maintain gender-identity non-discrimination policies for employment and students. On August 16, 2023 three veto-overridden laws took effect requiring educators to notify parents if a student requests a different name or pronouns, banning trans girls from team sports, and banning gender-affirming care for transgender minors, with House Bill 574 specifically banning individuals assigned male at birth from female sports and athletic teams. Since August 2023 minors cannot be prescribed puberty blockers or hormone therapy or receive gender-affirming surgery, and under HB 805 veto-overridden July 29, 2025, effective January 1, 2026 the state recognizes only male and female sexes and disallows state funds for gender transition care for minors and people in prison. On gender-marker documents, a June 26, 2022 federal ruling removed the undefined sex-reassignment-surgery requirement for North Carolina birth-certificate changes following a November 2021 Lambda Legal suit, but the July 29, 2025 HB 805 override requires amended certificates to continue displaying originally assigned sex alongside any change. Effective August 15, 2023 SB49 Parents' Bill of Rights bans K-4 instruction on gender identity, requires parental notification if a child requests a different name or pronoun in records or by personnel, and grants inspection and objection rights over instructional materials, while the state hate-crime statute does not cover gender identity. Private consensual same-sex sexual activity was decriminalized by Lawrence v. Texas (2003), but N.C. G.S. section 14-177 remains unrepealed and unenforceable for that conduct after State v. Whiteley (2005) upheld it facially only for minors, non-consensual or coercive conduct, public conduct, and prostitution. A prior state ban on local municipalities prohibiting sexual-orientation discrimination outside public employment expired December 1, 2020, while Durham and Guilford counties and Bessemer City, Durham, and High Point prohibit sexual-orientation discrimination in local public employment or discrimination and Charlotte and Wake County ordinances effective January 1, 2022 explicitly ban sexual-orientation discrimination. In public employment, the April 12, 2016 executive order and October 2017 extension bar sexual-orientation discrimination for state employees and contractors, with University of North Carolina campuses and the Housing Finance Agency maintaining sexual-orientation non-discrimination policies. The state hate-crime statute does not cover sexual orientation. In January 2021 a federal judge struck down North Carolina's exclusion of same-sex couples from domestic-violence protection, extending protections to them, and a 2008 Patients' Bill of Rights provision granted hospital visitation via designated visitor statute. In November 2021 a law banning sexual-orientation discrimination in foster-parenting placements was signed effective January 1, 2022, and on August 3, 2019 an executive order banned state funding of conversion therapy on minors.

66186276B80192890672447.summary:
Montana stands under the legal framework of the United States and under a state constitution whose equal-protection and dignity guarantees state courts have repeatedly applied to block or enjoin anti-trans legislation. In the July 2026 anti-trans national legal risk assessment, Montana is the only state whose standing improved, on the strength of that court record, even though the statutes that would otherwise place it among the most restrictive states remain enacted.

Senate Bill 458, signed in May 2023, codified sex as an immutable male-female binary determined at birth and unchangeable. District Judge Leslie Halligan struck it down in February 2025, holding that it violated the equal-protection clauses of the Montana Constitution by leaving a gap in sex-discrimination protection. Senate Bill 437, signed 24 March 2026, codified biological definitions of gender, male, female, man, woman, mother and father based on primary sexual anatomy, provides that gender means that sex definition and not gender identity, experienced gender, expression or role, and applies across more than 60 sections of state law including driver's licences, marriage licences and anti-discrimination protections, with applicants for driver's and marriage licences required to list sex as so defined. Representative Zooey Zephyr stated that the bill erases transgender, intersex and Two-Spirit recognition; in April 2026 plaintiffs sought to add it to the ongoing litigation as fundamentally identical to SB 458.

Changes to sex markers on Montana identity documents have been blocked in court since 2022. A rule of 9 September 2022 barring changes to sex identification on birth certificates absent proof of data-entry error or a DNA test was blocked by court order on 15 September 2022, which the Department of Public Health and Human Services complied with. A bill of 22 February 2023 prohibiting gender-marker changes on all identity documents, signed 19 May 2023, was stopped by a December 2024 injunction from District Judge Mike Menahan; after an April 2024 suit by two trans women unable to update driver's licences and birth certificates, Judge Menahan issued a preliminary block on 16 December 2024 pending trial on sex-discrimination grounds, which the Montana Supreme Court upheld on 15 April 2026, holding that the constitution requires treating individuals with dignity. A Helena district court's December 2024 order also enjoined the 2022 health department rule, the Motor Vehicle Division policy requiring a birth certificate to change a driver's-licence sex marker, and portions of SB 458, finding the plaintiffs likely to succeed on the claim that the restrictions constitute sex discrimination under the state constitution.

Facilities access is governed by a statute that is not in force. House Bill 121, passed in February 2025, requires bathrooms, locker rooms and sleeping areas in publicly funded facilities to be segregated by biological sex assigned at birth; the ACLU of Montana sued immediately, and on 2 April 2025 District Judge Shane Vannatta issued a temporary restraint, finding the law motivated by animus and supported by no evidence that the restrictions advance women's safety and privacy. A proposal to forbid trans people from using Capitol bathrooms aligned with their gender was voted down by the Montana House on 3 December 2024, and a 2018 ballot initiative requiring public bathroom use to match birth-certificate gender failed to gather signatures.

Gender-affirming care for minors is not prohibited in Montana. Senate 99, signed 28 April 2023, banned such care and was described as the most comprehensive prohibition in the United States; District Judge Jason Marks preliminarily enjoined it on 27 September 2023, ruling that discrimination against a person for being transgender inherently constitutes sex discrimination under Bostock v. Clayton County and served no compelling governmental interest in protecting minors. The Montana Supreme Court kept the injunction in place on 11 December 2024 on privacy grounds, with Justice Laurie McKinnon adding that transgender status should be treated as a suspect class, and Judge Marks permanently struck the ban down on 14 May 2025 for failure to establish a bona fide health risk clearly and convincingly or to show a change in the stance of major U.S. medical organizations.

A 2021 law barring transgender athletes from public school sports, contingent on continued federal education funding and signed the following month by Governor Greg Gianforte, was struck down in September 2022 by District Judge Rienne McElyea as unconstitutional on administrative grounds for infringing the authority of the Regents of the Montana University System.

Protection against discrimination is thinner than the court record suggests. By executive order Montana prohibits gender-identity discrimination in state employment and by state contractors and subcontractors, originating in 2000 personnel rules, broadened by Executive Order 41-2008 in November 2008 and expanded to gender identity and contractors in January 2016; federal Title VII protection for gender identity under Bostock v. Clayton County applies in Montana, and ordinances in Bozeman, Butte-Silver Bow County, Helena, Missoula and Whitefish prohibit gender-identity discrimination in public and private employment, housing and public accommodations, with Missoula County covering county employees only. Montana hate-crime statutes do not include gender identity, leaving prosecution to federal courts under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. In April 2021 Governor Gianforte signed legislation granting a right to discriminate where religious beliefs are substantially burdened, widely viewed as a licence to discriminate against LGBTQ people.

Same-sex marriage has been recognised in Montana since 19 November 2014, when Judge Brian Morris enjoined the state ban effective immediately, a ruling mooted by Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015; the Montana Supreme Court recognised a common-law same-sex marriage as retroactively valid in Adami v. Nelson on 10 December 2019. Montana permits adoption with no explicit prohibition on same-sex couples or second-parent adoption, affirmed 6-1 in Kulstad v. Maniaci on 7 October 2009, which granted parental rights and set precedent for stepparent adoptions by same-sex couples.

66186276B13694661525286.name: Missouri
66186276B13694661525286.summary:
Missouri's Save Adolescents from Experimentation (SAFE) Act, enacted in 2023 as Senate Bill 49, has been in force since 28 August 2023. It prohibits anyone under 18 from starting gender-affirming hormones or puberty blockers, allows those already in treatment to continue, and bans all transition-related surgery for minors. A state judge denied a preliminary injunction on 29 August 2023, and the statute took effect on schedule.

The same law bars MO HealthNet, the state Medicaid programme, from paying for gender-affirming care for a patient of any age, restricts treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres, and exposes providers who violate it to loss of their Missouri medical licence and to patient lawsuits brought up to 15 years after treatment.

Litigation began with a complaint filed 25 July 2023 in Cole County Circuit Court by Lambda Legal, the ACLU of Missouri and Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner, acting for three families of transgender young people, medical providers, PFLAG National and GLMA. Following a trial in September 2024, Judge Robert Craig Carter upheld the ban on 25 November 2024 and the plaintiffs announced an appeal. The Missouri Supreme Court affirmed unanimously on 13 January 2026, quoting the 2025 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that upheld Tennessee's comparable ban. The statute sunsets in 2027, lawmakers have stated they want it made permanent, and a November 2026 ballot initiative seeks to bar such care indefinitely.

Care in custody is separately restricted. Governor Mike Kehoe signed HB 2009, effective 2 July 2026, providing that no funds shall be expended for any cross-sex hormones or gender transition surgery undertaken for the purpose of any gender transition, with no taper plan for inmates already receiving care. Missouri became the seventh state to deny gender-affirming care to incarcerated people and the second in 2026 to do so. Florida, Kentucky and North Carolina have near-identical laws, while comparable measures in Idaho and Georgia were blocked by federal courts.

Trans athletes are barred from female sports. Senate Bill 39, signed 7 June 2023, requires public and private schools through college to restrict sports participation to sex assigned at birth; the ban carries a sunset clause repealing it automatically on 28 August 2027.

Identity documents carry a surgical requirement. A change of sex on a Missouri birth certificate requires a court order with certified proof on hospital letterhead, signed by the attending physician with licence and contact details, stating that the petitioner's physical sex has been altered and the surgical changes are irreversible, under Mo. Ann. Stat. § 193.215(9). Two 2013 cases that had permitted an exception were invalidated and reversed in May 2022, leaving no route around the surgical requirement. The Department of Revenue accepted Form 5532 for changing the gender designation on a licence or ID after policy review between 2016 and 2024, then reverted to requiring surgery documentation or a court order after an unspecified incident.

Protection machinery is uneven. Missouri's hate crime statutes explicitly cover gender identity, defined as "having a self-image or identity not traditionally associated with one's gender," while state non-discrimination legislation does not address gender identity at all.

Amendment 3, which would have prohibited abortion in most cases and prohibited gender transition procedures for minors under eighteen, was defeated by voters on 3 November 2026 with 45% support.

The same law bars this division's Medicaid programme from paying for gender-affirming care for a patient of any age, restricts treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres, and exposes providers who violate it to loss of their medical licence in this division and to patient lawsuits brought up to 15 years after treatment.

66186276B62688952876525.summary:
Alaska falls in the Moderate-Risk group of Erin In The Morning's July 2026 legal-risk assessment, alongside Kentucky and North Carolina. That tier is defined as states that have passed one or two laws aimed at transgender adults, enacted multiple laws targeting transgender youth, or are advancing negative laws quickly. It sits above the assessment's worst-law and do-not-travel tiers and below its protective groupings.

No statewide statute bars a transgender adult from using a public restroom or changing room matching their gender identity, and no statewide law bans gender-affirming care for adults. Pressure has reached Alaska through appointed regulatory boards rather than the legislature. Gov. Mike Dunleavy's earlier attempt to limit transgender students' access to single-sex facilities failed, while boards he appoints have restricted transgender girls' participation in girls' sports.

The State Medical Board, whose members Dunleavy appoints, voted unanimously on 22 August 2025 to recommend restricting medical care for transgender youth and approved a draft regulation that would classify providing gender-transition care to anyone under 18 as unprofessional conduct, exposing clinicians to disciplinary action. A board member had proposed the resolution in June 2025. The draft must be vetted by the Alaska Department of Law and then pass a 30-day public comment period before it can take effect.

The Alaska Board of Education voted 7-1 in September 2023 to bar transgender students from female sports and athletics statewide. Facilities policy below that level is set district by district. The Matanuska-Susitna Borough School District board voted 5-1 on 19 October 2022 to require transgender students to use bathrooms matching their sex assigned at birth or a private alternative such as the nurse's office, replacing guidance that had stood for more than seven years; the policy was described at the time as an apparent first for Alaska. It binds one district's schools and does not extend to adult facilities anywhere in the state.

Alaska's statewide nondiscrimination law does not cover gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations, and the 2002 executive order protecting state employees from discrimination addresses sexual orientation only. Four municipalities, Anchorage, Juneau, Sitka and Ketchikan, home to about 46% of the state's population, prohibit gender-identity discrimination in public and private employment, public accommodations and housing. Ketchikan's ordinance passed unanimously in July 2020 and took effect in mid-August 2020. Anchorage's ordinance passed 9-2 in September 2015 and survived a repeal attempt on 3 April 2018, when voters rejected Proposition 1 by 53% to 47%; that measure would have required people in public spaces to use bathrooms and locker rooms matching their sex assigned at birth. In Fairbanks, a February 2019 City Council ordinance covering gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations was vetoed by Mayor Jim Matherly.

Alaska's hate-crime statute does not list gender identity, so bias-driven violence against a transgender person does not trigger a state-level penalty enhancement. A visitor outside the four municipalities with local ordinances has no state or municipal recourse against discrimination in a hotel, restaurant or workplace.

Document changes are available and leave a record. An amended Alaska birth certificate with a corrected name and gender marker requires a Birth Certificate Request Form, a photocopy of identification, a letter from a medical or mental health provider attesting appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition, or a certified copy of a court-ordered change of sex, plus a fee. The amended certificate keeps the previous legal name printed at the bottom with a notation that it was originally issued under the former name and amended because of a change of name. Changing the gender marker on an Alaska driver's licence requires a letter from a licensed provider attesting clinical treatment, or an already-updated birth certificate or a court order for gender change.

Marriage licences have issued without regard to the sex of the spouses since 13 October 2014, after the federal district court in Hamby v. Parnell struck down the state's statutory and constitutional bans; the statutory ban had been allowed to become law without Gov. Tony Knowles' signature in 1996, and a constitutional amendment passed on 3 November 1998. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex under birth-sex status can therefore marry in Alaska.

Private consensual sex between adults is not criminalised. Alaska repealed its sodomy law with effect from 1 January 1980; the 1899 statute had punished the crime against nature with up to ten years in prison.

sources.summary: Alaska state law provides no protection against discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing, or public accommodations, and the 2002 executive order covering state employment addresses sexual orientation only with no gender identity provision. Four municipalities — Anchorage, Juneau, Sitka and Ketchikan, covering about 46% of the state population — ban discrimination based on gender identity in public and private employment, public accommodations and housing, with Ketchikan's unanimous ordinance passed in July 2020 effective in mid-August, and Anchorage's September 2015 ordinance (9-2) retained after voters rejected Proposition 1 to strip protections from transgender individuals on April 3, 2018 by 53% to 47%. In Fairbanks, a February 2019 City Council ordinance banning discrimination on gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations was vetoed by Mayor Jim Matherly. Under federal law, the June 15, 2020 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Bostock v. Clayton County holds workplace discrimination on gender identity is sex discrimination prohibited by Title VII, and the October 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act provides federal penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by actual or perceived gender identity prosecutable in federal court, while Alaska state hate-crime law does not cover gender identity. Transgender persons may obtain an amended birth certificate with corrected name and gender marker by submitting a Birth Certificate Request Form, ID photocopy, letter from a medical or mental health provider attesting appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition or certified copy of a court-ordered change of sex, plus fee, but the amended certificate retains the previous legal name at the bottom with notation it was originally issued under the former name and amended due to change of name. Changing the gender marker on a driver's license requires a letter from a licensed provider attesting clinical treatment or an already-updated birth certificate or court order for gender change. In September 2023 the Alaska Board of Education voted 7-1 to ban transgender individuals from participating in female sports and athletics statewide, while in August 2020 Anchorage voted 9-2 to ban conversion therapy on minors, the first such city ban in Alaska. Same-sex sexual conduct has been allowed since January 1, 1980 when Alaska repealed its sodomy law, which under the 1899 Alaska-specific statute had punished crime against nature with up to ten years in jail. Same-sex marriage has been legal since October 12, 2014 via the Hamby v. Parnell district court ruling declaring statutory and constitutional bans unconstitutional, with licenses accepted from October 13, 2014, following a 1996 statutory ban allowed to become law without Governor Tony Knowles' signature on May 6, 1996 and a constitutional amendment approved November 3, 1998. Alaska law does not address discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, housing, or public accommodations, except for a 2002 executive order prohibiting sexual orientation discrimination in state employment and a 1975 Human Rights Commission stance; a 2015 bill banning discrimination based on sexual orientation died without a vote. Anchorage, Juneau, Sitka and Ketchikan, representing about 46% of the population, ban sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations; Anchorage first passed an ordinance 7-4 in 2009 vetoed by Mayor Dan Sullivan, voters rejected Proposition 5 in April 2012 with 57% opposed, then passed an ordinance 9-2 in September 2015, and Ketchikan passed an ordinance unanimously in July 2020 effective mid-August, while Fairbanks limits protection to sexual orientation discrimination against city employees after mayoral veto of a broader 2019 ordinance. Federal protections apply via Bostock on June 15, 2020 holding workplace discrimination on sexual orientation violates Title VII, and the October 2009 Matthew Shepard Act providing federal penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by actual or perceived sexual orientation prosecutable in federal court, while Alaska state hate-crime law does not cover sexual orientation. Alaska permits adoption by married same-sex couples and recognizes the non-genetic, non-gestational mother as legal parent for a child born via donor insemination only if the parents are married, with lesbian couples having access to in vitro fertilization and courts generally favorable to surrogacy despite no surrogacy laws; Anchorage banned conversion therapy on minors in August 2020 by a 9-2 vote.

66186276B75419826371250.name: Georgia
66186276B75419826371250.summary:
Georgia's own law and practice diverge from the national layer in ways a trans visitor should weigh. Care for minors is banned by statute, the state employee health plan is under a court settlement requiring it to pay for gender-affirming care, and access to adult surgery narrowed abruptly in Savannah in 2025. Documented violence against transgender women in the state has centred on Atlanta.

Senate Bill 140, signed by Governor Brian Kemp on 23 March 2023 and in force since 1 July 2023, bars licensed medical professionals from providing hormone therapy or surgery for gender transition to patients under 18. Licence revocation is a possible penalty. Minors who began hormone replacement therapy before 1 July 2023 may continue under the law. The ACLU of Georgia said it would sue.

A settlement announced in October 2023 in federal court in Atlanta requires Georgia's State Health Benefit Plan to pay for medically necessary gender-affirming care for employees, their spouses and their dependents, after a December 2022 lawsuit alleged the plan illegally discriminated by refusing to pay. The plan's coverage of minors' care can extend to treatment obtained outside Georgia, even though that care is prohibited inside the state. The settlement keeps public-employee coverage in place alongside the 2023 ban.

Atlanta police said in April 2023 that they were investigating three violent crimes against transgender women in the city that year, after two Black transgender women were fatally shot a week apart; a January 2023 shooting that left a transgender woman in critical condition also remained open. The department described the violence against Black and Brown transgender women as epidemic-level. The sourcing gives raw counts without a denominator for the city's general homicide rate, so the figures establish that these attacks occurred and were under investigation, not that transgender residents face a risk measurably above the background rate of violence in the city.

Memorial Health University Medical Center in Savannah cancelled all gender-affirming surgeries on 13 February 2025, including a pre-approved double mastectomy for a 24-year-old transgender man. The hospital cited a responsibility to follow state and federal laws and regulations, and the cancellation came in the weeks after a January 2025 federal order denying Medicare and Medicaid funding to providers of youth gender-transition care. Savannah Pride Center said at least two other area residents were also denied care.

66186276B86627915353587.name: New Hampshire
66186276B86627915353587.summary:
New Hampshire is a state of the United States. Passports, visas, entry screening and federal facilities are governed by federal law; the findings below concern the state layer.

State anti-discrimination law has covered gender identity in housing, employment and public accommodations since June 2018. Coverage was extended to health care, public accommodations and jury selection effective 1 January 2020, and to public schools effective 17 September 2019, with the anti-bullying statute reaching gender identity and expression, including cyberbullying. Sexual orientation has been protected in public accommodations, housing and private and public employment since 1998.

Hate-crime penalty enhancements for offences motivated by gender identity took effect on 15 October 2019; sexual orientation has been covered since 1991. The gay and trans panic defence was abolished effective 1 January 2024, following passage in June 2023.

Enforcement of the state civil rights statute is documented. On 17 July 2026 the Merrimack County Superior Court found that a Concord man had violated the New Hampshire Civil Rights Act by striking a transgender woman.

GLAAD's 2025 national incident census recorded 72 anti-LGBTQ incidents in New Hampshire, the second-highest raw count of any state after California (198) and ahead of Texas (66), Ohio (50) and Washington (50). The census ranks by raw count and publishes no per-capita denominator, so the figure does not by itself establish New Hampshire's incident rate relative to larger states.

Identity documents are asymmetric. A New Hampshire birth certificate can be changed to reflect a different gender only on proof of sex reassignment surgery, legal in the state since 1990, together with a certified court order stating a "sex change," an application form, a photograph and fees. A reform bill was vetoed in July 2019 and the surgical requirement remains. Driver's licences have offered male, female and X markers since 1 January 2020, implemented in August 2021; the X marker is not available on birth certificates.

Care rules for minors have tightened. Laws passed on 18 July 2024 banned gender-affirming medicine for minors and, from 1 January 2025, banned reassignment surgery for transgender minors while retaining it for intersex people and circumcisions. House Bill 377 and House Bill 712, passed in August 2025 and effective January 2026, ban puberty blockers, hormone therapy and chest surgery for under-18 gender-affirming care, with a grandfather clause for treatment already under way as of 1 January 2026, disciplinary action against providers who violate the ban, and a right to sue. Those August 2025 laws removed access to gender-affirming care for transgender youth even where a physician judged it medically necessary.

The same July 2024 package barred transgender girls from girls' sports in grades 5 to 12 from 19 August 2024, with a birth certificate required to establish eligibility. A fourth bill in that package, which would have permitted discrimination against transgender people including adults, was vetoed. In August 2024 the state Supreme Court ruled 3-1 to protect transgender students in schools on privacy and autonomy grounds, and a judge granted a temporary stay of the sports ban pending investigation and appeals.

Marriage between two people of the same sex has been legal since 1 January 2010, following civil unions from 1 January 2008. An April 2021 Supreme Court ruling recognised adultery in such marriages, reversing the 2003 Blanchflower rule.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since the sodomy repeal of June 1975. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation, and 18 where one party is under the care, guardianship or authority of the other.

sources.summary: Gender identity has been protected against discrimination in housing, employment and public accommodations since June 2018, extended to health care, public accommodations and jury selection effective January 1, 2020, and to public schools effective September 17, 2019, with anti-bullying law covering gender identity and expression including cyberbullying. Hate crimes based on gender identity have been covered since 2019 with penalty enhancements effective October 15, 2019, and the gay and trans panic defence was abolished effective January 1, 2024 after passage in June 2023. Legal change of gender marker on a birth certificate requires sex reassignment surgery, legal since 1990, plus a certified court order stating a "sex change," application form, photograph and fees after a July 2019 veto of reform, while driver's licenses offer male, female and X since January 1, 2020 implemented in August 2021 with X unavailable on birth certificates, and the Medicaid ban on surgery coverage was lifted October 20, 2017. A June 30, 2016 executive order prohibited gender identity and expression discrimination in public employment, state programs and contracting, and a 2022 parental bill criticized as forcing schools to disclose gender identities died after a veto threat. July 18, 2024 laws banned trans girls from girls sports in grades 5 to 12 effective August 19, 2024 requiring a birth certificate for eligibility, banned gender-affirming medicine for minors, and allowed parental opt-out from instruction on gender identity or expression, while a fourth bill allowing discrimination against trans people including adults was vetoed. An August 2024 Supreme Court 3-1 ruling protected transgender individuals in schools on privacy and autonomy grounds, and a judge granted a temporary stay of the sports ban pending investigation and appeals. From January 1, 2025 reassignment surgery was banned for trans minors while retained for intersex people and circumcisions, and August 2025 House Bill 377 and House Bill 712 effective January 2026 banned puberty blockers, hormone therapy and chest surgeries for under-18 gender-affirming care with a grandfather clause for treatment ongoing as of January 1, 2026, disciplinary action for violating providers and a right to sue, alongside a conversion therapy ban for LGBT minors effective January 1, 2019. Same-sex sexual activity is legal after sodomy repeal in June 1975, with age of consent at 16 regardless of sexual orientation and at 18 where one party is under the care, guardianship or authority of the other. Sexual orientation has been protected in anti-discrimination law since 1998 covering public accommodations, housing and private or public employment, extended to public schools effective September 17, 2019 with anti-bullying coverage including sexual orientation and cyberbullying. Hate crimes based on sexual orientation have been covered since 1991 with penalty enhancements for actual or perceived orientation. The gay panic defence was abolished effective January 1, 2024. Conversion therapy on LGBT minors was banned effective January 1, 2019 after 2018 passage, with a 2022 repeal attempt dying in the House. Sexual orientation was explicitly listed within expectation of privacy legislation effective January 1, 2025, and same-sex marriage has been legal since January 1, 2010 after civil unions from January 1, 2008, with same-sex adultery recognized by an April 2021 Supreme Court ruling reversing the 2003 Blanchflower rule. 66186276B89395128410123.summary:
Arizona stands under the United States federal framework; the national layer is carried on the United States record rather than repeated here.

A national legal risk assessment published in July 2026 places Arizona in its Low-Risk States group, alongside Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, describing that group as jurisdictions that have largely refrained from targeting transgender adults. The same assessment names Arizona together with Virginia as a state whose youth-targeting anti-trans policies are judged unlikely to be extended to adults.

Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity is prohibited in Arizona through the 2020 federal Title VII rulings in Bostock v. Clayton County, Altitude Express v. Zarda and Harris Funeral Homes v. EEOC, reinforced by a January 2023 gubernatorial executive order banning gender-identity discrimination in state employment and contracts and a June 2023 Attorney General affirmation that state sex discrimination includes gender identity. Municipal ordinances in Phoenix (revised February 2013), Flagstaff (March 2013), Tempe (February 2014), Sedona (2015), Winslow (November 2018), Mesa (March 2021), Scottsdale (April 2021, effective 20 May), Glendale (May 2021) and Tolleson (June 2021) ban gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations, with exemptions for religious organizations, expressive groups, government agencies, private clubs and small businesses.

Arizona's hate-crime statute does not include gender identity, though the federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act has covered gender identity since October 2009. A gay and trans panic defence remains available under common law, with reform bills lapsing without action.

Gender-affirming care for minors is restricted. A March 2022 law signed by Governor Doug Ducey banned sex reassignment surgery on transgender children effective March 2023, with an exception permitting surgery on intersex children. A 1982 Arizona regulation bars Medicaid coverage of sex reassignment surgery; that ban was challenged in August 2020 by two transgender teenagers with NCLR, NHeLP and co-counsel as unconstitutional, following 2019 lawsuits seeking to void it. A June 2023 executive order granted Arizona government employees over age 21 full Medicaid access and insurance coverage for gender-affirming healthcare and services. Conversion therapy was banned in Pima County in August 2017 by a 3-2 vote with fines up to $2,500, alongside a June 2023 executive order barring government funding for conversion therapy.

Arizona's Supreme Court ruled on 25 April 2019 that family courts may determine care for a transgender child with gender dysphoria only in limited circumstances when divorced parents reach impasse, authorized to decide disputed parenting-plan elements narrowly tailored on evidence of imminent harm. In March 2023 the Arizona Department of Education introduced a hotline to report schools exposing children to topics including gender ideology for investigation. In June 2023 the Governor vetoed legislature-passed anti-trans bathroom and classroom pronoun-usage bills and vetoed an April 2023 bill targeting LGBT safe spaces in schools.

A second March 2022 bill signed by Ducey legally bars transgender children from female sports, athletics and Olympic competition, effective 30 days after enactment.

Arizona birth certificates and driver's licences carry distinct rules. In November 2020 three families with transgender children sued the Arizona Department of Health Services to permit birth-certificate gender change without sex reassignment surgery; litigation was ongoing as of August 2023 with all resident transgender individuals joined, and an August 2024 federal judge order permitted change without surgery. Driver's licence and state ID gender change requires a signed physician statement attesting the applicant is irrevocably committed to the gender-change process, without requiring surgery.

Same-sex marriage has been recognized since a U.S. district court decision on 17 October 2014 ended enforcement of statutory and constitutional bans, though those bans remain textually in the state constitution and Arizona Revised Statutes as unenforceable under Obergefell v. Hodges and, for out-of-state recognition, the 2022 Respect for Marriage Act. Voters rejected Proposition 107 in November 2006 and approved Proposition 102 in 2008 banning recognition, prompting Phoenix, Bisbee, Tucson and Flagstaff to enact domestic partnerships or civil unions.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal after the Arizona Equity Act of 2001 repealed sodomy laws. Adoption is permitted with no explicit prohibition on same-sex couples or second-parent adoptions, though primary consideration goes to married couples unless in the child's best interest or no married couple is available; the Arizona Supreme Court ruled unanimously in September 2017 that same-sex spouses have equal parental rights under Obergefell and Pavan v. Smith to list both names on birth certificates, with October 2020 appeals implementation. Surrogacy contracts are unenforceable though Soos v. Superior Court (1994) allows pre-birth orders for biological parents requiring second-parent adoption for a non-biological same-sex parent, and an April 2022 emergency law signed by Ducey allows religious organizations to legally discriminate against same-sex couples seeking to adopt or foster.

On 3 June 2026 Prism reported that Tucson Pride cancelled all 2026 events in January and effectively dissolved, citing a political and financial environment that made supporting queer events nearly impossible; Tucson was grouped with Tampa, Florida and Arlington, Texas as affected cities.

Proposition 318, approved by voters on 3 November 2026 with 59% support, prohibits schools and athletic associations from allowing a student, athlete, employee or other individual to use a restroom, locker room, shower room or other private space not designated for their sex.

66186276B53580985925186.name: Virginia
66186276B53580985925186.summary:
Virginia operates within the federal framework of the United States, and the national layer of exposure is carried in the country assessment. State law protects gender identity across several areas a visitor encounters directly, while the state's transgender-related restrictions are concentrated in schools and in rules covering minors.

The Virginia Values Act, passed 6 February 2020, signed 11 April 2020 and effective 1 July 2020, prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations and credit. It covers sexual orientation on the same terms and replaced earlier protections limited to state employment. A law signed 4 March 2020 with the same effective date authorises localities to enact their own sexual-orientation and gender-identity protections.

Violence motivated by gender identity falls within Virginia's hate crime law under legislation signed 4 March 2020 and effective 1 July 2020, which also added sexual orientation. HB 2132, repealing the gay and trans panic defence, passed in March 2021, was signed by Governor Northam, and took effect on 1 July 2021.

State identity documents are comparatively accessible. Virginia has offered an X gender marker on driver's licences since 1 July 2020, and since 1 September 2020 changing the sex designation on a birth certificate requires only "appropriate clinical treatment", replacing a surgery requirement that had been in force since 1979.

The state's criminal provisions on private sexual conduct no longer stand. §18.2-361 was struck down on 12 March 2013 and revised to remove the criminalisation of consensual same-sex relations, by a Senate vote of 40-0 on 7 February 2014 and a House vote of 100-0 on 6 March 2014, signed into immediate effect. §18.2-345 on lewd cohabitation was repealed in 2013 and §18.2-344 on fornication was repealed on 4 March 2020. The sodomy statutes had already been rendered unenforceable by Lawrence v. Texas in 2003.

Marriage between people of the same sex is recognised in Virginia and has been performed since 6 October 2014, when the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear the appeal in Bostic v. Rainey/Schaefer and marriages began at 1 p.m. that day. The statutory ban was repealed on 3 March 2020, and a codifying protection was signed in March 2024, effective 1 July. The 2006 constitutional amendment banning such marriages remains in the constitution, with repeal resolutions approved in January 2025 and January 2026 awaiting a voter referendum. A designated-visitor statute signed 26 March 2007 and effective 1 July 2007 extended hospital visitation rights to same-sex couples.

On schools, in 2014 a Gloucester County school board was held to have acted unlawfully in denying a transgender high school student use of the boys' bathroom, a ruling the U.S. Supreme Court allowed to stand in 2021. In July 2023 the state Department of Education adopted policies banning bathroom access and pronoun usage for transgender students, which were intended to be reversed in 2026. The Virginia High School League barred transgender athletes from girls' sports in February 2025. Virginia prohibits health care providers from attempting to change the gender identity of minors.

Official posture toward transgender students has moved in both directions through the courts. In September 2021 the Virginia Supreme Court upheld the reinstatement of a teacher suspended for speaking against transgender children and declining to use their pronouns on grounds of Christian belief. In May 2024 Governor Youngkin vetoed a bullying-definition bill that would have included gender identity.

A July 2026 legal risk assessment places Virginia in its Low-Risk States group alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, and names Virginia and Arizona as states that have enacted youth-targeting anti-trans policies which, on that assessment's reading of state-specific factors, appear unlikely to extend to adults.

Question 2, approved by voters on 3 November 2026 with 58% support, repeals the provision defining marriage as between one man and one woman and prohibits the state from denying a marriage licence to two adult persons based on sex, gender, or race.

sources.summary: Effective July 1, 2020, Virginia law prohibits discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations, and credit under the Virginia Values Act passed February 6, 2020 and signed April 11, 2020, and a March 4, 2020 law allows localities to enact their own protections on sexual orientation and gender identity. Virginia hate crime laws address violence based on gender identity under a bill signed March 4, 2020 and effective July 1, 2020, and HB 2132 repealing the gay and trans panic defense passed in March 2021, signed by Governor Northam, and went into effect July 1. Since September 1, 2020, changing sex on a birth certificate requires only “appropriate clinical treatment” rather than sex reassignment surgery required since 1979, and effective July 1, 2020 Virginia offers an “X” gender marker on driver’s licenses. A 2014 Gloucester County case denying a transgender high school student use of the boys’ bathroom resulted in a court ruling that the school board acted unlawfully, which the U.S. Supreme Court let stand in 2021, while in July 2023 the Department of Education passed policies banning bathroom access and pronoun usage for transgender individuals in schools, intended to be reversed in 2026. In February 2025 the Virginia High School League banned transgender athletes from girls’ sports following Trump’s executive order, and Virginia prohibits health care providers from trying to change the gender identity of minors. In September 2021 the Virginia Supreme Court upheld reinstatement of a teacher suspended for speaking out against transgender children and not using their pronouns on Christian-belief grounds, and in May 2024 Governor Youngkin vetoed a bullying-definition bill that would have included gender identity. Virginia statutes criminalizing sodomy and crimes against nature were effectively invalidated by Lawrence v. Texas in 2003, with §18.2-361 struck down March 12, 2013 and revised to remove criminalization of consensual same-sex relations by Senate vote 40-0 on February 7, 2014 and House vote 100-0 on March 6, 2014 signed into immediate effect, while §18.2-345 on lewd cohabitation was repealed in 2013 and §18.2-344 on fornication was repealed March 4, 2020. Same-sex marriage has been legal since October 6, 2014 after the Supreme Court refused appeal in Bostic v. Rainey/Schaefer with marriages beginning at 1 p.m. October 6, the defunct statutory ban was repealed March 3, 2020, and a codifying protection was signed in March 2024 effective July 1, while the 2006 constitutional ban remains pending repeal resolutions approved January 2025 and January 2026 for voter referendum. Effective July 1, 2020 the Virginia Values Act passed February 6, 2020 and signed April 11, 2020 prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, housing, credit and public accommodations, replacing prior limited state-employment-only protections, and a March 4, 2020 law effective July 1, 2020 added sexual orientation to hate crime laws. The 1934 ABC ban on gay bars was declared unconstitutional in 1991 in French Quarter Cafe v. Virginia Alcoholic Beverage Control Board, and hospital visitation rights were extended to same-sex couples through a designated visitor statute signed March 26, 2007 effective July 1, 2007 after unanimous House and Senate votes. Virginia allows single persons to adopt with no explicit prohibition on same-sex couples, but HB 189 and SB 349 signed April 9, 2012 effective July 1, 2012 authorize adoption agencies to refuse for religious reasons, while surrogacy contracts for same-sex couples were legalized by a bill passed February 2019 signed March 2019 effective July 1, 2019 and a February 2021 bill banned taxpayer dollars to religious organizations discriminating in adoption. Virginia prohibits health providers from attempting to change sexual orientation of minors, SB 1138 decriminalizing and modernizing HIV laws was signed March 31, 2021, a PrEP insurance anti-discrimination bill was vetoed in March 2025, and an archaic Code reference defining homosexuality as sexual conduct discovered August 2022 bars explicit sexual conduct materials from classrooms as a criminal offence since July 1, 2022.

66186276B94082813086253.name: District of Columbia
66186276B94082813086253.summary:
The District of Columbia stands under the national framework of the United States. It is the federal seat rather than a state, so national law applies directly within its boundaries and Congress retains authority over its local legislation and budget.

The District has no bathroom ban of its own. The facilities restriction in force there was attached by Congress, and on 5 December 2024 transgender-rights activists protesting that measure at the Capitol were arrested. The ban originates with Congress rather than with the District's elected legislature, so it is not something the local council can repeal.

A July 2026 legal risk assessment places the District of Columbia on its low-risk list alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia and Wisconsin, while cautioning that the District may no longer warrant its reputation as the most protective jurisdiction, because its law can be overridden by congressional action and by executive orders.

66186276B78821008370123.name: Maine
66186276B78821008370123.summary:
Maine law prohibits discrimination on the basis of actual or perceived gender identity or expression in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and education opportunity. The protections were added in 2005 and retained after a veto referendum on 8 November 2005, and LD 1688, signed on 17 June 2021, wrote gender identity explicitly into state statutes. The state hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for offences motivated by actual or perceived gender identity, and the gay and trans panic defence was abolished by legislation passed in June 2019 by 132-1 in the House and 35-0 in the Senate, effective 1 July 2019.

Gender markers on Maine driver's licences and state identification cards can be changed without medical provider certification, a rule in place since November 2019, on a completed Gender Designation Form offering male, female and X options. Birth certificates reflecting gender identity, including an X marker, have been issued since July 2020 on notarized affidavit. The X marker on a birth certificate requires a declaration from a licensed physician or mental health provider, and applicants who are minors require parental consent.

Maine has no state law restricting transgender people's use of sex-segregated facilities. The Maine Supreme Court ruled in January 2014 in Doe v. Regional School Unit 26 against a school district that had denied a student use of the bathroom aligned with her gender identity.

A law effective since July 2023 allows 16 and 17 year olds to obtain hormone therapy as gender-affirming care, and an April 2024 law explicitly protects, defends and safeguards gender-affirming healthcare. From 1 October 2026 healthcare facilities in Maine must mandate and include sexual orientation and gender identity data.

In June 2025 the Maine Senate rejected Legislative Document 233, which would have barred transgender women from competing in women's sports in state-funded schools. It was the only one of eight anti-trans bills introduced in the state in 2025 to pass the House.

The University of Maine System announced on 21 March 2025, with an update on 24 March, that it would comply with federal restrictions on transgender sports participation. The announcement followed the US Department of Agriculture's suspension of federal funding for research and programmes while it investigated possible sex-based discrimination in federally funded education programmes.

A July 2026 national anti-trans legal risk assessment places Maine in its Low-Risk States group. The same assessment separately flags that Maine's risk has increased because of the University of Maine System's capitulation on sports participation.

66186276B31549545599635.summary:
Delaware is a state within the United States and stands under the national framework carried by the national record and the parent bundle; what follows is Delaware's own law and practice.

A national trans legal risk assessment dated July 2026 places Delaware in its Low-Risk States group, alongside Arizona, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, defined there as jurisdictions that largely refrain from targeting transgender adults without specialising in their protection.

Delaware has no ban on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity; the Movement Advancement Project equality map records no such restriction for the state.

Since 2013, under SB 97, Delaware prohibits discrimination on the basis of actual or perceived gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations and other areas. The bill passed the Senate 11-7 on 6 June 2013, passed the House 24-17 with amendments, passed the Senate on amendments 11-9 on 18 June, was signed the next day and took effect immediately.

Since 2013 Delaware has imposed additional penalties for a violent crime motivated by the victim's actual or perceived gender identity.

HB142, which would formally repeal the common-law gay and trans panic defence and ban its use, was introduced in May 2023 and passed both houses of the Legislature in June 2023; the source records the Governor as having neither signed nor vetoed it.

Delaware allows a change of legal gender marker on state-issued identification on the signed statement of a licensed medical provider alone. Since 11 February 2017 sex reassignment surgery has not been an explicit requirement for an amended birth certificate, which instead requires a signed affidavit of surgical, hormonal, psychological or other treatment appropriate for gender transition. As of April 2020 Delaware did not offer a gender X marker on driver's licences.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 1 July 2013, with civil unions converted to marriages.

State-level protection machinery includes an Executive Order of 11 August 2009 extending anti-discrimination safeguards to state employees and applicants on the basis of gender identity, and an Executive Order signed in January 2025 by Governor Hall-Long creating Delaware's LGBTQ+ Commission.
