sources.title: Transgender legal history in the United States (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Federal policy on housing transgender prisoners has shifted repeatedly. A January 2015 ICE memo directed housing transgender immigration detainees according to gender identity, and in 2016 the US Department of Justice released guidelines forbidding corrections agencies from assigning trans inmates to men's or women's units solely on birth anatomy. In 2018 the Federal Bureau of Prisons revised its Transgender Offender Manual in the opposite direction, deleting the sentence that the Transgender Executive Council 'will recommend housing by gender identity when appropriate' and making placement 'a case-by-case basis' in which 'biological sex' is 'the initial determination', with gender identity used only 'in rare cases'. No Delaware-specific placement policy is documented.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Delaware (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2013 Delaware law prohibits discrimination on the basis of actual or perceived gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations, and other areas under SB 97, which passed the Senate 11-7 on June 6, 2013, passed the House 24-17 with amendments, passed the Senate on amendments 11-9 on June 18, was signed the next day, and took effect immediately. Since 2013 Delaware imposes additional penalties for committing a violent crime motivated by the victim's actual or perceived gender identity. HB142 to formally repeal the common-law gay and trans panic defense and ban its usage was introduced in May 2023, passed both houses of the Legislature in June 2023, with the Governor yet to either sign or veto. Transgender people are allowed to change their legal gender requiring only the signed statement of a licensed medical provider for the marker on state-issued identification, and as of February 11, 2017 sex reassignment surgery is no longer an explicit requirement for an amended birth certificate, requiring instead a signed affidavit of surgical, hormonal, psychological or other treatment appropriate for gender transition. A 2015 law signed June 25, 2015 and effective immediately allows inmates to access and/or change the name on birth certificates to reflect gender identity, where previously inmates could only change names due to religious beliefs. Since March 26, 2016 Delaware has prohibited discrimination based on gender identity within insurance contracts, including sex reassignment surgery. As of April 2020 Delaware does not have gender X available on drivers licenses, and an August 11, 2009 executive order protects employees of state executive branch departments and agencies from discrimination on the basis of gender identity. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since January 1, 1973 following repeal of the sodomy law in July 1972. Since 2009 Delaware law has prohibited discrimination on the basis of actual or perceived sexual orientation in employment, housing, public accommodations, and other areas, supplemented by an August 11, 2009 executive order for state executive branch employees, a May 2021 bill passed to repeal a loophole preventing claims based solely on just one exclusive sexual orientation with the Governor yet to sign or veto, and HB275 passed 21-15 in the House on March 28, 2024 to include asexuals and pansexuals in the definition of sexual orientation awaiting a Senate vote. Since 2001 Delaware has imposed additional penalties for violent crime motivated by the victim's actual or perceived sexual orientation. Civil unions granting the rights, benefits, protections, and responsibilities of married persons were available January 1, 2012, and same-sex marriage was legalized effective July 1, 2013 with conversion of civil unions to marriages. SB 65 banning conversion therapy on minors passed the Senate 12-3 on May 17, 2017 and the House 24-14 on June 7, 2018, was signed in July 2018, and went into effect immediately. In June 2021 a law was implemented to protect individuals from discrimination based on HIV medicine and Prep, and in April 2017 the Legislature passed a law allowing HIV patients to donate to other HIV patients, signed and effective January 1, 2018.

66186276B6628180846672.name: Pennsylvania
66186276B6628180846672.summary:
Pennsylvania's law operates inside the United States framework, which governs passports, visas, entry screening, federal custody and federally funded programmes; those national rules sit above the state layer and are not restated here. An independent anti-trans legal-risk assessment placed Pennsylvania in its low-risk tier in a July 2026 update, the category covering states that largely refrain from targeting trans adults without extending them specific protection.

Statewide discrimination protection is explicit. Since June 2023 discrimination on the basis of gender identity has been banned across Pennsylvania, with sexual orientation covered from the same date, and municipalities including Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, Allentown, Erie and Reading maintain their own bans. The Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission has interpreted the Human Relations Act's prohibition on sex discrimination to cover gender identity since August 2018, investigating complaints and awarding remedies that include stop orders, training and economic damages. Legally binding regulations signed in December 2022 define sex to include gender identity. State employees have held executive-order protection since 2003 and state contractors since 7 April 2016. A bill to write gender identity and sexual orientation protection into statute, House Bill 300, passed the House 102-98 in April 2023 and awaits a Senate vote, so the current statewide guarantee rests on commission interpretation and regulation rather than legislation.

State identity documents are comparatively open. Since August 2016 a transgender person can change the gender on a Pennsylvania birth certificate on a physician's note of appropriate clinical treatment, with no requirement for surgery and a parental request required below age 18; birth certificates carry no X option. Driver's licences and state IDs have offered X alongside M and F since 23 July 2020.

Philadelphia has built a local layer on top of the state rules. Ordinances adopted in November 2019 bar youth-serving organisations from discriminating against trans, nonbinary and gender-nonconforming youth, require at least one gender-neutral bathroom in every city-owned building, and confirm that the Fair Practice Ordinance protects nonbinary and gender-fluid people; in December 2021 X was added alongside male and female in all virtual public schools. On 17 October 2023 Mayor Jim Kenney declared Philadelphia a sanctuary for gender-affirming care by executive order, prohibiting the use of city resources to investigate or punish in-state or out-of-state residents seeking such care in the city, deprioritising enforcement of any future state or federal restriction, and shielding travellers from out-of-state enforcement.

Gender-affirming surgery is lawful in Pennsylvania, and no statewide prohibition on gender-affirming care for adults appears in the sources reviewed.

Violence motivated by anti-LGBTQ bias sits outside the state hate-crime statute. A 2002 hate-crime law covering LGBTQ people was struck down in 2008 on the constitutional ground that its content had been inserted into an agricultural terrorism bill; bills to reinstate it have never left committee, leaving no statewide hate-crime provision that reaches anti-LGBTQ violence. In April 2021 a Pittsburgh mayoral proposal sought a city ordinance explicitly naming gender identity; no enactment followed.

Restrictions on transgender participation in sport have moved through the legislature without becoming law. A June 2022 bill that would have required public K-12 schools and colleges to designate sports as male, female or coed, with female-designated teams restricted to athletes assigned female at birth, passed both chambers but was vetoed on 11 July 2022 by Governor Tom Wolf. On 6 May 2025 the Senate approved Senate Bill 9, the Save Women's Sports Act, reserving women's teams for "biological females" in K-12 and collegiate sport, and sent it to the House. On 22 April 2026 the Senate passed Senate Bill 1293 under the same title; Governor Josh Shapiro called supportive lawmakers "extremists", and it was unclear whether the House would take the bill up. All of these measures concern youth school sport rather than transgender adults or public facility access.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity is legal in Pennsylvania. The sodomy statute was held unconstitutional by the state Supreme Court in the 1980 ruling Commonwealth v. Bonadio on equal protection grounds, and the remaining sodomy laws were repealed in 1995. Marriage between two people of the same sex has been recognised statewide since Whitewood v. Wolf struck down the statutory ban on 20 May 2014; before that ruling the state recognised no marriages, civil unions or domestic partnerships. Philadelphia offers life partnerships for long-term committed couples with a city nexus, Pittsburgh provides domestic partnerships, and Luzerne County defines domestic partnership as between people of the same gender.

66186276B91272823970344.name: Wisconsin
66186276B91272823970344.summary:
Wisconsin is a state of the United States and stands under the national framework carried by the national record; the findings below are the Wisconsin-specific layer. A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment places Wisconsin in its low-risk group, alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia and the District of Columbia, describing jurisdictions that have largely refrained from targeting transgender adults while not taking extraordinary steps to protect them.

No statewide law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity, and gender identity is not a protected class under the state hate-crime statute, though sexual orientation is. Prosecutors have sometimes used perceived sexual orientation as the route to charge crimes motivated by a victim's gender identity. Local protection is patchwork: as of 29 May 2025, 21 per cent of the state's population lived in the ten cities with full employment, housing and public-accommodation ordinances covering gender identity, and 12 per cent in cities with partial ordinances. Dane and Milwaukee counties and the cities of Appleton, Cudahy, De Pere, Janesville, Madison, Milwaukee and Racine ban gender-identity discrimination; Oshkosh and Stevens Point extend protection only to transgender city employees. Executive Order #1, issued 7 January 2019, prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression in state employment, state contracting and the provision of state services, and directs state agencies to adopt and enforce nondiscrimination policies.

Wisconsin has no law barring transgender people from using government-building bathrooms or facilities consistent with their gender identity, no law defining sex to exclude transgender people, and no restriction on drag performance. The state's equality-map profile, current to 29 May 2025, records no ban on best-practice medical care for transgender youth and no shield law protecting providers or patients from out-of-state action.

Identity documents are the main friction point. Gender-marker change on a Wisconsin driver's licence is permitted only in limited circumstances, and change on a birth certificate is restricted: a person born in the state who has completed sex reassignment surgery may amend the birth certificate on documentation of the surgery and a name change. Neither licence nor birth certificate offers an X gender-neutral option, and the name-change process is restrictive.

State law does not ban gender-affirming care for minors. Governor Tony Evers vetoed Assembly Bill 465 on 6 December 2023, blocking a legislature-passed ban on gender-affirming health care for people under 18; he had earlier vetoed a June 2023 budget provision that would have barred Medicaid coverage of sexual reassignment surgery and other gender-affirming care for all individuals regardless of age. Care access nonetheless contracted under federal funding pressure: UW Health and Children's Wisconsin each announced on 13 January 2026 that they would pause gender-affirming pharmacologic care for patients under 18 after the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services said it would deny Medicaid and Medicare payments to hospitals providing such care to minors. Mental and behavioural health services continued. Wisconsin Attorney General Josh Kaul joined a multistate coalition seeking to block the HHS declaration. The pause follows federal funding pressure on Wisconsin hospitals rather than any state ban.

Marriage between two people regardless of sex has been recognised since 6 October 2014, when the Supreme Court declined the appeal in Wolf v. Walker and the district court's stay was lifted. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can expect that marriage to be recognised. Parenting rules allow individuals to adopt without regard to sexual orientation and married couples to adopt; access to IVF and artificial insemination is permitted, with state recognition of the non-genetic, non-gestational mother only if she is married. A September 2016 federal ruling required both parents to be recorded on birth certificates, and since 1 July 2021 birth certificates offer gender-neutral 'spouse' and 'parent 1'/'parent 2' options.

Private, non-commercial sexual conduct between consenting adults has been legal since 1983, when the state's sodomy provisions were repealed; the repealing legislation stated that Wisconsin did not approve of sexual conduct outside marriage.

The Milwaukee Police Department stopped listing the gender of crime victims in September 2023, alongside race, in order to avoid misgendering transgender people.

The Equality Map tracks state-level bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Wisconsin (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Wisconsin has no statewide anti-discrimination law covering gender identity and gender identity is not covered in the state's hate crime law, though perceived sexual orientation is often used as a medium to prosecute crimes based on the victim's gender identity; Executive Order #1 in January 2019 prohibited gender-identity discrimination in government employment, while Dane and Milwaukee counties and the cities of Appleton, Cudahy, De Pere, Janesville, Madison, Milwaukee and Racine ban gender-identity discrimination and Oshkosh and Stevens Point ban discrimination against transgender city employees only. A person born in the state who has completed sex reassignment surgery may amend their birth certificate upon documentation of surgery and name change, while persons on Wisconsin's sex offender registry are not allowed to change their names with no exception if the person is transgender. Sex reassignment surgery had to be explicitly included in Wisconsin Medicaid for government employees from January 2019 and was ordered extended to non-government employees in May 2019 under the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment, while a June 2023 budget bill passed by both houses banning Medicaid coverage of sexual reassignment surgery and other gender-affirming healthcare to all individuals regardless of age was vetoed under line-item veto power. People in prison are entitled to hormone therapy after the 2005 Inmate Sex Change Prevention Act denying hormone therapy to prisoners undergoing sex reassignment was ruled unconstitutional unanimously in Fields v. Smith by the Seventh Circuit on August 5, 2011, with Supreme Court denial of the state's appeal on March 26, 2012. Since September 2023 the Milwaukee Police Department no longer lists gender as well as race of victims to avoid misgendering transgender individuals in the future. On sports, a 2021 Republican bill banning transgender women from teams aligning with their gender passed the Assembly on party lines but was never voted in the Senate, was re-introduced in 2023, and a 2024 legislature-passed bill banning transgender individuals from female sports and athletics teams was vetoed by the Governor. On medical care, a 2021 Republican bill prohibiting insurers from covering gender-affirming care procedures for minors failed in committee, a re-introduced bill passed the Assembly October 12, 2023 and Senate October 17, 2023 and was vetoed December 6, 2023, and in December 2023 the Governor also vetoed a legislature-passed bill explicitly banning gender-affirming healthcare to individuals under 18. Consensual sodomy prohibitions originating in Michigan Territory in 1836 and retained at 1848 statehood, expanded to fellatio in 1897 and to cunnilingus with five-year penalties for sexual perversion in the 1950s, were reclassified as a misdemeanor punishable by nine months jail and/or 10,000 dollars in 1977 and legalized for private, non-commercial acts between consenting adults in 1983 with a statement that Wisconsin did not approve of any sexual conduct outside marriage. Same-sex marriage has been legal since October 6, 2014 when the Supreme Court refused appeal in Wolf v. Walker, lifting Judge Crabb's stay, while the Chapter 770 domestic partnership registry established in 2009 providing 43 of 200-plus spousal rights without stepchild adoptions was upheld unanimously in Appling v. Walker on July 31, 2014 and ended April 1, 2018, with same-sex partner benefits for state employees since 2009. Discrimination based on sexual orientation has been banned statewide in employment, housing, education, credit and all public accommodations since 1982, making Wisconsin the first U.S. state to do so, and sexual orientation is a protected class in hate crime law and under a 2001 law prohibiting sexual-orientation discrimination in schools. Parenting provisions allow individuals to adopt without respect to sexual orientation and married same-sex couples to adopt, allow lesbian access to IVF and artificial insemination with state recognition of the non-genetic, non-gestational mother only if married, required recording of both same-sex parents on birth certificates under a September 2016 federal ruling, and from July 1, 2021 provide gender-neutral spouse and spouse or parent 1 and parent 2 birth certificate options for children of same-sex couples. Conversion therapy on minors is banned in 14 communities including Milwaukee in March 2018, Madison in July 2018, Eau Claire in October 2018, plus Cudahy, Shorewood, Racine, Glendale, Sheboygan, Superior, West Allis by 6-3 in September 2020, Kenosha by 14-1 in October 2020 with maximum 1,000 dollar fine plus costs and 90 days in Kenosha County Jail and possible suspension of driving privileges up to five years, Sun Prairie, Appleton and La Crosse, while a June 2021 executive order banned state taxpayer dollars funding conversion therapy on LGBT minors, statewide ban efforts were blocked in June 2020 and January 2023, and in July 2025 the Wisconsin Supreme Court ruled 4-3 that bans can be enacted by regulation and executive order. A 2017 PRRI poll found 73% supported an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity with 20% opposed, distinct from 66% support for same-sex marriage with 26% opposed and 8% unsure. In October 2023 Governor Evers, speaking to "LGBTQ folks — especially our trans kids", said he would "veto any bill that makes Wisconsin a less welcoming, less inclusive, and less safe place for you to be who you are". Since September 2023 the Milwaukee Police Department has omitted victim gender to avoid misgendering transgender individuals in the future. Introductions of the transgender athlete and medical-care bills sparked significant backlash from organizational and community advocates, including Fair Wisconsin, GSAFE, and the ACLU of Wisconsin.

This division is a state of this country and stands under the national framework carried by the national record; the findings below are this division's own layer. A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment places this division in its low-risk group, alongside eight other divisions and the national capital district, describing jurisdictions that have largely refrained from targeting transgender adults while not taking extraordinary steps to protect them.

No division-wide law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity, and gender identity is not a protected class under this division's hate-crime statute, though sexual orientation is. Prosecutors have sometimes used perceived sexual orientation as the route to charge crimes motivated by a victim's gender identity. Local protection is patchwork: as of 29 May 2025, 21 per cent of the division's population lived in the ten cities with full employment, housing and public-accommodation ordinances covering gender identity, and 12 per cent in cities with partial ordinances. Two counties and seven cities ban gender-identity discrimination; two further cities extend protection only to transgender city employees. An executive directive issued 7 January 2019 prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression in divisional employment, divisional contracting and the provision of divisional services, and directs public agencies to adopt and enforce nondiscrimination policies.

This division has no law barring transgender people from using government-building bathrooms or facilities consistent with their gender identity, no law defining sex to exclude transgender people, and no restriction on drag performance. The equality-map profile for this division, current to 29 May 2025, records no ban on best-practice medical care for transgender youth and no shield law protecting providers or patients from out-of-jurisdiction action.

Identity documents are the main friction point. Gender-marker change on this division's driver's licence is permitted only in limited circumstances, and change on a birth certificate is restricted: a person born in this division who has completed sex reassignment surgery may amend the birth certificate on documentation of the surgery and a name change. Neither licence nor birth certificate offers an X gender-neutral option, and the name-change process is restrictive.

Divisional law does not ban gender-affirming care for minors. This division's governor vetoed a legislative bill on 6 December 2023, blocking a legislature-passed ban on gender-affirming health care for people under 18; he had earlier vetoed a June 2023 budget provision that would have barred public medical-assistance coverage of sexual reassignment surgery and other gender-affirming care for all individuals regardless of age. Private, non-commercial sexual conduct between consenting adults has been legal since 1983, when this division's sodomy provisions were repealed; the repealing legislation stated that this division did not approve of sexual conduct outside marriage.

66186276B37442548568489.summary:
The July 2026 anti-trans legal risk assessment map places Michigan in its 'Low-Risk States' tier, describing the state as having enacted fairly robust non-discrimination policies while falling short on healthcare equity and on protections for incarcerated transgender people.

Discrimination on the basis of gender identity is unlawful in Michigan under the Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act, following a July 2022 Michigan Supreme Court ruling that affirmed the Attorney General's appeal; the legislature codified the protection in a bill passed in March 2023 and signed by Governor Gretchen Whitmer on 8 March 2023. The ruling built on a 21 May 2018 Civil Rights Commission interpretation adopted 5-0 and on the 7 March 2018 Sixth Circuit decision in EEOC v. R.G. & G.R. Harris Funeral Homes holding that Title VII prohibits employment discrimination against transgender people. Sexual-orientation protection followed the same route, from a December 2003 executive order and a March 2013 marina-loan non-discrimination provision through the May 2018 commission interpretation to the March 2023 codification.

Hate-crime law covers gender identity implicitly within Michigan's 1992 hate-crime statute under the category 'gender', per an August 2021 court declaration. A hate-crime package adding 'gender identity or expression' explicitly passed the House in June 2023 and the Senate in December 2024, was signed in January 2025 and took effect 90 days after signature. Sexual orientation has been recognised for hate-crime data collection since 1992.

The gay and trans panic defence was abolished by a law passed, signed and implemented in July 2024.

Conversion therapy is banned statewide under a bill passed by both chambers in June 2023 and signed in July 2023, following a June 2021 executive order barring taxpayer dollars or funding for conversion therapy on minors.

Sex on a Michigan birth certificate can be changed without sexual reassignment surgery under a 30 June 2021 court ruling that declared the 1978 surgery and physician-statement requirement unconstitutional; the position was certified and codified by a bill passed in December 2024. Changing sex on a driver's licence or state ID requires a signed statutory declaration and a fee under the system in place since November 2019.

Marriage between two people of the same sex is legal in Michigan under Obergefell v. Hodges (26 June 2015). Michigan had barred it by a 1995 statute signed by Governor Engler and by the 2004 constitutional amendment Proposal 04-2, approved with 58.6% of the vote, which also barred civil unions. In DeBoer v. Snyder the district court held the ban unconstitutional on 21 March 2014; more than 300 licences were issued on 22 March 2014 before Sixth Circuit stays, and the Sixth Circuit reversed on 6 November 2014.

Michigan's sodomy statute has not been repealed by the legislature even though same-sex sexual activity is legal under Lawrence v. Texas (2003). The statute as written applied to both homosexual and heterosexual conduct, and Michigan and Massachusetts are the only northern states without statutory codification.

The Michigan Supreme Court announced a September 2023 decision on respecting an individual's pronouns for judges.

66186276B98615608994420.name: Nevada
66186276B98615608994420.summary:
Nevada stands under the United States federal framework, which governs passports, entry screening, federal custody and federal care measures; those apply within the state and are carried by the national record. The findings below are specific to Nevada.

A national legal risk assessment published in July 2026 places Nevada in its Low-Risk group, crediting the state with fairly robust non-discrimination policies while finding that it falls short on healthcare equity and on protections for incarcerated transgender people.

Nevada law prohibits discrimination based on gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public accommodation under provisions effective 1 October 2011 and extended throughout state statutes effective 1 July 2017. In November 2022 voters approved Question 1 by 58%, adding sexual orientation and gender identity or expression to the state Constitution's equal protection clause.

The state hate-crime law provides additional penalties for crimes motivated by actual or perceived characteristics. It was amended to add gender identity or expression after passage in May 2013, effective 1 October 2013, and a hate-crime reporting hotline was established in January 2025.

Identity documents can be changed without surgery. Since 2016 Nevada Vital Records issues a birth certificate with corrected gender on receipt of two affidavits reflecting preferred gender, and comparable changes are permitted for driver's licences and state IDs. The DMV and Vital Records offer an "X" third-gender designation on licences, birth certificates and state IDs with no medical documentation required, available from 2019. Legislation signed 22 June 2017 abolished the 1988 requirement that transgender people publish their names in newspapers before a legal sex change on government documents.

Gender-affirming care carries state-level protection. Health insurers are barred by state law from discriminating against transgender patients, the state Medicaid agency announced in March 2018 that it would cover sex reassignment surgery, and a bill passed in June 2023 and signed by the governor requires insurers including Medicaid to cover all medically necessary gender-affirming treatments effective 1 January 2024. The governor vetoed the broader SB 302 omnibus in 2023, which would have shielded gender-affirming care and mandated Medicaid surgery coverage.

In May 2023 the governor approved legislation explicitly protecting transgender and intersex people within state correctional facilities. The July 2026 assessment nonetheless finds Nevada short on protections for incarcerated transgender people.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 8 October 2014, when the Ninth Circuit struck down the state's marriage ban in Sevcik v. Sandoval. Voters removed the constitutional ban by approving Question 2 with 62% in November 2020, and in December 2020 the Nevada Supreme Court required retroactive recognition of out-of-state same-sex marriages performed before 2014.

The Movement Advancement Project's Equality Map records state-by-state rules on whether transgender people may use public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity, and is the source used to situate Nevada within that comparison.

66186276B21291522594454.name: Maryland
66186276B21291522594454.summary:
Maryland's gender-identity law is protective. The Fairness for All Marylanders Act of 2014, effective 1 October 2014, prohibits discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations statewide; before that date protection existed only in Baltimore City, Baltimore County, Howard County, Hyattsville and Montgomery County. Discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited statewide since the Antidiscrimination Act of 2001 took effect on 21 November 2001.

The hate-crime statute adds penalties for crimes motivated by actual or perceived gender identity, listed as a separate category by an amendment effective 1 October 2021. HB231, effective the same date, abolished the common-law gay and trans panic defence.

A 2024 law declaring Maryland a sanctuary state for the protection and defence of transgender individuals passed the Senate 33-13 and the House 97-38 and was signed by Governor Wes Moore, effective 1 October 2024. It followed a June 2023 executive order protecting unimpeded access to gender-affirming healthcare and an insurance law effective 1 January 2024 described in state-by-state rights research as the most transgender healthcare friendly in the United States.

Maryland stands under the United States federal framework. Passport and visa sex markers, federal facility rules, immigration detention and federal custody are governed nationally, not by the state.

State-level identity documents are accessible but not complete. Since 1 October 2015 a birth-certificate gender marker can be changed without surgery or sterilisation on certification from a licensed healthcare provider confirming gender identity; the X marker remained unavailable on Maryland birth certificates as of 2023. Motor Vehicle Administration IDs and voter registration have allowed X since 1 October 2019 without legal or medical documentation, and the University of Maryland will add X in 2026. HB39, effective 1 October 2021, repealed the 1971 requirement to publish a name in a newspaper before a legal change on a birth certificate.

Facilities and student access run in favour of transgender people. In March 2018 a federal court ruled that transgender students may use restrooms and locker rooms consistent with gender identity, striking down a Talbot County policy; Montgomery County adopted gender-neutral bathroom requirements by a 9-0 vote in July 2022 and Baltimore does so by ordinance. A February 2022 county report records that transgender athletes may participate according to gender identity without proof, documentation, or medical or legal transition, after bills in 2022 and 2023 that would have restricted teams by biological sex failed.

Violence against transgender people in Maryland is documented. On 11 September 2026 Sophie Lee, a 27-year-old Black trans woman, was found shot in Baltimore's Charles Village and died; she was the second Black trans woman shot to death in Baltimore within ten weeks.

Protection machinery includes Montgomery County's unanimous October 2020 LGBTIQ+ bill of rights ordinance, a 15-member Commission on LGBTIQ+ Affairs created by HB130 effective October 2021 and expanded to 21 members in April 2023, and HB1380, effective 1 October 2022, which automatically restores honorable discharges retrospectively to LGBT individuals who lived in Maryland at the time.

Marriage between people of the same sex has been legal in Maryland since 1 January 2013 under the Civil Marriage Protection Act, approved 72-67 in the House on 17 February 2012 and 25-22 in the Senate on 23 February 2012, signed 1 March 2012 and approved by 52.4% of voters on 6 November 2012, after a 1973 ban; domestic partnerships have existed since 2008 and out-of-state marriages have been recognised since 2010. A trans visitor whose relationship Maryland law reads as same-sex under birth-sex status can marry here.

Report of September 13, 2026: on Friday September 11, 2026 a 27-year-old Black trans woman (Sophie Lee) was found shot in Baltimore's Charles Village and died - the second Black trans woman shot to death in Baltimore within ten weeks.

Maryland's Trans Health Equity Act passed the Maryland House of Delegates as of May 20, 2024, sponsor Del. Anne Kaiser, D-Montgomery, extending Medicaid coverage of gender-affirming treatment. The measure's path runs through the Maryland Senate.

sources.summary: Federal policy on housing transgender prisoners moved in both directions between 2015 and 2018. A January 2015 ICE memo directed that transgender immigration detainees be housed according to gender identity, and in 2016 the US Department of Justice released guidelines forbidding corrections agencies from assigning trans inmates to men's or women's units solely on birth anatomy. In 2018 the Federal Bureau of Prisons revised its Transgender Offender Manual, deleting the sentence that the Transgender Executive Council 'will recommend housing by gender identity when appropriate' and replacing it with placement on 'a case-by-case basis' in which 'biological sex' is 'the initial determination' and gender identity is used only 'in rare cases'. No Delaware- or Maryland-specific placement policy is covered.

sources.title: Transgender rights in the United States (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Trans women held in men's facilities are subjected to V-coding, the assignment of trans women to aggressive cisgender male cellmates, characterized as 'a central part of a trans woman's sentence'. Trans women who physically resist sexual assault are often criminally charged with assault and placed in solitary confinement, with the charge then used to extend the sentence and deny parole. A 2021 California study found that 69% of surveyed trans women prisoners reported being made to perform unwanted sexual acts, 58.5% reported violent sexual assault, and 88% reported a 'marriage-like relationship'. sources.summary: Discrimination based on gender identity has been prohibited statewide since the Fairness for All Marylanders Act of 2014 took effect October 1, 2014, after prior coverage only in Baltimore City, Baltimore County, Howard County, Hyattsville, and Montgomery County. The hate-crime law provides additional penalties for crimes motivated by actual or perceived gender identity, clarified by a 2021 amendment effective October 1, 2021 to list gender identity as a separate category, and the common-law gay or trans panic defense was abolished by HB231 effective October 1, 2021. Maryland declared itself a sanctuary state for protecting and defending transgender individuals by a law passed 33-13 in the Senate and 97-38 in the House, signed by Governor Wes Moore and effective October 1, 2024, following a June 2023 executive order protecting unimpeded access to gender-affirming healthcare and a January 1, 2024 insurance law described as the most transgender healthcare friendly policies within the United States. Medicaid explicitly covers sexual reassignment surgery for eligible residents over 18 under a bill passed March 2023, signed April 2023, and effective January 1, 2024. Birth-certificate gender-marker change has been allowed since October 1, 2015 without surgery or sterilization upon certification from a licensed healthcare provider confirming gender identity, though X remains unavailable on birth certificates as of 2023, while Motor Vehicle Administration IDs and voter registration allow X since October 1, 2019 without legal or medical documentation, and the University of Maryland will add X in 2026. Name-change privacy reform HB39 effective October 1, 2021 repealed the 1971 requirement to publish names in a newspaper before a legal change on a birth certificate. On facilities and sports, a March 2018 federal court ruled transgender students may use restrooms and locker rooms aligning with gender identity striking down Talbot County policy, Montgomery County by 9-0 vote in July 2022 and Baltimore provide gender-neutral bathrooms by ordinance, and a February 2022 county report notes transgender athletes may participate per gender identity without proof, documentation, or medical or legal transition after 2022-2023 bills to restrict teams by biological sex failed. Private consensual same-sex sexual activity was invalidated by courts through Schochet v. State in 1990, Williams v. Glendening in October 1998 for oral sex, and a 1999 settlement for anal sex, with formal legislative repeal of the anal-sex provision effective October 1, 2020 and repeal of the oral-sex ban passed in 2023 and effective October 1, 2023 without Governor Wes Moore's signature. In July 2021 several men were arrested for gay sex but not heterosexual sex under the Unnatural or Perverted Sexual Practices Act still on the books because the 2020 Senate amendment left the oral-sex ban intact after a 2022 repeal attempt died in committee. Discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited statewide since the Antidiscrimination Act of 2001 effective November 21, 2001, and the hate-crime law adds penalties for crimes motivated by sexual orientation. Same-sex marriage has been legal since January 1, 2013 under the Civil Marriage Protection Act approved 72-67 in the House on February 17, 2012 and 25-22 in the Senate on February 23, 2012, signed March 1, 2012, and approved by 52.4% of voters November 6, 2012, following a 1973 ban, domestic partnerships since 2008, and recognition of out-of-state marriages since 2010. Conversion therapy by licensed practitioners on minors was banned effective October 1, 2018 after passage in April 2018 and signature in May 2018, with a federal constitutional challenge dismissed in September 2019. Protection machinery includes Montgomery County's unanimous October 2020 LGBTIQ+ bill of rights ordinance, a 15-member Commission on LGBTIQ+ Affairs established by HB130 effective October 2021 and expanded to 21 members in April 2023, and HB1380 effective October 1, 2022 automatically restoring honorable discharges retrospectively to LGBT individuals who lived in Maryland at the time.

66186276B43071933723331.name: California
66186276B43071933723331.summary:
California's care-access law is the most protective element of its own record. Governor Gavin Newsom signed SB 107 in September 2022, making California the first state to declare itself a sanctuary for transgender young people seeking medical care. Out-of-state youth can obtain hormones and puberty blockers in California, and the law shields families from child-abuse investigations or criminal prosecution for seeking gender-affirming care, including families who travel to California for it.

California's prison system is the one documented instance of identity-based placement in this inventory. As of January 2021 California is coded as the single state allowing transgender inmates to be housed according to their gender identity, with housing assigned identity-based within the general population and no trans-only separate facility documented. In 2015 California became the first state to fund gender-affirming surgeries for transgender prison inmates, and KPBS coverage of the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation's operational guidelines that year confirms the identity-based care and guidance posture while containing no explicit statement of a trans-only unit or segregation practice. The most recent documented statement of this housing practice in this record is dated January 2021; no later instance is documented.

Recorded hostility sits alongside that protective framework. The GLAAD ALERT Desk documented more than 1,000 anti-LGBTQ incidents nationwide in 2025, of which California recorded 198, the highest figure of any state. That ranking is by raw count only: the source supplies no population or per-capita denominator, so the count does not establish that California is riskier for an individual visitor than a smaller state.

A separate analysis of the same 2025 incident data reports a dramatic increase in anti-LGBTQ hate-crime reports in Los Angeles in law-enforcement data covering the same period as Governor Gavin Newsom's platforming of anti-trans figures.

A July 2026 analysis places California in the "Safest States" law band with a score of 4.1 and 1.9 recorded incidents, and argues that even the most protective statutory floors do not eliminate recorded hostility.

A budget appropriations bill passed on 9 July 2026 includes $26 million for gender-affirming healthcare protections, covering judicial and executive federal government litigation and liability administrative damages.

66186276B35012827062242.name: Colorado
66186276B35012827062242.summary:
Colorado's Anti-Discrimination Act prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity and gender expression in employment, housing, public accommodations, education and credit, a coverage in force since 2008 and expanded again by the 2025 legislature, as documented in the Colorado Legislature's own 2025 summary of gender-affirming-care and transgender legislation. As of 12 October 2026 the state's gender-identity policy score stands at 23.25 of 25 within an overall score of 44.5 of 47, and a July 2026 national legal-risk assessment lists Colorado among the most protective states for transgender people.

House Bill 1312, the Kelly Loving Act, was signed by Governor Jared Polis on 16 May 2025 after passing on 6 May. It requires employers and schools to use a person's chosen name and pronouns, prohibits deadnaming and misgendering in workplaces and schools with immediate effect, and requires schools with dress codes to allow a student to choose from any uniform option. Its provisions simplifying changes of gender identity on birth certificates and driver's licences, and changes of name on marriage licences, take effect on 1 October 2026.

Gender markers on state documents are changeable without surgery. The Board of the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment removed the surgical requirement unanimously in February 2019, ending a rule that had applied since 1 January 1984. A change is made by request, using a Change of Sex Designation form to the Division of Motor Vehicles for licences and IDs and Birth Certificate Correction and Sex Designation forms to the Department of Health for birth certificates. Birth certificates offer M, F, Intersex and X markers; IDs and licences offer male, female and X. Minors need parent or guardian consent plus confirmation from a medical or mental health professional.

Facilities access is protected. In 2013 the Colorado Civil Rights Division ruled that transgender six-year-old Coy Mathis could use the girls' restroom at her elementary school in Fountain, and in 2023 Colorado implemented a law granting full access to bathroom facilities for all genders. The state anti-bullying law prohibits bullying on the basis of gender identity and requires school districts to adopt prevention policies.

Colorado's hate-crime law has covered gender identity or expression since 2001, with penalty enhancements for bias-motivated crimes. In 2009 a Greeley jury convicted a man of first-degree murder with a hate-crime finding in a case described as the first murder trial applying a hate-crime law where the victim was transgender. The gay panic defence was abolished by a bipartisan bill passed in June 2020 and signed in July 2020, effective immediately.

Gender-affirming care is protected at state level but is under direct pressure. Legislation signed in April 2023 was enacted to protect, defend and guarantee gender-affirming healthcare services and to guarantee safe passage of transgender individuals from other states. 66186276B10610315112087.summary:
Minnesota sets its own civil, health-care and criminal law within the federal framework of the United States; federal rules on passports, visas, entry screening and federal custody are fixed nationally and are not restated here. On the matters a trans visitor encounters at state level, Minnesota law runs in a protective direction.

Minnesota Session Law 2023 ch. 29 (HF 146) declares that gender-affirming health care as defined in the Act "is against the public policy of this state and must not be enforced or applied" in pending cases, and amends state provisions on warrants, arrests and extraditions that arise from other states' laws on gender-affirming health care. The House passed the bill 68-62 on 24 March 2023 after a late-night debate, and Governor Tim Walz signed it. It followed a March 2023 executive order directing the Minnesota Department of Health to summarise the scientific literature on the safety and effectiveness of gender-affirming care and confirming that providers could bill insurance for such care.

The shield reaches out-of-state process. Minnesota authorities may not enforce subpoenas, arrest warrants or extradition requests issued elsewhere over gender-affirming care that is legal in Minnesota, and may not comply with out-of-state court orders to remove children from parental custody for having obtained such care. Families travelling to Minnesota for treatment fall inside that protection.

Anti-discrimination law covers gender identity. Minnesota has prohibited discrimination based on gender identity since 1993 in employment, housing, public accommodations, insurance, goods and services, contracts, health benefits and hospital visitation rights, and in that year became the first state to outlaw discrimination based on sexual orientation in the same fields. A May 2023 omnibus community justice bill protected "gender identity" as a category separate from sexual orientation and repealed exemptions for nonpublic service organizations, effective immediately. The same act repealed residual statutory language stating that the state "does not condone homosexuality or bisexuality" and did not authorise its promotion in educational institutions.

Hate-crime law has provided additional penalties for offences committed because of gender identity since that category was added in 1993; sexual orientation was added in 1989. The trans panic defence was abolished by the omnibus justice reforms signed on 29 May 2024 and effective 1 August 2024, which passed the Senate 34-33.

Identity documents are relatively open at state level. Changing the gender marker on a Minnesota birth certificate does not require sex reassignment surgery: it requires a physician's letter confirming appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition, or a court order for gender change, plus a notarised Birth Certificate Application and a fee, and the previous certificate is kept confidential. Driver and Vehicle Services updates a driver's licence or state ID on individual request with no documentation required, and since October 2018 licences and state IDs offer M, F or X on request, with no documentation needed for intersex, non-binary and ambiguous-sex applicants. Birth certificates carry no X option.

Care coverage is written into state policy. State Medicaid covers transgender-related care, and Minnesota law bars health insurers from excluding transgender-specific coverage or discriminating against transgender patients. Gender-affirming services were protected by the March 2023 executive order and codified by the legislation signed in April 2023. Conversion therapy is banned for minors and vulnerable adults under a law signed by Governor Tim Walz on 26 April 2023 and effective 1 August 2023, following a July 2021 executive order and city bans beginning with Minneapolis in November 2019. Practitioners may not advertise LGBTQ identities as a mental disease, disorder or illness or promise to change sexual orientation or gender identity; violations are subject to discipline by health licensing boards, and insurers and health plans may not pay for conversion therapy.

Private consensual conduct between adults is not criminalised. Minn. Stat. 609.293, which punished voluntarily engaging in or submitting to sodomy by the anus or by or with the mouth with up to one year's imprisonment and a fine of up to $3,000, was declared unconstitutional on 15 May 2001 as applied to private, consensual, non-commercial acts of adults, on privacy grounds under the Minnesota Constitution, in an unappealed class action decided two years before Lawrence v. Texas. The prohibition had been carried since the 1849 territorial adoption of Wisconsin law and the 1851 code, was raised in 1909 to 20 years' imprisonment, was expanded in 1921 to include fellatio, and was reduced in 1967 to a misdemeanour punishable by up to one year in jail or a $1,000 fine; a 1973 repeal attempt failed 46-69 with 19 abstentions, and formal repeal came in May 2023 through the Omnibus Judiciary and Public Safety Bill signed by Governor Tim Walz.

Marriage is recognised for relationships read locally as same-sex. Same-sex marriage became legal in Minnesota on 1 August 2013, after House passage 75-59 on 9 May and Senate passage 37-30 on 13 May, signed by Governor Mark Dayton on 14 May, following the defeat of a constitutional ban by 51.5% to 47.5% on 6 November 2012. A trans visitor married to a partner of any birth-sex configuration is recognised on that footing.

Custody placement practice has been documented along birth-sex lines. CeCe McDonald, a transgender woman, pleaded guilty to second-degree manslaughter and was sentenced on 4 June 2012 to 41 months; her attorneys acknowledged there was "no way" she would be sent to a women's prison and "really no history of transgender people being placed according to their gender identity" in the state. The Minnesota Department of Corrections placed her in an adult male facility, Minnesota Correctional Facility - St. Cloud, after a state gender assessment concluded she would be held in a men's facility, and although she was later transferred to a second facility she remained quartered with men throughout her imprisonment. She was held in segregated custody while awaiting trial. In May 2012 a fellow inmate attacked her with a glass, causing a wound that required eleven stitches; the attacker pleaded guilty in April 2013 to third-degree assault and received six months' jail time plus probation. A petition filed during her imprisonment led the department to administer the correct hormone regimen.

Hate-crime law provides additional penalties for crimes committed based on gender identity since its 1993 expansion to include that category. Changing legal gender on Minnesota birth certificates does not require sex reassignment surgery and requires a physician letter confirming appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition or a court order for gender change plus a notarized Birth Certificate Application and fee, with the old certificate kept confidential, while Driver and Vehicle Services updates a driver's license or state ID upon individual request with no documentation required. Since October 2018 driver's licences and state IDs allow M, F, or X upon request with no documentation for intersex, non-binary and ambiguous-sex people, but no X option is available for birth certificates. State Medicaid policy covers transgender-related care and Minnesota law prohibits health insurers from excluding transgender-specific coverage or discriminating against transgender patients, and gender-affirming services were protected by a March 2023 executive order codified in April 2023 by House File 146, the "Trans Refuge Bill," signed by Governor Tim Walz effective immediately. Conversion therapy was banned statewide effective August 1, 2023 after a July 2021 executive order and prior city ordinances, and the "trans panic defense" was abolished in the omnibus justice reforms bill signed May 29, 2024 effective August 1, 2024 after a 34-33 Senate vote. The Minnesota high school transgender athlete policy has been challenged in the courts by attorneys representing 3 school softball players. Bans on same-sex sexual activity dating to 1849 territorial adoption of Wisconsin laws and the 1851 code, increased in 1909 to 20 years imprisonment and expanded in 1921 to include fellatio, were reduced in 1967 to a misdemeanor punishable by up to one year in jail and/or $1,000 fine after a 1973 repeal attempt failed 46-69 with 19 abstentions, were invalidated for private adult consensual non-commercial acts in Doe et al. v. Ventura et al. (2001) by Judge Delila F. Pierce in an unappealed class action two years before Lawrence v. Texas, and were formally repealed in May 2023 by the Omnibus Judiciary and Public Safety Bill signed by Governor Tim Walz effective immediately. Minnesota became the first U.S. state in 1993 to outlaw discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, housing, public accommodations, insurance, goods and services, contracts, health benefits and hospital visitation, while retaining provisions that the state "does not condone homosexuality or bisexuality" nor "authorize the promotion of homosexuality or bisexuality in education institutions," which were formally repealed by the May 2023 omnibus. Hate-crime protections were expanded to cover sexual orientation in 1989, and same-sex marriage became legal August 1, 2013 after House passage 75-59 on May 9 and Senate passage 37-30 on May 13 and signature by Governor Mark Dayton on May 14, following November 6, 2012 voter defeat of a constitutional ban by 51.5% to 47.5%. Conversion therapy was banned statewide by legislation signed by Governor Walz effective August 1, 2023 following a July 2021 executive order and city bans beginning with Minneapolis in November 2019, and the "gay panic defense" was abolished in the law signed May 29, 2024 effective August 1, 2024. An August 2014 court settlement upheld marriage and sexual-orientation employment discrimination laws against a hunting club that refused a same-sex wedding, In re Guardianship of Kowalski on December 17, 1991 awarded guardianship to a lesbian partner over parents' objections, and adoption law allows single LGBTQ petitioning with no specific prohibition on joint or stepchild petitions by same-sex couples with IVF access and recognition of a married non-genetic, non-gestational mother via donor insemination while surrogacy is neither expressly prohibited nor permitted but courts have generally ruled for couples.

sources.title: Doe et al. v. Ventura et al. (2001)
sources.summary: On May 15, 2001, Minn. Stat. 609.293, which punished voluntarily engaging in or submitting to sodomy defined as carnally knowing any person by the anus or by or with the mouth with up to one year imprisonment and/or up to a $3,000 fine, was declared unconstitutional as applied to private, consensual, non-commercial acts of sodomy by consenting adults as violating the right of privacy guaranteed by the Minnesota Constitution.

sources.title: House File 146 - 'Trans Refuge Bill' and March 2023 Executive Order
sources.summary: On March 24, 2023 the Minnesota House passed House File 146 by 68-62 to protect transgender patients from other states and providers of gender-affirming care that is legal in Minnesota from legal action in states where such care is banned or restricted, prohibiting enforcement in Minnesota of out-of-state subpoenas, arrest warrants and extradition requests related to such care and barring compliance with out-of-state court orders to remove children from parental custody for obtaining such care, with Governor Tim Walz having signed an executive order protecting gender-affirming care and intending to sign the bill into law upon Senate passage after it cleared its final Senate committee.

sources.title: Minnesota conversion therapy ban - State law April 2023 and Executive Order July 2021
sources.summary: On April 26, 2023 Minnesota banned medical and mental-health practitioners from providing conversion therapy to minors and vulnerable adults, banned advertising that describes LGBTQ identities as a mental disease, disorder or illness or promises to change sexual orientation or gender identity, made violations subject to discipline by health licensing boards, and barred insurers and health plans from paying for conversion therapy, and enacted a gender-affirming-care shield law barring state authorities from honoring out-of-state subpoenas or arrest warrants for providing gender-affirming care, protecting families traveling to Minnesota for care, following a March 2023 executive order directing the Department of Health to summarize scientific literature on the safety and effectiveness of gender-affirming care and confirming providers could bill insurance for such care.

66186276B10610315112087.blindSummary:
This division sets its own civil, health-care and criminal law within the federal framework of this country; federal rules on passports, visas, entry screening and federal custody are fixed nationally and are not restated here. On the matters a trans visitor encounters at division level, this division's law runs in a protective direction.

Division Session Law 2023 ch. 29 (bill 146) declares that gender-affirming health care as defined in the Act "is against the public policy of this state and must not be enforced or applied" in pending cases, and amends provisions on warrants, arrests and extraditions that arise from other jurisdictions' laws on gender-affirming health care. The lower house passed the bill 68-62 on 24 March 2023 after a late-night debate, and the governor signed it. It followed a March 2023 executive order directing the division's public health agency to summarise the scientific literature on the safety and effectiveness of gender-affirming care and confirming that providers could bill insurance for such care.

The shield reaches out-of-jurisdiction process. This division's authorities may not enforce subpoenas, arrest warrants or extradition requests issued elsewhere over gender-affirming care that is legal in this division, and may not comply with court orders issued elsewhere to remove children from parental custody for having obtained such care. Families travelling to this division for treatment fall inside that protection.

Anti-discrimination law covers gender identity. This division has prohibited discrimination based on gender identity since 1993 in employment, housing, public accommodations, insurance, goods and services, contracts, health benefits and hospital visitation rights, and in that year became the first jurisdiction to outlaw discrimination based on sexual orientation in the same fields. A May 2023 omnibus community justice bill protected "gender identity" as a category separate from sexual orientation and repealed exemptions for nonpublic service organisations, effective immediately. The same act repealed residual statutory language stating that the division "does not condone homosexuality or bisexuality" and did not authorise its promotion in educational institutions.

Hate-crime law has provided additional penalties for offences committed because of gender identity since that category was added in 1993; sexual orientation was added in 1989. The trans panic defence was abolished by the omnibus justice reforms signed on 29 May 2024 and effective 1 August 2024, which passed the upper house 34-33.

Identity documents are relatively open at division level. Changing the gender marker on a birth certificate issued by this division does not require sex reassignment surgery: it requires a physician's letter confirming appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition, or a court order for gender change, plus a notarised certificate application and a fee, and the previous certificate is kept confidential. The licensing agency updates a driver's licence or division identity card on individual request with no documentation required, and since October 2018 both offer M, F or X on request, with no documentation needed for intersex, non-binary and ambiguous-sex applicants. Birth certificates carry no X option.

Care coverage is written into division policy. The public health insurance scheme covers transgender-related care, and this division's law bars health insurers from excluding transgender-specific coverage or discriminating against transgender patients. Gender-affirming services were protected by the March 2023 executive order and codified by the legislation signed in April 2023. Conversion therapy is banned for minors and vulnerable adults under a law signed by the governor on 26 April 2023 and effective 1 August 2023, following a July 2021 executive order and city-level bans beginning in November 2019 with the division's largest city. Practitioners may not advertise LGBTQ identities as a mental disease, disorder or illness or promise to change sexual orientation or gender identity; violations are subject to discipline by health licensing boards, and insurers and health plans may not pay for conversion therapy.

Private consensual conduct between adults is not criminalised. Division statute 609.293, which punished voluntarily engaging in or submitting to sodomy by the anus or by or with the mouth with up to one year's imprisonment and a fine of up to $3,000, was declared unconstitutional on 15 May 2001 as applied to private, consensual, non-commercial acts of adults, on privacy grounds under this division's constitution, in an unappealed class action decided two years before a landmark ruling of this country's highest court. The prohibition had been carried since the 1849 territorial adoption of the law of a neighbouring jurisdiction and the 1851 code, was raised in 1909 to 20 years' imprisonment, was expanded in 1921 to include fellatio, and was reduced in 1967 to a misdemeanour punishable by up to one year in jail or a $1,000 fine; a 1973 repeal attempt failed 46-69 with 19 abstentions, and formal repeal came in May 2023 through the omnibus judiciary and public safety bill signed by the governor.

Marriage is recognised for relationships read locally as same-sex. Same-sex marriage became legal in this division on 1 August 2013, after lower house passage 75-59 on 9 May and upper house passage 37-30 on 13 May, signed by the governor on 14 May, following the defeat of a constitutional ban by 51.5% to 47.5% on 6 November 2012. A trans visitor married to a partner of any birth-sex configuration is recognised on that footing.

Custody placement practice has been documented along birth-sex lines. A transgender woman pleaded guilty to second-degree manslaughter and was sentenced on 4 June 2012 to 41 months; her attorneys acknowledged there was "no way" she would be sent to a women's prison and "really no history of transgender people being placed according to their gender identity" in the division. The division's corrections department placed her in an adult male correctional facility after a gender assessment concluded she would be held in a men's facility, and although she was later transferred to a second facility she remained quartered with men throughout her imprisonment. She was held in segregated custody while awaiting trial. In May 2012 a fellow inmate attacked her with a glass, causing a wound that required eleven stitches; the attacker pleaded guilty in April 2013 to third-degree assault and received six months' jail time plus probation. A petition filed during her imprisonment led the department to administer the correct hormone regimen.

66186276B73434888205604.name: New Jersey
66186276B73434888205604.summary:
New Jersey's Law Against Discrimination, amended in 2006 to cover gender identity and expression and in 1991 to cover affectional or sexual orientation, bars denial of goods, services, facilities and lodging on those grounds in places of public accommodation, which state materials describe as including hotels, restaurants, stores and transportation, as well as in housing and employment. A trans visitor refused service or lodging can complain to the Division on Civil Rights, which investigates and can grant relief.

Bias-motivated crimes carry enhanced penalties where the bias rests on gender identity or expression, with sensitivity training available as a sentencing condition. A bill extending bias and intimidation protections to gender identity passed the lower house 71-0 in March 2021. The FBI's New Jersey division has reported gender X in its data since June 2021, a July 2022 police licensing system carries gender-identity protections, and state-run hospital patient records are required to protect sexual orientation and gender identity data.

State identity documents are comparatively open. Since 1 February 2019 a transgender person may obtain an amended birth certificate with corrected name and sex without surgery or any medical procedure, under three laws signed in June 2018; those laws also created an X marker on official documents and put transgender and intersex people on death certificates. Since February 2020 no doctor's note is required to change the M or F marker on a driver licence or state ID, and since April 2021 the X, M and F markers are all available. A November 2022 executive order provides privacy and confidentiality in legal name changes. These are state documents; passport and visa issuance is governed separately by federal rules.

An April 2023 executive order directs state agencies to protect and defend gender-affirming healthcare within New Jersey's borders, including access by people travelling in from other states.

The state has recognised and performed marriages of same-sex couples since 21 October 2013, following a 27 September 2013 court decision whose appeal was rejected on 19 October 2013; the legislature codified the position in December 2021 and the governor signed it on 10 January 2022, effective immediately. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can marry and have that marriage recognised here.

A January 2020 law bars the gay and transgender panic defence, providing that provocation is not objectively reasonable when based on actual or perceived gender identity or expression, including an unwanted non-forcible romantic or sexual advance. The bill passed both chambers 73-0 and 39-0.

A July 2026 legal-risk ranking built from a rubric over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills places New Jersey in the fifteen-state Most Protective tier, alongside California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington.

sources.summary: July 2026 national legal-risk ranking built from a rubric over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills (youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate/driver-license restrictions, end of legal recognition): New Jersey sits in the fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier (CA, CO, CT, HI, IL, MA, MD, MN, NJ, NM, NY, OR, RI, VT, WA), whose laws have 'gone above and beyond in safeguarding' trans rights. Contrast tier: worst-law states carry up to 5-year prison terms (Idaho) or arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use (Florida).

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in New Jersey (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: New Jersey Law Against Discrimination was amended in 2006 to include gender identity and expression as prohibited categories for employment, housing and public accommodations. Enhanced penalties apply for crimes with bias based on gender identity or expression with sensitivity-training sentencing options, the FBI New Jersey division reports gender X since June 2021, bill A-4833 on bias and intimidation based on gender identity passed the lower house 71-0 in March 2021, and July 2022 laws created a police licensing system with gender-identity protections and protected sexual orientation and gender identity data in state-run hospital patient records. Since February 1, 2019 transgender persons may obtain an amended birth certificate with corrected name and sex without surgery or medical procedures under three 2018 laws signed in June 2018 by Governor Phil Murphy that established a Transgender Equality Task Force, repealed the surgery requirement, created an X marker on official documents, and included transgender and intersex people on death certificates effective July 4, 2018. Since February 2020 no doctor's note is required to change driver license/ID sex marker M to F or F to M, since April 2021 X, M and F markers are available, and a November 2022 executive order provides privacy, dignity and confidentiality for legal name changes. An April 2023 executive order protects and defends gender-affirming healthcare within New Jersey borders including interstate access. The New Jersey State Interscholastic Athletic Association allows sports participation according to gender identity, and September 2018 school guidance promotes transgender-friendly policies on names and pronouns, participation in activities, use of facilities and student records. In June 2023 school boards in Middletown, Marlboro and Manalapan-Englishtown adopted parental notification policies outing transgender and non-binary students described as potentially violating discrimination and hate-crime legislation with a lawsuit by the Attorney General's office to block them, and the January 2020 law banning the gay panic defense provides provocation is not objectively reasonable if based on actual or perceived gender identity or expression including unwanted non-forcible romantic or sexual advance. Same-sex sexual activity is legal after State v. Ciuffini (1978) struck down sodomy laws as violating personal privacy and autonomy and the legislature repealed the sodomy law in 1978. LGBT persons were allowed to gather in drinking establishments after One Eleven Liquors, Inc. vs. Division of Alcoholic Beverage Commission in 1967 invalidated license revocations under the rule against serving female impersonators or persons of ill repute, with an official apology by Attorney General Gurbir Grewal in June 2021. Same-sex marriages have been recognized and performed since October 21, 2013 following a September 27 court decision whose appeal was rejected October 19, 2013, and were codified by legislation passed December 2021 and signed January 10, 2022 by Governor Phil Murphy effective immediately. The Law Against Discrimination was amended in 1991 to include affectional or sexual orientation prohibiting discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations including based on perceived orientation. Enhanced penalties apply for bias-motivated crimes based on sexual orientation with sensitivity-training sentencing options, and bill A1796 banning the gay panic defense for provocation based on affectional or sexual orientation including unwanted non-forcible advance passed 73-0 and 39-0 and was signed in January 2020 effective immediately. Sexual orientation change efforts directed at minors were banned by legislation passed June 2013 and signed August 19, 2013, upheld November 8, 2013 in District Court and September 11, 2014 in the Third Circuit with Supreme Court review declined in May 2015 and again April 15, 2019 in King v. Murphy, with a Hudson County ruling that claiming to cure a disorder is fraud. Knowing HIV nondisclosure in sexual activity was a third-degree offense versus fourth-degree for other STIs until bill S3707 signed January 18, 2022 reduced engaging in sex while infected with any STI including HIV to a disorderly persons offense.

66186276B99594608635082.summary:
Hawaii is a state of the United States and stands under the US federal framework; the national record carries federal law, passport rules and entry screening. The findings below concern Hawaii's own statutes and their application.

A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment, built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the withdrawal of legal recognition, places Hawaii in a fifteen-state Most Protective tier and describes the laws of that tier as having gone above and beyond in safeguarding transgender rights. The assessment is a rubric-based ranking of legislation rather than a measure of enforcement.

Hawaii holds a healthcare shield law or executive order, recorded as current on 27 September 2026, which protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where care that is lawful in Hawaii was banned in the patient's home state. For a trans visitor travelling from a state with a youth-care ban or another care restriction, this is the provision most directly relevant to obtaining care while in Hawaii.

State law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in housing and public accommodations since 2005 and 2006, in employment since 2011, in insurance contracts since 1 July 2016, and in jury selection under legislation signed in June 2022 and effective 1 January 2023. The same 2022 legislation created a state LGBTIQ+ commission and mandated state health insurance coverage for sexual reassignment surgery.

The hate-crime statute covers actual or perceived gender identity or expression, defined to include a person's actual or perceived gender, gender identity, gender-related self image, appearance or expression, whether or not it differs from that traditionally associated with the person's sex at birth. The gay and trans panic defences were abolished by a bill passed in April 2019, signed on 26 June 2019 and effective immediately.

Changing a gender marker on state documents does not require surgery. Since a law passed on 5 May 2015, signed 14 July 2015 and effective immediately, transgender people may change the marker by request; an updated birth certificate requires a completed Application for Amendment to Birth Record and an affidavit from a licensed physician, and an updated driver's licence or state ID requires a Gender Designation Form completed by a medical or social professional confirming gender identity. An X sex option on driver's licences and birth certificates, passed in May 2019, signed 26 June 2019 and effective 1 July 2020, is available by request with no medical documentation required.

Health insurance provisions include coverage of sex reassignment surgeries under the 2016 insurance nondiscrimination rule, mandatory coverage effective 1 January 2023, and the inclusion of transgender individuals in health insurance planning under a bill passed in May 2022 with an emergency clause signed a month later and effective immediately, replacing male-only and female-only planning in place since 1980. Conversion therapy on minors has been banned since 1 July 2018.

Marriage is open to couples regardless of gender under the Hawaii Marriage Equality Act, passed by the Senate 20-4 on 30 October 2013 and by the House 30-19 on 8 November 2013, given final Senate approval 19-4 on 12 November 2013 and signed on 13 November 2013, with marriages beginning 2 December 2013. The 1998 constitutional amendment that authorised the legislature to reserve marriage to opposite-sex couples was repealed by referendum on 5 November 2024, with 55.94 per cent voting to delete the opposite-sex limitation from Article I Section 23. Reciprocal beneficiary relationships have existed since 1997, civil unions were signed on 23 February 2011 and effective 1 January 2012, and benefits for the partners of state employees have been provided since 1997.

Parentage rules have moved toward gender neutrality. A bill passed in April 2021 and signed in July 2021 recognised unmarried same-sex parentage with immediate effect, and Act 298, effective 1 January 2026, implements gender-neutral parentage by voluntary acknowledgment or court adjudication.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since the 1972 repeal took effect in 1973, replacing an 1850 anti-sodomy statute; the age of consent has been 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation since 2001.
