66186276B11383391196245.summary:
Illinois is placed in the fifteen-state "Most Protective" tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking compiled from a rubric over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, which describes the tier's laws as having gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.

Discrimination on the basis of gender identity has been banned in employment, housing, credit and public accommodations since 1 June 2006, with "sexual orientation" defined to include gender-related identity whether or not traditionally associated with the sex assigned at birth. The exemption for employers with fewer than 15 employees was removed by legislation signed in August 2019 and effective 1 July 2020, following a 2018 veto, and discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in jury selection was banned effective 1 January 2020.

Hate-crime penalties were extended to gender identity by HB 3930, passed unanimously on 16 April and 20 May 2015, signed by Governor Bruce Rauner on 20 July 2015 and effective 1 January 2016; before that, such offences were covered only as perceived sexual orientation. The state's hate-crime statute has provided enhanced penalties for crimes motivated by actual or perceived sexual orientation since 1991. The gay and trans panic defence was repealed by SB1761, passed unanimously in June 2017, signed on 25 August 2017 and effective 1 January 2018.

Gender-affirming care is protected by legislation signed on 13 January 2023 and effective immediately, covering care provided within Illinois, including for people who travel from outside the state to obtain it. Under the shield law, patients and providers are protected from civil or criminal charges where care lawful in Illinois was banned in the patient's home state. Conversion therapy on minors under 18 by mental health providers has been banned under the Youth Mental Health Protection Act since 1 January 2016; a federal court dismissed a challenge brought by pastors on 15 February 2017, holding that private religious counselling is not trade or commerce.

Birth-certificate gender-marker changes no longer require surgery, under legislation passed on 31 May 2017 by 63-43 in the House and 32-22 in the Senate, signed on 25 August 2017 and effective 1 January 2018. An X option has been available since July 2020, and a self-attestation reform passed in January and February 2023 took effect on 1 July. Since 1 July 2024, people born outside Illinois can change the sex designation on an Illinois birth certificate. Driver's licences and state identification are corrected on a Gender Designation Change Form, with an X option available from 2024.

Single-occupancy public restrooms were designated gender-neutral by legislation passed 109-5 in the House and 53-0 in the Senate, signed in July 2019 and effective 1 January 2020. Chicago's Human Rights Ordinance, as amended in 2016, provides that each person determines their own gender identity, with no proof required beyond expression for bathroom access, and all Chicago public schools have had all-gender bathrooms by signage since December 2021. A May 2023 bill permitting use of multi-occupancy facilities consistent with a person's gender identity passed both chambers but had not been signed or vetoed.

Marriage equality was enacted by statute signed by Governor Pat Quinn on 20 November 2013 and effective 1 June 2014, after House approval 61-54 and Senate approval 32-21, superseding a 1996 statutory ban. Gender-neutral marriage certificates have been available under a July 2021 law, and 2023 legislation repealing out-of-jurisdiction null-and-void provisions took effect in 2024. Civil unions have been recognised since 1 June 2011 under a law signed on 31 January 2011, with out-of-state marriages of same-sex couples recognised as civil unions. The Illinois Domestic Violence Act is written in gender-neutral terms and applies to partners who share or have shared a dwelling or a dating relationship.

Private consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since 1 January 1962, when a new criminal code eliminated the state's sodomy law, making Illinois the first state to do so. The age of consent is 17, raised from 16 effective 1 January 2012.

66186276B15934532614691.name: Massachusetts
66186276B15934532614691.summary:
Massachusetts prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity and expression in credit, public and private employment, union practices and housing under legislation enacted on 23 November 2011 and in force from 1 July 2012, following an executive order of 17 February 2011 that barred state government and its contractors from discriminating against transgender state employees. Public-accommodation coverage was added by a Senate vote of 33-4 on 12 May 2016 and a House vote of 117-36 on 7 July 2016, signed by Governor Charlie Baker and effective 1 October 2016, and was retained at the ballot on 6 November 2018 by 67.8 per cent to 32.2 per cent, the first statewide popular vote of its kind in the United States. For a visitor these are the operative rules in hotels, restaurants, shops, transport and other places open to the public.

Gender identity was written into the hate-crime statute with effect from 1 July 2012. The framework defines a hate crime as a criminal act accompanied by overt actions motivated at least in part by prejudice, including on grounds of gender and sexual orientation, and requires incidents to be collected, summarised and publicly reported through the Crime Reporting Unit created by the 1990 Hate Crimes Reporting Act, involving the State Police, the Attorney General and legislative committees, alongside a Governor's Task Force on Hate Crimes established in 1991.

The state issues its own identity documents on self-declared terms. Birth certificates may be amended to reflect gender identity without sex reassignment surgery. Non-binary X markers on driver's licences and state identification cards have been available since November 2019 under a Registry of Motor Vehicles regulation, and non-binary X birth certificates and amendment of gender on marriage certificates were authorised by law signed on 29 July 2024 in the FY25 budget. Marriage licence forms in Boston have carried no gender or sex field since August 2023. Name changes can be obtained confidentially without public notice under An Act Protecting Personal Security, signed on 25 November 2025.

Health care is protected in two directions. A shield law in place since 2022 protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where care lawful in Massachusetts was banned in the patient's home state; this is the provision most likely to matter to a visitor travelling from a state that has banned the care. In July 2022 both chambers passed and the Governor signed a bill codifying gender-affirming healthcare protections, which took effect immediately under an emergency clause rather than after the usual 90-day period. Conversion-therapy practices on minors were banned by legislation passed 147-8 in the House on 13 March 2019 and 34-0 in the Senate on 28 March 2019, enacted on 4 April 2019 and signed on 8 April 2019 with immediate effect, making Massachusetts the sixteenth state with such a ban.

Marriage is open to same-sex couples following the Supreme Judicial Court's ruling of 18 November 2003, with licences issued from 17 May 2004 after the 180-day legislative window; attempts at a constitutional amendment failed and ended in 2007. The 1913 bar on non-resident marriages was repealed on 31 July 2008, so a couple travelling to Massachusetts can marry there, and 2012 rulings treat out-of-jurisdiction civil unions and California registered domestic partnerships as equivalent to marriage.

Two provisions of the criminal code remain on the books unrepealed: section 34, criminalising the abominable and detestable crime against nature, and section 35, covering any unnatural and lascivious act. Private consensual adult conduct has been outside their reach since the Supreme Judicial Court's 1974 decision in Commonwealth v. Balthazar, and the provisions are unenforceable as applied to such conduct. Repeal attempts repeatedly stalled in committee, including through the 2018 session that removed the abortion, adultery and fornication laws but left the sodomy, anal-sex and oral-sex provisions; the Senate passed repeal unanimously in January 2024, the House advanced it in June 2025, and a Senate committee scheduled it for floor consideration on 24 July 2025. Massachusetts is the only New England state, and one of two northern states, that still carries legislative criminalisation of same-sex conduct. A trans visitor in a relationship that local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status falls nominally within the statute's wording, though it is not enforced against private consensual conduct.

In a national legal-risk ranking published in July 2026, built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's-licence restrictions and removal of legal recognition, Massachusetts sits in the fifteen-state Most Protective tier.

66186276B2592965416524.name: New Mexico
66186276B2592965416524.summary:
New Mexico sits in the fifteen-state "Most Protective" tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking, compiled by applying a rubric to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the withdrawal of legal recognition. The ranking's authors describe the laws of this tier as having gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.

State law effective 1 July 2003 prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and union membership. The public-accommodations limb is the one a visitor interacts with directly: it covers restaurants, hotels, shops and other places serving the public. The 15-or-more-employees exemption was repealed effective 1 July 2019, and 2023 legislation explicitly extended coverage to local entities, counties, schools, universities and government-run agencies under an emergency clause; Albuquerque amended its Human Rights Ordinance in May 2024 to align.

Since 1 November 2019 transgender people may change legal gender without surgery. Legislation passed 26-13 in the House and 33-14 in the Senate and signed by Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham repealed the 1984 surgery requirement and provides male, female and X neutral designations on birth certificates, driver's licences and state IDs. An applicant submits a Request to Change Gender Designation on a Birth Certificate form with fees, with parental consent for minors, or a Request for Sex Designation Change form to the Motor Vehicles Division for licences and IDs. This replaced a prior requirement for a perjury statement from an institution or physician attesting surgical change plus a certified name-change order.

Since 1 July 2019 businesses and public facilities with single-occupancy restrooms must mark them gender-neutral and available to any person regardless of gender identity or sex, under legislation passed 54-12 in the House and 23-15 in the Senate and signed by the Governor. The state has no law prohibiting transgender girls' sports participation; eligibility is determined by birth certificate, original or amended, and the New Mexico Activities Association has issued no further guidance.

Gender-affirming care is protected rather than restricted. In March 2023 House Bill 7 codified protection for gender-affirming care and sex-reassignment surgery for adults on request without restrictions, including for interstate travellers, and is cited as establishing New Mexico as a refuge for transgender youths. The Movement Advancement Project's Transgender Healthcare Equality Map, data as of 27 September 2026, lists New Mexico as a state holding a shield law or 2023 executive order: the shield protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where the care is legal in New Mexico but banned in the patient's home state, which is directly relevant to a visitor travelling from a ban state. In 2026 the state health care authority announced use of state funds to maintain Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming care after a federal rule moved to exclude it.

Since 2003 New Mexico's hate-crime law has explicitly covered violence committed on the basis of actual or perceived gender identity. In February 2022 the Legislature passed omnibus crime bill HB68 repealing the common-law gay and trans panic defence, signed 9 March 2022. March 2019 school-bullying legislation protects students on the basis of gender identity and requires districts to adopt prohibition, reporting, investigation, disciplinary, prevention and staff-training policies, effective 1 July 2019.

Same-sex couples have had the same marriage rights as different-sex couples since the 19 December 2013 state Supreme Court ruling requiring equal marriage rights, making New Mexico the 17th state to recognise same-sex marriage; statutory codification passed 62-0 in the House and 39-0 in the Senate in March 2019 and took effect 1 July 2019. A trans visitor in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status therefore has that relationship recognised here.

Single persons, same-sex couples and second-parent adoptions are permitted with no prohibition, lesbian couples may access in vitro fertilization and donor insemination regardless of sexual orientation or marital status with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognized as legal parent, and no statute or case law prohibits gestational or traditional surrogacy which courts generally recognize. State law effective July 1, 2003 prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and union membership, supplemented by a 1985 executive order barring sexual-orientation discrimination in public employment, with enforcement upheld unanimously in Elane Photography v. Willock in 2013 for refusal to photograph a same-sex commitment ceremony. The common-law gay panic defence was repealed through omnibus crime bill HB68 passed in February 2022 and signed March 9, 2022 after unanimous Senate-only passages in 2019 and 2021 that died without House action. Historically the Navajo recognized four gender roles including nadleehi defined as a male-bodied person with a feminine nature, who due to perceived balance between sexes were typically chosen for certain societal and communal roles such as spiritual healers. They would traditionally wear female clothes and do female work, and some would have sexual relations with men which was accepted by the tribe, with similar recognized roles including Zuni lhamana and katsotse and equivalents among Mescalero Apache, Tiwa, Tewa and pueblos. As a result of colonization much of this cultural acceptance has disappeared, Navajo nadleehi became the subject of ridicule, and Christian converts among the Hopi were prohibited from attending the traditional snake dance because male cross-dressing could be observed. Will Roscoe is documented as writing about the "tolerance or even respect of transgender people" as fueling Spanish explorers' argument for colonization of native peoples and their lands in the name of Christianity. Today LGBTQ Navajo may find it difficult being accepted by family, with 70% of LGBT Navajo youth reportedly attempting suicide. Statewide polling showed 73% supported anti-discrimination legislation protecting LGBTQ people in 2018 and 64% supported a law covering sexual orientation and gender identity in 2017, while Santa Fe is cited as a gay capital and Albuquerque including its metropolitan area as a gay-friendly city.

66186276B43575054209436.summary:
New York sits in the fifteen-state "Most Protective" tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's-licence restrictions and withdrawal of legal recognition. The same ranking places the least protective states at the opposite end, with prison terms of up to five years for youth-care provision and arrest policies for gender-identity bathroom use.

Gender identity and expression have been protected statewide in credit, housing, employment, education and public accommodations since the Gender Expression Non-Discrimination Act was signed in January 2019 and took effect in February 2019, building on a 2009 executive order barring gender-identity discrimination in state employment and Division of Human Rights regulations issued 4 November 2015, effective 20 January 2016, covering transgender harassment and discrimination in those domains. A 2024 constitutional amendment explicitly bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity.

The Hate Crimes Act has covered gender identity and expression since 1 November 2019, with further anti-bias reform bills signed in November 2022. The gay and transgender panic defence was repealed in June 2019, effective immediately, making New York the sixth state to abolish it. Conversion therapy on minors has been banned effective 25 January 2019.

Since 2014 transgender adults could change the gender on birth certificates with a notarized medical affidavit verifying surgery or a gender dysphoria diagnosis; this was updated in 2020 to allow self-affirmation, with parental consent required for those under 17. The June 2021 Gender Recognition Act allowed an X marker on driver's licences and eased sealing of name- and gender-change records. An X marker on New York City birth certificates took effect 1 January 2019 and on death certificates from 2 January 2020; X was reported for state court and jury documents in November 2019 and in healthcare data from August 2020; X on all state forms was approved in April 2022 for 2023, with some organizations until 2024, alongside updatable marriage certificates. A November 2021 law effective 1 January 2022 requires utilities and municipalities to use preferred names and pronouns.

Shield protections apply. The MAP Transgender Healthcare Equality Map, data as of 27 September 2026, lists New York as a state with a shield law or executive order from 2023: the shield protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care legal in New York was banned in their home state, which is directly relevant to visitors travelling from ban states. Nationally, 16 states and the District of Columbia, covering 38% of the trans population aged 13 and over, hold shields, while 32 states and five territories, covering 56%, hold none. New York City issued an executive order on 12 June 2023 barring city resources from being used to detain, prosecute or investigate the provision or receipt of gender-affirming care. A state law of 25 June 2023, making New York the twelfth shield state, bars courts from enforcing out-of-state laws removing custody over youth gender-affirming care, bars treating such care as child abuse, and bars law-enforcement cooperation with out-of-state agencies. A September 2023 Ithaca ordinance and April 2025 City Council bills expanded provider protections.

Former Penal Law Section 240.37, in effect since 1976 and used by police to harass and arrest transgender individuals, was repealed in February 2021, effective immediately. Gender-neutral bathrooms were mandated by a law signed in December 2020, effective 23 March 2021. The anti-bullying law covers gender, including gender identity and expression, including cyberbullying, in all public elementary and secondary schools, with a 2019 loophole closure. A June 2023 law explicitly includes gender identity in drug treatment and addiction programmes, and a November 2020 law requires annual judiciary statistics by gender identity.

Nassau County remains the only county in New York banning transgender athletes from women's sports on county-run facilities, with a 2025 ruling finding no clear violation of anti-discrimination laws and an NYCLU lawsuit seeking inclusion.

Same-sex marriage became legal statewide under the Marriage Equality Act, passed 24 June 2011 and effective 24 July 2011, following a May 2008 directive recognizing out-of-jurisdiction marriages. Consenting adult same-sex sexual activity was legalized by New York v. Onofre in 1980, with defunct sodomy provisions affecting National Guard employees repealed effective 2000. A 2019 law granted state veterans benefits to those dishonorably discharged under Don't Ask, Don't Tell from 1993 to 2011.

On 16 December 2009 New York barred state agencies from discriminating on the basis of gender identity in all state-employment matters including hiring, termination, retention, appointment, promotion, tenure, recruitment and compensation, defining gender identity as having or being perceived as having a gender identity, self-image, appearance, behavior or expression whether or not different from sex assigned at birth, and ordered equal-opportunity efforts, consistent guidelines and swift confidential complaint investigations, effective immediately.

66186276B97229519707655.name: Oregon
66186276B97229519707655.summary:
Oregon sits in the fifteen-jurisdiction "Most Protective" tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking compiled from a rubric covering thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, among them youth care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's licence restrictions, and measures removing legal recognition. The rubric describes the laws in this tier as having gone beyond baseline safeguarding of trans rights.

Statewide anti-discrimination law covers the settings a visitor uses daily. The Oregon Equality Act, signed 9 May 2007 as Senate Bill 2 and in force since 1 January 2008, prohibits discrimination in employment, housing, public accommodation, public education and public services on the ground of gender identity. Sexual orientation is defined to include gender identity regardless of whether a person's identity, appearance, expression or behaviour differs from what is traditionally associated with sex assigned at birth. The protections apply uniformly across the state and do not depend on the locality; religious employers, organisations and institutions are exempt.

Bias-motivated violence carries enhanced penalties: state hate-crime statutes add punishment for crimes committed because of the victim's gender identity. SB704, passed and signed in May 2021 and effective 1 January 2022, abolishes the gay panic and trans panic defences in murder, manslaughter and hate-crime cases.

Identity documents are comparatively accessible. The driver-licensing agency has offered an X marker for neutral or non-binary identity on licences and state IDs since 1 July 2017, and X is also available on birth certificates. Sex reassignment surgery has not been required to change the gender marker on a birth certificate by request since 2014. Legislation in May 2017 abolished the 1991 requirement that transgender people publish their names in newspapers before a legal change of sex. A circuit court ruling on 10 June 2016 allowed a resident to change gender to non-binary, which the Transgender Law Center believed was the first ruling of its kind in the country. An October 2019 executive order added gender identity to a 1987 policy barring state agencies from unlawful discrimination and required a third gender option X; legislation signed in June 2021 updated the 2008 definition of gender identity.

Care is shielded for people arriving from states that have banned it. Oregon's shield law, signed by Governor Tina Kotek on 13 July 2023, protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges or investigation when care that is legal in Oregon was prohibited in the patient's home state. The House passed the bill in May 2023; the Senate passed a version with amendments after a Republican boycott.

Partner recognition does not turn on the parties' birth sex. Federal district judge Michael McShane struck down the 2004 constitutional amendment banning marriage for same-sex couples on 19 May 2014, marriages of same-sex couples performed elsewhere have been recognised since 16 October 2013, and gender-neutral marriage was codified effective 1 January 2016. Domestic partnerships have been available since 4 February 2008.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Oregon (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since January 1, 2008 Oregon has banned unfair discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations based on gender identity under the Oregon Equality Act signed May 9, 2007, where sexual orientation is defined to include gender identity regardless of whether identity, appearance, expression or behavior differs from that traditionally associated with assigned sex at birth, with an October 2019 executive order adding gender identity to a 1987 policy prohibiting state agencies from unlawful discrimination and requiring a third gender option X, and June 2021 legislation updating the 2008 definition of gender identity signed effective immediately. State hate crime statutes provide additional penalties for crimes committed based on the victim's gender identity, and SB704 passed and signed in May 2021 effective January 1, 2022 abolishes the gay panic and trans panic defenses in murder, manslaughter and hate crime cases. Since 2014 sex reassignment surgery has not been a requirement to change the gender marker on a birth certificate solely by request, a June 10, 2016 circuit court ruled a resident could legally change gender to non-binary in what the Transgender Law Center believed was the first ruling of its kind in the U.S., and since July 1, 2017 the Department of Motor Vehicles has offered X designating neutral or non-binary identity on licenses and IDs with X also available for birth certificates, while May 2017 legislation abolished the 1991 requirement for transgender people to publish names in newspapers before legal change of sex. In January 2013 as part of a discrimination settlement the state agreed to provide full medical insurance coverage for gender-affirming surgeries, drugs and related treatments for individuals on public employee health plans, and in August 2014 officials announced Medicaid would shortly begin covering gender-affirming hormone therapy and other gender-affirming healthcare. In May 2023 amid national backlash the House passed a bill to protect and defend gender-affirming healthcare especially for those entering Oregon from other states, frozen then passed in the Senate with watered-down amendments after a Republican boycott, signed July 13, 2023 by Governor Tina Kotek. A transgender-inclusive public schools policy survived challenge after the District Court ruled against plaintiffs July 24, 2018, the Ninth Circuit upheld February 12, 2020, and the Supreme Court denied certiorari in December 2020 in Parents for Privacy v. Barr, while April 2019 legislation signed May 6 amended a 1951 mental health law that equated transvestites with pedophilia after 58-2 House and 29-0 Senate votes. In July 2025 the 9th Circuit ruled the State adoption requirement to respect, accept and support a child's gender expression and sexual orientation was unconstitutional after the Department of Human Services prevented a woman seeking to adopt, and in June 2025 the U.S. Department of Education announced a Title IX investigation into the Oregon Department of Education for allowing transgender women to compete in women's sports. Oregon decriminalized same-sex sexual activity in 1972 after the 1971 repeal of the consensual sodomy law with an age of consent of 18, and a controversial lewd solicitation provision making it criminal to invite a person in a public place to have sexual intercourse was declared unconstitutional on free speech grounds in a unanimous 1981 Oregon Supreme Court decision. Same-sex marriage was legalized May 19, 2014 after Judge Michael McShane ruled the 2004 constitutional amendment banning such marriages via Ballot Measure 36 unconstitutional under the Equal Protection Clause, with same-sex marriages from other jurisdictions recognized since October 16, 2013 per Department of Justice opinion and gender-neutral marriage codified effective January 1, 2016, while domestic partnerships have been available since February 4, 2008 under the Family Fairness Act and benefits to same-sex partners of state employees have been provided since 1998. Since January 1, 2008 Oregon has banned unfair discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations based on sexual orientation under the Equality Act signed May 9, 2007, and the anti-bullying law prohibits bullying including cyberbullying and harassment on the basis of sexual orientation among other categories in all public schools. State hate crime statutes provide additional penalties for crimes based on the victim's sexual orientation, and SB704 passed and signed in May 2021 effective January 1, 2022 abolishes the gay panic defense in murder, manslaughter and hate crime cases. Oregon became the third state to ban conversion therapy on minors after House 41-18 on March 17, 2015 and Senate 21-8 on May 7, 2015 votes, signed May 18, 2015 by Governor Kate Brown effective July 1, 2015. Same-sex couples whether unmarried or married may apply to adopt and lesbian couples have access to assisted reproduction such as in vitro fertilization with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognized as legal parent if married, while surrogacy is neither expressly prohibited nor permitted but courts are generally favorable including for same-sex couples.

66186276B98073251815399.name: Rhode Island
66186276B98073251815399.summary:
A July 2026 anti-trans legal risk assessment map lists Rhode Island among its 'Most Protective' states for gender-identity nondiscrimination. The same map reports erosion at the federal layer and concludes that its top tier can no longer be considered most protective nationwide, so the ranking describes Rhode Island's own statute rather than conditions a visitor will meet at every point of the journey.

Discrimination based on gender identity or expression has been unlawful in Rhode Island since 2001 in employment, credit, housing and public accommodations under R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 28-5-3, 28-5-7, 34-37-4, 34-37-4.3 and 11-24-2. A bill signed in June 2023 added explicit bans covering patient care, nursing and related healthcare, and the long-standing housing exemption for dwellings with three occupants or fewer was repealed with effect from 1 January 2023.

Rhode Island hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by the victim's actual or perceived gender identity or expression, with the gender-identity coverage placed in statute at R.I. Gen. Laws § 42-28-46. The gay and trans panic defense was repealed in June 2018 by votes of 68-2 in the House and 27-0 in the Senate, signed by Governor Gina Raimondo the following month and effective immediately.

Identity documents are changeable on a self-declaration-plus-clinical-confirmation basis rather than a surgical one. Since 23 October 2014 a birth certificate gender change has required a Birth Certificate Request Form together with an affidavit from a physician, certified nurse practitioner or physician's assistant confirming transgender status, replacing the earlier sex reassignment surgery requirement. The Division of Motor Vehicles issues a corrected driver's licence on a Gender Designation Form signed by the applicant. A third gender marker, X, was announced for driver's licences and birth certificates in August 2019 with availability from July 2020, and a June 2018 law requires transgender people to be recorded correctly on death certificates.

Single-occupancy toilets may be designated gender-neutral with effect from 1 January 2022 under a bill signed in July 2021. Rhode Island also appears on the transgender healthcare equality map among jurisdictions covered by shield laws or executive orders from the 2023 and 2024 batches, which are drafted to make those protections enforceable against out-of-state action.

In March 2025 the Rhode Island Interscholastic League revised its transgender athletes policy. Transgender athletes remain able to compete, but member schools now carry responsibility for ensuring compliance with all applicable state and federal law when they determine gender-based eligibility, replacing the prior rule that allowed participation consistent with gender identity.

66186276B17406925856308.name: Vermont
66186276B17406925856308.summary:
As of July 2026 Vermont is listed among the most protective states on gender-identity nondiscrimination. State law bans discrimination based on gender identity in employment, public accommodations, education, housing, credit, insurance and union practices. The provision was added after a 2006 veto, passed again in 2007, was signed by Governor Jim Douglas on 22 May 2007 and took effect on 1 July 2007. For a visitor the public-accommodations coverage is the operative part: hotels, restaurants, shops and service providers fall under it.

Hate-crime law provides additional penalties for an offence committed because of the victim's gender identity, added in 1999 to a 1990 statute that originally covered sexual orientation. The gay and trans panic defence was abolished and repealed by legislation that passed the House 144-1 in March 2021 and the Senate 29-0 in April 2021, was signed by Governor Phil Scott on 5 May 2021 and took effect on 1 July 2021.

Single-user public bathrooms have had to be marked gender-neutral since 1 July 2018, under a bill signed in May 2018.

Vermont's shield laws, enacted in 2023 and 2024, are enforceable against out-of-state action and place the state among those protecting transgender and non-binary people who travel in for gender-affirming healthcare; the 2023 measure took effect immediately by emergency clause.

Partner recognition is settled. Civil unions were introduced in July 2000 as the first state status identical to marriage, following a 1999 Vermont Supreme Court ruling on equal marriage benefits, and marriage for same-sex couples has been legal since 1 September 2009, the first state to adopt it through the legislature and governor rather than a court decision.

Proposal 4, approved by voters on 3 November 2026 with 79% support, prohibits the denial of rights to an individual based on race, ethnicity, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, or national origin.

Hate crime law provides additional penalties for a crime committed based on the victim's gender identity, added in 1999 to the 1990 law that originally covered sexual orientation. The gay and/or trans panic defence was abolished and repealed by legislation passed 144-1 in the House in March 2021 and 29-0 in the Senate in April 2021, signed May 5, 2021 by Governor Phil Scott and effective July 1. Texas. Vermont law permits single LGBT individuals and same-sex couples to petition to adopt, provides lesbian couples access to in vitro fertilization with recognition of the non-genetic, non-gestational mother as legal parent to a child born via donor insemination irrespective of marital status, and in June 1993 the Vermont Supreme Court ruled in favor of a lesbian seeking to adopt her partner's two biological sons. Discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, public accommodations, education, housing, credit, insurance and union practices was banned with protections added in 1992, with the anti-bullying law also prohibiting bullying including cyberbullying and harassment based on sexual orientation in all educational institutions. Hate crime legislation enacted in 1990 including sexual orientation provides additional penalties for a crime committed based on the victim's sexual orientation. Use of conversion therapy on LGBT minors was banned by a bill approved unanimously in the Senate March 17, 2016, approved with amendments in the House April 26, accepted by the Senate April 29, signed May 25 by Governor Peter Shumlin and effective July 1, 2016, and the gay panic defence was abolished and repealed by the 2021 bill passed 144-1 and 29-0 and signed May 5, 2021 effective July 1.

Washington operates under the United States framework on passports, entry screening, federal facilities and federal custody, which are set nationally. State law and state institutions govern health care, insurance, the state prison system and state ballot measures.

A July 2026 legal-risk assessment of United States anti-trans measures places Washington among the most protective states in the country. The same assessment flags two Washington ballot initiatives, I-001 and I-638, due for a November vote, as targeting transgender residents; whether they pass decides whether that protective posture holds.

Washington has shield laws or executive orders from the 2023 and 2024 batches that are enforceable against out-of-state action, and a nationwide tracker of such measures lists the state among those covered. For a trans visitor who travels to Washington for gender-affirming care, these measures bear on whether another state's action can reach care provided in Washington.

Washington state prisons have been legally required since October 2023, under court order and rulings, to provide gender-affirming healthcare and, where indicated, sex-reassignment surgery to inmates. In July 2024 a transgender woman prisoner was transferred out of a women's prison back to a men's prison as punishment for consensual sex with a cisgender inmate of the women's prison, so housing assigned by birth sex functioned as the disciplinary sanction.

Initiative 638, approved by voters on 3 November 2026 with 56% support, requires school and voluntary nonprofit athletics to prohibit biologically male students from competing with and against biologically female students.

sources.summary: Prison section: in October 2023, Washington state prisons (under court order and rulings) were legally required to provide gender-affirming healthcare and/or sexual-reassignment surgery to inmates; in July 2024, a trans woman prisoner was transferred from a women's prison back to a men's prison as punishment for consensual sex with a cisgender inmate of the women's prison. Placement outcome documented: birth-sex (men's) housing used as sanction in 2024.

Ballotpedia list of Washington ballot measures. Records Initiative 638, approved 3 November 2026 with 56% support, requiring school and voluntary nonprofit athletics to prohibit biologically male students from competing with and against biologically female students. The October dossier already flagged this initiative as pending a November vote; the result is new.

66186276B98555229882405.blindSummary:
This division operates under this country's framework on passports, entry screening, federal facilities and federal custody, which are set nationally. Division law and division institutions govern health care, insurance, the division's prison system and ballot measures.

A July 2026 legal-risk assessment of this country's anti-trans measures places this division among the most protective divisions in the country. The same assessment flags two ballot initiatives due for a November vote, one designated I-001 and the other I-638 in the source material, as targeting transgender residents; whether they pass decides whether that protective posture holds.

This division has shield laws or executive orders from the 2023 and 2024 batches that are enforceable against action originating in another division, and a nationwide tracker of such measures lists this division among those covered. For a trans visitor who travels to this division for gender-affirming care, these measures bear on whether another division's action can reach care provided here.

Correctional practice in this division carries a documented reversal. Prisons in this division have been legally required since October 2023, under court order and rulings, to provide gender-affirming healthcare and, where indicated, sex-reassignment surgery to inmates. In July 2024 a transgender woman prisoner was transferred out of a women's prison back to a men's prison as punishment for consensual sex with a cisgender inmate of the women's prison, so housing assigned by birth sex functioned as the disciplinary sanction.

The second of those two initiatives, approved by voters on 3 November 2026 with 56% support, requires school and voluntary nonprofit athletics to prohibit biologically male students from competing with and against biologically female students.
66186276B98555229882405.localsOnly:
State law requires health insurance to cover facial hair removal and an expanded range of gender-affirming procedures, a coverage set the July 2026 assessment identifies in only four states. Residents receive that coverage regardless of where the care is sought under the shield measures.

Washington extends refugee protections to people leaving states with hostile regimes, as recorded in the same assessment.

12653393B40111500734429.name: Kandahar
12653393B40111500734429.summary: Kandahar is subject to Afghanistan's national regime in full, with no local exception. It is the Taliban movement's historic and spiritual heartland: the supreme leader and senior clerical establishment are based here, and the Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice has an unusually strong local presence. The city's Ghazi Stadium carries a record of staged public punishments, and public flogging for moral offences remains prominent. Morality officers and checkpoints are pervasive, giving a visitor frequent opportunities for scrutiny, while deep Pashtun-conservative social policing and strict gender segregation mean local hostility reinforces the official moral framework rather than softening it; local tribal and clerical authority strengthens the national system. There is minimal foreign-visitor infrastructure, no meaningful tourism, and no known civil-society, NGO, diplomatic or consular presence able to intervene for a foreigner — the few foreigners present are conspicuous, and suspicion of foreigners runs high amid insecurity and an ISIS-K presence that also targets perceived moral deviants. Discovery of a transgender visitor would foreseeably mean detention by Taliban security or morality officials, document checks, abuse in custody, referral to moral courts and public corporal punishment, with no local protection, sanctuary or remedy documented. Conditions here operate at least as strictly as the national picture, with less discretion and fewer mitigating channels than in Kabul; nothing distinguishes the region favourably.

12653393B56617740339660.name: Zabul
12653393B56617740339660.summary: Zabul is subject to Afghanistan's Taliban national regime in full, with no local exception of its own. Zabul is a remote, predominantly Pashtun, rural province in southern Afghanistan and a historic Taliban heartland — among the most conservative in the country. Virtue-and-vice enforcement operates at street level here, and conservative social norms reinforce family and community reporting, so an outsider who stands out attracts attention quickly. There is no tourist or foreign-facing economy, little urban anonymity, and no NGO shelter, civil-society or protective infrastructure; suspected moral offences are handled through local Taliban and community channels rather than any impartial process, and rule-of-law recourse is minimal. A visitor discovered as transgender would therefore face exposure with less recourse than in provincial capitals. No Zabul-specific trans-visitor incident or distinct local policy has been documented, and the precise likelihood of detention or lethal harm after discovery remains uncertain — the absence of a recorded local case should not be read as evidence of safety.

12653393B46006342616872.name: Uruzgan
12653393B46006342616872.summary: The region is subject to Afghanistan's Taliban national regime in full, with no local exception. Uruzgan is a remote, predominantly rural and Pashtun tribal province administered from Tarin Kowt, with almost no foreign presence, tourism infrastructure, or independent institutions — few hospitals, no advocacy organisations, no independent courts, and no media able to report or intervene. Local conditions make scrutiny far harder to escape than in larger cities: small communities offer little anonymity, a trans visitor is conspicuous on sight, and social conservatism shaped by Pashtunwali alongside Taliban authority means enforcement discretion sits with local Taliban commanders and tribal elders, with family, community and militia structures more likely to participate than to protect. Corporal punishment for moral offences is treated locally as a live practice. There are no known local safeguards, complaint mechanisms, consular access, or protective facilities for a trans visitor discovered here, and no documented local tolerance or exception. Region-specific case records for Uruzgan are sparse, so the lack of reported incidents should be read as uncertainty rather than safety; neither a local protective arrangement nor an inevitable worst-case outcome is established for the province.

12653393B78791504725813.name: Daykundi
12653393B78791504725813.summary: Daykundi is subject to Afghanistan's national Taliban regime in full, with no documented local exception. Daykundi is a remote, mountainous and largely rural province in the central highlands, overwhelmingly Hazara and Shia, where Taliban authorities hold administrative and security control. It sees very few foreign visitors: tourism infrastructure is minimal, hotels are scarce, medical services are limited, and there is little NGO or consular presence, with long distances to Kabul. A foreign trans visitor would be conspicuous in small towns and on checkpointed roads, so discovery would likely be quick and unmediated by any local advocate or timely consular or medical support; police, courts and community authority function as the enforcement mechanism rather than a remedy. Moral enforcement appears somewhat less systematically patrolled than in Kabul because of remoteness and reliance on local elders, but this does not reduce exposure: Taliban vice-and-virtue administration and the document regime operate as they do nationally, while small, conservative communities with strong family and honor-based norms intensify communal scrutiny, leaving little privacy and few escape options. Neither remoteness nor the province's comparatively low armed violence and lack of a record of intensified morality sweeps softens a state-directed moral-enforcement regime. No safe zone, tolerant enforcement tradition, protective institution or community infrastructure for gender-diverse visitors is documented, and the province has no visible trans community or independent legal help. The absence of recorded local incidents reflects absent documentation and monitoring rather than safety, and no distinct protection is documented for minors or travelling families.

12653393B29313712249365.name: Ghanzi
12653393B29313712249365.summary: Ghanzi is subject to Afghanistan's national Taliban regime in full, with no local exception. It is a remote, sparsely populated rural area with a strongly conservative Pashtun and Baloch tribal society, a largely desert character, and essentially no tourism or visitor-facing infrastructure — so there is no documented lighter enforcement, tourist-facing tolerance, or protective local practice distinguishing it from the national picture. Practically, this means anonymity is unavailable: a visibly gender-nonconforming or openly trans visitor would stand out sharply, and there is no trans or LGBT support infrastructure, community contact, or outside-observer presence of the kind that marginally shields people in larger cities. Distance from embassies and aid organisations, together with the absence of independent institutions, means discovery would leave no realistic consular or legal remedy. Disputes are settled through Taliban officials and tribal structures rather than formal courts, and rural isolation removes even the thin cover that contact with outsiders might otherwise provide. No reliable province-specific evidence establishes how often trans people are targeted here, and no local safeguard — including for a travelling minor accompanied by a parent or guardian — is documented against outing, scrutiny or coercion.

12653393B93572570471663.name: Paktika
12653393B93572570471663.summary: Paktika is subject to Afghanistan's national Taliban legal framework in full, with no local exception. The province lies in the country's southeast on the Pakistan border: rural, overwhelmingly Pashtun and tribal, a Taliban heartland that has been under the movement's administration since 2021, with negligible tourism or foreign-facing infrastructure. Moral enforcement is carried out locally by Taliban morality committees alongside tribal elders and community authority rather than through courts, reinforced by identity checks, security checkpoints, gender-segregated social norms and informal policing of honour norms. There is little anonymising urban space outside small towns such as Sharana, so a foreign visitor is conspicuous by definition and any discovery would be immediate and highly local. Custody would be by birth sex in a province where detainee abuse and public corporal punishment are documented nationally, and there is no functioning police or judicial remedy, no trans community or advocacy infrastructure, and no local protective or oversight institution; medical, consular and advocacy resources available in Kabul would require travel there. Visible gender nonconformity invites family and community violence with little or no external scrutiny, and no region-specific mitigation is known. Specific Paktika case records are sparse, and that absence is not evidence of safety.

12653393B66876919073955.name: Khost
12653393B66876919073955.summary: Khost is subject to Afghanistan's Taliban national law in full, with no local exception, and no tolerance zone or protective recourse is known to exist here. Khost is a remote, socially conservative Pashtun province on the Pakistan border in the country's southeast, with limited international presence and little infrastructure for a foreign visitor to seek help, leave quickly or report abuse. Authority is associated with Haqqani-network-linked governance, historically known for strict moral policing, while rigid gender segregation and tribal Pashtunwali norms leave little space for visible gender nonconformity and informal tribal justice operates alongside the security forces. International monitoring and media attention concentrate on Kabul, so provincial oversight and consular visibility are thinner than in the capital. Discovery routes are unusually dense: Pakistan-facing border passes and checkpoints add routine document scrutiny, and hotel registration and tribal gossip in a small, tightly networked province mean exposure can come from many directions. A visibly gender-nonconforming visitor, or one whose documents are questioned, would depend on local discretion at every stage; family and community exposure is a serious additional risk, and detention conditions are unlikely to be safe. No visible LGBT or protective community infrastructure exists in the province. No specific recent trans-targeting incidents in Khost are established in the available evidence, but that gap does not indicate safety — local conditions suggest enforcement at least as harsh as, and likely harsher than, the national picture, with less institutional restraint.

12653393B16859990709200.name: Paktia
12653393B16859990709200.summary: Paktia is subject to Afghanistan's Taliban national regime in full, with no local exception. The province in eastern Afghanistan, with Gardez as its capital, is overwhelmingly rural and Pashtun-majority tribal, under direct Taliban administration with a strong Haqqani network presence, and has essentially no tourist economy, advocacy networks or international presence of the kind that might marginally moderate enforcement in Kabul. Anonymity is scarce for a trans visitor anywhere in the country and scarcer here: tight kinship networks, pervasive community and religious surveillance and the absence of urban anonymity mean a visibly foreign or gender-nonconforming person cannot move unnoticed. Discovery can run through borders, lodging, medical care, police stops and contact with local families, with tribal honor dynamics and local morality officers reinforcing one another. There is no functioning court, police complaint or consular channel to turn to, no visible LGBT community infrastructure or legal-aid presence, and community and family offer no reliable protection; detention is by birth sex in Taliban custody, and exit would be remote and slow. No region-specific record documents how transgender visitors are specifically treated in Paktia, but that silence reflects absent research rather than safety, and the province's structural conditions sit at the harsher end of the national picture.

12653393B769191277822.name: Logar
12653393B769191277822.summary: Logar is subject to Afghanistan's national Taliban regime in full, with no local exception. The province is largely rural and heavily conservative, with a Pashtun-majority population, a strong Taliban administrative presence and an active vice-and-virtue enforcement footprint, lying a short distance south of Kabul. There is no tourist economy, no visible queer community or NGO infrastructure, and no urban anonymity to fall back on: foreign visitors are rare, movement passes through checkpoints and small, close-knit village and district networks, and a stranger whose presentation diverges from gender norms attracts immediate community and informal-enforcement attention. Discovery through documents, family contacts or daily interaction is highly plausible, and once found out a visitor would almost certainly become known locally, amid near-total absence of independent oversight and the added threat of family or community hostility. No local protective exception, tolerance or tourism-facing accommodation is known, and nothing in the province mitigates the inherited regime. Local records do not establish a Logar-specific rate or enforcement pattern distinct from the national picture, so how much harsher conditions are than the national average remains uncertain — but the province's isolation, tight social networks and conservative vigilance leave a trans visitor essentially no anonymity and no local recourse.

12653393B94990201402617.name: Wardak
12653393B94990201402617.summary: Wardak lies wholly within Afghanistan's Taliban national regime in full, with no local exception. Maidan Wardak is a rural, socially conservative province on Kabul's south-west approaches, historically a Taliban stronghold with strong Pashtun communities and a heavy clerical and militant presence. It has no international tourist infrastructure, no protected venue, and none of the anonymity a large city affords — smaller communities mean discovery would most likely come through family, neighbours, tribal elders, mosques, road checkpoints and local morality networks rather than any formal process. The province's authorities are themselves the enforcing body, and police and courts offer no independent recourse. No shelter arrangement, advocacy organisation, protective institution or accepting space for gender-nonconforming visitors is documented in Wardak, and past instability and active militant policing make evasion harder than in larger urban areas. Reporting from the province is sparse: there are no documented trans-specific local enforcement campaigns, but the absence of local incident reports does not establish safety, and no local mitigation is known. Conditions are understood to be at least as severe as the national picture, with less cover than Kabul, and family and community honour-based pressure compounding whatever risk the state apparatus itself carries.

12653393B60423242182357.name: Kabul
12653393B60423242182357.summary: Kabul is subject to Afghanistan's national regime in full, with no local exception. As the capital and the seat of Taliban central administration, including the ministry responsible for public morality, the city concentrates checkpoint presence, document and identity checks, and surveillance of public conduct, making enforcement there more visible and more immediately centralised than in remote districts; cases are routed through central courts and custody facilities, and neither foreigner status nor presence in the embassy district offers documented protection once discovery occurs. Urban density gives some anonymity compared with rural areas, but that anonymity does not survive being outed, and no Kabul-specific safeguard, tolerant enclave or effective avenue of complaint is documented for a trans visitor. The departure since 2021 of the foreign presence, aid organisations and informal safe venues removed the cover that once made the city easier to navigate; reports have described LGBT Afghans hiding in Kabul and street attacks on men read as gay. A stranger whose documents or presentation diverge from expectations is conspicuous in a heavily regulated public space. Reports documenting serious consequences for LGBT Afghans in the city do not establish how often foreign visitors are affected, but they give no reliable basis to expect protection or consular access. Local conditions concentrate the national picture rather than soften it.

The region is subject to Afghanistan's Taliban national regime in full, with no local exception. Local conditions intensify that inherited exposure rather than soften it. Taliban authority is present but thinly institutionalised: disputes are worked out through tribal and clerical channels rather than courts, and there is no independent advocacy infrastructure, legal aid or realistic consular reach in the province. The Zaranj border crossing and the checkpoints along major land routes mean identity documents and personal presentation come under close inspection, limiting anonymity for a visitor whose gender expression draws attention. In a small, honour-sensitive border community, visible gender nonconformity is unlikely to be tolerated or quietly mediated, and word of a discovery can travel through family and tribal networks as well as officials. The province has little tourist or service infrastructure, and its isolation means a visitor who is outed would find no reliable police recourse or protective services locally; port or trade anonymity does not extend to official encounters.

Almost no foreign visitors, diplomatic presence, international organizations or independent civil society operate here, and there is no legal aid, affirming healthcare or community network to turn to; local Taliban networks, tribal codes and active religious enforcement can intensify the consequences for a trans visitor who is discovered or outed, including forced outing to family or neighbours. The provincial capital Lashkar Gah is more urban and somewhat more visible, but that brings little practical protection. No Helmand-specific pattern of treatment of trans visitors has been documented, so nothing in the record distinguishes the province as safer than the country overall; that silence reflects the near-total absence of observers rather than any tolerance, and should not be read as reassurance. Small, close-knit communities, mountainous isolation, scarce transport and border checkpoints make being noticed and reported more likely, and local officials and residents are unlikely to separate foreign status from a moral offence. Discovery would leave no reliable recourse — no independent police, courts or trusted local help — and no documented local mitigation of the national consequences. 26408823B93569072225888.name: Cunene

The province is far from Luanda-based LGBTQI+ advocacy and legal support, and there are no local trans organisations, campaigns, or gender-aware health and support services recorded; health facilities around Ondjiva are limited. Police and courts are distant and under-resourced, and formal complaint and legal-aid channels reach the province more weakly than in the capital, so whatever protection national law offers is difficult to invoke in practice here. Social unfamiliarity with gender nonconformity means discovery would likely bring intense community scrutiny, possible refusal of lodging or services, and forced disclosure to officials; friction may escalate without institutional correction, and arbitrary questioning or extortion at checkpoints and border crossings is plausible. Document checks at the Namibia crossings and the reduced anonymity of a small, rural population compound exposure. No documented local pattern of violence, organised hostility, or official targeting of trans visitors is known — the main exposure is social conservatism plus thin recourse rather than state threat — but absence of documented incidents should not be read as safety, and there is no local evidence distinguishing enforcement of trans visitors' treatment from the national picture.

Consequences are more likely to be social suspicion and gossip, service refusal, intrusive questioning, delayed recourse, and bribery or extortion by undertrained officials, with police harassment more plausible than in Luanda; detention would carry birth-sex custody risk and health facilities are limited, while police accountability is weak. Document mismatch, service denial and harassment are possible, and the province's remoteness and thinner institutional capacity leave less practical recourse than in the capital, with reliance on family, employer and community gatekeeping making discovery less safely handled. There are no concentrated LGBTQ venues, no local trans community or advocacy group, and no safe venue in the province; the nearest organised support and specialist legal help are in Yerevan, several steps away. If a trans visitor is harassed or denied help, practical options are correspondingly thinner than in Yerevan, and any complaint would run through provincial police, whose response has been reported as uneven outside the capital. No distinct local policy, no local protective machinery, and no documented pattern of targeting transgender visitors in Aragatsotn is known; that gap in reporting should not be read as evidence of safety. Entry clearance is essentially the only official encounter: paperwork is checked by visiting officials with no local registry, police post or court on the island to consult. Any dispute, complaint or medical emergency means leaving the island, with handling and recourse depending entirely on Antiguan authorities reached at a distance; emergency care requires evacuation to Antigua. The lack of a resident community also means there is no local social picture to read — no documented record of tolerance or hostility exists in either direction, and an empty island should not be read as acceptance. Practical exposure for a trans visitor therefore sits almost wholly at the entry-and-evacuation layer, where national conditions apply without any local institution to soften or sharpen them.

Paro's tourism-facing economy means hospitality, transport and airport staff handle foreign documents daily and are accustomed to foreign guests, which softens routine dealings compared with more remote districts. Most visitors move through licensed, guided itineraries, giving some hospitality oversight while limiting independent contact with local residents. Paro town is small, socially conservative and generally considered more conservative than Thimphu, so a visitor who is outed has little anonymity, and no trans-specific support organisation or drop-in resource is identifiable in the district. Healthcare and security responses here remain national in character. No district-specific protection, local ordinance, court practice or policing pattern distinguishing Paro from the national record was documented; that lack of local evidence should not be read as evidence of safety. Tourism infrastructure does not itself provide a remedy if a visitor is outed or mistreated, and no local safeguard attaches to airport, hotel or guide encounters.

The consequences are therefore mainly social and practical rather than criminal, with weak recourse: no trans-specific service, oversight body or local protective practice is recorded. Proximity to Gaborone is the district's main practical advantage: legal, medical and advocacy services, and relatively more tolerant urban norms, are a short journey away, while day-to-day recourse inside Kgatleng generally means travelling to the capital. In villages and traditional-community settings, privacy is thinner than in a large city, so discretion about accommodation, relationships and document details remains sensible. Ordinary bureaucratic friction and inconsistent official understanding are the likeliest local difficulties rather than state targeting.

Tourism-facing lodges and their staff are regularly in contact with foreign guests and are generally used to international visitors. Local conditions are less supportive than the national picture. Social attitudes are conservative, with a strong rural churchgoing culture, and in small settlements a visibly gender-nonconforming or outed visitor can expect immediate curiosity and gossip. Trans-specific community infrastructure and legal aid do not exist locally — advocacy and support organisations are based in Gaborone. Police stations, courts and health facilities are few, spread over vast distances and have limited familiarity with gender-identity cases, so document checks, emergencies, medication continuity, complaints and remedies may be handled slowly, or with insensitivity, compared with the capital. Rural scrutiny and thin services leave somewhat less margin for a trans visitor than in Gaborone, though the more likely difficulties are questioning, misgendering or inconsistent service than any state threat. No Ghanzi-specific record documents anti-trans violence, police targeting, facility exclusion or discriminatory incidents, and none documents local protections beyond the national framework either.

27767025B11866847137657.name: Centre
27767025B11866847137657.summary: The Centre Region is Cameroon's political capital: Yaoundé houses the presidency, the courts, the gendarmerie and police high commands, and a dense network of checkpoints and identity controls. A visibly gender-nonconforming visitor moving through the capital meets a heavier concentration of official scrutiny than in other regions — routine document checks, stops and questioning, and a greater chance that appearance alone draws attention from security personnel. Social attitudes in the city are conservative and official-facing, and state-controlled media are concentrated here, so exposure carries a real risk of public outing. The region is subject to Cameroon's national law in full, with no local exception. Documented appearance-based prosecutions have run through Yaoundé's courts, including a 2011 case of people jailed for wearing women's clothing and the case of Jean-Claude Roger Mbede, whose sentencing proceeded through Kondengui Central Prison in the capital; an appeals court here has overturned a comparable appearance-based conviction, so appeal is possible though not dependable. Custody after an arrest in the capital would most likely be at Kondengui, where conditions for detainees held on such grounds are described as harsh. Yaoundé's large diplomatic, expatriate and NGO presence and its urban anonymity offer some practical cover and modestly better access to consular and legal contact than elsewhere in the country, but they do not shield a visitor from state scrutiny once noticed, and no local protective measure, tolerance or enforcement exception is known here.

27767025B65184844379073.name: Far North
27767025B65184844379073.summary: The Far North is subject to Cameroon's national law in full, with no local exception. Small towns such as Maroua and the settlements around the Lake Chad basin offer little anonymity, and outside Waza National Park tourism is minimal, so a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor stands out quickly. Security is militarised: frequent army and gendarmerie checkpoints, armed-community vigilance and displacement linked to the Boko Haram insurgency mean encounters with officialdom are more common than in the south, while state presence and rule of law are weaker and further reduced by recent insurgency-related insecurity. There is no local LGBTQ support organisation, no visible trans community infrastructure, and markedly fewer willing defence lawyers and accessible courts than in Douala or Yaoundé, so detention, coercive questioning, extortion and hostility from civilians or armed groups are realistic local outcomes, and routes to release, appeal or outside help are slower from remote districts. No local protections, documented tolerance or region-specific prosecutions are on record here; the absence of regional case detail reflects thin reporting rather than safer conditions, and it should not be read as reassurance. Where local conditions meet the national framework, they intensify exposure rather than soften it: deeper conservatism, low anonymity and heavy surveillance make discovery more likely to escalate, with thinner institutional recourse once it happens.

27767025B74489197250691.name: North-West
27767025B74489197250691.summary: North-West, centred on Bamenda, falls under Cameroon's national regime, in which consensual same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity are criminalised and arrests proceed on clothing and presentation, carrying penalties of six months to five years' imprisonment; cybercrime provisions also reach gender presentation. Documented cases include the 2021 Douala convictions of two transgender women (Shakiro and Patricia) for wearing women's clothing, the 2011 dress-based convictions, and courts imposing maximum terms for gender expression, alongside 2022 reports of group attacks and gendarme beatings of detained LGBTI people and 2022 findings of arbitrary arrest and abuse of gender-nonconforming people. Police and gendarmes have detained, beaten and extorted people over alleged same-sex conduct or gender nonconformity, generally with near-total impunity, while few lawyers will defend the accused. The region itself has been gripped by the Anglophone conflict since 2016–2017, with non-state separatist groups and state security forces both operating and separatist control across much of the countryside; this brings military and armed-group checkpoints, roadblocks, curfews, identity checks, arbitrary and mass detention, an emergency posture, and a severely degraded rule of law in which functioning courts, legal aid, LGBTQ services and ordinary policing are largely absent. Social attitudes, including local religious conservatism, are strongly conservative, little tourism infrastructure exists, and no region-specific record of trans tolerance, protection or documented trans-targeted incidents has been found — an absence that does not indicate safety, and no distinct local pattern of targeting transgender visitors is established either. For a transgender visitor who is out or discovered, these conditions compound the inherited criminal exposure: discovery is likely to be read as immorality or illegality, with foreseeable arrest, beatings, extortion, detention in poor conditions and custodial violence, while the militarised environment and competing authorities make severe harm unpredictable and effective recourse, protection or consular assistance minimal. Impunity and the collapse of ordinary policing are worse locally than nationally, leaving exposure higher and protection weaker than the national average, with few offsetting safeguards.

27767025B54850051814081.name: South-West
27767025B54850051814081.summary: The region is subject to Cameroon's national law in full, with no local exception. What distinguishes the South-West is its security environment rather than any local variant of that law. The Anglophone conflict since 2016–2017 has concentrated military and gendarmerie checkpoints along roads around Buea, Limbe and Kumba, alongside separatist-imposed curfews and 'ghost-town' lockdowns, stop-and-search and routine identity checks by both state forces and armed separatist groups, which operate with practical impunity in places. Beating and unrecorded detention in security custody are live risks there, and a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor's documents are more likely to be examined and any subsequent detention to disappear from view. Policing, courts and legal aid are weaker than in Douala or Yaoundé, with fewer functioning lawyers, courts and advocacy groups available after an arrest, and improvised routes around checkpoints are difficult. Local social conditions cut both ways. Attitudes in the South-West are broadly conservative, more so than on the francophone coast, while Limbe's coastal tourist economy, the Mount Cameroon area and Buea's university population bring some familiarity with foreign visitors. Neither offers a documented exception to national enforcement practice: no trans-specific local protection, support organisation or protective machinery is known anywhere in the region, and no distinct local pattern of anti-trans targeting has been established either. Border treatment of foreign documents, facility access and placement in custody are likewise not specifically documented for the region, and that uncertainty should not be read as safety.

28894549B37294008176905.name: Équateur
28894549B37294008176905.summary: Équateur is a remote northwestern province centred on the Congo River port of Mbandaka, one of the least-governed parts of the country, with very few foreign visitors, thin infrastructure and no tourism economy to speak of. The region is subject to DR Congo national law in full, with no local exception. Outside Mbandaka, police, courts and legal aid function weakly, medical infrastructure is limited, and nothing documented locally softens national practice for a trans visitor: there are no known protective services, no local tolerance and no trans community infrastructure to turn to. Police and officials are underpaid and resort to extortion, so an outed visitor could face detention, humiliation, coerced disclosure, denial of care or violence with effectively no working recourse. Church and customary authority shape strong social disapproval; a travelling minor could additionally face family or community "correction" or state inquiry. Unlike the conflict-affected east, no armed-group campaign against LGBTQ people is documented in Équateur, but weak state presence leaves poorly controlled security personnel as the practical exposure rather than militia. Document checks at river and air transport points can draw attention to papers or presentation, and riverine and rural isolation makes a discreet exit difficult once questions arise. How national provisions are applied to trans visitors specifically is uncertain, and no Équateur-specific protective measures or reliable visitor remedies are established.

Consular and legal help is distant, and no local tolerance or protective exception distinguishes the region from the national picture. Exact enforcement against trans foreigners is poorly documented, and no region-specific records of trans-specific enforcement or facility rules were found — a gap that does not establish safety. It has markedly less anonymity than Djibouti City: fewer tourist-facing or hospitality services, thinner institutional presence, and close-knit community networks shaped by strong Afar and Somali customary and religious conservatism, where social framing sits at hostility rather than mere friction. A visibly transgender visitor, or one whose presentation does not match local expectations, would stand out far more than in the capital, with little realistic expectation of tolerant anonymity. Border and gendarmerie checkpoints along the Ethiopian route raise the chance that a mismatch between foreign documents and presentation becomes a public matter, since scrutiny here is more routine and more personal than in the capital. The national human-rights commission is sited in Djibouti City, so complaint-based recourse is at a practical distance, and no local trans community, protective infrastructure, or documented local safeguard is known. No recorded local incidents or distinct local enforcement pattern have been documented either way, and the thinness of reporting should not be read as evidence of safety; discovery in a small community carries a high social cost, including shunning, harassment, denial of services or discretionary police action, with little effective local remedy.

No local ordinance, practice or incident distinguishes the parish from the national picture, so conditions there follow Dominica's framework: in April 2024 the High Court read down sections 14 and 16 of the Sexual Offences Act so that private consensual adult same-sex activity is no longer criminalised, though the provisions remain on the statute book and say nothing about transgender status. No law protects gender identity or gender expression, there is no anti-discrimination law, and same-sex unions are not recognised. Across the country, police responses to anti-LGBT violence have been documented as dismissive or ridiculing, including a refusal to investigate an attack on a gay complainant, alongside a killing of a man accused of watching another man and violence against people read as gender-nonconforming. Organised religious hostility toward LGBT visitors is also recorded, including a 2009 call by an evangelical leader for gay tourists to be kept away. No trans-specific prosecution, gender-marker or documentation rule, facility or detention rule, or healthcare provision is documented nationally or locally. For a transgender visitor who is discovered or outed, this means possible social hostility and service refusal with unreliable police recourse, but no documented criminalisation of trans identity or expression.
