8384693B50697642267539.name: Tartous
8384693B50697642267539.summary: Tartous is subject to Syria's national law in full, with no local exception. The governorate occupies Syria's Mediterranean coast, with beach tourism around Tartous city, Banyas and Safita, a tourism-dependent economy and a long-standing foreign presence; its population is mixed Alawite, Sunni and Christian, and local social character is commonly described as comparatively secular and relaxed, though conservative attitudes and close scrutiny in small coastal communities remain a real factor for a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor. Tartous never fell under Islamic State or Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham territorial control, so the armed-group violence documented elsewhere in Syria is not a local operative regime, and no local raid, arrest or targeting of trans visitors is specifically documented. That silence is not evidence of safety: nothing here records local tolerance, protective enforcement or practical relief either. Security services are pervasive, there is no visible trans community or advocacy infrastructure, and police discretion remains the operative risk once a visitor is discovered. Since the change of government in late 2024 the governorate has been administered by the post-Assad authorities, and conditions have proved volatile — sectarian unrest and security-force abuses affecting Alawite communities in March 2025 showed how quickly the coastal area can deteriorate, even though nothing in that episode was trans-specific. Being outed in a small, socially watched community, document scrutiny and weak rule of law make informal exposure more salient here than formal enforcement. Distinct local rules on visitor documents or custody practice are not documented, and such gaps should not be read as reassurance.

8384693B23566608622518.name: Dar'a
8384693B23566608622518.summary: Dar'a is subject to Syria's national legal regime in full, with no local exception. The province is a largely rural, tribally structured southern border district adjoining Jordan, where extended-family and religiously conservative norms govern social life and anonymity is scarce: in small communities a visibly trans or outed visitor would stand out, and the discreet gathering places available in Damascus have no counterpart here. Security conditions distinguish Dar'a further. Frequent checkpoints and border screening between Syria and Jordan expose travellers to repeated identity scrutiny, while fragmented armed factions, widespread weapons, an active kidnapping and extortion economy, and weak, contested state authority — following the province's role as the cradle of the 2011 uprising, its 2018 reconquest under Russian-brokered reconciliation and the 2024-25 transition — make policing unreliable, with residual ISIS-affiliated cell activity and periodic assassinations adding to the unpredictability. Within that institutional vacuum, discovery by police, a local armed group or community figures can lead to detention, extortion or family and community coercion rather than protection. No documented local tolerance, visitor infrastructure or trans-specific protection exists to soften the national position, so outcomes for a trans visitor are less predictable and harder to contain than in Syria's major cities. No record of trans-targeted enforcement in Dar'a itself is established; given the province's insecurity and conservative climate, that gap reflects absent documentation rather than evidence of safety.

8384693B61807023607014.name: As-Sweida
8384693B61807023607014.summary: As-Sweida is subject to Syria's national law in full, with no local exception. The governorate is a small, tightly knit Druze-majority area in southern Syria where a foreigner is conspicuous: family and clan networks, religious authority and village-level social surveillance mean an outed or outable trans visitor is likely to be noticed quickly, and the anonymity Damascus's size once offered does not exist here. Local norms around gender and sexuality are reported as stricter than the national average. Social and religious authority rests with Druze sheikhs and community elders rather than a vice-police apparatus, which has historically kept private conduct at arm's length from central morality enforcement, but it also means that any sanction would be communal rather than official. Security has fragmented: sectarian clashes in July 2025 between government forces and Druze armed groups, de facto control of the governorate by Druze armed and religious leadership since mid-2025, and active checkpoints leave policing divided among local factions rather than a dependable state force, making any attempt to seek help after an assault, extortion or confinement unpredictable. Since 2024–2025 ISIS-affiliated cells have carried out attacks in and around the governorate, so extremist hostility is a live local hazard rather than a distant one, and visible outsiders have historically faced kidnapping and extortion risk. As-Sweida retains a small tourism economy built on its Roman sites and desert scenery, and lies outside the areas historically ruled by Islamic State or Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham. No trans-specific campaign or protective institution is documented here, and such a silence should not be read as safety: the local environment offers no tolerant spaces or reliable recourse.

8384693B30882548325909.name: Quneitra
8384693B30882548325909.summary: Quneitra is subject to Syria's national law in full, with no local exception. The governorate is a heavily militarised, largely depopulated border district on the armistice line with the Israeli-occupied Golan: the destroyed city stands mostly empty, with residents spread among villages such as Khan Arnabeh, Al-Baath and Hader and around Madinat al-Baath, and control of the wider area is fragmented between state security, former opposition factions and forces in the UNDOF buffer zone, so predictability and access to protection vary from place to place. Movement is saturated with checkpoints and crossings where identity documents are routinely examined, and a foreign visitor is conspicuous at once — discovery is hard to avoid, and a document discrepancy can bring questioning, arbitrary detention or private hostility. Communities are close-knit, conservative tribal, Druze and Bedouin structures with little tolerance of visible gender nonconformity. There is no LGBT or visitor-support infrastructure, no organised local community and no local protective institution, while health and legal services are limited or destroyed, leaving nowhere practical to turn after harassment, extortion or violence. No trans-specific enforcement pattern or protective practice is documented in Quneitra; the absence of recorded local incidents reflects thin documentation, not safety.

36821470B25997690360286.name: Nakhon Ratchasima Province
36821470B25997690360286.summary: Nakhon Ratchasima (Korat) inherits Thailand's national framework for transgender travellers: the Immigration Bureau's Welcome Pride arrival accommodation when a passport does not match a traveller's appearance, legal same-sex marriage, the Gender Equality Act's gender-identity discrimination ban, and no criminalisation of transgender identity or hate-crime designation — though enforcement of those discrimination provisions is spotty, and a documented 2025 murder of a trans woman led to no hate-crime designation. Legal gender recognition and passport marker change remain unavailable, title prefixes are locked to sex at birth, name-change approval is discretionary, and detention or hospital placement can turn on sex at birth or medical verification, including separated custody units. Because the province is not a major international tourist destination, the Welcome Pride scheme and visitor-facing services are less established locally. No province-specific punitive measure, targeted policing, organised hostility, documented anti-trans violence, or local protective ordinance distinguishes treatment there from the national picture. As Isan's main gateway city and a large regional transport, military and university centre, Korat has a visible transgender presence in markets, beauty services and entertainment, and Isan cultural norms are generally tolerant of visible kathoey presence. Outer districts are largely rural and agricultural, and local life is more socially conservative and religiously conservative than Bangkok, Pattaya, Phuket or Chiang Mai, with stronger expectations of conventional presentation, thinner trans-specific services and advocacy, fewer English-speaking or LGBTQ-aware settings, and frontline police, hotels and hospitals that may be less experienced with gender-diverse foreign visitors. A trans visitor who is outed would more likely encounter curiosity and social awkwardness, bureaucratic friction, service denial or harassment, and custody placement uncertainty — at a provincial system whose officials' practice is uneven, including at Korat Central Prison, one of the country's largest men's facilities — rather than severe punishment.

36821470B94320894939793.name: Surat Thani Province
36821470B94320894939793.summary: Surat Thani Province applies Thailand's national framework with no province-specific protective law, hostile legislation, local ordinance, or documented trans-targeted policing, raids, or region-specific record of anti-trans violence; police checkpoints exist but are not trans-specific. Nationally there is no legal gender recognition or marker change (title prefixes follow sex at birth), anti-discrimination coverage for gender identity under the Gender Equality Act is enforced unevenly and less visibly than in Bangkok or Pattaya, and there is no hate-crime statute, so anti-trans violence is prosecuted as an ordinary offence — a documented 2025 murder of a trans woman was handled without bias protections, alongside the 2015 Nachacha Kongudom case. Arrival is eased by the Immigration Bureau's Welcome Pride accommodation for passport–appearance mismatch, and the airport's immigration practice follows that national policy. Custody and hospital placement follow national Department of Corrections and health rules: placement turns on medical verification, with men's cells or segregation the usual alternative (only medically transitioned trans women approach women's facilities, and a separated-wing precedent exists in Pattaya), possible solitary confinement, and ward placement following documents; provincial prisons and hospitals do not reduce these risks, while gender-affirming care is widely available nationwide. Within the province, Koh Samui, Koh Phangan and Koh Tao are tourism-dependent international destinations with large foreign visitor populations, where visibly gender-nonconforming foreigners are routine, immigration desks and hospitality staff are accustomed to international documents, and transgender women work visibly and unremarkably in cabaret, entertainment and hospitality — a limited contextual positive rather than evidence of trans-specific acceptance or protection. The mainland districts, provincial town and rural and Muslim-majority communities are more conservative and less familiar with visible gender diversity than Bangkok, local clinics and police are less accustomed to trans-specific issues, and enforcement of equality protections is weaker than in Bangkok or Pattaya, raising friction and casual disclosure risk. For a visitor whose status becomes known, the likely harms are staring, misgendering, bureaucratic hesitation, refusal or awkwardness in services, and less competent custodial or hospital placement rather than imprisonment or lethal state action; beach and nightlife settings carry ordinary social friction rather than organized hostility, and the accountability gap for anti-trans violence remains operative.

No province-specific protection, ordinance, police practice or incident record involving transgender visitors was found, and that lack of a local record reflects the limits of documentation here rather than any assurance of safety. Detention is geographically concrete: Bang Kwang Central Prison, a major correctional facility, lies within the province, and detainees there fall under national custody arrangements rather than any local safeguard. Visitors whose documents do not match their presentation should expect bureaucratic friction and document-based checks in official encounters, as elsewhere in the country.

36821470B69255687394343.name: Prachuap Khiri Khan Province
36821470B69255687394343.summary: Prachuap Khiri Khan is subject to Thailand's national regime in full, with no local exception. The province is a quiet coastal strip dominated by the Hua Hin and Cha-am beach resorts — a royal-resort area known for family, golf and retiree-facing tourism — alongside quieter districts such as Pranburi and Kui Buri. In the tourist belt, hospitality staff and businesses are accustomed to foreign guests, and transgender people are visible in service and entertainment work, so varied presentation attracts little attention. Beyond that belt the character changes: rural and interior districts are more socially conservative, and in smaller towns a visitor may draw more staring and curiosity, with thinner trans-aware medical or legal help and less routine familiarity among local officials, hotels and public hospitals than in Bangkok, Pattaya or Phuket. The province has a low-anonymity social fabric with little visible LGBTQ nightlife or community infrastructure, so someone who is outed has fewer accepting venues and support networks than in the larger centres. No province-specific ordinance, facility ban, organised sweep or documented pattern of police targeting, exclusion or violence against trans visitors is known — but local records are thin, particularly in rural and border districts, and thin documentation should not be read as safety. Hospital or custody placement remains document-based, and bias incidents would be pursued through national institutions only, with no local remedy machinery, advocacy presence or protective mechanism operating for visitors. In practical terms the province sits close to the national baseline: everyday social exposure is modestly higher in small conservative towns, while recourse, when needed, depends on the same discretionary officials found elsewhere in the country.

36821470B65611179255944.name: Songkhla Province
36821470B65611179255944.summary: Songkhla is subject to Thailand's national legal framework in full, with no local exception or additional provincial rule. Within it, conditions vary sharply across the province. Hat Yai — the largest city and a commercial, medical, university and tourism centre — has a visible transgender presence in its service sector and nightlife, established accommodation and clinic infrastructure, and heavy cross-border Malaysian visitor traffic, so discreet visitors there generally meet ordinary, internationally accustomed friction. Songkhla city and the rural interior are quieter and more socially conservative, with fewer trans-specific services, less visible community support and greater community scrutiny. In Muslim-majority districts toward the Malaysian border, gender norms are stricter than the national picture, with tighter gender segregation at religious and community sites raising outing friction, and Islamic family-law jurisdiction applies to Muslim residents. Parts of the province near the border fall under an Emergency Decree, bringing heavier security checkpoints and wider detention discretion — measures not directed at transgender people specifically, but which increase general police encounters. The Sadao border crossing to Malaysia can involve additional document checking. No region-specific pattern of trans-targeted policing, raids, hostile local legislation or visitor incidents is documented, but local protection and support appear thinner outside Hat Yai, where social friction rather than official action is the likelier exposure.

36821470B89498504013794.name: Phuket Province

The residual exposure is institutional rather than street-level: custody, policing and medical handling outside the large resorts, and anything arising during an emergency or detention, remain less predictable and can follow documentation that does not match a visitor's presentation. Scams, harassment and service friction in nightlife areas remain a background concern, and local police discretion is a variable.

36821470B74825096412992.name: Chon Buri Province
36821470B74825096412992.summary: Chon Buri Province is subject to Thailand's national law in full, with no local exception. The province is anchored by Pattaya, a resort city whose tourism and nightlife economy is built partly on a long-established, highly visible transgender community of performers and workers; hotels, clinics, attractions and cabaret venues routinely handle foreign guests whose documents do not match their presentation, so everyday presence there is less exceptional than in most Thai provinces. Private and international hospitals along the Pattaya–Si Racha corridor are accustomed to foreign patients, though ward treatment can be inconsistent. Against that, Pattaya carries elevated street crime, police corruption and sex-industry exploitation. Bars, sex-tourism venues and dating-app meetups are where extortion, violence and exploitative policing concentrate, and visibility itself is not a safeguard. A trans woman was murdered in Pattaya in April 2025 after refusing a client's request for sex; it is a single incident rather than a documented pattern, but it occurred in a high-general-crime tourist city, and the community's public response to it signals real local organisation. Locally, Pattaya Remand Prison holds transgender inmates in a dedicated block rather than the usual men's facilities — a concrete mitigation — but that does not guarantee placement with women and time there can still involve segregation or solitary confinement. Outside the Pattaya–Si Racha corridor the province is more conventional in attitude and official discretion is wider, with no documented trans-specific local harm. The tourist-facing Pattaya strip is the province's most relaxed part; adult-entertainment settings remain its least.

17741764B49308440506872.name: Nanumanga
17741764B49308440506872.summary: Nanumanga is a small, remote outer atoll reached only by boat, with infrequent inter-island transport, only a few hundred residents, no tourist infrastructure, and no court, place of detention, or NGO, legal or consular presence; island life is centred on the dominant Protestant congregation and the local kaupule, which tends toward conservative social norms, and visitors are few. There is no local legal regime or trans-specific service distinct from the national picture: Tuvalu's Penal Code provisions on male same-sex conduct and gross indecency (maximums of 14, 7 and 5 years) remain on the books and would by their terms reach a trans woman whom authorities classify as male if she has sex with a man, alongside a 2023 constitutional ban on same-sex marriage, no gender-identity protection or recognition, no hate-crime law, and no recognition of same-sex relationships. No prosecutions of consenting adults are documented, though the documented absence dates to 2013 and UN human-rights statements were made in 2011; Tuvalu's longstanding pinapinaaine gender-diverse tradition and recent official recognition of transgender people in health planning provide some cultural familiarity, while religious and social discrimination persists in the wider context. With no anonymity available, a visibly transgender visitor would be known to the whole community within hours, facing community scrutiny, possible moral or religious condemnation, difficulty finding accommodation or local help, and a higher chance that any police interaction turns on a document or appearance mismatch. Formal recourse would require slow travel to Funafuti, since any arrest or custody is handled there under national practice, including birth-sex custody and facility placement, leaving thinner practical recourse rather than evidence of specific local hostility. No region-specific incident, enforcement, custody or official hostility record distinguishing Nanumanga from the national picture is documented, and the absence of records is not evidence of safety.

17741764B36602748519227.name: Nanumea
17741764B36602748519227.summary: Nanumea is Tuvalu's remote northern atoll: a community of a few hundred people organised around kinship, customary elders and a strong church presence, with no tourist or guesthouse infrastructure and no anonymity — a foreign visitor is known as soon as they arrive. Medical cover is a single clinic and transport is irregular, so a care need or an incident cannot be resolved locally, or escaped quickly, and outside help is slow to reach. The region is subject to Tuvalu's national law in full, with no local exception. Outer-island conservatism runs stronger than in the capital, and discovery by neighbours or family is likelier here than in Funafuti. Tuvalu's recognised pinapinaaine tradition gives gender diversity a familiar cultural place, but on Nanumea that familiarity sits inside tight church and family networks, where the plausible response to a visibly trans visitor is intense curiosity, gossip, moral disapproval, communal pressure or friction in getting services — not, on any documented record, physical violence. 36957248B77241623821364.name: Iringa
36957248B77241623821364.summary: Iringa is subject to Tanzania's national law in full, with no local exception. Iringa is an inland southern-highlands region and town, largely rural and predominantly Christian, that serves as a gateway to Ruaha's safari routes. Social norms are conservative and traditionally religious; there is a university population but no visible transgender community, advocacy groups, queer venues or legal-aid infrastructure. Civil society, media scrutiny and legal support are thinner here than in Dar es Salaam, and foreign visitors are few and mostly safari-bound, which limits anonymity for outsiders. Discovery in Iringa would most plausibly come through hotel registration, document checks or public attention in a small town where faces are known. Local authorities have no documented history of handling such cases more softly than the national norm, and no local incident record exists — the absence of documented cases should not be read as safety, since local enforcement and the treatment of an outed visitor remain untested. Ruaha-linked tourism may produce courteous service, but that hospitality is discretionary and does not extend to border, lodging, hospital or police encounters, where hostile local attitudes can meet official procedure with no local remedy in place. Compared with the coastal cities, Iringa has less organised anti-LGBT campaigning but also far less support and greater visibility, so the local climate reinforces rather than mitigates national exposure.

36957248B13188202009922.name: North Pemba
36957248B13188202009922.summary: North Pemba falls under Tanzania's national regime in full, and additionally under Zanzibar's separate penal statutes. Beyond that framework, the island's own conditions shape daily risk. North Pemba is a predominantly rural, closely knit Muslim Swahili island of fishing and farming communities, with a far smaller tourism sector than Unguja and few settings where a visitor can go unnoticed. Local religious and social authority is strong, civil society is weaker than on Unguja or the mainland, and there are minimal visible queer venues and no known local trans community, advocacy group or safe-accommodation network. A visibly trans or outed visitor is likely to be noticed and discussed: discovery through neighbours, community gossip or lodging staff is comparatively easy, and small-island privacy is limited. Recourse is thinner here than in Dar es Salaam or Stone Town. Courts and policing are less accessible in rural districts, official harassment or extortion is not uniformly documented for this district, and violence by private actors is more likely to go unanswered. No North Pemba-specific incidents involving trans visitors are recorded, and no local protective practice is documented — that silence reflects limited monitoring rather than safety, and local conditions lean toward the more restrictive end of the national picture.

36957248B25003810903493.name: South Pemba
36957248B25003810903493.summary: South Pemba lies within semi-autonomous Zanzibar, so in addition to Tanzania's national laws it sits under Zanzibar's own 1934 Penal Code and 2004 Penal Decree, which broadly define gross indecency and criminalise sex between women, with penalties of up to five years' imprisonment; these statutes target conduct rather than trans identity as such, but they contribute to a hostile legal climate. Nationally, same-sex conduct is criminalised, life imprisonment applies to same-sex acts between men on the mainland, and there is no legal gender recognition or anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity anywhere in the country. Documented national patterns include police-custody torture and forced or anal examinations, extortion, state-led anti-LGBT campaigns, the 2018 Dar es Salaam crackdown, vigilante violence, and the 2024 abduction and mutilation of a transgender activist that drew no known prosecution. Zanzibar authorities have separately moved against LGBT-friendly civil society, the Zanzibar AIDS Commission suspended HIV outreach to men who have sex with men, and Islamic religious authorities — the Mufti and Kadhi courts — shape a morality-oriented enforcement environment. There is no documented routine pathway to imprisonment for trans identity alone. Pemba itself is markedly more socially conservative, religiously observant, rural and tightly knit than Unguja's tourist centre or the mainland cities — almost entirely Muslim, with minimal tourism, almost no foreign community, no visible LGBT venues, no trans community or support infrastructure, and legal-aid and advocacy concentrated elsewhere; police oversight is weaker than in Dar es Salaam, and there is no documented record of police or official relief for LGBT people there. A gender-nonconforming foreigner stands out with limited anonymity, and in small communities outing spreads quickly through documents, appearance or gossip; police, health services and community authorities may treat such travellers as morally suspect, raising risks of arrest, detention, extortion, abuse, violence, deportation and communal hostility, with no realistic local remedy. No South Pemba-specific incident of police targeting or anti-trans violence, and no specific tourist case, is documented; trans-specific border or document practices, facility rules and effective visitor protections are likewise undocumented, and absence of documentation is not evidence of safety.

17295835B48340970483027.name: Central Region
17295835B48340970483027.summary: The region is subject to Uganda's national Anti-Homosexuality Act 2023 regime in full, with no local exception. Central Region contains Kampala, the capital, along with the Wakiso and Mukono districts and Entebbe airport, and it concentrates the country's police headquarters, state institutions, embassies, hospitals and tourist-facing services. Documented enforcement and anti-LGBT harm in Uganda is disproportionately reported from this part of the country: shelter raids, mob violence and app-based entrapment cluster around the capital, where police, media and mobs tend to treat gender nonconformity as evidence of offending. Entebbe's border screening creates exposure for travellers whose documents do not match their presentation, and the country's only recorded legal gender-marker change was issued here. Kampala is more cosmopolitan than the rest of the country, and its size, foreigner presence, NGO and clinic network, hotels and private spaces offer more anonymity and access to care or consular help than elsewhere; the city hosts an organised if largely hidden community. These advantages are limited — the support spaces themselves have been raided, and being outed can still lead to questioning, detention, extortion, eviction or communal violence without reliable official protection. Outside the capital the region's rural districts are more conservative, with fewer services and little recourse, and no local legal protection offsets the national regime anywhere in the region.

14850775B13681962240800.name: Volyn Oblast
14850775B13681962240800.summary: Volyn Oblast is a predominantly rural, socially and religiously conservative region in Ukraine's northwest, centred on Lutsk with small towns where a visibly transgender visitor is likely to attract attention and anonymity is limited. Ukraine's national framework applies in full, with no local exception: there is no separate local law, protective regime, or documented campaign targeting trans people here. No trans-specific community infrastructure or support services are known in the oblast, and LGBT presence is far less visible than in Kyiv or Lviv, so friction in daily life is more likely to take the form of social disapproval, service refusal, or indifference from local officials than organised hostility. The region's border character shapes practical exposure. Volyn sits on land crossings into Poland and Belarus, so the national screening of travellers at checkpoints is encountered here directly rather than as an abstract possibility; delays, secondary interviews, document scrutiny and placement according to marked sex are the realistic outcomes at oblast crossings, and no specific local remedy is established. Proximity to Poland also offers an exit route, though it runs through the same checkpoints. Specialist health services are sparse outside Lutsk, and the diagnosis gatekeeping that trans people face nationally is harder to navigate from here than from a major city, with refusal or delay of care a plausible consequence of being outed. Thin local recourse is the recurring theme: discovery is more likely to produce bureaucratic exclusion, stigma and delays than state persecution, but this limited local information does not establish safety, and the national concerns remain fully applicable.

The main local exposure is therefore social and administrative rather than legal.

14850775B31033086218351.name: Luhansk Oblast
14850775B31033086218351.summary:
The occupied parts of the oblast run under Russian-appointed authorities applying Russian federal law — the all-audiences "propaganda" law, the 2023 transition ban, and the LGBT-movement "extremist" designation (participation punishable by up to 12 years) — plus wartime arbitrariness. The self-proclaimed LPR shared the DPR's original constitutional ban on same-sex unions and the same persecution pattern documented by ADC Memorial's interviews with displaced residents: targeted hunting of gay people, informal detention for ransom and forced labour, and violence with total impunity.

Freedom House (2022) records that discovery of LGBT identity by the military or occupation administration brings insults, violence, extortion, restriction of freedom and threats to life; the PROJECTOR project documented occupying forces specifically searching for LGBTIQ+ people (81 known victims). UN reporting (2025) finds LGBTQ+ persons at acute risk of sexual violence, particularly in detention. Arbitrary detention in unofficial sites without lawyers or family access is documented across the occupied areas (State Department 2024).

Transgender residents face appearance-document mismatch that blocks checkpoint passage and exit, plus discrimination in work, services and housing. Almost all openly LGBT residents have fled; no public expression of identity or support is possible, and no monitor or remedy operates.

sources.title: ADC Memorial & Center for Civil Liberties — Violation of LGBTI Rights in Crimea and Donbass (2016)
sources.summary: Interview-based report (Dec 2015–Mar 2016) with LGBTI people and experts from Crimea, Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts, many displaced. Documents physical attacks and targeted hunting of gay people, including a foreigner lured through a fake social-network date into an apartment where five men stripped him, beat him in a shower, forced him to lick a toilet and drink vodka, filmed the assault and posted the video online. In the self-proclaimed DPR and LPR, respondents report a gay man shot and buried behind the Yasynuvatskyi checkpoint near Donetsk, and people brought to "the Basement" for intimidation, ransom and forced labour. Transgender people face document-appearance mismatch that prevents them from leaving, and discrimination blocking work, services and housing. The first DPR constitution expressly provided that "perverted unions between people of the same sex are prosecuted by law"; the clause was later removed but persecution continued. Respondents who stayed in Crimea hoping to use Russian legal gender-change procedures found them unusable in practice under the occupation authorities.

sources.title: Hromadske / Krym.Realii — How LGBT People Are Treated in Russia-Occupied Territories
sources.summary: About 10,000 LGBT people lived in Crimea before annexation; the Simeiz drag bar scene ended as a public scene in 2014 when the Russian propaganda law was imposed and homophobic Russian nationalist movements arrived. Occupation head Sergey Aksenov threatened in September 2014 that "self-defense forces and police will react" if gays take to the streets; no public LGBT event has occurred in Crimea since. When activist Nikolay Alexeyev sent hate-crime alerts in 2016, deputy head Dmitry Polonsky told LGBT people to leave for "Gayrope", and the "Crimean self-defense" militia publicly threatened to "pack and post" proponents of same-sex relationships. International human-rights organisations and UN missions are barred from the peninsula. In the occupied east, support for LGBT people cannot be expressed publicly at all.

sources.title: Gwara Media / PROJECTOR — systemic violence against LGBTQ+ people in occupied regions
sources.summary: Documentation project on war crimes against LGBTQ+ people under occupation: Russian military specifically searched for people related to the LGBTIQ+ community; monitors know of 81 people who went through detention/violence, 20 interviewed. A 20-year-old endured a month and a half of detention and torture in occupied Kherson on suspicion of separatism. Cases include insults, violence, extortion, restriction of freedom and threats to life once the military or occupation administration learns a person belongs to the LGBT+ community.

sources.title: Freedom House — Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine, Freedom in the World 2025
sources.summary: Russian authorities disseminate anti-LGBT+ propaganda and regularly threaten LGBT+ people with aggressive rhetoric; violent attacks against LGBT+ people and people perceived as LGBT+ are reported. The November 2023 Russian Supreme Court designation of the "international LGBT public movement" as an extremist organisation applies in the occupied territories, with participation or financing punishable by up to 12 years in prison; LGBT+ organisations' human-rights work has become impossible. Russian law imposed in the occupied areas bans changing sex and gender in public records and via medical procedures (narrow congenital-anomaly exception) and recognises no same-sex unions. Hate crimes by private actors draw only small fines or short administrative detention. Rights groups report almost all LGBT+ individuals have long since fled the occupied areas; those who remain do not openly or visibly express their identity. Free movement is severely restricted; residents without a Russian passport are treated as stateless.

sources.title: UN Ukraine — LGBTQI+ survivors of conflict-related sexual violence in occupied Ukraine (2025)
sources.summary: UN account of conflict-related sexual violence against LGBTQI+ people under Russian occupation, citing the Secretary-General's 2025 annual report finding that LGBTQ+ persons were at acute risk of sexual violence, in particular in detention settings. Survivors describe rape, threats of rape, sexual torture, forced nudity and sexual humiliation committed in occupation and detention contexts, intersecting with discrimination based on actual or perceived sexual orientation or gender identity.

sources.title: US State Department — Ukraine, Russian-Occupied Areas 2024 Human Rights Report
sources.summary: Occupation authorities arbitrarily detain civilians without lawful grounds or procedural guarantees, hold people in unofficial detention sites (warehouses, barns) without access to relatives or lawyers, and commit torture and ill-treatment; the whereabouts of many detainees are unknown. Russian federal law, including the anti-LGBT propaganda and extremism framework, is applied throughout the occupied areas.

The oblast is largely rural and strongly church-influenced — Greek Catholic, Orthodox and Reformed congregations, with Hungarian-minority areas — and more socially conservative than Kyiv or Odesa. Queer community life is small, with essentially no trans-specific services outside Uzhhorod; the few public LGBT events held there have met counter-demonstrations and small attacks, and police responsiveness in towns and villages is uneven, with smaller police and border units on the scene. No trans-specific incident record exists for the oblast itself, which marks genuine uncertainty rather than safety. Everyday exposure for a discreet visitor is more likely to be staring, refusal of service or intrusive questioning than violence; Carpathian resort areas may draw less casual attention than villages, and distance from the front lines lowers general rather than trans-specific risk.

27058087B19329078127106.name: Canelones
27058087B19329078127106.summary: Canelones is the department ringing Montevideo, taking in the commuter communities of Las Piedras and La Paz, Ciudad de la Costa, and the Costa de Oro beach resorts such as Atlántida, Marindia, Parque del Plata and Solís, along with Carrasco International Airport, plus wine towns and a rural north. It operates entirely under Uruguay's national framework with no departmental variation: the 2018 Comprehensive Law for Trans People remains in force after a failed 2019 repeal attempt, gender recognition is by self-declaration under Laws 19684 and 18.620 (with only female and male markers available), the Penal Code enhances penalties for identity-motivated crimes, the health system carries a non-discrimination obligation, marriage equality and equal age of consent apply, gender expression is not criminalised, and a trans prisoner may choose men's or women's placement. Courts, police and civil-registration institutions are national, and no local ordinance, police practice, facility exclusion or border-screening rule creating extra restrictions for trans visitors is documented here. conditions differ mainly in social familiarity rather than in law: the metropolitan and coastal belt adjoining Montevideo is largely suburban with steady domestic tourism, while smaller, more conservative towns and the rural interior are less accustomed to visible gender diversity and thinner on trans-specific community and health supports, so a visitor who is outed there may meet more curiosity, staring, misgendering, service hesitation, bureaucratic unfamiliarity, slower or uneven handling of complaints, and less institutional experience than in central Montevideo. Everyday exposure therefore depends chiefly on local attitudes and on access to supportive institutions outside the capital, while discovery itself brings no criminal exposure, no custody or facility restriction, and the same national anti-discrimination and health protections as elsewhere. Documented national shortcomings — uneven enforcement, gaps in implementation, hospital or service friction such as the 2024–2025 Maldonado hospital and BROU discrimination cases (which occurred outside this department and involved residents rather than visitors), recorded mistreatment in bureaucratic or hospital settings, national prison-placement practices, and a national record of substantial violence against trans residents — apply as countrywide conditions, and no Canelones-specific pattern of any of them affecting visitors is established; the absence of region-specific documentation reflects limited evidence rather than confirmed safety.

42786344B61423155075663.name: Bolívar
42786344B61423155075663.summary: Bolívar is subject to Venezuela's national law in full, with no local exception. Local conditions, however, shape how that regime plays out. In the southern mining arc, including the Sifontes area, illegal mining has left armed non-state groups exercising de facto control, so police and judicial protection thins out further there. For a trans visitor, identity or appearance checks at checkpoints and in routine services are the flashpoints: outcomes depend heavily on which actors are present, and discovery can lead to humiliating scrutiny, detention for payment or extortion, with effectively no remedy. What differs here is who enforces it: the governorate lies on an active front line, with southern separatist forces holding the south including the city of Ad Dali', Houthi forces in the north around Damt, and contested districts between them, so the authority a visitor encounters — court, militia or tribal body — depends on where they are. Local conditions compound that fragmentation. Authority is exercised through tribal and armed-group checkpoints rather than reliable civil policing, and ID checks on roads mean a visibly trans or gender-nonconforming traveller can be identified long before any formal process begins. The governorate is rural, conservative and tribal, with essentially no tourist infrastructure and no documented local organizations, clinics or legal remedies serving trans people, so an exposure is likely to be handled by family, tribe or militia rather than by institutions. Militia custody adds risk of arbitrary detention, extortion and mistreatment, while private or vigilante violence is difficult to hold accountable. Active conflict and collapsed public services also restrict access to medical care and consular assistance, making any incident harder to recover from than the legal exposure alone suggests. No local protective regime, documented tolerance or safer treatment under any of the competing authorities is on record, and there is no indication that moving between areas of control improves a trans visitor's position.

6923714B34072001548912.name: Southern
6923714B34072001548912.summary: Southern Province operates under Zambia's national regime with no known regional exception: consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised and enforced, gender-nonconforming presentation can be treated as evidence of immorality, and there is no legal gender recognition or broad anti-discrimination protection — only narrower health-care guidelines that may not reach visitors. Should a trans visitor be discovered or outed, the national exposures apply — stop-and-search, bribery and extortion demands, arrest under public-order or same-sex-conduct laws, prolonged detention, threatened charges, documented police violence and harassment, forced anal examinations in custody or used as court evidence, and mob violence including a documented attack involving police officers; a relationship read as same-sex can also trigger the law. SYN-ABW.name: Aruba
SYN-ABW.summary:
Aruba is a constituent territory within the Kingdom of the Netherlands and stands under that framework; the island's own Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, carries the anti-discrimination provisions in force here. Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting the recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life, and Articles 2:61 and 2:62 set penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover heterosexual or homosexual orientation only. Gender identity and gender expression are not addressed, and no transgender-specific provision is cited in the sources.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16, equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. This is the only youth-specific legal threshold in the record; no findings on education, schools, or minors' access to services or documentation appear in the sources.

Partner recognition is established at two levels. On 8 September 2016 the Aruban Parliament voted 11 to 5, with four abstentions per the Associated Press account of 9 September 2016, to extend civil-code marriage articles to registered partnerships open to both opposite-sex and same-sex couples, granting spousal pension and emergency medical decision rights. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 12 July 2024, when the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal in Aruba. Since the Dutch Supreme Court ruling of 13 April 2007, Aruba must recognize same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024, immediately before the July 2024 ruling. SYN-AIA.name: Anguilla
SYN-AIA.summary:
Anguilla is a British Overseas Territory and the law that governs a visitor is local law; United Kingdom legislation reaches the island only where an Order in Council extends it, so no United Kingdom-level anti-discrimination floor applies of its own force.

Private consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised by order of the Privy Council on 5 January 2001, in a decision that also covered the Cayman Islands, the British Virgin Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands. The order was issued unilaterally after the local legislatures refused to repeal their statutes, and religious leaders protested the decision. Anguilla had never carried the prohibition in exactly the same statutory form as those other territories.

Anguillian law provides no protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The Constitution's anti-discrimination clause reaches race, political opinions, colour, creed, sex and place of origin, so gender identity sits outside the protected categories and a trans visitor has no statutory non-discrimination footing in local law.

The age of consent is 18 for same-sex conduct and 16 for different-sex conduct. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore carries legal exposure that a different-sex couple does not face.

The Marriage Act defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman as husband and wife. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal, and Anguilla is among the British overseas territories that have not legislated for civil partnerships. A commercial destination-wedding service marketing ceremonies on the island states that same-sex marriage is not recognised under Anguillan law, so a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has access only to a symbolic, non-legal ceremony. Non-legal ceremonies of same-sex couples have taken place there.

Public LGBT life is highly constrained. A subdued and subtle climate of homophobia has pushed local LGBT people toward secrecy. The island has no pride events, gay organisations, venues, bars or clubs and no community infrastructure, which the source attributes to a population of about 15,000. The only recorded public event is a small protest on 17 May 2011 in The Valley marking the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia.

Visiting same-sex couples have described the island as gay-friendly and reported that nobody was discriminatory in any way, though the same source cautions that the position of local people may differ. A 2023 first-person account by a queer family found same-sex conduct legal under the British order but the scene muted rather than openly visible, an outcome that account attributes to decriminalisation imposed from outside rather than to local initiative.

The Marriage Act defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman as husband and wife. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal, and Anguilla has not legislated for civil partnerships. A commercial wedding service states same-sex marriage is not recognised under Anguillan law, so a trans visitor in a locally classed same-sex relationship has access only to a symbolic non-legal ceremony. Such non-legal ceremonies have taken place. Public LGBT life is highly constrained, with a subdued and subtle climate of homophobia pushing local LGBT people toward secrecy. The island has no pride events, gay organisations, venues, bars or clubs and no community infrastructure, attributed to a population of about 15,000. The only recorded public event is a small protest on 17 May 2011 in The Valley marking the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia. Visiting same-sex couples have described the island as gay-friendly and reported nobody was discriminatory in any way, though the same source cautions local people may differ. A 2023 first-person account by a queer family found same-sex conduct legal under the British order but the scene muted rather than openly visible, an outcome that account attributes to externally imposed decriminalisation rather than local initiative.

SYN-BES.summary:

No source in the inventory describes a provision that addresses trans visitors directly. The protection that exists on these islands is carried by marriage registration and general anti-discrimination law, not by text naming gender identity, gender markers or facilities.

The Census Office in Saba registered the Caribbean Netherlands' first same-sex union on 4 December 2012: Aruban Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez (26) wed Venezuelan Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto (27), both visiting residents. Same-sex unions have therefore been registrable in these islands since 2012, and the island registry has performed one for visitors. This 2012 registration is the only dated union event in the sources; no later instance is documented.

For a trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex, that registration evidences a working route rather than a paper right. Civil ceremonies on Saba run through the island registry, with the Court Room in the Administrative Building recorded as the simplest venue for an efficient ceremony and registrar Julieta Woods documented as flexible about couples' wishes. Full destination-wedding suppliers, including caterers, florists and accommodation, operate on the island.

SYN-BLM.name: Saint Barthélemy
SYN-BLM.summary:
Saint Barthélemy is a French overseas collectivity, and the national framework of France applies here as it does in metropolitan France: its criminal law, identity documents, anti-discrimination statute and marriage regime govern the island.

Medical capacity is the sharpest practical constraint. The island covers about 8 square miles and holds roughly 10,000 residents, and the single red flag recorded against it in an aggregate travel-safety rating is limited healthcare access. Prescriptions and ongoing gender-affirming treatment cannot be assumed to be available locally, and a visitor who depends on either should carry supplies and confirm provision before arrival.

The same aggregate index rates Saint Barthélemy 7.7 out of 10, counting nine positive rights against the one healthcare red flag.

Anyone detained in Saint Barthélemy falls under the French prison administration, whose placement policy recognises only biological sex; trans detainees, overwhelmingly women, are held under birth sex. The controller-general of detention places, in an opinion of 25 May 2021 drawing on about 40 referrals received since 2010, found that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with recommendations that also cover intersex and non-binary persons.

Socially the island is discreet rather than permissive. It has no LGBTQ venues, no Pride events and no visible scene; same-sex couples attract no attention, crime is low, and the sources record no hostility toward gay or trans visitors. The luxury-yacht economy has long welcomed gay couples, and hospitality staff are described as trained for a diverse clientele.

Politically, Saint Barthélemy's joint deputy with Saint Martin was among 11 overseas deputies who voted against the 2013 law opening marriage to same-sex couples.

BLM detainees fall under this French system.

France's Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté opinion of 25 May 2021 on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty draws on about 40 referrals since 2010. It finds serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with recommendations applicable also to intersex and non-binary persons.

The French framework applies in Saint Barthélemy: legal gender-marker change without surgery or sterilisation, hormone therapy and surgery available since 1975, anti-discrimination coverage; non-binary recognition limited.

Full equality under French law applies across about 8 square miles and about 10,000 residents. The luxury-yacht economy has long welcomed gay couples, with no visible scene; discretion is the norm and same-sex couples attract no attention.

Aggregate rating 7.7/10, with 9 positive rights and 1 red flag: legal gender change without surgery, anti-discrimination law in place but limited healthcare access. No government LGBT+ travel advice exists; FCDO shows no warnings. No trans-specific visitor tips have been submitted.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Saint Barthélemy (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: French law banned discrimination on the basis of "sexual identity" in July 2012 and replaced that term with "gender identity" by the law of 18 November 2016 amending article 225-1 of the Penal Code; Chapter 2 of the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships or training and sanction, dismissal or discriminatory measures on account of gender identity. Since 1 January 2017 transgender people have been allowed to change legal gender without sex reassignment surgery, sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates or medical diagnosis under the law signed 18 November 2016 after Constitutional Council approval on 17 November 2016, but they must go before a court to change the gender marker while first-name change can be done at the registry office. France legalised gender affirmative surgery domestically in 1979, removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree in 2010 as the first country to declassify gender dysphoria, with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, though transgender rights organizations stated nothing changed beyond the announcement. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location for gender affirming healthcare and recommended informed consent and self-determination, while the National Academy of Medicine characterized increased demand as an "epidemic-like phenomenon" advising extreme caution without changing practice, and in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued first guidelines recommending puberty blockers plus calcium and vitamin D from at least Tanner stage 2. In 2017 transphobia became an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison, and police identified around 1,870 victims of transphobic and homophobic attacks in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018. Conversion therapy was legally banned by a bill passed by the Senate on 7 December 2020, concurred by the National Assembly on 25 January 2022 and published 1 February 2022, with proposed punishments of two years' imprisonment and/or a 30,000 euro fine. A Senate-passed bill of May 2024 to ban medical transition under age 18, following a March 2024 Senate-commissioned report criticizing youth care, is opposed by the Macron government, unlikely to pass the National Assembly and had no update since 23 July 2024. All sodomy laws were repealed in 1791 during the French Revolution with no mention of private same-sex relations in the Penal Codes of 1791 and 1810, while a 1960 ordinance inserting article 330 alinea 2 doubling the penalty for indecent exposure for homosexual activity, adopted via the Mirguet amendment, was repealed in 1980, and the discriminatory age of consent raised to 21 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual in 1942 and lowered to 18 in 1974 was equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982 under President François Mitterrand. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a bill for compensation to gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980, still awaiting Senate vote. National legislation since 1985 prohibits sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public and private goods and services, and the law of 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic comments with a maximum penalty of 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment and increased penalties when physical assault or murder is motivated by sexual orientation, enforced with the first conviction in January 2006 later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Civil solidarity pacts (PACS) were enacted in 1999 for same-sex and unmarried opposite-sex couples, and same-sex marriage became legal nationwide including all overseas departments and territories after National Assembly approval 12 February 2013 by 329-229, Senate approval 12 April, Constitutional Council validation 17 May 2013, presidential signature 18 May 2013 and first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier, with joint adoption legal since May 2013. The historic MSM blood-donation ban dating to 20 June 1983 was recalled 12 January 2009, replaced by one-year abstinence from 10 July 2016, reduced to four months from 2 April 2020, and fully removed 16 March 2022 so policy applies regardless of sexual orientation. Same-sex marriage is legal in Saint Barthélemy but its joint deputy with Saint Martin was among 11 overseas deputies voting against, while Guadeloupe, Martinique, Saint Martin and Saint Barthélemy are noted for gay bars, discos, saunas and beaches, and Saint Barthélemy's reputation as an international celebrity tourist destination is stated to have produced a more open and relaxed social climate for LGBTQ people than other French Caribbean territories. President Emmanuel Macron in October 2018 denounced homophobic violence as "unworthy of France" and announced future concrete measures after a rise in attacks.

SYN-BMU.name: Bermuda
SYN-BMU.summary:
Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory of the United Kingdom in which local legislation governs; United Kingdom statutes do not extend automatically. Bermuda has no legal recognition of transgender people. The Human Rights Act has prohibited discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 2013, when the Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act, which also banned age discrimination; gender identity is not a protected ground, so trans people have no statutory protection against discrimination. Proposals to extend that protection were failed or dropped in 2004–2006 and again in 2009.

The sources identify no Bermuda-specific provisions on identity documents or gender markers, border or airport screening, restroom and facility access, custody, healthcare, penalties or protection machinery for transgender people. The absence of gender identity as a protected ground is the only trans-specific legal finding the record carries.

The record describes expression of gender identity as often difficult and documents one instance of official interference: in 2006 the Government attempted to bar Mark Anderson, the drag performer known as the "Queen of Bermuda" Sybil, from participating in a parade, stating that he contradicted local mores and sensitivities. The most recent documented instance of this kind in the record is from 2006; no later instance is documented.

Same-sex marriage has been unavailable since 2022. The Supreme Court legalised it in May 2017 in the Godwin and DeRoche case; the Domestic Partnership Act 2017, given royal assent 7 February 2018 and effective 1 June 2018, replaced marriage with domestic partnerships for both same-sex and heterosexual couples, making Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality. The Supreme Court restored marriage on 6 June 2018 and the Court of Appeal on 23 November 2018, but the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council banned it again on 14 March 2022, with July 2022 laws retrospectively backdating prior legality. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship should expect no marital recognition.

Consensual sex between adult men was decriminalised in 1994 when the House of Assembly voted 22–16 to remove two Criminal Code sections, replacing prior liability of up to ten years' imprisonment for anal and oral sex; lesbian activity was never illegal. As of 2022 the age of consent stands unequal at 18 for consensual anal intercourse under the law effective 1 November 2019 against 16 for other sexual activity, and the gross indecency provision between men was repealed in 2019.

Organised religious hostility toward visible same-sex couples is documented: Bermuda's AME and other churches protested a gay cruise (the Norwegian Dawn, New York–Bermuda, 12 July) as "incompatible with the word of God and the Christian moral fibre". Such hostility is aimed at couples read locally as same-sex, which would reach a trans visitor whose relationship is read that way.

Royal Gazette (14 May 1994): the House of Assembly voted 22–16 to decriminalise consensual sex between adult men, removing two Criminal Code sections. The debate split the island, with religious leaders divided and the Christian Coalition staging marches against it.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Bermuda (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The article states there is no legal recognition of transgender people in Bermuda. The article states that, by omission, there is thus no protection from discrimination for transgender people. The article states that the ability of persons to express their gender identity is often difficult. As its example, the article states that in 2006 the Government attempted to ban Mark Anderson, also known as the drag queen "Queen of Bermuda" Sybil, from participating in a parade, stating that he contradicted local mores and sensitivities. The article provides no transgender-specific provisions on documents, screening, facilities, custody, care, enforcement, penalties, or protection machinery beyond that omission and example. Homosexuality is legal in Bermuda; lesbian activity has never been illegal, while consensual private sexual conduct was legalised by the Stubbs Bill in 1994 after prior liability of up to ten years' imprisonment for anal and oral sex. As of 2022 the age of consent remains unequal at 18 years for consensual anal intercourse under the law effective 1 November 2019 versus 16 for other sexual activity, after a prior higher age of 18 for gay male conduct found in violation of the European Convention on Human Rights, and the Criminal Code provision on gross indecency between men was repealed in 2019. The Human Rights Act has prohibited discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation since 2013, following failed and dropped proposals in 2004-2006 and 2009. Same-sex marriage is not legally available since 2022, having been legalised by the Supreme Court in May 2017 in the Godwin and DeRoche marriage-license case under the Marriage Act 1944 and Human Rights Act, replaced by domestic partnerships by law given royal assent 7 February 2018 and effective 1 June 2018, restored by the Supreme Court on 6 June 2018 and Court of Appeal on 23 November 2018, then banned again by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council on 14 March 2022 with July 2022 laws retrospectively backdating prior legality. Same-sex couples are allowed to adopt equally under the Adoption of Children Act following the February 2015 Supreme Court ruling on marital-status and sexual-orientation discrimination, and binational same-sex partners were granted equal employment and benefits by the Supreme Court in November 2015. The Bermuda Regiment, formed by random lottery-style conscription, does not discriminate on grounds of sexual orientation and officially prohibits discrimination or harassment of LGBT soldiers, though such activities have been reported as tolerated by officers to the extent one conscript described the Regiment as "the most homophobic environment that exists". Gay and bisexual men may donate blood with the Bermuda Hospitals Board if they have not had sex with another man in the past 12 months, with a 12-month deferral likewise for women who have sexual relations with men who have sex with men. In November 2020 reporting, the government spent approximately £150,000 to legally appeal an unconstitutional case of a man charged and threatened with jail under the archaic "obscene behaviour law" for importing DVDs of gay porn into Bermuda.

The 1994 decriminalisation debate split the island: religious leaders were divided and the Christian Coalition staged marches against the change, evidence of an organised constituency for the conduct-based restrictions that remained in the Criminal Code.

In November 2020 reporting, the Government spent approximately £150,000 to appeal an unconstitutional case against a man charged and threatened with jail under the "obscene behaviour law" for importing DVDs of gay porn into Bermuda, an expenditure of public funds defending a prosecution of same-sex material.

The sources identify no territory-specific provisions on identity documents or gender markers, border or airport screening, restroom and facility access, custody, healthcare, penalties or protection machinery for transgender people. The absence of gender identity as a protected ground is the only trans-specific legal finding the record carries.

The record describes expression of gender identity as often difficult and documents one instance of official interference: in 2006 the government attempted to bar a drag performer, known by a stage name styling him the "Queen" of this territory, from participating in a parade, stating that he contradicted local mores and sensitivities. The most recent documented instance of this kind in the record is from 2006; no later instance is documented.

Same-sex marriage has been unavailable since 2022. The highest civil court legalised it in May 2017 in a named case; a partnership statute of 2017, given royal assent 7 February 2018 and effective 1 June 2018, replaced marriage with domestic partnerships for both same-sex and heterosexual couples, making this territory the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality. The highest civil court restored marriage on 6 June 2018 and the appellate court on 23 November 2018, but the highest court of appeal banned it again on 14 March 2022, with July 2022 laws retrospectively backdating prior legality. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship should expect no marital recognition.

Consensual sex between adult men was decriminalised in 1994 when the lower chamber voted 22–16 to remove two sections of the criminal code, replacing prior liability of up to ten years' imprisonment for anal and oral sex; lesbian activity was never illegal. As of 2022 the age of consent stands unequal at 18 for consensual anal intercourse under the law effective 1 November 2019 against 16 for other sexual activity, and the gross indecency provision between men was repealed in 2019.

Organised religious hostility toward visible same-sex couples is documented: churches of a prominent denominational tradition and others protested a gay cruise (a cruise ship travelling from a major city in a neighbouring country to this territory on 12 July) as "incompatible with the word of God and the Christian moral fibre". Such hostility is aimed at couples read locally as same-sex, which would reach a trans visitor whose relationship is read that way.
SYN-BMU.blindTangential:
The 1994 decriminalisation debate split this island: religious leaders were divided and a religious advocacy group staged marches against the change, evidence of an organised constituency for the conduct-based restrictions that remained in the criminal code of this division.

In November 2020 reporting, the government of this division spent approximately 150,000 in public funds to appeal an unconstitutional case against a man charged and threatened with jail under the "obscene behaviour law" for importing DVDs of gay porn into this island, an expenditure of public funds defending a prosecution of same-sex material.

A prior higher age of consent of 18 for gay male conduct was found in violation of the regional human rights convention to which this country is a party, which produced the equalised-but-still-split consent structure in force from 1 November 2019: 18 for anal intercourse, 16 for other sexual activity.
SYN-BMU.blindLocalsOnly:
Same-sex couples may adopt equally under the adoption statute following the February 2015 ruling of the highest court on marital-status and sexual-orientation discrimination, and the highest court granted binational same-sex partners equal employment and benefits in November 2015.

The territorial regiment, formed by random lottery-style conscription, officially prohibits discrimination or harassment of LGBT soldiers and does not discriminate on grounds of sexual orientation, though such conduct has been reported as tolerated by officers to the extent that one conscript described the unit as "the most homophobic environment that exists".

Gay and bisexual men may donate blood through the territorial blood service if they have not had sex with another man in the past 12 months, with a 12-month deferral likewise applied to women who have sexual relations with men who have sex with men.

Protection on the ground of sexual orientation arrived only after failed and dropped proposals in 2004–2006 and 2009; gender identity was not added at any point in that sequence.
SYN-BMU.blindOutOfScope:
Whether local authorities recognise a changed gender marker on a foreign passport or identity document is not sourced; the record contains no provision either way, and this remains unresolved rather than permissive or restrictive.

The record contains no trans-specific violence or homicide figures for this division, so no comparison against the general homicide rate can be made, and no incident involving a transgender person after the 2006 parade episode is documented. An undocumented present is not evidence of an absent risk.

The year of the cruise ship protest recorded on 12 July is not given in the source, which dates it only to that day; the year remains unresolved.

Whether the equality statute's sexual-orientation protection has ever been applied to conduct or presentation read as gender-nonconforming is not sourced, and no reported enforcement or complaint machinery specific to transgender people is identified.

SYN-COK.name: Cook Islands
SYN-COK.summary: The Cook Islands is the entire jurisdiction, so a single national legal framework applies across all islands with no subnational variation. Geographically it is a small, tourism-oriented Polynesian archipelago whose economy, centred on Rarotonga, routinely absorbs foreign visitors, and everyday hostility toward trans guests tends to be lower than in less tourism-dependent places. Traditional Cook Islands culture recognises gender-diverse people, referred to locally as akava'ine (with raerae and māhū used in related regional usage), and an established community gives trans visitors a degree of visibility and social acceptance. Against this, churches and family life are broadly conservative Christian, and the small, close-knit society means anonymity is minimal: once known, a visitor's gender history can become common knowledge quickly, with misgendering, curiosity, privacy exposure or disapproval more likely outcomes than state hostility. No trans-specific criminal offence, border or police targeting, facility restriction or pattern of violence against trans visitors is documented — but coverage is thin, so this absence should not be read as proof of safety. Practical protections are limited: there is no local legal gender recognition, no gender-identity anti-discrimination or hate-crime coverage, and facilities and custody arrangements follow birth sex in practice. Gender-affirming healthcare is scarce, service and care continuity can be uneven, and formal recourse through small institutions is thin, with outer islands having fewer services than Rarotonga. Overall, conditions cut both ways — a low general-crime, hospitable, tourism-facing setting alongside church-influenced conservatism where being outed can invite social friction rather than detention.

sources.summary: PinkNews (14 Apr 2023): Cook Islands parliament voted on Friday to remove the never-enforced 'indecent acts between males' law — exposure of up to 10 years under the 1969 Crimes Act — through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023; a note in the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBTQ+ people, and the bill also adds protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault. Same-sex marriage remains outlawed under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000.

PinkNews (1 Oct 2020): decriminalisation stalled again — MPs deferred the Crimes Bill report by three months. Traces the full path: colonial-era 1969 sections 154/155 (up to 7 years for sex between men) criminalise; a 2017 select committee recommended removing them and 'indecent acts between men'/sodomy were struck from the draft, but MPs later backtracked and the kick-down-the-road continued; notes colonisation introduced the taboo into a historically accepting society.

PinkNews (3 Aug 2017): draft Crimes Bill, written with New Zealand help, would remove sections 154/155 of the 1969 Crimes Act — up to 7 years for gay sex and 5 years for 'any indecent act with or upon any other male', with consent explicitly not a defence. Population 21,000; the country's only LGBTI community group, Te Tiare Association, welcomed the move (member Valentino Wichman quoted on the law's homophobia).

RNZ Pacific (10 Aug 2017): public submissions opened in parliament on the Cook Islands Crimes Bill intended to replace the widely considered outdated 1969 Crimes Act. The clerk of Parliament, John Tangi, confirmed a submission from the Te Tiare Association representing the country's LGBTI community was already before the select committee; at least three lawyers expected to speak on penalties and sentencing.

SYN-COK.tangentialFactors: The repeal concluded a reform process that had run since 2017, when a draft Crimes Bill written with New Zealand legal assistance would have removed sections 154 and 155; a select committee recommended deletion and the offences were struck from the draft, after which members reversed that decision and, in October 2020, deferred the bill's report by a further three months. Public submissions on the 2017 bill were taken by a parliamentary select committee in a country of roughly 21,000 people, and at least three lawyers were expected to address penalties and sentencing.
SYN-COK.localsOnly:
Te Tiare Association is the country's LGBTI community organisation, and its submission was before the select committee examining the 2017 draft Crimes Bill. The offences struck from the draft at that stage were restored by members before the 2023 amendment finally removed them.

The Marriage Amendment Act 2000 continues to govern who may marry locally, so same-sex marriages cannot be entered into in the Cook Islands.

No sourced material in the inventory addresses gender-marker or passport policy for trans travellers, gender-recognition procedures, healthcare access, facility use, hate-crime or anti-discrimination protection, or police practice in the Cook Islands. Nothing in the available sources documents a trans-specific prosecution, enforcement action or violent incident.

The maximum penalties recorded for the repealed sections 154 and 155 are inconsistent across sources: seven years and five years in the 2017 reporting, up to ten years in reporting on the repeal. The discrepancy is unresolved, and whether the offences were ever applied before living memory is not established either.
