SYN-CUW.name: Curaçao
SYN-CUW.summary:
Curaçao is an autonomous constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, with full autonomy except in defence, foreign affairs and matters reserved to the Supreme Court of the Netherlands.

Both male and female same-sex sexual activity is legal, with an equal age of consent of 16 for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. A trans visitor in a relationship read locally as same-sex faces no conduct offence on that basis.

Same-sex marriage has been legal in Curaçao since 12 July 2024, when the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld an Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation. Before that ruling, Curaçao recognised as valid same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, but offered no in-island marriage, civil union or other form of recognition.

Recognition arrived by court order rather than by statute. A limited-rights proposal was put to the Estates of Curaçao in 2017, and a marriage bill submitted on 4 June 2019 was withdrawn in September 2020 for lack of support. In April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed that LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should receive equal rights quickly, and the August 2015 Oliari and Others v. Italy judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, applicable to Curaçao, required legal recognition.

The Criminal Code enacted in 2011 prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds that include heterosexual or homosexual orientation. Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any distinction affecting the recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights in political, economic, social, cultural or other social life, and Articles 2:61 and 2:62 set penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The protected grounds named in the source material do not include gender identity, and no Curaçao-specific authority on gender-identity coverage was identified.

Official rhetoric has not consistently governed practice. In April 2015 commissioner Marvelyne Wiels of Pueblo Soberano publicly backed equal rights for everyone in the local press, while her party colleague Winifred Raveneau opposed the rights push fiercely and used a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit requirement to force Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel premises. Public LGBT assembly on the island can be obstructed through administrative permitting at short notice.

Curaçao opened an LGBT community centre, the Pink House, in 2010, and alongside Aruba and Sint Maarten has acted as a driver of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom. Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag cites an IGLTA award naming the island the most gay welcoming in the region, and a rights wishes-package was delivered to ministers in The Hague.

No Curaçao-specific sourcing was found on gender markers in locally issued identity documents, entry or border screening triggered by gender presentation, access to gender-affirming care, or the designation of facilities. Those areas are unassessed rather than cleared.

SYN-CYM.name: Cayman Islands
SYN-CYM.summary:
The Cayman Islands' constitutional discrimination grounds were drafted in 2009 without sexual-orientation protection. The omission drew criticism from the United Kingdom parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee, which called it deplorable and warned that Cayman courts could afford less protection than Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights requires; the Foreign and Commonwealth Office answered that the list of grounds was open-ended. No enumerated constitutional ground anchors a discrimination claim, and no trans-specific ground is listed.

No domestic route to marriage exists. In March 2019 Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie struck down the statutory prohibition on same-sex marriage; the Court of Appeal overturned that ruling in August 2019 and restored the ban. Recognition survives at the level of immigration administration: in December 2020 immigration authorities recognised the overseas marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder, who had wed in Ireland, and the Court of Appeal held that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds. For a trans visitor whose relationship would be locally classed as same-sex, an overseas marriage therefore carries immigration effects even though the territory offers no domestic route to marry.

Public visibility in the tourist-facing environment is high. Around 600 people, among them the premier, the governor, ministers and members of the Legislative Assembly, joined the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation's first Pride parade on 7 August 2021, with broad official participation.

No trans-specific legal provision is documented for the Cayman Islands. Nothing in the available sources addresses gender recognition, identity documents, single-sex facilities, healthcare access or hate-crime protection, and no trans-specific incident or enforcement action is recorded.

sources.summary: PinkNews (11 Aug 2009): UK MPs on the Foreign Affairs Committee criticised the Cayman Islands' draft constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission 'deplorable' and warning the drafting could leave Cayman courts affording citizens less protection than the European Convention on Human Rights Art 14 requires; the FCO countered that the discrimination-grounds list was open-ended. Early-dated evidence of London–local friction over LGBT protections that frames the later recognition rulings.

Cayman News Service (29 Jul 2021): around 600 people — including the premier, the governor, ministers and MLAs — joined the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation's first Pride parade (Sat 7 Aug 2021 debut), an historic turnout with broad official participation; participants were asked to refrain from excessive displays of affection (organisers' condition amid public-space sensitivities). Evidence of high official tolerance in the tourist-facing environment.

Washington Blade (30 Dec 2020): immigration authorities recognised the overseas same-sex marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder, who wed in Ireland. The Court of Appeal held that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds. Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie had struck down the same-sex marriage ban in March 2019; that ruling was overturned on appeal in Aug 2019, while the recognition-for-immigration-effects line survived.

SYN-ESH.name: Western Sahara
SYN-ESH.summary:
Western Sahara is a disputed territory with no single legal order running through it. Morocco controls most of the ground and Moroccan security services, courts and detention facilities operate there; the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic claims sovereignty and governs through exile institutions and refugee camps in Algeria. Which framework a visitor stands under depends on which part of the territory they are in.

Moroccan jurisdiction reaches into the territory in practice. On 9 December 2005 Human Rights Watch reported the trial of seven human-rights defenders from Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara on charges of fomenting illegal protests, called the charges dubious and demanded a fair trial. The case shows Moroccan courts and detention operating on Sahrawi political cases, not only on paper.

Same-sex intimacy is criminalised under both frameworks. Moroccan law carries six months to three years of imprisonment. For the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, the Council for Global Equality, Equaldex and ILGA record same-sex sexual activity as illegal for both men and women, punishable by up to three years, and a July 2017 PinkNews roundup listed the SADR among jurisdictions where homosexuality is illegal for men and women and had been for decades. A trans visitor in a relationship that local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status therefore stands inside a criminal prohibition in either part of the territory.

The SADR's own position is contested. In 2010 Ahmed Mulay Alli, the SADR's diplomatic representative in Mexico, said the Constitution 'does not refer to homosexuality or any other sexual practice... it does not punish it'. The Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid (CEAR) reads the same silence as leaving LGBTQ people with no legal protection against discrimination or violence. Constitutional silence is not decriminalisation, and no statute in the inventory decriminalises anything.

The only documented account of the Sahrawi authorities applying such charges comes from a 2009 USCRI report: officials running the refugee camps in Algeria said they were holding some prisoners on 'homosexuality' charges while alleging facts that would more fittingly describe rape. The charge sits in the hands of camp administration rather than a court.

Social exposure is high. Most residents are Muslim, and relationships between people of the same sex are widely read as a foreign phenomenon.

No source in the inventory records a trans-specific statute, a protection mechanism, or a documented case of a trans visitor being processed under either framework.

The partially-recognised state, an African Union member since 2016, claims sovereignty over Western Sahara. The status recorded for July 2017 is criminalised.

SYN-FLK.name: Falkland Islands (Malvinas)
SYN-FLK.summary:
The Falkland Islands are a British Overseas Territory with their own Legislative Assembly, which legislates locally; the United Kingdom is responsible for the territory's defence. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and Gender Recognition Act 2004 do not extend to the Islands, so legal protection and gender recognition depend on the territory's own ordinances.

Same-sex activity has been legal since 1989 and the age of consent has been equal since 2005.

Marriage and civil partnerships have been available since 29 April 2017. The Legislative Assembly passed the bill in March 2017 by 7 votes to 1, and the registrar general confirmed by reply in June 2017 that it is law. Civil partnerships are open to opposite-sex as well as same-sex couples, and a trans visitor whose relationship would be classed as same-sex under local birth-sex status can marry or register a civil partnership on the same terms. A public consultation ahead of the bill recorded 90% support for same-sex marriage and 94% for civil partnerships in a territory of roughly 3,000 residents.

Legal gender change has been possible since 2014 under the CPE Ordinance 2014. There is no self-identification route and no recognition of non-binary status. Holders of a UK Gender Recognition Certificate are recognised in their acquired gender under that ordinance.

The Constitution Order 2008, at Article 16, bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The provision covers sexual orientation only; no gender-identity ground is identified in it.

Two ordinances frame the criminal-justice treatment of bias. The Crimes Ordinance 2014 provides for hate-stirring on grounds of sexual orientation, and the CPE Ordinance 2014 makes sexual orientation an aggravating factor in sentencing. On the sources available, neither ground extends to gender identity.

sources.summary: PinkNews (12 Apr 2017): the Legislative Assembly passed same-sex marriage (7-1) plus civil partnerships open to same-sex AND opposite-sex couples, after a public consultation showing 90% support for same-sex marriage and 94% for civil partnerships in the ~3,000-resident territory — the operative equality reform.

Rob Salerno blog (22 Jun 2017): the Falklands registrar general confirmed by reply that the same-sex marriage and civil partnership bill passed in March is law, resolving the outstanding question of its assent; the same registrar confirmed that same-sex marriage is not legal in the South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands dependency.

SYN-FRO.name: Faroe Islands
SYN-FRO.summary:
The anti-discrimination provision in force since 1 January 2007 makes anyone who publicly makes a statement threatening, insulting or degrading a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation liable to a fine or up to two years' imprisonment. Gender identity is not among the listed grounds. On the sourced account this made the Faroe Islands the last Northern European jurisdiction to prohibit discrimination and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation.

Before that provision took effect, homophobic conduct was legally unaddressed. In 2006 the openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host Rasmus Rasmussen was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out; he and his family then received threatening telephone calls, and police refused to handle the case because no Faroese law banned discrimination against sexual minorities at the time. He was later moved to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression exacerbated by the beating, never recovered, and died by suicide in 2012. The most recent documented assault in this record is that 2006 attack; no later instance is documented.

A second documented attack dates from 2005, when the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men intent on physically assaulting them in Tórshavn; the group was not attacked anywhere else on its tour.

Hostility from elected office is documented across a decade. In September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for the visiting Icelandic prime minister and her partner, citing his religion. In June 2015 Løgting Speaker Jógvan á Lakjuni published a letter attacking the national broadcaster Kringvarp Føroya for the space it gave LGBT Føroyar and condemning a drag show at the Nordic House as 'non-culture', asking whether 'these people do not feel any shame'. The same year av Rana demanded that Pride be banned and repeatedly compared LGBT Føroyar to Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters, and his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality. Singer Eivor Pálsdóttir publicly urged people to ignore him, documenting organised public pushback alongside the hostility.

Public expression has been contested since the first gay pride march in 2005, which provoked substantial controversy; in 2015 av Rana also suggested the Tórshavn pride parade be moved out of the city centre.

Partner recognition is unresolved in this record. In 2006 LGBT activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures demanding an end to sexual-orientation discrimination and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics; at that point the Faroe Islands, with a population of about 47,000, had neither protection nor partnership recognition. No later sourced statement establishes the current status of partnership or marriage registration here.

sources.summary: PinkNews (9 Nov 2006): LGBT activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures demanding an end to sexual-orientation discrimination and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics; at the time the Faroes (population ~47,000, self-governing within Denmark) had neither protection, leaving homophobia legally unaddressed.

PinkNews (7 Sep 2010): Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for visiting Icelandic PM Johanna Sigurdardottir and her partner, citing his religion — signals the prominence of religiously motivated opposition to openly gay public figures in Faroese politics.

SYN-GGY.name: Guernsey
SYN-GGY.summary:
Guernsey is a self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, the States of Guernsey, and its own statute book. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex services code issued under it in 2025 do not apply here automatically; United Kingdom measures reach Guernsey only by Order in Council.

Same-sex sexual activity is lawful for men and women. Decriminalisation preceded 1983, when the age of consent was set at 21 in line with the United Kingdom; the male same-sex age of consent fell to 18 in 2000 and was equalised at 16 by legislation approved in 2011 that took effect on 5 November 2012. Guernsey nonetheless retains specific male homosexual offences in its criminal law, including a ban on homosexual sexual acts not conducted in private, which can expose men to prosecution for private-life conduct that is lawful elsewhere.

Transgender people have been able to legally change their gender since 2007, including obtaining a new birth certificate. Guernsey law only allows a new birth certificate to be issued and does not amend or remove records from existing birth certificates, so prior gender markers remain on the original record.

Guernsey is the only part of the British Isles never to have enacted civil partnership legislation, though United Kingdom civil partnerships were recognised for succession purposes from 2 April 2012. The States of Guernsey approved same-sex marriage on 10 December 2015 by a vote of 37 to 7, rejecting both a civil-partnership-only option and a single 'Union Civile' alternative; implementing legislation was to be separate and was not expected before 2017.

A 2004 law enabled the States of Guernsey to pass Ordinances banning discrimination, and the Sex Discrimination (Employment) (Guernsey) Ordinance, 2005 banned discrimination based on gender identity. As of 2020 no equivalent Ordinance had specifically outlawed discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Anti-discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity existed in child welfare proceedings in Guernsey and Alderney since 2008 and in Sark since 2016. In September 2022 the States of Guernsey passed a comprehensive anti-discrimination bill unanimously (33-0) explicitly including sexual orientation, rejecting all amendments proposing exemptions for small businesses of five employees or fewer and for religious affiliations; it takes effect from 1 October 2023.

Guernsey's only prison, Les Nicolles, opened in 1989 and holds male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages; it has 11 wings, capacity 139, is operated by the States of Guernsey, and held about 99 prisoners in November 2024. No rule on housing prisoners by birth sex versus gender identity, no separate unit for trans prisoners, and no solitary or segregation practice for them is recorded.

The States of Guernsey repealed the 50-year Adoption Law's ban on unmarried couples adopting on 24 June 2015, agreeing that same-sex couples may adopt, with civil partnerships recognised and equal parental responsibility for both partners; Jersey had approved the same change two days earlier. The Billet d'État of 24 June 2015 records the review of Adoption Law at p.1170, which led to adoption rights for same-sex couples.

Guernsey adopted the United Kingdom's relaxed blood-donor rules on 23 September 2011, making gay and bisexual men eligible after a 12-month deferral, targeted to around 7 November 2011 to match the United Kingdom change, ending the local 1980s HIV-era ban; other donation restrictions were unchanged.

SYN-GIB.name: Gibraltar
SYN-GIB.summary: The region is subject to Gibraltar's national law in full, with no local exception. Gibraltar is a single compact jurisdiction, so the territory-wide legal picture is what a visitor meets on the ground: British-style courts and policing operate in a small, English-speaking, tourist-facing place where visitors are routine, openly LGBT people are visible, and an annual Pride is held. Discretion is limited by the density of the territory — a close-knit, partly socially conservative community where a trans visitor is conspicuous and anonymity is scarce, so encounters in hotels, clinics and with police turn largely on the individuals involved. Friction, stares and the occasional service problem are the more plausible forms of difficulty here. The frontier with Spain is operated under Spanish procedures outside Gibraltar's control, so checks there are not governed by the territory's own institutions. No incidents of police targeting, facility exclusion or violence against trans visitors are documented in the material available for Gibraltar; equally, how officials handle document discrepancies, how the protections operate in practice, and current social attitudes toward trans visitors are not established — that gap should not be read as reassurance.

sources.summary: The UK House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee's Seventh Report (2007-08) on Overseas Territories sets accountability and good-governance expectations that apply to Gibraltar as an overseas territory; it also records corruption concerns raised in Turks and Caicos.

El País in English (15 Aug 2016): Gibraltar put a draft bill amending the Civil Marriage Act for same-sex marriage before Parliament after a December 2015 consultation that left Gibraltarians polarized; a government minister presided over an inter-ministerial committee weighing all viewpoints, with popular consultation and main parties suggesting support for the change.

Gibraltar Chronicle (22 Jul 2021): the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would 'urgently' consider legislation to tackle 'disgusting lurking homophobia' following an incident of anti-gay abuse.

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror): LGBTQ rights in Gibraltar - legal since 1993, equal age of consent since 2012, adoption right by Supreme Court ruling 2013, civil partnerships since 2014, same-sex marriage since Dec 2016 (passed unanimously), discrimination protections for sexual orientation and 'gender reassignment' since 2007; transgender persons not allowed to change legal gender.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Gibraltar's Parliament passed a bill on 19 September 2013, given royal assent on 25 September and in force on 10 October, amending the Crimes Act 2011 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation as a hate crime. In July 2021 the Justice Ministry began investigating a further proposal to make denigration of a person on the basis of sexual orientation a specific criminal offence, prompted by what Chief Minister Fabian Picardo called 'disgusting lurking homophobia' on social media during Pride month. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for 'transgender identity'. The Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, de jure legalising LGBT adoption, after a long-term lesbian couple denied adoption for lack of legal recognition of their relationship challenged the law; the government amended the law through the 2014 civil partnership legislation. The Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024 and explicitly allows same-sex couples to adopt children without discrimination. In February 2021 Gibraltar enacted a surrogacy law permitting non-commercial, altruistic surrogacy for married couples or civil partners unable to conceive, with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination. In June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority approved an amendment to its in vitro fertilisation policy allowing lesbian couples to access assisted reproductive technology. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practice conversion therapy. The age of consent for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender was equalised at 16. The Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 8 April 2011 that the higher age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set an equal age of consent of 16 that took effect on 23 November 2012. Before that, gay male minors faced a discriminatory age of 18, and a private member's bill to equalise consent was defeated in Parliament on 18 May 2009. The Foreign Affairs Committee's 2008 enquiry into overseas territories recommended making discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status illegal in all overseas territories.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Gibraltar (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The Equal Opportunities Act 2006, in force on 1 March 2007, prohibits discrimination in employment and the provision of goods and services on the ground of "gender reassignment". The Act defines "gender reassignment" as "a process for the purpose of reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex". The 2008 Foreign Affairs Committee enquiry into the overseas territories concluded that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status should be made illegal in all overseas territories. In July 2026, Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for "transgender identity". In July 2026, Parliament passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practice conversion therapy, stated generally without specifying sexual orientation versus transgender scope in the excerpt. Male same-sex sexual activity defined legally as male sodomy was decriminalized in Gibraltar in 1993 following pressure from the European Court of Human Rights and Government of the United Kingdom, with no equivalent provision for women because Victorian-drafted law only addressed men. The Supreme Court ruled on 8 April 2011 that an age of consent of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, mandating 16 and decriminalising heterosexual anal sex at 16, implemented in statute by the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011 approved in August 2011 and effective 23 November 2012 setting 16 regardless of sexual orientation. Civil partnerships have been available since March 2014 granting most rights of marriage including adoption as mandated by the 2013 ruling, and same-sex marriage was legalised by the Civil Marriage Amendment Act 2016 passed unanimously on 26 October 2016, receiving royal assent on 1 November and taking effect on 15 December 2016 with the first marriage the next day, requiring assignment of an alternative registrar where a deputy registrar opts out. The 2006 Constitution does not mention sexual orientation after 2002 proposals omitted it, but the Equal Opportunities Act 2006 effective 1 March 2007 prohibits discrimination in employment and goods and services on grounds including sexual orientation defined as orientation towards persons of the same sex, opposite sex, or both. Amendments to the Crimes Act 2011 approved 19 September 2013, assented 25 September and effective 10 October 2013 criminalised hatred and harassment on the ground of sexual orientation, while in July 2021 the Justice Ministry was investigating proposals against lurking homophobia including a possible specific offence of denigrating a person as a result of sexual orientation.

SYN-GIB.displaySummary: Gibraltar is a self-governing British Overseas Territory with its own Parliament and Supreme Court; the national record for United Kingdom covers the federal layer in detail. The principal legal gap facing a trans visitor is gender recognition: no process exists in Gibraltar for changing a legal gender marker, and transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore travels on a document whose marker cannot be altered by any local route, and can expect to be read at the border and in public under that marker. Statutory discrimination protection covering gender reassignment has been in place since the Equal Opportunities Act 2006 took effect on 1 March 2007. The Act prohibits discrimination in employment and in the provision of goods and services on the ground of gender reassignment, defined as a process for the purpose of reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex. Sexual orientation is a protected ground under the same Act. Hate-crime coverage extends to trans people. Parliament amended the Crimes Act 2011 in September 2013 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, with approval on 19 September, royal assent on 25 September and effect from 10 October 2013. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for transgender identity. In July 2021 the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would urgently consider legislation to tackle what the Chief Minister, Fabian Picardo, called "disgusting lurking homophobia" on social media during Pride month, following an incident of anti-gay abuse. The proposal at that stage concerned sexual orientation; the trans-inclusive amendment came in July 2026. In July 2026 Parliament also passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practise conversion therapy; the sourced excerpt states the offence generally without specifying whether its scope covers sexual orientation, transgender identity, or both. Partner recognition is established locally. Civil partnerships have been available since March 2014, and same-sex marriage since 15 December 2016, after the Civil Marriage Amendment Act passed unanimously on 26 October 2016, received royal assent on 1 November and took effect on 15 December, with the first marriage the following day. A deputy registrar may opt out, requiring assignment of an alternative registrar. Because no gender-recognition route exists, a trans visitor's legal sex for marriage purposes remains that recorded at birth; a relationship locally read as same-sex can be registered. Adoption is open to same-sex couples. The Supreme Court ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, and the Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024, expressly allowing same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination. The age of consent is 16 for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender. The Supreme Court ruled on 8 April 2011 that the previous age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set the equal age of 16 with effect from 23 November 2012.

SYN-GLP.name: Guadeloupe
SYN-GLP.summary:
Guadeloupe is a French overseas department. Criminal law, identity-document rules, custodial conditions and the national preventive mechanism are set at the national level and carried by the parent record; this assessment covers what is specific to the island.

Guadeloupe's first LGBT+ centre, the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened on 24 April 2024, run by a federation of Guadeloupean associations. It offers reception, support and orientation for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities.

The opening was attended by the visiting national minister Aurore Bergé, who announced measures to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence and discrimination in Guadeloupe, with structures adapted for the overseas territories. The centre's opening was presented as a concrete step toward inclusion and safety.

Community organisations Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova partnered on a year of LGBT-friendly social events across Guadeloupe in 2025, described locally as a potential 'annus mirabilis' for the island's community.

A September 2023 interview with Leïla of Secret's Out reported that community members increasingly reconcile their lives with their orientation, and described activism on the island as advancing after neighbouring Martinique; the interview also featured Prisca Melyon-Reinette of Amalgame Humani's.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: French law applicable in Guadeloupe decriminalised same-sex relations in the Penal Code of 1791 and retained this in the 1810 Code, while public morality laws continued to be used against LGBTQ people; in Alsace and Lorraine, annexed in 1940, men were interned in Nazi camps and persecuted under Vichy despite the absence of a sodomy law. Vichy's article 334 of 6 August 1942 (later 331) set consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. The Mirguet amendment of 1960 doubled penalties for indecent exposure in homosexual activity (art. 330, 2nd alinea), repealed in 1980. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for men arrested under article 330 before 1980; the Senate has yet to vote. A conversion therapy ban passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and was published on 1 February 2022, carrying two years' imprisonment and/or €30,000. The law of December 2004, passed 31 December 2004, made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal, with a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment; civil liberties groups including Reporters Without Borders called it a serious infringement of free speech. It created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité and amended the 1881 Freedom of the Press Law to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination on grounds of gender, sexual orientation or disability. Christian Vanneste, an MP from the ruling UMP party, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006, though that conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Pride has been held in Paris since 4 April 1981 (Place Maubert, about 10,000 people), reaching 500,000 participants in 2019, with events in dozens of other cities. Transgender people have changed legal gender without surgery or medical diagnosis since 1 January 2017 (law signed 18 November 2016), but must still appear before a court to change the gender marker; a first name change can be done at the registry office. Self-certification of gender and proof of medical treatment were both dropped from the final bill. Until 2015 France refused to recognise surrogate children as French citizens, leaving many in legal limbo; the Court of Cassation ruled on 5 July 2017 that a child born to a surrogate abroad can be adopted by the partner of the biological father, the Court of Appeal of Paris held in May 2019 that a Canadian birth certificate must be recognised, and in December 2019 the Court of Cassation ruled that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France. In 2022 a court of appeal ruled that a transgender woman should be considered the mother of the child she conceived before her sex change, while a 2017 legal bid for 'neutral sex' classification was rejected by the Court of Cassation. In 2010 France became the first country to declassify gender dysphoria as a mental illness, removing gender identity disorder by decree, though French trans rights organisations said nothing changed beyond the announcement; transsexualism remains under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender-affirming surgery has been legal domestically since 1979. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems in gender-affirming healthcare: lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, recommending an informed-consent, self-determination model. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned the Little Mermaid Observatory, a group opposed to all gender transition for minors, to report on youth gender care, which called transition a 'health scandal' and transness a 'social contagion'; a bill to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, opposed by the Macron government, with no update since 23 July 2024, while in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first trans youth guidelines recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2. Blood donation deferrals for gay and bi men were cut to four months in April 2020 and abolished entirely on 16 March 2022. The French Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and 'a primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access, though this did not change actual practice. In October 2018 President Macron denounced homophobic violence as 'unworthy of France' after a rise in attacks, and a report released 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against about 1,380 in 2018. In 2022 it emerged that the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, France's interministerial body against racism, anti-Semitism and anti-LGBT hatred, was a member of The Little Mermaid Observatory; one member resigned and the president stepped away. In March 2008 Education Minister Xavier Darcos announced a policy fighting all forms of discrimination including homophobia in schools as one of 15 national education priorities for 2008–2009. In January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the campaign 'Tous égaux, tous alliés' to tackle anti-LGBTQ bullying, providing reporting services, a helpline for students and staff, and requiring all French schools to give guidance on LGBTQ issues, with 17 May as a special sensitisation day. In March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms; in February 2019 the use of 'parent 1' and 'parent 2' on school enrolment forms caused widespread conservative outrage. Legislation to ban medical transition for under-18s passed the Senate in May 2024, prompting large-scale protests, making trans minors a direct legislative target.

SYN-GUF.name: French Guiana
SYN-GUF.summary:
French Guiana is an overseas department of France and has no gender-identity legislation of its own. Criminal law, identity documents, anti-discrimination provisions and the marriage regime that operate here are the French national ones, applied without local variation.

Detention carries the most serious documented risk. No local protocol governs the custody of transgender detainees, so placement in French Guiana's facilities follows the national practice: assignment to a men's or women's wing is based on the detainee's legal gender and decided case by case, without a consistent protective standard.

Specialist gender-affirming care is not provided locally on the same basis as in metropolitan France. Patients travel to the mainland for surgery and specialist assessment, and the journey adds cost and delay to every medical step, including any undertaken during a stay in the department.

Transphobia and cultural taboos discourage visibility in the department, and abuse is less likely to be reported, including to the police. Under-reporting is a feature of the local situation rather than evidence that abuse is rare.

CGLPL opinion (25 May 2021) on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: serious violations persist across French places of detention, applicable in French Guiana.

Grokipedia page on transgender rights in French Guiana: France's national framework applies — simplified legal gender recognition since 2017 (administrative declaration, no surgery/sterilisation/diagnosis), anti-discrimination protections since 2012, hate-crime provisions 2017; specialised trans healthcare limited by remoteness; societal transphobia and cultural taboos discourage visibility and reporting.
No usable finding on the safety of trans visitors in French Guiana.

GayOut travel guide for French Guiana: same-sex relations legal, same-sex marriage legal (French law), Pride events held; rated 'Very Safe for LGBTQ+'; no listed venues - a small scene anchored in Cayenne.
Gayther LGBTQIA+ country guide for French Guiana covers equality index, gender-identity recognition, and same-sex union and marriage data; no specific figures or findings were available from it.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in French Guiana (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: France removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree in 2010, becoming the first country to declassify gender dysphoria as mental illness, with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale. Since 1 January 2017 under the law signed 18 November 2016 after the Constitutional Council ruling of 17 November, transgender people may change legal gender marker by court order without sex reassignment surgery, sterilisation, psychiatrist certificate or medical diagnosis, with first-name change available at the registry office. This followed a decades-long legislative ban on legal gender change despite the 1959 change for Coccinelle and 1979 legalisation of gender-affirming surgery inside France, overturned only after the 1992 B. v France case at the European Court of Human Rights. Discrimination on the ground of "sexual identity" was prohibited from July 2012, with the term replaced by "gender identity" on 18 November 2016 amending Penal Code article 225-1 and Labour Code protections covering recruitment, internships, training, sanction and dismissal. Since 2017 transphobia is an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison, and police identified around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018. Gender-affirming healthcare was found by a 2022 ILGA-Europe report to lack self-determination with extended waiting times and location-dependent inequitable access recommending informed consent and self-determination, while the National Academy of Medicine advises extreme caution and actual practice is unchanged. For youth, the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the first national guidelines in late 2024 recommending puberty blockers from at least Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D supplements, while a Senate-passed May 2024 bill to ban medical transition under age 18 following the March 2024 Little Mermaid Observatory report has had no update since 23 July 2024 and is opposed by the Macron government. Private same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 and retained in the Penal Code of 1810 applied to nations and French colonies, ending ancien régime capital punishments including castration, dismemberment and burning with the last burning on 6 July 1750. A discriminatory age of consent of 21 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual relations introduced 6 August 1942 as article 334, moved to article 331 in 1945 and lowered to 18 in 1974, was equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982 under President Mitterrand, while the discriminatory 1960 Mirguet amendment to Penal Code article 330 alinea 2 doubling penalty for homosexual indecent exposure was repealed in 1980 with a March 2024 National Assembly unanimous compensation bill for pre-1980 Article 330 victims pending Senate vote. Discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since 1985 in employment, housing and public and private provision of goods and services, codified in the Labour Code. The law of 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments with a maximum penalty of 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months imprisonment and amended the Law on Freedom of the Press of 29 July 1881 to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination based on gender, sexual orientation or disability, while physical assault or murder motivated by victim sexual orientation carries increased penalties, and created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité. Same-sex marriage following civil solidarity pacts in 1999 was legalised in 2013 with the law signed 18 May 2013 after the 17 May Constitutional Council ruling and first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier, and is legal in all overseas departments and territories, with French Guiana's two deputies recording one vote in favour and one abstention. Lesbian, gay and bisexual people may serve openly in the Armed Forces, men who have sex with men blood-donation abstinence requirements of one year from 10 July 2016 and four months from 2 April 2020 were fully removed 16 March 2022 to an orientation-neutral policy, and the conversion therapy ban passed the Senate 7 December 2020, the National Assembly 25 January 2022 and was published 1 February 2022.

Specialist gender-affirming care is not provided locally on the same basis as in metropolitan France. Patients travel to the mainland for surgery and specialist assessment, and the journey adds cost and delay to every medical step, including any undertaken during a stay in the department. SYN-IMN.name: Isle of Man
SYN-IMN.summary:
The Isle of Man is a self-legislating Crown Dependency of the United Kingdom. Tynwald enacts its own statutes on gender recognition, equality and criminal law, and United Kingdom legislation reaches the island only when extended by Order in Council rather than automatically.

The Gender Recognition Act 2009 (c.11) allows transgender people to change their legal gender and to have the new gender recognised. The Equality Act 2017, granted royal assent on 18 July 2017 and largely in force from 1 January 2019, lists gender reassignment as a protected characteristic and as a ground on which discrimination is prohibited.

A ban on conversion therapy covering sexual orientation and gender identity was passed in 2020 as an amendment to the sexual offences bill in the Legislative Council and took effect in 2024. In 2024 the Isle of Man became the first British territory, and the first part of the British Isles, to prohibit the practice.

In July 2022 community consultation progressed on a hate crime bill that would explicitly include gender reassignment alongside sexual orientation and marital or civil partnership status. The bill's status after that consultation is not sourced.

Sexual offences law applies gender-neutrally. Private consensual male homosexual acts were decriminalised in September 1992 with an age of consent of twenty-one, lowered to eighteen by the Criminal Justice Act 2001 (c.4), then lowered to sixteen and made gender-neutral for all sexual conduct regardless of gender and sexual orientation by the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2006 (c.3). Until 2021, Section 9 of the Sexual Offences Act 1992 retained offences of buggery and gross indecency between men if under sixteen or committed elsewhere than in private; in 2021 the more-than-two-persons specification was deleted and language on indecent exposure and sexual activity in a public place was made gender-neutral under the Sexual Offences and Obscene Publications Act 2021, which received royal assent in July 2021 and took effect on 1 July 2022 by proclamation.

On partner recognition, same-sex couples have held civil partnerships since 6 April 2011 under the Civil Partnership Act 2011 (c.2), and marriage has been available since 22 July 2016 following royal assent on 19 July 2016. Existing civil partnerships could be converted without a second ceremony, and the first conversion was completed within days of entry into force. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as same-sex enters a jurisdiction that recognises the union.

Family law has not kept pace with that recognition. Under the Civil Partnership Act 2011, same-sex couples have had equal access to full joint or stepchild adoption since 6 April 2011 and lesbian couples have access to artificial insemination, but as of an August 2023 consultation same-sex couples are not recognised as parents on birth certificates in cases of IVF and surrogacy, and no law on the island acknowledges surrogacy.

SYN-MSR.name: Montserrat
SYN-MSR.summary:
Montserrat is a British Overseas Territory and stands under the United Kingdom's framework, including the European Convention on Human Rights and its non-discrimination and equality obligations.

Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults in private has been lawful since 2001, when the prohibitions were swept away retrospectively by an Order in Council under Sections 3(1) and 3(7) of the Caribbean Territories (Criminal Law) Order, 2000. Lesbian conduct was never an offence. Group sex and sex in public remain criminal offences for all persons.

The age of consent is 18 for homosexual activity and 16 for heterosexual activity. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex therefore falls under the higher threshold of 18.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal. Article 10(1) of the Constitution protects only opposite-sex marriage, providing that every man and woman of marriageable age has the right to marry a person of the opposite sex and to found a family. A trans visitor's partner would not be recognised as a spouse or civil partner.

Article 16 of the Montserrat Constitution and Article 79 of the Labour Code prohibit discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, defining 'discriminatory' as affording different treatment on grounds such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion or other status. Neither provision names gender identity among the enumerated grounds, which end with an open-ended 'other status'.

There are no gay bars, nightclubs or other dedicated venues on the island. Several hotels welcome gay tourists and operate non-discrimination policies, which is the main documented point of entry for a visitor seeking a welcoming environment.

sources.summary: GlobalGayz 'Gay Life in Montserrat' (Sept 2012): a 104 km2 island reshaped by Hurricane Hugo (1989) and the 1995 Soufriere Hills eruption, which wastelanded the south and displaced over half the population north. Gay life barely exists locally: 'gays are everywhere but hardly here,' and the social scene is decimated.

Associated Press report (Jan 2001, via GLAPN): Britain scrapped the anti-gay statutes in five Caribbean territories including Montserrat and Turks & Caicos, saying they violated signed international human rights agreements — the legal basis on which Montserrat's prohibitions were eventually swept away; local politicians and religious leaders opposed, framed as a cultural rift with London.

SYN-MTQ.name: Martinique
SYN-MTQ.summary:
Martinique is an overseas department of France and stands under the French national framework in full: Article 73 of the Constitution applies French law to the island, so the identity documents, criminal law, anti-discrimination provisions and marriage regime a visitor would rely on are national law operating locally. A trans visitor is subject to the same substantive rules as in metropolitan France, administered through the department's own courts, administrative services and registry offices, and no island-specific procedure or exemption applies.

Martinique's correctional establishments are French prisons, so the national placement rules and the national detention watchdog's findings on transgender detainees apply to them by virtue of being French places of deprivation of liberty; no rule specific to the department governs placement, isolation or safety there. The watchdog's on-site interviews were conducted at establishments outside the department, so that finding rests on referrals and inspections elsewhere while still binding Martinique's prisons.

Same-sex conduct has been lawful in Martinique since 1815. The 2013 marriage-equality law applies in the department, discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation has been prohibited in goods and services since Law No. 2001-1066 (Penal Code articles 225-1 and 225-2) and in employment since 2008 (Labour Code article L1132-1), and gender-identity discrimination has been prohibited since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, with the term "sexual identity" replaced by "gender identity" in 2016.

Community infrastructure operates on the island. JM Concept 972 runs information, meetings and services for Martinique's LGBT community, and LGBTQ organisations listed for the overseas departments include AIDES Territoire Martinique, KAP Caraïbe, Tjenbé Rèd Prévention and SAFE SXM.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News feature (12 Jan 2018): trans women in France are held in prisons matching the gender marker on their identity documents (Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code) — most end up in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them ('we don't want any women here'), placement following the ID marker rather than anatomy. The French prison framework applies to the department's establishments as French law.

Opinion of the CGLPL, France's detention-places watchdog (25 May 2021): finds 'the persistence of serious violations' of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees across ALL French places of deprivation of liberty, based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons plus on-site inspections (eight trans women and one trans man interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse sites). sources.summary: French law governs Martinique, and the following national provisions apply in the department. Homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic public comments were made illegal by a National Assembly amendment approved 31 December 2004, carrying a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment; the same law amended the 1881 Law on the Freedom of the Press to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence, and discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation. Christian Vanneste, an MP in Chirac's UMP party, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006, though the conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Since 1 January 2017 transgender people can change their legal gender without surgery or a medical diagnosis, but must still go before a court to change the gender marker, while a first name change can be done at the registry office. The bill was signed 18 November 2016 after passing the Senate on 6 November 2015 and the National Assembly, with the Constitutional Council ruling it constitutional on 17 November 2016 and dropping the original self-certification provision; before that, legal gender change had been banned for decades until the 1992 European Court of Human Rights case B. v. France. A report released 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose by 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims, up from about 1,380 in 2018. Penalties increase where physical assault or murder is motivated by the victim's sexual orientation, and since 2017 transphobia has been an aggravating cause for all crimes punishable by prison. Conversion therapy was banned by a bill published 1 February 2022. Assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and single women took effect in September 2021 with state cover for women under 43, and the MSM blood donation deferral was removed on 16 March 2022. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems with gender-affirming healthcare, including extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, with treatment covered by Sécurité Sociale under ALD 31. In March 2024 centre-right Republican senators commissioned The Little Mermaid Observatory to report on youth gender care, after which legislation to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, opposed by the Macron government with no update since 23 July 2024; in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first guidelines for trans youth, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D. The Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access. Earlier state hostility includes the 1960 Mirguet amendment treating homosexuality as a 'national scourge' alongside alcoholism and the Vichy age-of-consent law of 6 August 1942 setting 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. SYN-MYT.name: Mayotte
SYN-MYT.summary:
Mayotte is a French overseas department in the Indian Ocean and stands under the French national framework, including its places of deprivation of liberty.

Trans detainees in Mayotte's establishments are held according to the gender shown on their identity document under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code, which in practice places trans women in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them; placement follows the document marker rather than anatomy.

France's detention-places watchdog, the CGLPL, reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty, based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons and on-site inspections in which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse. The opinion extends to Mayotte's local jails as French establishments.

Legal gender change without surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatric certificates or proof of medical intervention was approved by the Senate on 6 November 2015 and the National Assembly on 24 May 2016, modified on 12 July 2016 to drop self-certification, re-approved on 12 October, ruled constitutional on 17 November, signed 18 November 2016 and effective 1 January 2017; a court appearance is still required to change the gender marker, while a first-name change can be done at the registry office. The National Assembly also voted the simplification of legal gender change. French law bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity: article 225-1 of the Penal Code was amended on 18 November 2016 to replace 'sexual identity' with 'gender identity', and the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships or training and sanction, dismissal or discriminatory measures on that account. Since 2017 transphobia has been an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison.

Formal entitlement and lived experience diverge. A teacher at the university centre of Mayotte and his Malagasy partner married at Sada town hall in 2023, after what reporting described as a long and complicated path, on a predominantly Muslim island where the written law is not the whole of what a couple faces. Same-sex marriage has been legal here since Mayotte voted to remain part of France in 1975.

Legal representation is thinly available locally. A French-language directory of LGBT-friendly lawyers returns no referenced practitioner for Mayotte's towns, including Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi and Sada, while listing a Paris-based lawyer admitted to the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, including persons and family law, as available.

A 16 May 2020 French report recorded a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019, with around 1,870 victims identified by police compared with around 1,380 in 2018; the figure is national and covers homophobic and transphobic incidents together, not Mayotte alone.

Healthcare provision was found by a 2022 ILGA-Europe report to suffer lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned a report critical of youth gender-affirming care, after which legislation to ban medical transition under age 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 but is opposed by the government, with no update since 23 July 2024; in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued first national youth guidelines recommending puberty blockers with calcium and vitamin D supplements from at least Tanner stage 2.

sources.summary: French law bans discrimination on the basis of 'sexual identity' since July 2012, with article 225-1 of the Penal Code amended on 18 November 2016 to replace 'sexual identity' with 'gender identity', and the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships or training and sanction, dismissal or discriminatory measures on account of gender identity. Legal gender change without sex reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates or proof of medical interventions was approved by the Senate on 6 November 2015 and the National Assembly on 24 May 2016, modified on 12 July 2016 to drop self-certification, re-approved on 12 October after rejecting Senate amendments requiring medical treatment, ruled constitutional on 17 November, signed 18 November 2016 and effective 1 January 2017, but still requires going before a court for the gender marker while first-name change can be done at the registry office. In 2017 transphobia became an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison, and hate-crime provisions cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination, with a 16 May 2020 report recording a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019 with around 1,870 victims identified by police compared to around 1,380 in 2018. Healthcare provision was found by a 2022 ILGA-Europe report to suffer lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location, with a recommendation for informed consent and self-determination, while the National Academy of Medicine has characterized increased demand as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and 'primarily social problem' advising extreme caution without changing actual practice. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned a report critical of youth gender-affirming care, after which legislation to ban medical transition under age 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 but is opposed by the Macron government with no update since 23 July 2024, while in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued first national youth guidelines recommending puberty blockers with calcium and vitamin D supplements from at least Tanner stage 2. Transgender individuals are allowed to serve openly in the French Armed Forces, conversion therapy was banned by Senate vote 7 December 2020, National Assembly concurrence 25 January 2022 and publication 1 February 2022 with proposed punishments of two years' imprisonment and/or 30,000 euros fine, and in March 2019 the Minister of Higher Education sought use of transgender people's preferred names on student cards and exam forms. Same-sex sexual activity in private was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 with no mention of same-sex relations, retained in the Penal Code of 1810 and followed in nations and French colonies adopting the Code, while a discriminatory age of consent under Vichy article 334 moved to article 331 on 8 February 1945 set 21 years for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual, lowered to 18 in 1974, and repealed 4 August 1982 under President François Mitterrand to equalise at 15. A 1960 Mirguet amendment inserting article 330 alinea 2 doubled the penalty for indecent exposure for homosexual activity to repress pimping and other national scourges, was repealed in 1980 as part of an act redefining sexual offenses, and in March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980 with Senate vote still pending. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation has been banned since 1985 in employment, housing and public and private provision of services and goods, and the law of 31 December 2004 made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal with maximum penalty of 45,000 euros fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment, created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité, and amended the Press Law of 29 July 1881 for injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination with increased penalties when assault or murder is motivated by sexual orientation. sources.summary: Transgender people can change legal gender without sex reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates or medical diagnosis under the law signed 18 November 2016 after a 17 November Constitutional Council ruling, effective 1 January 2017, but must still go before a court, while first-name change can be done at a registry office. Discrimination on the basis of "sexual identity" has been banned since July 2012, with the term replaced by "gender identity" in Penal Code article 225-1 on 18 November 2016, and the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, sanction, dismissal or discriminatory measures on that ground. Since 2017 transphobia is an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison, and conversion therapy was banned by a law passed by the Senate 7 December 2020, concurred by the National Assembly 25 January 2022 and published 1 February 2022, following a 2019 proposal for two years' imprisonment and/or a 30,000 euro fine. For care, a 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location and recommended informed consent and self-determination, the National Academy of Medicine characterised increased demand as an "epidemic-like phenomenon" and "primarily social problem" advising extreme caution without changing practice, and late-2024 pediatric guidelines recommend puberty blockers from at least Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D. Private same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 and that approach was retained in the Penal Code of 1810 applied in adopting French colonies, ending ancien régime capital punishment involving castration, dismemberment and burning with the last burning on 6 July 1750. SYN-PCN.name: Pitcairn Islands
SYN-PCN.summary:
The Pitcairn Islands are a British Overseas Territory. The United Kingdom reserves defence and external affairs, while local ordinance governs the constitutional, criminal and family law that a visitor would deal with on the island.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001, so a trans visitor whose relationship would be locally classed as same-sex faces no criminalisation exposure under local law.

The Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010 has prohibited discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 2010. The guarantee is constitutional rather than an offence provision, and it names sexual orientation and not gender identity, so a trans visitor has no express constitutional protection on gender-identity grounds.

The Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 made same-sex marriage legal on 14 May 2015 and defines marriage as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity. That definition is the only express reference to gender identity in the territory's legislation recorded in these sources. The ordinance was approved unanimously by the Island Council on 1 April 2015, signed by Governor Jonathan Sinclair on 5 May 2015 and published on 13 May 2015.

The same ordinance recognises civil partnerships performed outside the Pitcairn Islands, so a partnership or marriage entered abroad is recorded as recognised locally.

No incident of violence targeting a trans person is documented for the Pitcairn Islands in these sources, and no dated case of any kind appears in the record.

SYN-PYF.name: French Polynesia
SYN-PYF.summary:
French Polynesia is an overseas collectivity of France, and French law governs justice and civil status in the territory while territorial institutions in Papeete regulate much of daily life.

Gender-diverse healthcare in the territory is limited by the small number of specialists available locally. Under Vice-President Eliane Tevahitua, the territorial government tabled a social-security bill that would have fully reimbursed hormonal treatment with progesterone and testosterone, matching mainland France; after heated debate in the Territorial Assembly the bill did not obtain sufficient support and lapsed. For a trans visitor staying any length of time, the gap between the law on paper and the care actually reachable in the archipelago is the most concrete material constraint.

The mahu role, a traditional Polynesian recognition of gender diversity in which individuals embody both male and female qualities and hold recognised standing, predates colonisation, and mahu and rae-rae are visible across the islands in daily life. Reporting from OutTraveler in July 2025 described this openness as ingrained in the culture rather than secured by law, noting that a visiting gay couple checked online whether the destination was safe before travelling and found mainstream inclusivity and acceptance operating without pride flags or organised protest. The 118-island territory has no Pride movement to speak of, which visitors read either as reassurance or as evidence that visibility is tolerated rather than defended.

CGLPL opinion (25 May 2021) on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: since France's Law 2016-1547 civil-status gender change no longer requires medical transition/surgery, yet no norms were added on how to house detainees accordingly - serious violations persist across French detention. French-framework treatment applicable in French Polynesia's prisons.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News feature (12 Jan 2018): in France, where prisoners are placed by the sex on their ID under Article D248 of the criminal procedure code, transgender women held in male prisons fall into a legal grey area and are 'punished for a lot more than their alleged crimes' — the piece follows cases including a trans woman held at Lille in 2014 amid inmate threats. French framework applying to Réunion as a department.

Opinion of 25 May 2021 of the French places-of-deprivation-of-liberty watchdog (CGLPL): finds 'the persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across French custody facilities, based on referrals since 2010 covering some forty transgender persons, interviews with associations and experts, and on-site/document inspections, with recommendations to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries. National framework covering Réunion.

PinkNews (26 Aug 2012): PM Jean-Marc Ayrault announced the same-sex marriage and adoption bill would go to the National Assembly and Senate in October 2012, fulfilling President Hollande's campaign pledge; both houses had to approve, and the Catholic Bishops Conference came out against adoption. The marriage statute that subsequently applied to Réunion with the 2013 metropolitan law.

Yagg (25 Jul 2012, French): the harassment bill adopted by the National Assembly amended Penal Code article L225-1 to add 'identité sexuelle' as a discrimination ground, making transphobia prosecutable; deputies Sergio Coronado (EELV) and Elisabeth Pochon (PS) intervened in the debate. This is the discrimination-protection basis in force in Réunion.

Yagg (19 May 2016, French): the National Assembly adopted amendment 282 — tabled by about forty Socialist deputies — inserting a Civil Code section to facilitate legal gender change for trans people, though the government's three sub-amendments could limit its scope. The gender-change framework applying to Réunion as state law.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Réunion (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: In 2010 France became the first country to declassify gender dysphoria as a mental illness by decree, though transgender rights organizations stated nothing changed beyond the announcement, with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale. Discrimination on the basis of "sexual identity" was banned in 2012, with the term replaced by "gender identity" in 2016 including amendment of article 225-1 of the Penal Code on 18 November 2016 and protection in the Labour Code, and since 2017 transgender people have been allowed to change legal gender without surgery or medical diagnosis. The legal gender-change regime took effect 1 January 2017 after Senate approval 6 November 2015, Assembly approvals 24 May 2016 and 12 July 2016 and 12 October 2016, Constitutional Council ruling of constitutionality 17 November 2016, signature 18 November 2016 and publication the next day, requiring application before a court without psychiatrist certificates or proof of reassignment surgery while first-name change can be done at the registry office. In 2017 transphobia became an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison, and a 16 May 2020 report recorded police identification of around 1,870 victims of transphobic and homophobic attacks in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018. Gender-affirming surgery within France was legalised in 1979, and a 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location and recommended informed consent and self-determination. The National Academy of Medicine has characterized increased treatment-seeking as an "epidemic-like phenomenon" and "primarily social problem" advising extreme caution without changing actual practice, while a March 2024 Senate-commissioned report led to a Senate-passed May 2024 bill to ban medical transition under 18 opposed by the Macron government and unlikely to pass the Assembly with no update since 23 July 2024, and in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommended puberty blockers from at least Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D supplements. Transgender individuals are allowed to serve openly in the French Armed Forces, conversion therapy was banned by a bill passed by the Senate 7 December 2020, concurred by the Assembly 25 January 2022 and published 1 February 2022 with proposed punishments of two years' imprisonment and/or 30,000 euro fine, and in March 2019 the Minister of Higher Education announced institutions should use transgender people's preferred names including on student cards and exam forms. Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 with no mention of same-sex relations in private, retained in the Penal Code of 1810 and followed in French colonies adopting the Code, while a discriminatory age of consent of 21 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual introduced 6 August 1942 and lowered to 18 in 1974 was repealed 4 August 1982 to equalise at 15, and a 1960 provision doubling penalty for homosexual indecent exposure under article 330 alinea 2 was repealed in 1980. Civil solidarity pacts (PACS) were enacted in 1999 for same-sex and unmarried opposite-sex couples affording most marriage protections, and France became the thirteenth country to legalise same-sex marriage through a bill approved by the Assembly 12 February 2013 by 329-229 and Senate 12 April 2013, ruled constitutional 17 May 2013, signed 18 May 2013 with first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier, with joint adoption legal since May 2013. National legislation prohibiting sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and goods/services was enacted in 1985 and incorporated in the Labour Code, and the law of 31 December 2004 made homophobic comments illegal punishable by up to 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment and amended the Press Law of 29 July 1881 to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred/violence or discrimination based on gender, sexual orientation or disability, while physical assault or murder motivated by sexual orientation carries increased penalties. The December 2004 law created the High Authority against Discrimination and for Equality, the Ministry of Education announced anti-discrimination including homophobia as a 2008-2009 priority and launched the January 2019 Tous égaux, tous alliés campaign with reporting services, helpline and LGBTQ guidance plus observance of 17 May, and lesbian, gay and bisexual individuals are allowed to serve openly in the Armed Forces. A ban on men who have sex with men donating blood dating to 20 June 1983 was recalled 12 January 2009, replaced by one-year abstinence effective 10 July 2016, reduced to four months from 2 April 2020, then removed 16 March 2022 applying the same policy regardless of sexual orientation, and in March 2024 the Assembly unanimously passed a bill for compensation to gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980 pending Senate vote.

SYN-SHN.name: Saint Helena
SYN-SHN.summary:
Saint Helena is a British Overseas Territory. United Kingdom legislation reaches it only where extended by order, so the territory's own ordinances and institutions, not United Kingdom law, determine what a visitor encounters. No transgender-specific criminal, documentation, screening, facilities, custody, care or violence provision is documented in territory law.

Consensual same-sex activity has been lawful since 2001, and the age of consent is equalised at 16 across Saint Helena, Ascension Island and Tristan da Cunha. No penalty provision specific to transgender people is documented.

The St Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha Constitution Order 2009 bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and has been in force since 2009. It defines "discriminatory" as affording different treatment to different persons on any ground such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, association with a national minority, property, age, disability, birth or other status. The enumerated grounds do not include gender reassignment, and no extension of the ban to gender reassignment is documented.

The Commission for Equality and Human Rights Ordinance 2015 defines "gender reassignment" as an intended, current or past process, or part of such a process, for reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex, or the state of mind whereby a person psychologically identifies with a gender inconsistent with, or not culturally associated with, their assigned sex at birth. The same ordinance defines sexual orientation as a person's orientation towards persons of the same sex, the opposite sex, or either sex.

The Equality and Human Rights Commission in Saint Helena monitors human rights laws, promotes understanding of the importance of equality, and works towards the elimination of unlawful discrimination. It may conduct inquiries and investigations into persons suspected of having committed an unlawful act, including unlawful discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender reassignment.

Same-sex marriage is legal on Ascension Island under the Marriage (Ascension) Ordinance 2016, approved by the Ascension Island Council on 31 May 2016 by 5 votes to 0, signed and gazetted on 20 June 2016, and commenced on 1 January 2017. On Tristan da Cunha it has been legal since 4 August 2017 under the Marriages (Tristan da Cunha) Ordinance 2017, which defines marriage as the union of two persons regardless of sex and extends eligibility, formalities, rights and recognition to same-sex couples on equal terms with opposite-sex couples. On Saint Helena it has been legal since 20 December 2017 under the Marriage Ordinance 2017; the first same-sex marriage there took place on 31 December 2018. No marriage provision specific to transgender people is documented.

Adoption by same-sex couples has been permitted since 2017. Under the Saint Helena Welfare of Children Ordinance 2010, covering Saint Helena and Tristan da Cunha, and the Ascension Island Child Welfare Ordinance 2011, single and married people may adopt regardless of sexual orientation. No adoption provision specific to transgender people is documented.
