No extension of the Constitution Order 2009 sexual-orientation discrimination ban to gender reassignment, and no transgender-specific marriage, adoption, or penalty provisions, are documented. Homosexuality is legal in Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha. The St Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha Constitution Order 2009 bans discrimination based on sexual orientation, defining "discriminatory" as "affording different treatment to different persons on any ground such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, association with a national minority, property, age, disability, birth or other status." SYN-TCA.summary:
The Turks and Caicos Islands is a British Overseas Territory standing under the United Kingdom framework, and its own ordinances and courts govern immigration status, family recognition and non-discrimination. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal there since 2001, and the constitution prohibits discrimination on the ground of sexual orientation.

In a Court of Appeal ruling, the Director of Immigration was ordered to issue a residence permit to Timothy Haymon as the spouse of Richard Sankar. The court read "spouse" in the Immigration Ordinance to include a spouse lawfully married in another jurisdiction, and held that refusing the permit on sexual-orientation grounds contravened the constitution's equality, non-discrimination and private-and-family-life guarantees. The statutory definition of marriage was left untouched, so the decision creates no local right to marry. A trans visitor whose relationship local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status can rely on a marriage lawfully entered elsewhere to support residence in the territory, in the same way as the spouses of residents.

Document handling for trans people runs through United Kingdom channels. The HM Passport Office knowledge-base profile for the Turks and Caicos Islands, official operational guidance published in 2025, states that transgender citizens are recognised in the territory and that the passport office processes gender-recognised documents for this jurisdiction. A visitor presenting a United Kingdom passport with a changed gender marker can expect it to be treated as valid in the territory. No local statute or instrument giving effect to that recognition is identified in the available sources.

Visibility is low. A resident account published in 2009 described virtually no information about gay life in the territory and no visible social scene, with privacy as the everyday norm; the account attributed this partly to a population in which roughly two-thirds of residents are not originally from the islands, leaving full-citizen Belongers a demographic minority. That account is dated and impressionistic, and does not establish anything about current violence risk.

SYN-VAT.name: Holy See
SYN-VAT.summary:
No criminal provision in Vatican City law reaches consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults in private and non-commercial. The territory's legal code derives from the Italian Zanardelli Code of 1889 and has carried no such offence since 1890, including through the founding of the sovereign state in 1929. Nothing in the criminal law addresses being transgender.

The age of consent is 18 for all persons regardless of gender. A lower age of 14 applies to sexual relations within a marriage recognised as valid by the Catholic Church and by Vatican City law.

Vatican City has no legal mechanism for changing a gender marker on identity documents, and no anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity applies in the territory. No rule governs access to single-sex facilities for a trans visitor, and no document-amendment route exists for a resident or a visitor.

Vatican City operates no prison system. It maintains a few cells for pre-trial detention, and a person sentenced to imprisonment by Vatican City serves the term in Italian prisons at Vatican expense. There is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy and no documented case of a trans prisoner held under Vatican City's authority.

The Congregation for Catholic Education's 2019 document 'Male and Female He Created Them' frames 'gender theory' as denying the difference and reciprocity of man and woman and as eliminating the anthropological basis of the family. It is an educational instruction addressed to Catholic institutions rather than a rule binding visitors, but it states the governing institution's position on gender identity.

A 2023 declaration by the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith permitted spontaneous blessings for same-sex couples while forbidding any rite resembling marriage. A January 2024 press release reiterated that blessings never extend to the unions themselves.

Vatican City has consistently rejected civil recognition of same-sex unions, same-sex marriage, and the granting of adoption rights to same-sex couples. Pope Francis in 2023 expressed support for same-sex civil unions outside the Catholic Church while maintaining that the Sacrament of Marriage is between a man and a woman as instituted by God.

In 2021 Vatican foreign minister Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher wrote to the Italian ambassador to the Holy See objecting to an Italian parliamentary bill meant to protect LGBTQ Italians against violence and discrimination. The objection targeted the provision prohibiting incitement of hatred on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity, which the letter described as a violation of freedom of speech and of religion, and asked for the draft law's text to be reformulated.

On 13 January 1998 the activist Alfredo Ormando set himself on fire on St. Peter's Square, under Vatican jurisdiction, in protest at the Catholic religion's refusal of homosexuality. He died days later in hospital from severe burns.

SYN-VGB.name: British Virgin Islands
SYN-VGB.summary:
Same-sex intimacy has not been a criminal offence in the British Virgin Islands since January 2001, when the United Kingdom's Privy Council ordered the repeal of the sodomy laws across the territory and four other remaining British Caribbean territories after the local legislatures declined to act. The change came by order of the United Kingdom's highest court of appeal rather than by enactment of the local House of Assembly; local legislator Orlando Smith said at the time that "there is nothing we can do."

The British Virgin Islands stands under the United Kingdom's constitutional framework, and measures of the United Kingdom's Parliament extend to it only when brought into force by Order in Council. A trans visitor should not assume that United Kingdom discrimination and service-access protections, including the Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code, are available in the territory by default; any such protection must be traced to British Virgin Islands legislation or to a specific extension order.

Whether a marriage between two people of the same sex validly contracted elsewhere is recognised under British Virgin Islands law remains contested rather than settled. The case testing whether the United Kingdom marriage of Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome is valid locally was still running when, on 29 July 2022, the BVI Christian Council lost its bid to appeal the case-management orders of Justice Adrian Jack, as reported by BVI News. That refusal cleared a procedural obstacle and left the proceedings in place; it is not a ruling on recognition. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be classed locally as same-sex cannot rely on recognition being settled.

No criminalisation of trans people, and no trans-specific protection machinery, appears in the sources for the territory. The visitor-relevant legal questions are the framework relationship with the United Kingdom and the unsettled recognition of marriages contracted elsewhere.

SYN-WLF.name: Wallis and Futuna Islands
SYN-WLF.summary: Wallis and Futuna is subject to French national law in full, with no local exception. What shapes a trans visitor's daily experience is the local texture: a territory of roughly 11,000 people spread across small, remote islands where anonymity is scarce, so a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor becomes known quickly across communities governed by customary authority, a dominant Catholic Church and strong Polynesian social norms. Traditional gender-variant roles comparable to fakafafine exist culturally, but they coexist with stigma and concealment rather than openness, and nonconformity is typically managed through curiosity, gossip, moral discomfort and service friction rather than official action; foreignness may buffer some of that scrutiny. Healthcare is thin, with a small hospital at Mata-Utu and serious or specialist cases evacuated to Nouméa or metropolitan France, so an emergency or inpatient stay is a realistic point of discovery, and a mismatch between documents and presentation can compound practical disruption. There is no local trans or LGBT support infrastructure, and everyday hostility has no practical remedy beyond appeal to distant French institutions, leaving the formal protections weaker in effect than in metropolitan settings. No local campaign or documented pattern of official targeting against trans visitors has been identified, but that silence should not be read as evidence of safety, and locally available continuity of care remains uncertain.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News (Jan 2018): trans women in France whose legal gender is marked male — largely those without sex-reassignment surgery — are incarcerated in all-male establishments, a documented legal grey area; example of a trans woman transferred to Lille's men's facility in 2014. Relevant as the French prison framework Wallis and Futuna inherits (French law applies unless locally overridden).

CGLPL (French national preventive mechanism) opinion of 25 May 2021 on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: serious violations of fundamental rights persist in French detention, based on referrals about ~40 transgender detainees since 2010 and interviews with associations/experts; extends a 30 June 2010 opinion on trans prisoners. This French detention framework applies in Wallis and Futuna as a French collectivity.

Grokipedia compilation on transgender rights in Wallis and Futuna: French civil-law gender-marker recognition available without surgery or diagnosis since the 2016-17 French reforms; gender-identity discrimination protections since 2012 (employment, housing, services); but ~11,000 population, isolation and dominant Catholic/Polynesian norms leave practical healthcare and acceptance barriers, with fakafafine-type roles coexisting alongside stigma/concealment.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Wallis and Futuna (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Discrimination on the basis of 'sexual identity' has been banned since 2012, with the term replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016 amending article 225-1 of the Penal Code, and the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships, sanctions, dismissal or discriminatory measures on account of gender identity. Effective 1 January 2017 after a Constitutional Council ruling on 17 November 2016, signature on 18 November 2016 and publication the next day, transgender people can legally change gender without sex reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates or medical proof, but must go before a court, while first-name change can be done by registry office after the self-certification provision was dropped. Gender identity disorder was removed as a diagnosis by decree in 2010 with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender affirmative surgery has been legal domestically since 1979. Since 2017 transphobia is an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison, and police identified around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018. Transgender individuals are allowed to serve openly in the French Armed Forces, and in March 2019 the Minister of Higher Education sought use of transgender people's preferred names including on student cards and exam forms. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and location-dependent inequitable access to gender-affirming healthcare and recommended informed consent and self-determination, while the National Academy of Medicine characterized the rise as an epidemic-like and primarily social phenomenon urging extreme caution without changing practice. After a March 2024 Senate-commissioned report critical of youth gender-affirming care, a bill to ban medical transition under age 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 but is opposed by the Macron government and stalled since 23 July 2024, while late-2024 guidelines from the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommended puberty blockers with calcium and vitamin D supplements from at least Tanner stage 2. Private same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 retained in the Penal Code of 1810 for colonies, while the 1960 Mirguet amendment doubling the penalty for homosexual indecent exposure under article 330 alinea 2 was repealed in 1980 and the discriminatory age of consent of 21 then 18 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual relations was equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980, still pending Senate vote. Sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public and private goods and services has been banned since 1985 with Labour Code protection, and same-sex marriage signed 18 May 2013 after Constitutional Council approval 17 May 2013 with first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier following PACS partnerships from 1999 and joint adoption since May 2013 is stated as legal in all overseas departments and territories. The law of 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic comments punishable by up to 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months imprisonment and amended the Press Law of 29 July 1881 to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination based on sexual orientation, with increased penalties when assault or murder is motivated by sexual orientation, creating the High Authority against Discrimination and for Equality. Police identified around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks in 2019 versus around 1,380 in 2018, after President Macron in October 2018 denounced homophobic violence as unworthy of France. Conversion therapy was banned by law published 1 February 2022 after Senate passage 7 December 2020 and Assembly concurrence 25 January 2022 carrying two years imprisonment and/or 30,000 euro fine, and the MSM blood-donation ban from 20 June 1983 recalled in 2009 moved from one-year abstinence effective 10 July 2016 to four months from 2 April 2020 to removal on 16 March 2022 for all regardless of orientation, with lesbian, gay and bisexual individuals allowed to serve openly in the Armed Forces.

72843720B863019116732.name: Centro
72843720B863019116732.summary:
Centro stands under Italy's national framework on legal gender recognition, discrimination and asylum. The findings specific to this region are judicial and documentary: a regional distribution of recorded anti-LGBT violence, an administrative ruling in Rome, and a homicide acquittal in Perugia.

Progetto Gionata's region-by-region study of anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence, covering 2012 to 2025, ranks six Italian regions at the top by victim count. Lazio and Toscana, both within Centro, are two of the six, alongside Lombardia and Piemonte in the north-west and Campania and Puglia in the south. The ranking is by raw victim counts, which track population, and the study supplies no per-capita denominator, so it does not establish that any one of these regions carries a higher rate of violence than another.

In Rome, the municipal administration announced on 30 August 2025 that the Consiglio di Stato, the country's highest administrative court, had upheld the city's 2022 removal of Pro Vita & Famiglia posters attacking "gender" ideology in schools. The court found the images discriminatory, one of them showing a boy being handed a red hairbow, and held that public spaces may not be used for messages that generate alarmism, fear or serious disturbance, particularly where minors are concerned. The campaign behind the posters had collected 105,000 online signatures. The outcome confirms that anti-trans public messaging can be restricted in the region's largest city.

In Perugia, the Court of Cassation confirmed on 5 March 2026 the appeal acquittal of a trans woman, Pinheiro Reis Duarte Hudson, known as Patrizia, over the death of Samuele De Paoli on 27 April 2021. The court held that the death resulted from cardiac arrhythmia caused by accidental compression during a scuffle that De Paoli started, making the acquittal on the homicide charge final. The case was a national anti-trans media flashpoint, and the definitive judicial outcome favoured the trans defendant in the region's main university city.

This is the strongest judicial recognition of transphobic aggravation recorded in Italy.

Progetto Gionata's region-by-region study of anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence, covering 2012 to 2025, names the Italian regions with the highest victim counts, six regions ranking at the top. Nord-Ovest stands under the national framework of Italy; the findings below are specific to this region. Milan operates Italy's first gender registry, the registro di genere, which allows transgender people to use their chosen name on civic and municipal documents. LifeGate presents the registry as a milestone for transgender rights in the country and ties it to a 2022 council motion by the country's first elected transgender councillor. Turin runs a parallel practice, Identita Alias, at municipal offices and libraries. Both instruments are city-level, and the inventory documents no region-wide equivalent.

Progetto Gionata's breakdown of anti-LGBT aggressions by region and city for the period 2012–2025 places two of the region's constituent regions among Italy's six highest-victim regions for anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence. The ranking is by raw count of victims; the source supplies no population denominator, so it does not measure per-capita risk and does not show that a larger regional population is more dangerous than a smaller one.

sources.title: Italy 'to open first prison for transgender inmates' | BBC News
sources.summary: BBC News (12 Jan 2010): Italy announced plans for one of the world's first dedicated transgender prisons at Pozzale, near Florence - converting a nearly empty medium-security women's prison into a specially equipped detention centre for about 30 of Italy's roughly 60 transgender prisoners (mostly convicted of drug or prostitution offences); gay-rights groups welcomed the dedicated space and its psychological support. The report states that until then transgender prisoners had been located in women's prisons 'where they are often segregated for their own safety' - the documented 2010 baseline for placement practice in Italy. Repubblica (2013) later reported the Pozzale project was abandoned.

sources.title: La doppia sofferenza delle trans in carcere | La Repubblica (Inchieste)
sources.summary: La Repubblica investigative report 'La doppia sofferenza delle trans in carcere' (28 Aug 2013): at that date the prison administration counted 69 transsexual prisoners spread across ten Italian facilities, with placement tracking legal sex - female hormones could not be prescribed to prisoners who 'according to their identity card, count as men,' trans women were held in men's sections, and those who had already undergone sex-change surgery were 'destined for the women's sections.' Segregation practice: in some prisons trans prisoners were put in isolation when cells were lacking - described as the most inhumane way to preserve their safety - and protected sections such as the G8 section at Rebibbia (Rome) and the protected section at Poggioreale (Naples) imposed limitations, including on partner visits. Documented ruling: the 2011 Terni case in which the Spoleto surveillance magistrate ordered the local health authority to pay for the prisoner's hormone therapy 'to guarantee psychophysical integrity'; the ruling was appealed and followed by a July 2012 appellate decision. The dedicated Pozzale transgender prison project (2008-2010), which would have drawn trans women from the special wing of Sollicciano (Florence), was shelved.

72843720B59566147937015.summary:
Visitors to Nord-Est stand under the national framework of Italy. Entry rules, identity documents, legal gender recognition, criminal law and the national protection and health-care layers are set by Italy and are recorded in the country's own dossier. The material identified at region level concerns Veneto and, in narrower form, Emilia-Romagna.

The Veneto Regional Council passed motion n.340 at its 178th public session in Venice on 3 July. Deliberation n.92 of 14 October 2014 approved that motion, committing the regional government to a mandatory 'Natural Family Day' observance on the last school day before Christmas and rejecting the aims of gender-awareness content in schools. The official regional government bulletin carries the primary-source text of the deliberation. The most recent documented instance of this instrument in this record is 14 October 2014; no later amendment, repeal or successor measure is documented here.

The Veneto measure operates through the school calendar and regional policy statements. It creates no criminal offence, no penalty and no restriction on entry, documents or movement, and it does not alter the national rules on legal gender recognition or anti-discrimination protection.

sources.summary: Regional council records: motion n.340 passed at the 178th public session in Venice on 3 July. Deliberation n.92 of 14 October 2014 approved the motion that committed the regional government to a mandatory 'Natural Family Day' observance on the last school day before Christmas.

Official regional government bulletin: deliberation n.92 of 14 October 2014 carries the primary-source text of the Veneto regional council motion instituting the 'Natural Family Day' school observance and rejecting the aims of gender-awareness content.

sources.title: Italy 'to open first prison for transgender inmates' | BBC News
sources.summary: BBC News, 12 January 2010: Italy announced plans for one of the world's first dedicated transgender prisons at Pozzale, near Florence, converting a nearly empty medium-security women's prison into a specially equipped detention centre for about 30 of Italy's roughly 60 transgender prisoners, mostly convicted of drug or prostitution offences. Gay-rights groups welcomed the dedicated space and its psychological support. Before then transgender prisoners had been held in women's prisons, 'where they are often segregated for their own safety', which established the 2010 placement practice in Italy. Repubblica reported in 2013 that the Pozzale project was abandoned.

sources.title: La doppia sofferenza delle trans in carcere | La Repubblica (Inchieste)
sources.summary: La Repubblica investigative report 'La doppia sofferenza delle trans in carcere', 28 August 2013: the prison administration counted 69 transsexual prisoners across ten Italian facilities. Placement tracked legal sex, so female hormones could not be prescribed to prisoners who 'according to their identity card, count as men'. Trans women were held in men's sections, and those who had already undergone sex-change surgery were 'destined for the women's sections'. In some prisons trans prisoners were put in isolation when cells were lacking, described as the most inhumane way to preserve their safety. Protected sections such as the G8 section at Rebibbia in Rome and the protected section at Poggioreale in Naples imposed limitations, including on partner visits. In the 2011 Terni case the Spoleto surveillance magistrate ordered the local health authority to pay for the prisoner's hormone therapy 'to guarantee psychophysical integrity'; the ruling was appealed and a July 2012 appellate decision followed. The Pozzale transgender prison project of 2008-2010, which would have drawn trans women from the special wing of Sollicciano in Florence, was shelved.

72843720B88210905209841.name: Sud
72843720B88210905209841.summary:
Sud is a region of Italy and stands under the Italian national framework. No regional statute, court ruling or administrative measure specific to Sud addressing gender identity or sexual orientation was identified in this inventory, so the assessment rests on documented incidents within the region.

ILGA-Europe's annual country review for Italy, published in February 2025, records a troubling increase in the number and geographic spread of bias-motivated violence against LGBTI people in 2024, with incidents reported almost monthly. One such incident fell within this region: in March 2025 a young man was assaulted by attackers on a scooter in Scampia, a neighbourhood of Naples.

On 13 October 2025 a 63-year-old man was arrested in Torre Annunziata, in the province of Naples, after making stabbing threats against a young LGBTQIA+ activist; Il Gazzettino described it as a grave homophobic episode in the Naples area.

On detention, no dedicated transgender prison facility exists in Italy. A 2010 announcement that Pozzale, near Florence in Tuscany, would become one of the world's first prisons for transgender inmates was never realised; as of 2013 the facility had not been created, and trans detainees remain within the ordinary men's and women's prison circuit, including in this region.

On 26 April 2025 three young men were beaten at a fast-food restaurant in Catania because they were gay. The Procura etnea, the Catania prosecutor's office, reconstructed a sequence of insults and threats that preceded the physical assault, and video of the attack circulated publicly.

A Catania outlet's follow-up of 5 June 2026, titled "Omofobia in Sicilia, continuano le violenze", catalogues continuing assaults and suicide cases across Sicilian towns, indicating that the pattern of attacks recorded in 2025 has not stopped.

82249235B5553315981608.name: Alberta
82249235B5553315981608.summary:
Alberta's trans-specific lawmaking is a package of three statutes that passed final legislative stage on 4 December 2024. The Education Amendment Act, 2024 introduced parental opt-in for classroom instruction on sexuality and rules governing students' preferred names and pronouns and their participation in school sport. The Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024 bars certain gender-affirming care for minors. The Fairness and Safety in Sport Act bars trans women from women's sport.

Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, passed at the tail of the fall sitting and invokes the Charter's notwithstanding clause to shield the three trans-youth laws from legal challenge for years. Egale Canada, the Skipping Stone Foundation and five families announced constitutional litigation, calling the package discriminatory, and state that their court challenge continues regardless; the laws are in force with constitutional litigation pending.

Premier Danielle Smith's 12 February 2024 announcement of the package stated the bans would not include a ban on women's shelters, women's prisons or women's changing rooms, and Alberta's statutory trans package deliberately excluded jail and prison settings. No provincial placement-by-birth-sex rule for trans prisoners was enacted, and no Alberta-specific trans-prisoner placement, special unit or segregation case is documented in this record.

Provincial correctional policies vary and no Alberta-specific rule is documented. Federal corrections operations inside Alberta accommodate offenders based on gender identity rather than sex assigned at birth: since 2018 the Correctional Service of Canada permits gender-diverse offenders to request placement or transfer to a men's or women's institution aligned with their gender identity or expression, regardless of anatomy or the sex/gender marker on identity documents, with requests refused only where CSC finds unresolvable overriding health or safety concerns. As of 2025 CSC reported 90 self-identified transgender women in federal institutions, 73 housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's. The Office of the Correctional Investigator called CSC's 2022 gender-diversity policy an important change but flagged the lack of clear parameters for what counts as an overriding health or safety concern and the absence of a dedicated mechanism for gender-diverse prisoners to report abuse.

Alberta's Human Rights Commission handles discrimination complaints in areas of provincial responsibility, and gender identity and gender expression are prohibited grounds in employment, housing and public and private accommodations across Canadian jurisdictions as of 2017. Section 15 of the Charter applies to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities, and Supreme Court jurisprudence has interpreted sex and physical disability in section 15 to include transsexuality. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in Alberta under provincial vital statistics rules governing identity documents such as birth certificates.

Since 2022 the Criminal Code statutorily bans conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults, making it a crime to subject anyone to it as defined by statutory law. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 20 July 2005 under the federal Civil Marriage Act; Alberta's 2000 Marriage Act defining marriage as between a man and a woman and invoking the notwithstanding clause was invalid because capacity to marry is exclusive federal jurisdiction and its five-year exemption expired in 2005.

In a poll commissioned for the Privy Council Office reported for 2020, 87.6% of those surveyed said they would be comfortable if a neighbour was a transgender person. This figure is a general-population attitude finding from 2020, not a measure of current risk or of violence.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Alberta (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Federal, provincial and territorial human rights acts prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations, with all jurisdictions explicitly including gender identity as a prohibited ground as of 2017. Supreme Court jurisprudence has interpreted the concepts of sex and physical disability in section 15 of the Charter to include transsexuality and HIV/STDs, and section 15 applies to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities, while private-sector complaints proceed under applicable federal or provincial human rights statutes. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules, with vital statistics including identity documents such as birth certificates falling under provincial jurisdiction. In 2023 Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents’ Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoking the notwithstanding clause, which requires schools to obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity and has prompted calls for repeal and legal action. In 2024 Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, the Education Amendment Act, 2024 and the Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges in Alberta courts, and in 2025 Alberta passed Bill 9: Protecting Alberta’s Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 using the notwithstanding clause to block those Charter challenges. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer Communities, acknowledged contribution to institutional bias, intolerance and violation of human rights and personal suffering, shame, trauma and distrust, stated “We must stand together against homophobia, transphobia, and any other kind of marginalization, shaming, disrespect or hate,” and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers. Since 2022 the Criminal Code statutorily bans conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults and makes it a crime to subject anyone to it as defined by statutory law. British Columbia, Ontario and Saskatchewan grant parental status to three or more intentional parents, allowing for a wider range of queer and trans families in addition to or in place of the birth parent. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized June 27, 1969 by the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968–69 (Bill C-150), and the remaining anal-intercourse offence in section 159 was repealed June 21, 2019 by Bill C-75 after courts in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Alberta each declared it unconstitutional under Charter equality provisions, leaving a general age of consent of 16 since June 2019 and 18 where there is trust, authority, dependency or exploitation. In Egan v Canada (1995) the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under section 15 as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta (1998) held failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law itself violated section 15, with all provinces, territories and the federal government explicitly including sexual orientation as a prohibited ground of discrimination in employment, housing and public and private accommodations as of 2017. Same-sex marriage became legal nationwide July 20, 2005 by the federal Civil Marriage Act, making Canada the fourth country worldwide and first in the Americas to do so with no residency requirement, following court rulings in several provinces and one territory between 2002-2005, while Alberta’s 2000 Marriage Act defining marriage as between a man and a woman and invoking the notwithstanding clause was invalid because capacity to marry is exclusive federal jurisdiction and its five-year exemption expired in 2005. Same-sex adoption was legalized province by province from British Columbia in 1996 to Nunavut in 2011 as the last jurisdiction, with Alberta legalizing stepchild adoption in 1999 and joint adoption in 2007. In 2022 Canada became the third country worldwide and first in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults, making it a crime under the Criminal Code to subject anyone to it as statutorily defined. On November 28, 2017 the Prime Minister issued a formal parliamentary apology for oppression of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and two-spirit communities, and on June 21, 2018 the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act received royal assent allowing RCMP and federal departments to destroy or remove judicial records for pre-1969 homosexual acts or section 159 convictions, requiring notification to involved provincial or municipal police and courts, available to living and deceased persons and distinct from pardon or record suspension as recognition the act should never have been a crime. In December 2020 Canada’s police chiefs apologized for decades of oppression and opposition from the 1960s to the present, acknowledging institutional bias, intolerance and human rights violations. In a poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office reported for 2020, 91.8% of those surveyed said they would be “comfortable” if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual, a sexuality-tolerance finding distinct from transgender tolerance. In that same 2020 Privy Council Office poll, 87.6% said they would be “comfortable” if a neighbour was a transgender person, the article’s documented transgender-specific tolerance statement. 2020 Pew Research showed 85% of Canada’s general population (92% among Canadians aged 18-29) favoured social acceptance of homosexuality, up from 80% in 2013, and June 2013 polls showed majority support for same-sex marriage available since 2005, with 70% agreeing same-sex couples should have same adoption rights and 76% agreeing they are just as likely to successfully raise children, all sexuality-specific findings. The article notes Canada was ranked first indicating least dangerous in Asher & Lyric’s LGBTQ+ Danger Index in 2023, first in the Gay Travel Index in 2024, and ninth in the Equaldex Equality Index in 2024, general LGBTQ rankings not disaggregated for transgender people.

82249235B71336988791422.name: Saskatchewan
82249235B71336988791422.summary:
Saskatchewan's human rights legislation lists gender identity and gender expression as prohibited grounds of discrimination in employment, housing, and public and private accommodations, giving a visitor or resident a provincial complaints route.

Change of legal gender is a provincial function and is available in Saskatchewan under the province's own rules.

On 22 August 2023 the Saskatchewan education ministry announced parental inclusion and consent policies. Schools must seek parent or guardian permission before changing the preferred name and pronouns of students under 16, parents must be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and third-party school programs were paused. That release initiated the court challenge.

The Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 was passed with the province invoking the notwithstanding clause, a five-year override of the Charter. It requires schools to obtain parental consent for students under 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity. Human rights groups called for repeal, and the invocation of the clause may prevent legal action from succeeding on Charter grounds.

On 11 August 2025 the Court of Appeal for Saskatchewan (2025 SKCA 74) set aside the 2023 chambers decision, so the pronoun-notice policy stands. The appeal court held that Charter breaches under sections 1 and 15 cannot be tested where section 33 has been invoked. Reporting on the same judgment states that the appeal was granted in part, that a judge has jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits Charter rights, and that UR Pride's litigation may continue in the Court of King's Bench.

Amnesty International Canada participated as an intervenor in the appeal and welcomed the 11 August 2025 decision as a meaningful victory for the protection of human rights in Canada. Amnesty argued that courts can still determine whether the province's anti-trans pronoun law violates the Charter and issue a declaration to that effect even where the notwithstanding clause shields the law from being struck down, and that use of the clause must align with Canada's international-law obligation to provide an effective remedy.

Egale Canada co-counsel Bennett Jensen said UR Pride will continue the litigation, noting that students had been living under the reality of the law for two years.

On 6 November 2025 the Supreme Court of Canada said it will hear the appeals in the challenge to the school pronoun law. Both the province and UR Pride appealed the Court of Appeal decision and asked for the hearing to be expedited alongside the challenge to Quebec's Bill 21. No merits ruling has changed the policy, and the constitutionality of the shielded consent rule is now before Canada's highest court.

This division's human rights legislation lists gender identity and gender expression as prohibited grounds of discrimination in employment, housing, and public and private accommodations, giving a visitor or resident a complaints route within this division.

Change of legal gender is a function of this division and is available here under this division's own rules.

On 22 August 2023 this division's education ministry announced parental inclusion and consent policies. Schools must seek parent or guardian permission before changing the preferred name and pronouns of students under 16, parents must be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and third-party school programs were paused. That release initiated the court challenge.

The 2023 amendment act of the legislature creating a parents' bill of rights was passed with this division invoking section 33, a five-year override of the constitution's bill of rights. It requires schools to obtain parental consent for students under 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity. Human rights groups called for repeal, and the invocation of the section may prevent legal action from succeeding on bill-of-rights grounds.

On 11 August 2025 the appeal court (2025 appeal ruling, division code in the neutral citation redacted) set aside the 2023 chambers decision, so the pronoun-notice policy stands. The appeal court held that breaches of sections 1 and 15 of the constitution's bill of rights cannot be tested where section 33 has been invoked. Reporting on the same judgment states that the appeal was granted in part, that a judge has jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits bill-of-rights guarantees, and that the complainant organisation's litigation may continue in the superior trial court.

An international human-rights organisation participated as an intervenor in the appeal and welcomed the 11 August 2025 decision as a meaningful victory for the protection of human rights in this country. It argued that courts can still determine whether this division's anti-trans pronoun law violates the constitution's bill of rights and issue a declaration to that effect even where the override shields the law from being struck down, and that use of the section must align with this country's international-law obligation to provide an effective remedy.

Co-counsel for a national equality organisation said the complainant organisation will continue the litigation, noting that students had been living under the reality of the law for two years.

On 6 November 2025 this country's highest court said it will hear the appeals in the challenge to the school pronoun law. Both this division and the complainant organisation appealed the appeal court decision and asked for the hearing to be expedited alongside the challenge to a neighbouring division's contested bill. No merits ruling has changed the policy, and the constitutionality of the shielded consent rule is now before this country's highest court.

82249235B4167839012994.name: New Brunswick
82249235B4167839012994.summary:
New Brunswick sets its own schools policy on sexual orientation and gender identity inside the Canadian legal framework. Policy 713, issued by the Department of Education and Early Childhood Development, has been in force since 17 August 2020 and was revised on 1 July 2023, 23 August 2023 and 1 January 2025.

In the version effective 1 January 2025, students of any age may choose the names and pronouns used for them in informal school settings; parental consent is encouraged but not required. Formal records for students under 16 still require parental consent. The revision went further than the recommendations of child advocate Kelly Lamrock.

The policy's application clause covers the school environment and names all students together with school personnel, contract and casual employees, visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers and visitors, so its rules reach adults present in New Brunswick classrooms who do not live in the province.

From 1 July 2023 until the January 2025 revision, the policy barred teachers from using the chosen name and pronouns of a student under 16 without parental consent, reversing a three-year-old rule that required teachers to obtain the student's informed consent before discussing names and pronouns with parents. The 1 July 2023 change also dropped explicit wording letting students take part in extracurricular activities, including sports teams, reflecting their gender identity. Premier Blaine Higgs's Progressive Conservative government made the change without a legislative vote, citing complaints from parents and teachers; two ministers resigned in protest and two were removed, and eight party members including six cabinet ministers sat out question period in June 2023 to protest the lack of process. Dissidents called for a leadership review. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said trans kids in New Brunswick "need to feel safe, not targeted by politicians".

The proposed changes drew public opposition before they took effect: about 350 people rallied at the New Brunswick legislature on 14 May 2023 to protest the review, and Education Minister Bill Hogan confirmed the review was under way. Gail Costello of Pride in Education, who helped write the policy, told the rally that "we know it saves lives" and warned that "with this policy changed or removed, we're going to lose kids".

The policy as adopted in 2020 requires schools to respect students' chosen names and pronouns and to provide gender-neutral bathrooms. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association mounted a constitutional challenge to the 2023 parental-consent rule.

sources.summary: Federal, not provincial, rules govern a trans prisoner held in federal custody in New Brunswick. Correctional Service Canada's 2022 gender-diversity policy allows gender-diverse offenders to request placement or transfer to a men's or women's institution aligned with their gender identity or expression, regardless of anatomy or the sex marker on identification documents; each request is assessed individually and may be refused where an unresolved 'overriding health or safety concern' exists. As of 2025 CSC recorded 90 self-identified transgender women in federal custody, 73 housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's, and between fiscal years 2017-18 and 2024-25 it received 129 placement or transfer requests from people assigned male at birth to women's institutions: 35 approved, 72 denied, 22 withdrawn. Provincial correctional policies vary, and no New Brunswick provincial-jail placement rule is documented here. The Correctional Investigator has criticised the policy's unclear 'health or safety' override criteria and the lack of a dedicated abuse-reporting mechanism.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in New Brunswick (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations is prohibited by all provinces and territories as well as the federal government, explicitly listed as a prohibited ground in human rights acts as of 2017. The concepts of sex and physical disability in section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms have been interpreted to include transsexuality, with section 15 applying to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities but requiring private complaints to be brought under federal or provincial human rights statutes. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. In 2023 Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoking the notwithstanding clause to require schools to obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, prompting legal action by human rights groups. In 2024 Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024, and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges in Alberta courts but were shielded by Bill 9: Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 using the notwithstanding clause. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for institutional bias, intolerance and violation of human rights against Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans, Transgender, and Queer communities, stating police must stand against transphobia and creating the Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 when the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 (Bill C-150) was brought into force upon royal assent. In Egan v Canada in 1995 the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under the equality clause in section 15 of the Charter as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta in 1998 found failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law violated section 15. Since June 2019 the general age of consent for all sexual activities has been 16, rising to 18 where there is a relationship of trust, authority or dependency or exploitation, with limited close-in-age exceptions for ages 12 through 15. Former Criminal Code section 159 criminalizing anal intercourse was held unconstitutional by courts in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Alberta and was repealed on June 21, 2019 through Bill C-75. Same-sex marriage became legal nationwide on July 20, 2005 through the federal Civil Marriage Act, making Canada the fourth country in the world and first in the Americas to legalize it. The Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act granted royal assent June 21, 2018 allows the RCMP and federal departments to destroy or remove judicial records for pre-1969 homosexual acts or section 159 convictions, available to living and deceased persons and distinct from pardon or record suspension. In 2022 Canada became the third country in the world and first in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for minors and adults and make it a crime to subject anyone to it as defined in the Criminal Code. 2020 Pew Research showed that 85% of Canada's general population, including 92% among Canadians aged 18 to 29, favoured social acceptance of homosexuality, up from 80% in 2013. June 2013 polls showed a vast majority blessed same-sex marriage available since 2005, with 70% agreeing same-sex couples should have the same rights to adopt and 76% agreeing same-sex couples are just as likely to successfully raise children. A poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office reported for 2020 found 91.8% would be "comfortable" if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual. That same Privy Council Office poll found that 87.6% said they would be "comfortable" if a neighbour was a transgender person.

14339913B23556801435424.name: Scotland
14339913B23556801435424.summary:
Scotland is a constituent nation of the United Kingdom. Criminal law, policing, prisons and family law are devolved to the Scottish Parliament, while legal gender recognition and equality law are set at United Kingdom level; the findings below are those specific to Scotland.

Trans people in Scotland change their legal gender under the United Kingdom Gender Recognition Act 2004. A Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill was introduced to the Scottish Parliament in March 2022 and passed in December 2022 by 86 votes to 39, applying only to Scotland, but the United Kingdom government blocked the Bill under section 35 of the Scotland Act 1998 while it awaited royal assent — the first time that power has been used to overturn Scottish legislation — so the reformed procedure is not in force in Scotland.

The Equality Act 2010 forms part of the law of Scotland, and the UK Supreme Court's unanimous judgment in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers (16 April 2025) held that 'woman' and 'sex' in that Act mean biological woman and biological sex, so a gender recognition certificate does not entitle a trans woman to the Act's sex-based protections in Scotland. The Equality and Human Rights Commission, the body enforcing the Equality Act 2010 across England, Wales and Scotland, updated its code of practice on 20 May 2025 following that judgment, advising that services and businesses may ask for a birth certificate where there is 'genuine concern' about biological sex and that trans people may be excluded from single-sex sport 'when necessary' for safety or fair competition; its interim guidance shortly after the judgment said trans women should not be permitted to use women's facilities in workplaces and public-facing services such as shops and hospitals. This is the operative guidance a trans visitor encounters at venues, transport and services in Scotland, already applied within Scotland at Holyrood, where the Scottish Parliamentary Corporate Body announced in May 2025 that toilets designated male or female would be interpreted as meaning biological sex, with new gender-neutral toilets open to anyone.

Hate crime in Scotland is governed by the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021, passed by the Scottish Parliament in March 2021 by 82 votes to 32, given royal assent a month later and brought into force on 1 April 2024, which lists gender identity as a protected characteristic. Earlier Scottish legislation enacted in 2009 provides penalty enhancements where an offence is motivated by the victim's gender identity.

The Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service publication 'Hate crime in Scotland, 2025-26', issued 30 June 2026, records 7,115 hate-crime charges in total, up 17% on 2024-25 and the highest since 2003-04, with transgender-identity aggravation accounting for 104 charges, up 21% from 86 the previous year and the highest level since the 2021 Act took effect, and sexual-orientation aggravation accounting for 2,062 charges, the second commonest category.

Police Scotland recorded 8,538 hate crimes in 2024-25, according to the Scottish Government report published 17 February 2026, the first annual report under the 2021 Act, with the highest rates per 10,000 residents in Glasgow City and City of Edinburgh at about 32.25 each, and 62 per cent of recorded hate crimes carrying a race aggravator and just over a quarter a sexual-orientation aggravator, while the report gives no per-resident rate for the transgender-identity category.

Police Scotland published interim guidance on 25 June 2025 providing that searches involving the removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear are conducted on the basis of biological sex, in both custody and stop-and-search contexts. Where a person's lived gender differs from their sex at birth, efforts will be made to provide an officer of that lived gender on request.

On 19 June 2026 in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Judge Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, struck down the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory guidance on trans custody as unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis after the guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in establishments matching their gender identity. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Scotland since 16 December 2014 under legislation passed by the Scottish Parliament on 4 February 2014 by 108 votes to 15 and given royal assent on 12 March 2014, with the first ceremonies on 31 December 2014 and no religious organisation or celebrant obliged to perform such marriages.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Scotland (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Under the Gender Recognition Act 2004, transgender people in Scotland may change their legal gender. In 2018 the Scottish Government announced plans to provide an "X" sex descriptor on identity documents and to lower the minimum age of transition to 16. A Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill to reform the 2004 Act was introduced in March 2022 and passed in December 2022 by 86-39, applying only to Scotland. The Bill was blocked by the UK government under section 35 of the Scotland Act 1998, the first use of that power to overturn Scottish legislation, while awaiting royal assent. The Equality Act 2010 covers gender reassignment and outlaws discrimination, harassment and victimisation because a person belongs to, is thought to belong to, or is associated with a protected group. Scotland enacted 2009 legislation providing penalty enhancements where crime is motivated by the victim's gender identity, and hate-crime legislation passed in March 2021 by 82-32, receiving royal assent a month later and taking effect 1 April 2024, explicitly includes gender identity. Same-sex sexual activity was legalised in Scotland by Section 80 of the Criminal Justice (Scotland) Act 1980, in force 1 February 1981, and the age of consent was equalised at 16 in 2001. Section 2A prohibiting promotion of homosexuality was repealed in Scotland by the Ethical Standards in Public Life etc. (Scotland) Act 2000. The Historical Sexual Offences (Pardons and Disregards) (Scotland) Act 2018, passed in June 2018 and effective in October 2019, issued symbolic pardons to men convicted of consensual same-sex activity before decriminalisation and allows an accepted disregard application to prevent inclusion in disclosure checks and treat the offence as not occurred. Civil partnerships for same-sex couples have been available since 2005 under the Civil Partnership Act 2004, conferring property, inheritance tax, social security, pension, parental responsibility, maintenance, tenancy, insurance and next-of-kin rights with formal dissolution akin to divorce. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 16 December 2014 under the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Scotland) Act 2014, passed 4 February 2014 by 108-15 with royal assent 12 March 2014, with first ceremonies 31 December 2014 and no obligation on religious organisations or celebrants to perform them. Same-sex couples obtained joint and stepchild adoption rights from 28 September 2009, with the Looked After Children (Scotland) Regulations 2009 allowing consideration as foster parents on the same basis as others. The Equality Act 2010 outlaws discrimination, harassment and victimisation based on sexual orientation, and 2009 legislation provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by sexual orientation, with sexual orientation explicitly included in the 2021 hate-crime law effective 1 April 2024.

The two hate-crime series measure different things over different periods. The COPFS figures count charges decided by the prosecution service in 2025-26; the Scottish Government figures count crimes recorded by the police in 2024-25. Within the 2025-26 charge totals, transgender-identity aggravation at 104 charges stands well below sexual-orientation aggravation at 2,062. Mexico City recorded 17 homicides of LGBT+ people in 2024, 11 of them trans women, the highest raw state count in the country that year and the first time the city has led the count, according to annual monitoring published in May 2025 by a Mexican LGBT+ news collective. These are raw counts. The sources supply no per-capita denominator and no general homicide rate for the city, so the figure cannot be presented as a rate or as a measure of risk relative to other jurisdictions.

The city's congress approved transfeminicidio as a distinct offence in the local penal code in July 2024, reported as 18 July and 19 July in different sources. The reform is known as the Ley Paola Buenrostro, after a trans woman murdered in 2016, and made Mexico City the second state to create the offence. Article 148-Ter, added to the code on 23 August 2024, defines transfeminicidio as the killing of a trans woman or feminine-spectrum person by reason of gender identity or expression.

In December 2024 the city created a dedicated Transfeminicide Investigation Unit. Its investigators may no longer demand legal name or gender change or medical documentation from trans people.

The prosecution-service agreement FGJCDMX/04/2025 sets initial-response protocol rules for transfeminicide cases alongside feminicide investigations.

On 25 August 2025 the mayor launched a Gender Police with 30 patrol units to handle cases of violence against women and girls in the city. The sources do not state whether its remit covers trans women.

The city's congress approved transfeminicidio as a distinct offence in the local penal code in July 2024, reported as 18 July and 19 July in different sources. Article 148-Ter, added to the code on 23 August 2024, defines transfeminicidio as the killing of a trans woman or feminine-spectrum person by reason of gender identity or expression. The prosecution-service agreement FGJCDMX/04/2025 sets initial-response protocol rules for transfeminicide cases alongside feminicide investigations. On 25 August 2025 the mayor launched a Gender Police with 30 patrol units to handle cases of violence against women and girls in the city; the sources do not state whether its remit covers trans women.

31927357B49073316106075.name: Michoacan de Ocampo
31927357B49073316106075.summary:
Michoacán, one of Mexico's states, has not typified the killing of LGBT people as a hate crime under state law, and the majority of attacks on the community concentrate in Tierra Caliente, the subregion under armed-group influence.

Six LGBT+ homicides were recorded in the state in the first four and a half months of 2026, among them the killing of Daniela, a trans woman found beaten to death in a drainage channel in Morelia on 2 April 2026; a suspect was arrested in April 2026. Civil-society groups place the six cases in Morelia (three), Uruapan, Ocampo and Maravatío, and count at least 56 registered aggressions against the community in the state since 2014.

The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes contra Personas LGBT recorded 46 LGBT+ homicides in Michoacán between 2015 and 2024. Morelia accounts for the largest number at 11, followed by Lázaro Cárdenas with 6, Apatzingán and Uruapan with 5 each and Zamora with 4; 2015 was the deadliest year with 10 victims. Trans women were the most affected group, 27 of the 46, and people aged 25 to 39 the most affected age bracket. Thirteen disappearances of LGBT+ people were reported between 2022 and 2024. These are raw counts without a population denominator, so ranking municipalities by number of cases reflects population size as much as risk.

Enforcement is minimal. Of the 46 hate-crime cases recorded by civil society in the state since 2015, only one was being processed for judicialization, the murder of Meredith Escarlet, a trans woman killed in Tarímbaro, and the state prosecutor's office keeps no disaggregated data on such crimes.

sources.summary: El Sol de Morelia reports that the majority of attacks on the LGBT community in Michoacán concentrate in Tierra Caliente, and that the state has not typified the murder of sexual-diversity people as a hate crime.

La Jornada (15 Apr 2026) reports the arrest of a suspect in the killing of 'Daniela', a trans woman found beaten to death in a drainage channel in Morelia (2 Apr 2026), and counts six LGBT+ homicides in the state in the first four and a half months of 2026.

31927357B5337219705256.name: Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
31927357B5337219705256.summary:
Veracruz was among the last Mexican states to legislate legal gender recognition. Its Congress reformed the Civil Code in 2025 to create an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, with no age requirement. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state survey covers Veracruz only in relation to identity documents held by the civil registry; it documents no prison-placement rule for the state and no information on where transgender prisoners are housed.

Violence against LGBT+ people is recorded in high raw numbers. Diario de Xalapa reported that Veracruz closed 2025 with 15 recorded hate crimes against the LGBT community. The Letra S annual impunity report published on 7 May 2026 counts six of the 60 LGBT+ murders recorded nationwide in 2025 as occurring in Veracruz, level with Guanajuato and behind Puebla's seven; the same tally includes the November 2025 killing of a trans woman at a motel in Oluta. These are raw counts published without a per-capita denominator, so the state ranking is by raw count only and does not by itself establish that a visitor faces higher risk in Veracruz than in a less populous state.

Earlier counts run the same direction. Letra S's 2021 report found that Veracruz led the national count of violent deaths of LGBT+ people for the fourth consecutive year, with 10 recorded cases, ahead of Guanajuato (9), Estado de México (7) and Chihuahua (6); 19 of the 32 states recorded victims that year. The same report documents systematic under-counting: in a third of the 2021 cases no name was published, and in 43 percent the sex was recorded as male with no attention to gender identity. State figures are compiled for the LGBT+ category as a whole, so no trans-specific homicide rate for Veracruz is published.

Prosecution is the weak point. The state prosecutor's office holds several open files on LGBT murders, according to the activist Leonardo Ruiz of Orgullo Xalapa, among them the case of Edhibaldo Presa Parra, a Universidad Veracruzana professor found dead on 7 January. Activists argue that hate-crime classification in these cases rests on inference from motive patterns and aggravating circumstances rather than direct evidence, and place responsibility for the absence of outcomes on the FGE. Not every monitoring source points the same way: data from the group Soy Humano put Veracruz's 2024 figures below the national average.

31927357B6525686063804.name: Oaxaca
31927357B6525686063804.summary:
Oaxaca stands under Mexico's national framework on legal gender recognition; the findings below are specific to the state. Oaxaca created an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition through a 2019 reform to its civil code. A 2021 decree extended the procedure to people aged 12 and over, and a June 2023 Supreme Court ruling reopened access for children under 12, leaving the route open across age groups.

Oaxaca's only documented gender-identity legislation governs identity documents.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people and against muxes is documented at state level. Oaxaca's human-rights ombudsperson opened 34 investigations into attacks on LGBTIQ+ people between 2015 and 2022. Muxe teacher Marimar 'Estrellita' Santiago was killed in 2022 on the road to Huilotepec, in the Istmo de Tehuantepec, prompting community demands for justice.

A profile published by Trendencias in April 2025 describes Oaxaca as Mexico's fastest-growing tourist destination and, at the same time, the country's most dangerous state for the LGBT+ community. It reports violent incidents under investigation with possible municipal-police involvement in municipalities where armed groups operate, and names two victims: muxe Cristian Hernández Cutino, 31, and stylist Zulma Hernández Mendoza, 43. The ranking is stated without per-capita figures, so it cannot be weighed against the state's general homicide rate.

The state's response has concentrated on visitor security rather than institutional reform, according to the same profile.

1811400B57209440839078.name: Tripura
1811400B57209440839078.summary:
Tripura stands under India's national framework, and the national assessment of legal recognition, identity documents, entry, facilities and healthcare applies to visitors here without regional modification. The region's own sources contain no Tripura statute, court order or state policy on any of those questions.

What the region's sources document is checkpoint and transport-hub enforcement in which gender presentation is treated as a possible concealment method. On 2 August 2024, police at the Panisagar check post in North Tripura district stopped a bus on the Assam-Agartala highway bound for Mumbai via Guwahati and detained seven Bangladeshi nationals, two of them transgender and five described by police as disguised as third gender; the case was registered as one of fraudulent documents and border crossing.

A separate report of the same period records 15 Bangladeshi nationals, seven of them transgender, apprehended in separate incidents within 24 hours, carrying fake Aadhaar and PAN cards. The two accounts differ on the number detained at Panisagar and on how many of them were transgender.

On 9 November 2024 a joint 24-hour operation detained 12 Bangladeshi nationals, among them minors and transgender people. Six, including three transgender persons, were held after midnight while travelling to Mumbai; a second group of six, including three children from Khulna, was held at Udaipur Railway Station. A local facilitator was arrested for moving them.

Tripura shares an 856-km border with Bangladesh, and these checkpoints sit on the highway and rail routes running from that border towards the rest of the country. Police in the operations treated third-gender presentation as a disguise, and transgender people were among those detained. The operations were immigration enforcement directed at Bangladeshi nationals, and the sources do not record whether the same scrutiny falls on transgender residents or on visitors whose documents and appearance diverge. The figures are raw counts from individual operations, with no denominator for the number of people passing through these checkpoints.

1811400B32673734874058.name: West Bengal
1811400B32673734874058.summary:
West Bengal is a state of India and stands under the national framework on transgender recognition, identity documents and healthcare, which the national record carries. This record covers enforcement, institutions and documented incidents specific to the state.

In August 2024 a group of trans women travelling to RG Kar Medical College in Kolkata filed an FIR alleging that a Railway Protection Force constable at Rabindra Sadan metro station groped one of them while checking her gender and made inappropriate remarks. Metro Railway and the RPF denied the allegation and filed a counter-FIR against the group; video footage showed the complainant in tears. The episode records gender-checking conduct by uniformed personnel in the state.

West Bengal accounted for three of the seven cases registered nationally under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021, the joint highest count that year alongside Assam and Kerala. The national total is small: 20 cases between 2019 and 2023, which the reporting attributes to police-registration bias rather than to low levels of violence. Official case counts in the state therefore understate what trans people there experience.

On border enforcement, South Dinajpur police arrested a transgender woman from Sirajganj district in Bangladesh on allegations of infiltrating India, together with the e-rickshaw driver who had brought her across. The person arrested was a foreign national entering without authorisation, not a visitor on a visa, and the single case does not establish a pattern of targeting trans travellers at the state's land border.

West Bengal is among the 12 states and union territories that notified a transgender welfare board. A Right to Information investigation published in November 2024 found the state's board operating without a functioning policy framework, and that most boards nationally have met less than once a year since being constituted, with several lacking a compliance mechanism or any decision-making power.

sources.title: LGBT rights in India - Wikipedia
sources.summary: On September 6, 2018 a five-judge bench of the Supreme Court ruled unanimously in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India, striking down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code insofar as it criminalised consensual same-sex acts, holding that discrimination based on sexual orientation violates the Constitution, and preserving the provision for non-consensual acts. In July 2024 the Indian Penal Code was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which omits Section 377 entirely. The 2014 NALSA judgment recognised a legal third gender and the right to self-identified gender identity, codified by the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, which bans discrimination in education, employment, healthcare and housing. All of these determinations bind Punjab. No Punjab-specific statute or institution targeting trans people exists.

sources.title: Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 - Wikipedia
sources.summary: The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 (Act No. 40 of 2019) is the national statute governing transgender people in Punjab. It was passed by the Lok Sabha on August 5, 2019 and the Rajya Sabha on November 26, 2019, received presidential assent on December 5, 2019, and has been in force since January 10, 2020. Following the Supreme Court's 2014 NALSA ruling, it grants transgender people the right to declare self-perceived gender identity without undergoing sex reassignment surgery, bans discrimination, creates a National Council for Transgender Persons, and prescribes imprisonment of not less than six months up to two years plus a fine for crimes against transgender people; criticism holds that it omits mandatory reservations in jobs and education. On January 27, 2020 the Supreme Court issued notice in a petition challenging the Act's constitutionality. No statute in Punjab targets trans people, and this is the framework a trans visitor to Amritsar stands under.

1811400B21167269026319.name: Tamil Nādu
1811400B21167269026319.summary:
Tamil Nadu stands under India's national framework for legal gender recognition, identity documents and criminal law. The state layer governs welfare provision, healthcare access and the administrative categories used in state records and services.

Tamil Nadu was the first Indian state to adopt a transgender welfare policy. Its transgender welfare portal publishes the operative paperwork for changing gender in state records: an affidavit form, a certificate of identity for change of gender, relaxation of membership identification requirements, and user manuals. The thirunangai and thirunambi categories are embedded in state governance rather than sitting outside it.

State provision includes free sex-reassignment surgery in government hospitals, and access to housing and citizenship schemes through the state regime.

The Madras High Court, in its order of 4 August 2025 in WP 7284 of 2021, recorded that the government had brought the Tamil Nadu State Policy for Transgender Persons 2025 into effect. The court described the policy as a victory for transgender and intersex persons after a long struggle and commended the government for it.

Prosecution data place Tamil Nadu ahead of other states in reaching court on transgender offences. A civil-society crime-data analysis published on 30 January 2026 records Tamil Nadu as the only state with a case under the Transgender Persons Act in 2020 (one of one nationally) and in 2022 (one), and as the source of seven of the eleven national cases in 2023. The same analysis warns that registration bias shapes these figures, so the counts measure reporting and prosecution reachability rather than the incidence of violence. The 2023 figure is a share of the national total, not a per-capita rate; no population denominator is given.
