27671186B79778155682183.name: Niger
27671186B79778155682183.summary:
Niger is an independent country with its own criminal law; the assessment below is national.

Article 25 of the Refoundation Charter, adopted in March 2025, criminalises all lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex and asexual acts or practices, expressly including transgender acts or practices. The February 2026 penal code punishes LGBTQIA+ acts or practices with 5 to 10 years' imprisonment and a fine of up to 100 million CFA francs, and the punishable practices expressly include changing or attempting to change one's birth sex. Same-sex sexual relations carry the same 5 to 10 year term and fine, covering same-sex sexual activity and public announcement of a romantic relationship with a person of the same sex.

Creating, managing, financing or participating in LGBTQIA+ organisations, clubs and social venues, directly or indirectly, is punished with 10 to 20 years' imprisonment and a fine of up to 500 million CFA francs. Mitigating circumstances and suspended sentences cannot be applied to these penalties.

Since March 2025, Article 24 defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman. Since June 2026, marrying a person of the same sex and officiating, organising or bearing official witness to a same-sex wedding is punished with 10 to 20 years' imprisonment.

There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on gender identity or sexual orientation. Article 95 of Law 2022-59 punishes collecting and processing data revealing sexual life or sexual orientation with three months to five years' imprisonment and a fine of 5,000,000 to 50,000,000 CFA francs; Law 2015-36, which had prohibited discrimination including on grounds of sexual orientation, was repealed in 2023 with convictions expunged.

Same-sex sexual activity was explicitly outlawed in 2025 and penalised in 2026. Before that change the age of consent stood at 13 for heterosexual acts and 21 for homosexual acts.

After the 2026 code took effect, dozens of people were arrested across the country and some imprisoned, including military officials, and LGBTQ people went into hiding. Organisations providing HIV prevention services to men who have sex with men stopped working, ending access to condoms, HIV testing and PrEP.

Documented enforcement includes two men caught naked in a parked car arrested for public indecency and fined; two young women in Maradi in 2022 prosecuted for lesbianism and acquitted for lack of legislation but imprisoned for two years for posting nude videos allegedly portraying a lesbian act; and two young women reported as lesbians in Niamey in 2025 prosecuted for public indecency but acquitted because the facts did not pertain to the public sphere, with the judge allegedly sanctioned for leniency. As of 8-9 December 2022 Niger had no specific law criminalising same-sex relationships, and Maradi lawmaker Nana Djibou Harouna had presented to the Speaker of Parliament a proposal backed by nearly all MPs to criminalise same-sex relationships, with punishment unspecified and no debate scheduled.

No violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity was reported and no documented cases of discrimination in employment, housing, education, health care or statelessness on those grounds were recorded, though stigma or intimidation probably prevented incidents from being reported. Two gay rights organisations operated in secret, partly because they were not formally registered.

Asylum seekers from Cameroon, Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire who held LGBTQ public demonstrations in Niamey in 2022 were denied refugee recognition, hindering relocation, and faced shops refusing to serve them and verbal or physical violence from strangers.

Gay men and lesbians face strong pressure to conform to societal norms, leading many to lead socially acceptable lives in public while seeking LGBT relationships privately. The 2025 acquittal of two women prosecuted for public indecency caused widespread debate ranging from approval to outrage. The only official cultural-values statement in the record concerns LGBTQ practices generally: "all LGBTQ practices, whatever they may be (...) are not in line with our social and cultural values". The record contains no statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (2004) 'Nigeria: Unconsensual Sodomy Laws' documents the wave of Sharia adoption across northern Nigeria, listing the twelve states concerned: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. It traces the wave from Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law, promulgated 27 October 1999 and in force 27 January 2000. Niger State's presence in that list places it within the northern-bloc criminalisation claim, and the provisions remain in force.

UK Home Office Country Policy and Information Note, 'Nigeria: Sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics' (version 4.0, June 2025), sets out Nigeria's hybrid legal system, the 12-state Sharia criminal layer and its coverage of women, and the limits of the available arrest data.

sources.title: Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria 1999-2006: A Sourcebook, Vol. IV, Ch. 4 Part IV — The Niger State Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 (Ostien, ed.)
sources.summary: Ostien's sourcebook reproduces Niger State's own Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 in full — a law to amend Penal Code Law Cap 94, Laws of Niger State, to review the punishments therein, gazetted in the Niger State of Nigeria Gazette No. 8, Vol. 25 of 9 March 2000 (pp. B29-B36) and coming into force on 4 May 2000. The enactment defines 'adultery' to include sodomy and inserts section 68A, under which a Muslim convicted of a listed offence and proved against him to the Islamic evidentiary standard receives the harsher Sharia-specified punishment (with amputation added to the caning paragraph of section 68), while the ordinary Penal Code punishment otherwise applies. State-level statutory proof that Niger, like the other northern bloc states, built a distinct criminal track for Muslim defendants — the legal layer this record identifies as the visitor-facing risk beyond federal law.

sources.title: Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria 1999-2006: A Sourcebook, Vol. IV, Ch. 4 Part III — The Sharia Penal Codes (Ostien, ed.)
sources.summary: Niger: Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 (HB.4/2000) was signed into law on 22 February 2000 and came into operation on 4 May 2000, gazetted as Niger State Gazette Vol. 25 No. 8 of 9 March 2000. The editor notes that it is not a complete Sharia Penal Code: it amends the Penal Code of 1960 so that certain sections, applied to Muslims, carry different burdens of proof and different punishments than when applied to non-Muslims, and it is printed in its entirety in Part IV of the same chapter. An outed Muslim visitor in Niger State therefore stands under a harsher parallel legal frame than federal law alone.

27671186B8148656125930.name: Imo
27671186B8148656125930.summary:
Imo is a state in south-eastern Nigeria and stands under the national legal framework. Its own record covers enforcement action taken inside the state against private gatherings and against people accused of same-sex conduct in public.

On 26 April 2018 two men in Imo State were stripped, beaten and paraded through the streets after being accused of gay sex. An inquiry by NoStringsNG found that the victims were then arrested by the police themselves, and that they might need legal support. The state's role in the episode was to detain the people who had been attacked, not the crowd that attacked them.

Enforcement continued into 2025. On 19 February the Imo Police Command broke up a party at Graziella Hotels in Orogwe, Owerri West, arrested many of those present, described as gay and lesbian suspects, and placed attendees who fled on a police search list. The event was a private hotel gathering, and the police treated it as an operation with names attached to people who were not detained.

Seven years separate the two documented episodes, and they occurred in different parts of the state: a street in 2018, a hotel in Owerri West in 2025. Police action in Imo is therefore not confined to a single locality, and it has not been limited to public conduct. Both a public street and a closed private venue appear in the record as points of exposure, and leaving before an arrest did not remove people from the search.

27671186B63712480376187.name: Edo
27671186B63712480376187.summary:
Edo State stands under Nigeria's national legal framework. Its own documented record is one of mob violence against people accused of same-sex conduct, and it contains no instance in which police protected the person accused.

In February 2008, in a remote community in Edo State, police declared Ugbogbo Ovbukhan wanted over 'gay practice' after he and his partner Jerry were found together. A mob beat both men for desecrating the community; Ovbukhan escaped before police arrived and police arrested Jerry for interrogation. The Nigerian Observer reported the wanted declaration on 15 August 2008.

On 10 June 2010, The Nigerian Observer reported from Benin City, in Oredo local government area, that Mark Osato Edomwonyi narrowly escaped being killed by a mob after he was found with his partner Paddy in Paddy's rented apartment. A neighbour raised the alarm; Edomwonyi fled through the backyard before the mob arrived, and the crowd then, in the newspaper's words, 'unleashed terror' on Paddy. No police intervention, arrest or prosecution appears in the report, and Edomwonyi's whereabouts were still unknown when it was filed.

In May 2018, at Ekpoma, a mob lynched one of two men found together while the other escaped. The report presented the killing as an 'abominable act' against traditional heritage, treating it as community redress.

For a visitor, the documented exposure in Edo comes from community perception rather than from a prosecution: in these accounts it is neighbours, not patrols, who raise the alarm, and the single police action documented across the three cases was taken against the couple rather than against those who beat them. The cases reported involve men accused of same-sex conduct, and the inventory holds no Edo case in which a report identifies the victim of violence as a transgender person. Risk to a trans visitor therefore has to be read from the way accusations of sexual and gender nonconformity mobilise a crowd, not from a documented attack on a trans person in the state.

The figures are national in scope, with no Edo-specific breakdown, and TIERs states they represent only a fraction of the true scale.

65028918B93184959873838.name: Aceh
65028918B93184959873838.summary:
Aceh stands under Indonesia's national legal framework; the national layer is carried by the parent record. The region-specific layer is a provincial sharia criminal code. Special autonomy granted in 2005 authorised the introduction of Islamic criminal law for Muslim residents, and Qanun Aceh Nomor 6 Tahun 2014 tentang Hukum Jinayat, enacted in 2014, has been enforced since 23 October 2015. Aceh is Indonesia's only province that criminalises same-sex relations and enforces Islamic law in addition to the national criminal code.

Article 63 of the Qanun defines liwath as sexual acts between males and Article 64 defines musahaqah as sexual acts between females, each determined by sex at birth. Each offence carries up to 100 lashes, up to 100 months' imprisonment, or a fine of up to 1,000 grams of gold. Because the definitions turn on birth sex rather than presentation or legal gender marker, a trans visitor whose documents, presentation or partner's sex are read as same-sex conduct falls within the provision and faces caning, imprisonment or a fine.

Public caning is the province's standing punishment for sharia offences. On 23 May 2017 an Islamic court in Banda Aceh applied the 2014 provisions for the first time, ordering two men caned 82 times each before hundreds of spectators outside a mosque; in 2017 two further men, aged 20 and 23, were sentenced to public caning for same-sex relations.

The most recent documented enforcement in this record is from 2025. Two men aged 20 and 21 were sentenced on 11 August 2025 to public caning for kissing, after an April 2025 arrest in which police broke into a toilet; CBS News and the Associated Press reported on 26 August 2025 that two men were publicly caned in the province after a sharia court convicted them of hugging and kissing. No later Aceh enforcement incident is documented in this record.

Trans people in Aceh have faced targeted enforcement. In January 2018 police in North Aceh arrested twelve transgender women, forcibly cut their hair, compelled them to wear men's clothing and closed their beauty salons. In a separate parlour raid in Aceh in January 2018 police tortured detainees, shaved the heads of transgender women, removed their shirts and bras, and paraded them through the street forcing them to shout that they were to become men.

sources.summary: QURU: Journal of Family Law and Culture (doi 10.59698/quru.v3i1.405): 'The Increasing Number of Waria in Banda Aceh: Between Social Challenges and Law Enforcement' by UIN Ar-Raniry scholars (keywords: Law Enforcement, Waria, Aceh, Islamic Law, Qanun). Aceh legal scholarship analysing the rise of waria cases through a sharia-law-enforcement lens.

CBS News/AP (26 Aug 2025): two men were publicly caned in conservative Aceh province after a sharia court convicted them of hugging and kissing. Public caning is the province's standing punishment for sharia offences.

iNews Aceh (undated local report, Feb-2025 round-up context): Satpol PP and Wilayatul Hisbah Banda Aceh secured an alleged gay couple in a boarding house; a local advocate urged police to investigate and boarding-house owners to monitor tenants. The report concerns a gay couple, and no trans person is identified in it.

UNSW Human Rights Research Centre reports that transgender women face the highest rates of violence among LGBTIQ Indonesians, with survey data on relative social hostility. The report covers the January 2018 detention of twelve transwomen. Its scope is Indonesia-wide rather than Aceh-specific.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Aceh (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Cross-dressing is not per se illegal in Indonesia, and transgender identity (also called waria) has long been part of Indonesian culture and society. Transgender people are allowed to change their legal gender on official documents after undergoing sex reassignment surgery and receiving a judge's approval, after which they can marry a person of the opposite legal gender, exemplified by Vivian Rubiyanti Iskandar as the first trans Indonesian legally recognized as female and by Aprilio Manganang in 2021 as the first service member to legally change gender from female to male although his case was intersex assigned female at birth. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with identification papers including Kartu Tanda Penduduk for residents of Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung and Papua, recognizing only male and female descriptors with no third gender/X option and printing gender at birth unless court recognition was already obtained, on the stated reasoning that many were undocumented where families did not approve. Indonesian law does not explicitly protect transgender people from discrimination or harassment, and transgender people who do not hide their gender identity often find it challenging to maintain legitimate employment and are thus often forced into prostitution and other illegal activities to survive. In Aceh transgender people have faced targeted enforcement: in January 2018 police in North Aceh arrested twelve transgender women, forcibly cut their hair, compelled them to wear men's clothing, and closed their beauty salons, and in a January 2018 parlour raid in Aceh police tortured LGBTQ citizens, shaved the heads of transgender women, stripped their shirts and bras, and paraded them in the street forcing them to shout "to become men". In Jakarta the Social Agency declared waria to be socially dysfunctional and regularly conducts raids against transgender women, taking detained individuals to city-owned rehabilitation centres where they are incarcerated with homeless people, beggars and street buskers and only released upon documentation of lack of homelessness and a signed promise not to repeat the offence, with officials stating this is to create a deterrent against being transgender and continued violations will result in jail time. The Indonesian Ulama Council ruled transgender persons must live in the gender they were born with, stating if not willing to cure themselves medically and religiously they must accept their fate to be ridiculed and harassed, while the judicial system takes the contrary position recognizing actual genders and authorities have in some cases arrested and prosecuted perpetrators of hate crimes against the transgender community. Aceh has special autonomous status implementing Islamic Sharia-based criminal law (Qanun Jinayat), with authority granted in 2005 to introduce Sharia law for Muslim residents and the 2014 Qanun Jinayat providing that consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults are punishable by up to 100 lashes or up to 100 months (8 years) imprisonment, set for enforcement by the end of 2015. Enforcement outcomes in Aceh include the 2017 sentencing of two young gay men aged 20 and 23 to public caning, several high-profile cases of men publicly caned after guilty findings for same-sex relations, and the 11 August 2025 sentencing of two men aged 20 and 21 to public caning for kissing after April arrest when police broke into a toilet. Nationally Indonesia has allowed private consensual same-sex activity since 1993 at age 18, has no explicit sodomy law unlike Malaysia, and the Penal Code does not prohibit non-commercial private consensual activity between consenting same-sex adults. In December 2022 Parliament passed a Penal Code criminalizing sex outside marriage upon complaint by immediate family, set to take force on 2 January 2026 with up to one year imprisonment for unmarried partners, with the spokesperson stating the draft will not criminalize private sexual orientation including LGBTQ persons and Coordinating Minister Mahfud MD stating it did not criminalize an LGBTQ person and only targets adults committing sexual violence or rape of underage same-sex children and immoral acts in public, while Article 421(1) punishes obscene acts against a same-sex person in public with maximum 1 year and six months imprisonment or maximum fine category III. Indonesian law does not recognise same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships, households headed by same-sex couples lack the same legal protections as opposite-sex couples, and same-sex couples are ineligible to adopt as only married husband-wife couples can adopt. As of 2019 no specific law protects from discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity nor prohibits hate crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity, though a 2015 police circular states processing of hate speech related to sexual orientations and gender identity and Head of National Police Regulation No. 8 of 2009 stipulates the duty to protect special rights of minority groups including sexual orientation. Police have conducted repeated raids and detentions for gay parties and saunas under pornography-related offences, including the November 2016 Jakarta raid after an Islamic Defenders Front tip-off, May 2017 arrest of 141 men for a gay sex party with ten charged and detention of 144 in the Atlantis Gym raid, October 2017 arrest of 51 in a Central Jakarta sauna with six charged including the owner, and 2025 raids detaining 56 on 1 February, nine on 24 May, and arresting 75 on 22 June near Jakarta. The article states: "While transgender people in Indonesia are generally more accepted than gays, lesbians and bisexuals, they have, in recent years, faced growing discrimination and rejection, mostly from sharia-supporting Muslim groups, which have become more and more popular in Indonesia." The article states "some public tolerance is given to some transgender people working in beauty salons or the entertainment industry, most notably the celebrity talk show host Dorce Gamalama." The article states transgender identity (also called waria) has long been part of Indonesian culture and society. The article states discrimination and harassments directed at transgender people is not uncommon, though violence is quite rare, and transgender people who do not hide their gender identity often face employment exclusion forcing reliance on prostitution and other illegal activities. The article reports officials justify rehabilitation detention as creating a deterrent against being transgender and cites the Ulama Council position that those unwilling to cure themselves medically and religiously must accept their fate to be ridiculed and harassed, evidencing institutional rejection despite noted cultural presence.

sources.title: Qanun Jinayat (2014 Aceh Sharia Criminal Code)
sources.summary: Qanun Aceh Nomor 6 Tahun 2014 tentang Hukum Jinayat enacted in 2014 and enforced from 23 October 2015 defines liwath in Article 63 as sexual acts between males and musahaqah in Article 64 as sexual acts between females as determined by birth sex and punishes each with up to 100 lashes, up to 100 months imprisonment, or a fine of up to 1,000 grams of gold, thereby exposing trans visitors in Aceh to caning, imprisonment and fines where presentation, identity documents, or partner sex are policed as same-sex conduct.

sources.title: 2017 Aceh public caning case - two young gay men aged 20 and 23
sources.summary: Aceh is Indonesia's only province that criminalizes same-sex relations and enforces Islamic law in addition to the national criminal code, and on May 23, 2017 in Banda Aceh an Islamic court applied its 2014 anti-homosexuality provisions for the first time by having two men publicly caned with 82 lashes each for gay sex before hundreds of spectators outside a mosque.

65028918B93184959873838.modelContext: Aceh: Indonesia's only province with formal sharia criminal law (qanun jinayat) — caning for same-sex intimacy documented (2017 caning of two men), wilayatul hisbah morality police patrol public behavior; the most dangerous province in Indonesia for a discovered trans visitor.
65028918B93184959873838.blindSummary:
This division operates under this country's national legal framework; the national layer is carried by the parent record. The region-specific layer is a provincial sharia criminal code. Special autonomy granted in 2005 authorised the introduction of Islamic criminal law for Muslim residents, and the provincial sharia criminal code enacted in 2014 has been enforced since 23 October 2015. This division is the only provincial-level jurisdiction in this country that criminalises same-sex relations and enforces Islamic law in addition to the national criminal code.

Article 63 of the code defines liwath as sexual acts between males and Article 64 defines musahaqah as sexual acts between females, each determined by sex at birth. Each offence carries up to 100 lashes, up to 100 months' imprisonment, or a fine of up to 1,000 grams of gold. Because the definitions turn on birth sex rather than presentation or legal gender marker, a trans visitor whose documents, presentation or partner's sex are read as same-sex conduct falls within the provision and faces caning, imprisonment or a fine.

Public caning is the division's standing punishment for sharia offences. On 23 May 2017 a regional sharia court in the administrative capital applied the 2014 provisions for the first time, ordering two men caned 82 times each before hundreds of spectators outside a mosque; in 2017 two further men, aged 20 and 23, were sentenced to public caning for same-sex relations.

The most recent documented enforcement in this record is from 2025. Two men aged 20 and 21 were sentenced on 11 August 2025 to public caning for kissing, after an April 2025 arrest in which police broke into a toilet; two major news organisations reported on 26 August 2025 that two men were publicly caned in this division after a sharia court convicted them of hugging and kissing. No later enforcement incident in this division is documented in this record.

Trans people in this division have faced targeted enforcement. In January 2018 police in a northern district arrested twelve transgender women, forcibly cut their hair, compelled them to wear men's clothing and closed their beauty salons. In a separate parlour raid in this division in January 2018 police tortured detainees, shaved the heads of transgender women, removed their shirts and bras, and paraded them through the street forcing them to shout that they were to become men.

65028918B88589358118692.name: Lampung
65028918B88589358118692.summary:
Lampung stands under Indonesia's national legal framework, which the parent record carries in full. The province's own documented record of official conduct toward transgender people is a November 2018 operation in which the Satpol PP, the regional morals-and-order force, raided three trans women, detained them at the Satpol PP office and hosed them down at the firefighter building while an officer recorded the incident.

OutRight International's Creeping Criminalisation study names Lampung as one of eight Indonesian provinces whose discriminatory regional regulations it analyses, and it examines those rules at both province and district level. Restrictive rules in Lampung therefore operate below the national tier as well as at it, and enforcement of morals and order in the province rests with a regional force rather than solely with the national police.

For a trans visitor, the exposure documented in Lampung is sub-national: regulations analysed at province and district level, and a regional morals-and-order force with a documented raid and degrading treatment of trans women, sit alongside the national provisions that apply throughout Indonesia.

sources.summary: UNSW human-rights review of anti-trans violence in Indonesia: documents that in November 2018 three transwomen were raided by Satpol PP (the regional morals-and-order force) in Lampung province — detained at the Satpol PP office and hosed down at the firefighter building, with an officer recording it — alongside a national pattern of transwomen murdered in 2017 (Bone, Semarang, South Sulawesi) and election-cycle anti-LGBT bylaw lobbying from 2016 onward; an SMRC survey of 1,520 Indonesians (Nov 2016) found LGBT people hated by 16.6%.

OutRight International's Creeping Criminalisation study analyses discriminatory regional regulations in eight Indonesian provinces — Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatera, South Sulawesi, South Sumatera and Yogyakarta — at both province and district level. Lampung is named among them.

65028918B84835514626455.name: West Papua
65028918B84835514626455.summary:
West Papua operates no provincial criminal law reaching sexual conduct or gender expression. The province stands under Indonesia's national framework without local additions, and no regency-level regulation on dress, public morality or gender presentation is documented in this inventory.

Security-force conduct is the province's defining documented risk. A report published on 22 July 2025 by the Asia-Pacific Solidarity Network recorded 138 acts of torture or other ill-treatment by police and military against people in detention in Maybrat and the Central Highlands through early 2025, with most victims male and under 24, seven female, and seven minors aged 15 to 17; the report's framing is 'impunity, secrecy and silence', indicating near-total absence of accountability. Any visitor to the province, including a visibly gender-nonconforming one, stands in this security-force environment.

The Papua human-rights monitor's Q3 2025 quarterly records a notable increase in military deployments and operations in West Papua's highland regions since August 2025. In Sorong, police arrested over a dozen protest participants in August 2025. On 27 September 2025 a military task force opened fire on civilians in Agats, Asmat Regency, alongside ongoing displacement and racial tension affecting indigenous Papuans. No trans-specific finding accompanies this pattern, but it amplifies exposure for a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor.

Provincial document practice follows the national pattern: since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with Kartu Tanda Penduduk, including residents of Papua, but the card recognises only 'male' and 'female' with no third gender or X designator, and prints gender at birth unless a court recognition is obtained. Families' disapproval can block the documentation process, which officials cite as leaving some residents undocumented and unable to access work or social services.

Legal gender recognition is available nationally after sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, after which the person may marry someone of the opposite legal gender. The judicial system has recognised trans status: Vivian Rubiyanti Iskandar was the first trans Indonesian legally recognised as female, and there are documented cases where perpetrators of hate crimes against the transgender community were arrested and prosecuted.

Indonesian law does not explicitly protect transgender people from discrimination or harassment. The Indonesian Ulama Council ruled that transgender persons must live in the gender they were born with, stating that if they are 'not willing to cure themselves medically and religiously' they must be willing 'to accept their fate to be ridiculed and harassed'. This religious-body position sits alongside the judicial system's contrary practice.

Targeted enforcement documented against trans people includes the January 2018 North Aceh police arrest of twelve transgender women, during which their hair was forcibly cut, they were compelled into men's clothing, and beauty salons were closed. The Jakarta Social Agency declared waria socially dysfunctional and conducted regular raids and incarceration in city-owned 'rehabilitation' centres alongside homeless people, beggars and buskers, requiring documentation and a signed pledge before release; officials stated this was intended as a deterrent against being transgender and warned that continued violations would result in jail time. These are national-level actions, not West Papua ones, but they set the enforcement backdrop.

Discrimination in employment is documented: transgender people who do not hide their gender identity often find it challenging to maintain legitimate employment and are frequently pushed into prostitution and other informal or illegal activity to survive, with discrimination and harassment described as not uncommon though violence as quite rare. The article also notes that gays in jails are often sexually abused because of their orientation and do not report it, due to trauma and fear of return.

The control environment includes the 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction, which prohibits presentations suggesting same-sex relations and carries a fine or up to seven years' imprisonment; a March 2016 broadcasting commission policy banning programmes that make LGBTQ behaviour appear 'normal' and discouraging effeminate, transgender or cross-dressing figures; bans on sites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ terms including Grindr; and widely practiced, openly advertised conversion therapy, including rehabilitation-centre treatment with de facto legalisation by some city governments after the 'RUU Ketahanan Keluarga' Family Resilience draft was rejected by 5 of 9 factions.

Care context: a 2012 Health Ministry estimate put the number of transgender women at around 31 thousand. Yayasan Srikandi Sejati, founded 1998, focuses on transgender health, providing HIV/AIDS counselling and free condoms to transgender sex workers at a free health clinic, operating amid a lack of school sex education and a historical movement focus that led the public to believe AIDS was a 'gay disease'.

Cultural context: transgender identity, also called waria, has long been part of Indonesian culture and society, and some public tolerance is given to transgender people working in beauty salons or the entertainment industry. The article states that while transgender people in Indonesia are generally more accepted than gays, lesbians and bisexuals, they have in recent years faced growing discrimination and rejection, mostly from sharia-supporting Muslim groups, which have become more popular in Indonesia.

Military service context: in 2021 Aprilio Manganang became the first service member to legally change gender from female to male, though his case involved an intersex person assigned female at birth and raised as a girl.

Direct security-force risk context for any visitor to the province.

Papua human-rights monitor quarterly, Q3 2025: notable increase in military deployments and operations in West Papua's highland regions since August 2025. In Sorong police arrested over a dozen protest participants in Aug 2025. On 27 September 2025 a military task force opened fire on civilians in Agats, Asmat Regency, alongside ongoing displacement and racial tension affecting indigenous Papuans. No trans-specific finding is recorded; the general security-force pattern amplifies exposure for a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor.

Transgender people who do not hide gender identity often find it challenging to maintain legitimate employment and are thus often forced into prostitution and other illegal activities to survive, with discrimination and harassments not uncommon though violence quite rare. In the military, Aprilio Manganang in 2021 became the first service member to legally change gender from female to male, although his case was intersex assigned female at birth and raised as a girl. Private, non-commercial consensual sexual activity between consenting adults of the same sex has been allowed nationally since 1993 at 18 years of age, with no explicit sodomy law unlike Malaysia, and a 2003 national bill to criminalize same-sex activity with cohabitation, adultery and witchcraft failed with no subsequent reintroduction. Security-force conduct is the division's defining documented risk. A report published on 22 July 2025 by a regional solidarity network recorded 138 acts of torture or other ill-treatment by police and military against people in detention in a riverine district and the highlands through early 2025, with most victims male and under 24, seven female, and seven minors aged 15 to 17; the report's framing is 'impunity, secrecy and silence', indicating near-total absence of accountability. Any visitor to the division, including a visibly gender-nonconforming one, stands in this security-force environment.

The division's human-rights monitor's Q3 2025 quarterly records a notable increase in military deployments and operations in the division's highland regions since August 2025. In a major port city, police arrested over a dozen protest participants in August 2025. On 27 September 2025 a military task force opened fire on civilians in a riverside town in a coastal sub-district, alongside ongoing displacement and racial tension affecting indigenous residents of the division. No trans-specific finding accompanies this pattern, but it amplifies exposure for a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor.

Provincial document practice follows the national pattern: since June 2021 the national home-affairs ministry has conducted outreach to issue transgender citizens of this country with the national identity card, including residents of this division, but the card recognises only 'male' and 'female' with no third gender or X designator, and prints gender at birth unless a court recognition is obtained. This country's law does not explicitly protect transgender people from discrimination or harassment. 65028918B28198720309323.summary:
Central Kalimantan stands under Indonesia's national framework, and the sources reviewed identify no provincial-level legal divergence. OutRight Action International's 2022 mapping of Indonesian laws and regional regulations that violate the rights of women and LGBTIQ people lists eight provinces with discriminatory regional regulations; Central Kalimantan is not among them. No provincial enforcement action, police operation, prosecution or incident directed at trans or LGBTIQ people in Central Kalimantan appears in the sources reviewed. Absence from a list of discriminatory regulations is a legal finding only. It does not establish how provincial police, local officials or communities treat trans visitors in practice, and nothing in the sources reviewed addresses that question.

sources.title: 2023 Indonesian Penal Code – Wikipedia

This is the national criminal baseline applying to a visitor in Central Kalimantan, whose risk follows the country's national framework rather than any local divergence.

65028918B37605681672150.name: North Sumatra
65028918B37605681672150.summary:
North Sumatra is a province of Indonesia and stands under the national legal framework, which applies here as it does nationwide.

North Sumatra is one of eight provinces covered by OutRight Action International's mapping of national laws and discriminatory regional regulations. That mapping documents regional rules imposing dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear, with significant variation between regions; the report states its findings hold for areas beyond the provinces it examined directly.

Medan, the provincial capital, is the site of the only documented legal-process case for a transgender person in North Sumatra. Dimas Cahya became the first transgender man in the city to change his name legally to match his identity, and the Medan District Court granted the application after a six-week process. The judge warned that the change would 'erase my identity' but declined to engage with LGBTI issues, and no enforcement action against the couple is recorded.

UNAIDS reporting describes Medan as conservative, with LGBTI people regarded locally as 'immoral'.

sources.summary: OutRight Action International's 'Creeping Criminalisation: Mapping of Indonesia's National Laws and Regional Regulations That Violate Human Rights of Women and LGBTIQ People' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa; 2022 file copy) maps national laws and discriminatory regional regulations across eight focus provinces: Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta. It finds much overlap but significant regional variation in dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear, and states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set.

sources.title: The first but not the last: Indonesian transgender man fights for recognition | UNAIDS
sources.summary: Dimas Cahya, a transgender man from Medan, North Sumatra's capital, told UNAIDS how he became the first transgender man in Medan to legally change his name to match his identity. After a six-week process the Medan District Court granted the application; the judge warned that the change would 'erase my identity' but stayed out of LGBTI issues completely. The article frames Medan as conservative, with LGBTI people deemed 'immoral', and reports that a Medan legal-aid organisation asked the couple invasive questions before the case. This is the only documented legal-process case for North Sumatra: a local court handled a trans person's application neutrally, and the article records no enforcement action against the couple.

65028918B6070530336190.name: Special Region of Yogyakarta
65028918B6070530336190.summary:
The Special Region of Yogyakarta carries its own layer of discriminatory regional regulation. A 2022 mapping of Indonesia's national laws and regional regulations that violate the rights of women and LGBTIQ people examined eight focus provinces, Yogyakarta among them, and found substantial overlap alongside significant regional variation. The regulations it documents include dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear. The mapping states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the eight it examined, so the categories it identifies are not confined to the provinces it names.

The most fully documented enforcement action against a trans institution in Yogyakarta is the February 2016 closure of Pondok Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah, a religious school where trans women study Islam. The hardline Front Jihad Islam threatened to seal the school, and on the night of 24 February 2016 a two-hour meeting at the Jagalan ward office in Yogyakarta ended with an agreement to shut it. Those present included ward and residents' officials, the lurah and the local military district commander; an earlier session on 19 February was attended by the Banguntapan camat and the local police sector chief. The district head justified the closure on the grounds that the pesantren lacked a permit, conflicted with Islamic values and had once had alcohol found on site. Its founder, Shinta Ratri, said about 20 waria attended the weekly weekend classes, which taught ordinary Islamic instruction.

A waria witness at the meeting said a Front Jihad Islam leader delivered anti-LGBT remarks to shouts of "Allahu Akbar" and vowed the group would keep hunting LGBTI people wherever they gather. The Governor of the Special Region of Yogyakarta, Sultan Hamengku Buwono X, publicly urged restraint on both sides, called LGBT people "sama-sama anak bangsa" (fellow children of the nation) and said the regional government would study the issue. The shutdown concluded on administrative and community grounds; no provincial anti-trans statute was cited.

The pesantren and the Yogyakarta waria community were operating again years after the closure, and economic and social marginalisation of trans people in the province persists.

76434192B26311534340602.name: KwaZulu-Natal
76434192B26311534340602.summary:
KwaZulu-Natal is a province of South Africa and stands under the national framework: the constitutional equality guarantee, the Equality Court under the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act, legal gender recognition, the 2024 hate-crime statute and the national correctional rules for transgender inmates apply here as they do elsewhere in the country. No provincial law, by-law or provincial institution departing from that layer is documented in the sources.

The provincial evidence on violence and victimisation is a 2024 masters thesis in criminology at the University of KwaZulu-Natal in Durban. It interviewed 15 self-identifying queer participants recruited through the Imvelo Yesizwe Organisation in KwaMashu township and reports substantial queerphobic violence and victimisation in that township setting. The study also examines whether the support and interventions available to those residents were adequate, and what safety strategies they used.

The study is small and its participants were purposively recruited, so it records the experiences of that group rather than a measured rate of violence. It does not disaggregate transgender participants from other sexual minorities, and no source gives a KwaZulu-Natal figure for violence against transgender people. A trans visitor to the province has no validated local victimisation figure to work from.

PinkNews (26 Jan 2012): Zulu King Goodwill Zwelithini's anti-gay remarks at a harvest festival prompted demands for apology; police opened investigation, with the KwaZulu-Natal Premier and Contralesa weighing in on the royal family's account. Region-specific evidence of top traditional authority hostility toward gay people in the province.

sources.title: Transgender prisoners challenge prison authorities (GroundUp)
sources.summary: GroundUp news feature (6 Aug 2025, Elna Schutz) documenting where transgender prisoners are held in South Africa: Jade September, a transgender woman, was imprisoned in the male section of Pollsmoor and won her 2019 Equality Court case against the Minister of Correctional Services, which ruled that not allowing her to express her gender identity was unfair discrimination. Reports that the resulting Department of Correctional Services standard operating procedure (SOP) for LGBT+ prisoners requires a safety-risk assessment within the first six hours of admission and stipulates that transgender men and transgender women are to be detained or transported only with other transgender men or transgender women respectively, alongside respectful-search and communication rules. Also notes Lawyers for Human Rights representation of 'NM', a transgender woman serving a long-term sentence at Johannesburg Correctional Centre, in litigation against DCS over gender-affirming healthcare, and rights organisations' concern about implementation of the SOP.

sources.title: Nthabiseng Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre - Lawyers for Human Rights
sources.summary: Lawyers for Human Rights case page (14 Nov 2025): the South African High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, ruled in favour of transgender inmate Nthabiseng Mokoena against the Department of Correctional Services (DCS), finding unfair discrimination and harassment because DCS refused to allow her to express her gender identity (feminizing attire, she/her pronouns) and failed to provide appropriate accommodation. The court held that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at State expense, rejected DCS's contrary argument, and ordered DCS to immediately implement accommodations, enforce its own SOPs relating to transgender inmates, and provide the prescribed medical care. Subject-verified: documents that trans inmates are accommodated inside the standard national corrections system (here Johannesburg Correctional Centre) and that placement/accommodation obligations rest on DCS SOPs enforced through litigation.

sources.title: Media Statement: National Preventive Mechanism welcomes the High Court ruling affirming the rights of transgender persons in correctional facilities (SAHRC)
sources.summary: South African Human Rights Commission, acting as the National Preventive Mechanism under OPCAT (designated 4 Dec 2024), media statement (14 Nov 2025) welcoming the Gauteng Division of the High Court, Johannesburg, judgment (delivered 10 Nov 2025) in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others (Case No. 2024/070075). Describes Mokoena, assigned male at birth and identifying as female from early childhood, being restricted from wearing feminine clothing and makeup and misgendered while in a correctional facility. Subject-verified: an official state human-rights body confirming that transgender persons are held in the ordinary correctional system and that the 2025 ruling affirms their rights in correctional facilities, including accommodation.

76434192B51294388644125.name: Nothern Cape
76434192B51294388644125.summary:
The Northern Cape is a province of South Africa, and the national record carries the country's constitutional discrimination guarantees, hate-crime statute, gender-recognition rules and corrections standards. What follows is specific to the province.

On the night of 14 May 2024, Jo-Ann Isaks, a 27-year-old transgender woman, was found dead in her burning room in the Paballelo location of Upington. She had multiple stab wounds to the upper body. A family member noticed the fire at about 23:00. Police in the ZF Mgcawu District confirmed a murder case had been opened, described the investigation as at a critical stage and reported no arrests; the same statement identified her publicly by a male name. Jenny Sambok, an LGBTIQ+ leader in the district, said the community in the ZF Mgcawu region had been shaken.

Karabelo Pudumo, an 18-year-old transgender Grade 10 learner at Pescodia High School in Kimberley, the provincial capital, was stabbed to death on 1 June 2024. A man she had been drinking with allegedly turned on her after realising she was transgender and stabbed her more than 20 times. A suspect was reportedly arrested, a detail the outlet reporting the case could not confirm with the authorities. More than 300 children and community members attended a memorial service at the school. Her death was the second suspected hate-crime murder of a transgender person in the province in under a month.

A third LGBTIQ+ resident, Lazarus Ikaneng Thomas, a 50-year-old gay man, was murdered in September 2024. The three deaths are raw counts for one province in one year, and the sources provide no per-capita or general homicide rate against which to measure them.

Organised community presence in the province is recent. The first Northern Cape Pride was held on 30 November 2024 at the Galeshewe Open Air Arena in Kimberley under the theme 'Pride with a Purpose', with a morning parade, speakers and community activities. Pride Committee member Tebogo Makwati called it a historic moment for the province.

76434192B92524600968894.name: Mpumalanga
76434192B92524600968894.summary:
Mpumalanga is a province of South Africa and stands under the national framework; the constitutional guarantees, the criminal-law position on consensual conduct, the gender-recognition statute, the hate-crime provisions and the national correctional rulings are carried by the national record. The findings below are those specific to the province.

Traditional-authority structures have been openly opposed to legal recognition of same-sex relationships. A published letter of June 2010, issued by the National House of Traditional Leaders together with its provincial houses after a meeting held at Hazyview in Mpumalanga, stated that traditional leaders were disappointed that the Constitutional Court's marriage judgment had given what the letter called an immoral practice a lifeline, declared that they did not support legalisation of same-sex marriage, warned of ostracism and violence, and committed to a five-year campaign against it. The same structure asked Parliament in 2016 to review the constitutional clause protecting people against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

Violence against people read as sexuality- or gender-nonconforming has produced both a killing and a mass response inside the province. Portia Mtsweni, a 25-year-old lesbian, was found dead near Zamani Primary School in Tweefontein, in Thembisile Hani Local Municipality, in the early hours of Sunday 29 December 2019; she was half naked and had stab wounds. On 2 January 2020 about 800 people marched in the same municipality in protest, in a demonstration organised by Lasiphumakhona LGBTI, the ANC Women's League and others. Thembisile Hani mayor Nomsa Mtsweni called on parents, leaders and churches to stand united against gender-based violence.

Public LGBTIQ+ presence has also drawn official cooperation. Mpumalanga's first Pride march and celebration was held on Saturday 9 August 2014 in the provincial capital, then Nelspruit and now Mbombela, under the theme 'Moving Forward, Proud, Strong & United'. Around 1,000 participants marched from the SABC offices to Nelspruit Plaza, followed by a picnic at Oorwesig Garden Park. The organiser, Joy Kunene, said police were visible and supportive and supplied about 20 police and traffic officers; the event launched the LGBTI Mpumalanga Movement, an umbrella body for the province's LGBTI organisations.

Police conduct is the most consistently reported grievance. At a Pride Flag Tour event held at the eMbalenhle Sasol Club on 18 August 2026, LGBTIQ+ community members led by the Rainbow Seed Institute raised concerns about discrimination and stigmatisation at government institutions, particularly police stations. Participants said they were ridiculed, questioned or treated unfairly when seeking assistance, and one member alleged that after she was sexually assaulted in eMbalenhle months earlier, an officer at eMbalenhle Police Station asked why she had not fought back. Attendees said they fear reporting crimes because of stigmatisation.

The documented pattern is community-level violence and police mistreatment inside a protective national legal framework. Enforcement appears to turn on the individual station, municipality or venue rather than on any province-wide practice, and the sources identify no Mpumalanga-specific court ruling, provincial policy or facilities rule.

76434192B37104984973577.summary:
Limpopo is a province of the Republic of South Africa and stands under the national legal framework. The province-specific material in the source inventory concerns the reach of customary law and traditional authority in the rural districts that formed part of the former Bantustans.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 May 2012 that the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament would create a parallel customary-law justice system covering people living in the former Bantustan areas, with no provision allowing anyone to opt out of its jurisdiction. The same report states that rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, and that chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas.

Mamba Online reported on 18 April 2012, in a piece by Melanie Judge, that the bill was under debate in provincial public hearings and would re-criminalise gay and lesbian conduct in former-Bantustan areas through a separate customary system. Lesbians were reported punished at chiefs' homesteads and tribal offices, and those able to do so were expected to leave rural areas. Traditional leaders were also reported to have opposed the Civil Union Act of 2006.

The most recent documented instance in this record dates from 2012; no later instance is documented.

76434192B85643022077130.name: North West
76434192B85643022077130.summary:
North West is a province of South Africa and its law sits inside the national framework; the South Africa record carries the constitutional protections, legal gender recognition, marriage law and hate-crime statute. The findings below are those specific to the province.

The clearest practical obstacle for a trans visitor who depends on prescribed hormone treatment is the provincial health system. No public health facility in North West provides hormone replacement therapy for transgender people, and the North West Department of Health confirmed that position to the South African Human Rights Commission in response to a complaint lodged by Action for Social Justice International. Residents travel sometimes hundreds of kilometres, most often to Soweto in Gauteng, to obtain treatment. A visitor whose supply runs out in the province cannot expect a public clinic or hospital to fill or continue the prescription.

Institutional enforcement of gendered appearance is documented in the province. In March 2016 an 18-year-old, Zinzi Manini Molema, was barred from attending school at Maphoitsile village after refusing to wear a skirt; the principal sent her home on the stated ground that she must wear a skirt because she was a girl, and she missed three weeks of classes. The case concerns a pupil rather than a visitor, but it records a North West school applying a dress rule against a gender-nonconforming person rather than accommodating her.

The province's quantitative evidence on anti-LGBT discrimination rests on a single survey. Conducted during 2009 and 2010 under the auspices of the UNISA Centre for Applied Psychology with OUT LGBT Well-being, OUT North-West and Gay Umbrella, it surveyed 319 LGBT people, most of them from rural backgrounds in one of the country's poorest and least populated provinces, and asked about openness about same-sex sexuality, how LGBT people perceive their environment, and experiences of sexual abuse and discrimination. Campaign research published in 2016 lists that North West study alongside only two others as the quantitative South African studies of anti-LGBT hate crime conducted up to that point.

sources.summary: HRW (29 May 2012) reported that the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament threatened LGBT South Africans by creating a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustans. HRW reported that rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, that chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas, and that the bill offered no opt-out from customary jurisdiction.

Love Not Hate campaign research (GALA-hosted, conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being, 2016) records that only three quantitative studies of hate crimes against LGBT people have been done in South Africa: the 2003 empowerment study across Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and Western Cape, a 2010 North West province study, and this national campaign study, which measures levels of discrimination against LGBT people nationally.

sources.title: North West trans community desperate for hormone replacement services
sources.summary: The trans community in North West province cannot access hormone replacement therapy (HRT) at any public health facility in the province and residents are forced to travel sometimes hundreds of kilometres to Soweto in Gauteng to get it, MambaOnline reported on 21 February 2023. The North West Department of Health confirmed it has no facilities providing HRT for transgender people, in its response to a complaint lodged by Action for Social Justice International with the SA Human Rights Commission. Documents the province-level absence of trans-specific healthcare that a trans visitor reliant on prescribed HRT would confront on the ground.

sources.title: Lesbian pupil banned from school in North West
sources.summary: MambaOnline (23 March 2016, citing the Taung Daily News) reported that 18-year-old lesbian Zinzi Manini Molema of Maphoitsile village, North West, was barred from attending school for refusing to wear a skirt; the principal sent her home saying she must wear a skirt 'since I was a girl', and she stayed home for three weeks without attending any classes. Records a North West institution enforcing a gendered dress code against a gender-nonconforming pupil, illustrating the province's socially conservative enforcement climate.

It surveyed 319 LGBT people from a largely rural background in one of the country's poorest and most under-populated provinces, asking about openness about same-sex sexuality, how LGBT persons perceive their environment, and sexual abuse and discrimination.

76434192B98113213215773.name: Eastern Cape
76434192B98113213215773.summary:
Eastern Cape stands under the national framework of South Africa. The province's trans-relevant law is the national layer: the constitutional prohibition on unfair discrimination, the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act and its Equality Court, the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024, and legal gender recognition under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003.

Transgender prisoners held in Eastern Cape correctional centres, among them St Albans, Mthatha and East London, are governed by the national placement standard rather than any provincial rule. Under the regulations to the Correctional Services Act on the accommodation of vulnerable inmates, and the Department of Correctional Services' standard operating procedures, inmates are to be housed in cells appropriate to their gender identity where that is feasible and safe, and transgender inmates are to be held in single cells. No Eastern Cape-specific transgender placement case is on record, so the province's custody practice is read entirely from the national instruments.

Rural districts under customary jurisdiction carry a risk that does not apply in the metropolitan centres. A bill before the national parliament in 2012 would have created a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustan areas, with no opt-out from customary jurisdiction. Human Rights Watch reported at the time that rural LGBT people already faced discrimination, violence and poor cooperation from police, and that chiefs' courts punished lesbians in rural areas.

Gender-affirming care in the province runs through the public hospital system and is documented as slow. In December 2024 LGBT activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over year-long delays in transgender healthcare. A trans visitor who depends on the public system in the Eastern Cape should plan for waiting times rather than immediate access.

Supports the province's framing of traditional-court rural jurisdiction as the defining risk factor for LGBT travellers off the main cities.

1st Afrika (2 May 2025): Eastern Cape police arrested four suspects over the killings of two women in Gqeberha whose bodies were found at separate locations the prior week; the murders sparked public outrage and renewed calls to confront rising gender-based violence in the province. sources.title: Nthabiseng Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others, Case No. 2024/070075 - High Court of South Africa, Gauteng Local Division, Johannesburg (Fisher J), judgment of 10 November 2025
sources.summary: National placement standard governing trans prisoners in every province including Eastern Cape: the judgment records that DCS agrees that, under the regulations to the Correctional Services Act relating to accommodation of vulnerable inmates and the DCS Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), inmates should be accommodated in cells appropriate to their gender identity where feasible and safe; DCS further conceded its own SOPs prescribe single-cell accommodation for transgender inmates. The Equality Court, applying these instruments, ordered the DCS to accommodate the complainant in a single cell or in the same cell with inmates of the same gender identity. This is the operative rule for where trans prisoners are housed in Eastern Cape correctional centres (e.g., St Albans, Mthatha, East London), no province-specific trans-placement case being on record.

76434192B69392740373411.name: Gauteng
76434192B69392740373411.summary:
Gauteng's documented record of violence against transgender people rests on a single recent case. Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old transgender woman from Soshanguve who was living in Winterveld (both in Tshwane), was attacked at about 1:30 am on 26 December 2024 in a tavern in Tshwane. A man had been saying that gay and lesbian people 'don't deserve to live'; he smashed a bottle into her face as she lit a cigarette and told her 'I told you I'm gonna kill you'. The cuts to her mouth, lips, nose, cheek and forehead were stitched after treatment at Kgabo Clinic. She opened an assault case at Dube Police Station, which had shown no progress when MambaOnline reported on 6 January 2025. The incident is the province's most recent documented trans-specific hate crime on record.

On 10 November 2025 the Gauteng Division of the High Court, Johannesburg, sitting as an Equality Court under the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act, delivered judgment in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others (Case No. 2024/070075). The court found that the Department of Correctional Services had engaged in unfair discrimination and harassment of a transgender woman inmate by refusing to allow her to express her gender identity and by denying her prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy. It held that the right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at state expense, and ordered the Department to implement the required accommodations and to enforce its own standard operating procedures for transgender inmates. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling on 14 November 2025. The orders are enforceable against the Department in the province, giving trans people in Gauteng an operational equality-court remedy for discrimination of this kind.

The same judgment records the only documented determination of how transgender prisoners are housed in Gauteng. Mokoena, a transgender woman serving a life sentence at Johannesburg Correctional Centre, was initially held in the Medium A section, where she could express her gender identity through long hair, makeup and women's clothing. She was later moved to the Medium C section, and at the time of judgment was held in C Single Section, a segregated unit used for solitary confinement, and was accommodated with cisgender male cellmates despite asking for a single cell; she was first housed with two cisgender gay men and then with one cisgender man, an arrangement the Department justified by overcrowding. The court found that its standard operating procedures prescribe accommodation appropriate to gender identity where that is feasible and safe, that no basis existed for refusing her single accommodation, and ordered that she be held in a single cell or with inmates of the same gender identity and that the procedures be enforced.

For a transgender visitor, the risk documented in Gauteng concentrates in unprovoked violence against visibly transgender people and in the police response to it, while the province's courts have ordered enforceable protections for a transgender person in custody.

sources.summary: 'Hate Crimes Against Gay and Lesbian People in Gauteng: Prevalence, Consequences and Contributing Factors' - Joint Working Group research initiative conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being with the UNISA Centre for Applied Psychology (authors Wells & Polders), the first representative quantitative provincial hate-crime study in South Africa (2003/04); partner roster includes Behind the Mask, Triangle Project, GALA and the Durban Lesbian & Gay Community & Health Centre.

Love Not Hate campaign research (GALA-hosted, conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being, 2016): the companion review of hate crimes against LGBT people in South Africa states that only three quantitative studies have ever been done - the 2003 empowerment study across Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and Western Cape; a 2010 North West province study; and this national campaign study - and measures levels of discrimination against LGBT people nationally.

sources.title: Transgender Woman in Brutal Hate Crime Attack in Tshwane Tavern
sources.summary: Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old transgender woman originally from Soshanguve and living in Winterveld (both in Tshwane, Gauteng), was assaulted at a local tavern at about 1:30 am on 26 December 2024 after a man began saying gay and lesbian people 'don't deserve to live'; he smashed a bottle into her face as she lit a cigarette, saying 'I told you I'm gonna kill you', leaving deep cuts to her mouth, lips, nose, cheek and forehead that were stitched after treatment at Kgabo Clinic. She opened an assault case at Dube Police Station, which MambaOnline (6 January 2025) reported had shown no progress. The province's most recent documented trans-specific hate incident on record.

sources.title: Media Statement: National Preventive Mechanism welcomes the High Court ruling affirming the rights of transgender persons in correctional facilities
sources.summary: The SA Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism (14 November 2025) welcomed the judgment of the Gauteng Division of the High Court, Johannesburg, in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others (Case No. 2024/070075), delivered on 10 November 2025. The court found the Department of Correctional Services engaged in unfair discrimination and harassment of the transgender inmate by refusing to allow her to express her gender identity and denying her prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy, and held that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at state expense, ordering the DCS to implement accommodations and enforce its own SOPs. Demonstrates an operational Gauteng court remedy, under PEPUDA, for discrimination against a trans person.

sources.title: Nthabiseng Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others, Case No. 2024/070075 - High Court of South Africa, Gauteng Local Division, Johannesburg (Fisher J), judgment of 10 November 2025
sources.summary: The only documented determination of where trans prisoners are housed in Gauteng. Mokoena, a transgender woman serving life, is held at Johannesburg Correctional Centre: initially housed in Medium A section where she could express her gender identity (long hair, makeup, women's clothing); later transferred to Medium C section; at the time of the judgment she was housed in C Single Section, a segregated/solitary-confinement unit of Medium C, and - despite requesting a single cell - was accommodated with cisgender male cellmates (first two cisgender gay men, then one cisgender male), which DCS justified by overcrowding. The court found the DCS's SOPs prescribe accommodation appropriate to gender identity where feasible and safe and that no basis existed for refusing single accommodation, ordering DCS to house her in a single cell or with inmates of the same gender identity and to enforce its transgender-inmate SOPs.

76434192B69392740373411.blindSummary:
This division's documented record of violence against transgender people rests on a single recent case. A 23-year-old transgender woman from one town in the principal city's municipality, who was living in a nearby settlement within the same municipality, was attacked at about 1:30 am on 26 December 2024 in a tavern in the principal city. A man had been saying that gay and lesbian people 'don't deserve to live'; he smashed a bottle into her face as she lit a cigarette and told her 'I told you I'm gonna kill you'. The cuts to her mouth, lips, nose, cheek and forehead were stitched after treatment at a local clinic. She opened an assault case at a police station in the principal city, which had shown no progress when a publication reported on 6 January 2025. The incident is the division's most recent documented trans-specific hate crime on record.

On 10 November 2025 the highest civil court of this division, sitting in the principal city as an equality court under national equality legislation, delivered judgment in an application brought by a transgender woman inmate against the head of a correctional centre and others. The court found that the prison service had engaged in unfair discrimination and harassment of a transgender woman inmate by refusing to allow her to express her gender identity and by denying her prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy. It held that the right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at state expense, and ordered the prison service to implement the required accommodations and to enforce its own standard operating procedures for transgender inmates. The national human rights commission's preventive mechanism welcomed the ruling on 14 November 2025. The orders are enforceable against the prison service in this division, giving trans people in this division an operational equality-court remedy for discrimination of this kind.

The same judgment records the only documented determination of how transgender prisoners are housed in this division. The applicant, a transgender woman serving a life sentence at a correctional centre in the principal city, was initially held in a general section, where she could express her gender identity through long hair, makeup and women's clothing. She was later moved to a different section, and at the time of judgment was held in a single-cell section, a segregated unit used for solitary confinement, and was accommodated with cisgender male cellmates despite asking for a single cell; she was first housed with two cisgender gay men and then with one cisgender man, an arrangement the prison service justified by overcrowding. The court found that its standard operating procedures prescribe accommodation appropriate to gender identity where that is feasible and safe, that no basis existed for refusing her single accommodation, and ordered that she be held in a single cell or with inmates of the same gender identity and that the procedures be enforced.

For a transgender visitor, the risk documented in this division concentrates in unprovoked violence against visibly transgender people and in the police response to it, while the courts here have ordered enforceable protections for a transgender person in custody.

'Hate Crimes Against Gay and Lesbian People in Gauteng: Prevalence, Consequences and Contributing Factors' was conducted in 2003/04 by OUT LGBT Well-being with the University of South Africa Centre for Applied Psychology, under the Joint Working Group research initiative, with authors Wells and Polders; partner organisations included Behind the Mask, Triangle Project, GALA and the Durban Lesbian & Gay Community & Health Centre. It is described as the first representative quantitative provincial hate-crime study in South Africa.

A 2016 Love Not Hate campaign review, hosted by GALA and conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being, measures levels of discrimination against LGBT people nationally and records that only three quantitative studies of hate crime against LGBT people have ever been carried out; the 2003/04 Gauteng study is one of them. The province's hate-crime baseline therefore rests on a study more than two decades old, drawn from gay and lesbian respondents rather than transgender people.

76434192B56312278962278.name: Western Cape
76434192B56312278962278.summary:
The Western Cape has no provincial law or municipal by-law that bars transgender people from gender-segregated facilities; access is decided venue by venue, by the operator's own rules and by the staff enforcing them. On 19 February 2025 Taswald Ruiters, a transgender woman from Eerste River, was threatened with removal from the Green Point Athletic Stadium in Cape Town after using the women's bathroom. A security guard told her "Look at you, you're a man", directed her to the men's bathroom and said he had the final say. Police were called four times and had not arrived after nearly three hours. The stadium is a public facility operated by the City of Cape Town; on the day it was rented by Western Province Athletics, which was responsible for the security services on site.

The incident records a gap between the absence of any provincial restriction on facility access and the response a visibly trans person actually received in the province's best-resourced metro. The Western Cape stands under the national framework of South Africa; the constitutional guarantees, the criminal-law position, the hate-crime statute, legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care are national provisions carried by the national record, and the provincial layer neither adds to nor subtracts from them.

The Western Cape High Court appeal decision in 'Khoin v Jenkins in re: Observatory Civic Association v Trustees ... Liesbeek Leisure Properties Trust' [2023] 1 All SA 110 (WCC) recognised intangible heritage in South African heritage law and found a failure to consult First Nations communities. Peter Kantor's case note (2023, PER/PELJ vol. 26) analyses the decision as a cultural-heritage recognition dispute, not a matter of morality or criminal jurisdiction.

19338628B22645672383103.name: Île-de-France
19338628B22645672383103.summary:
Île-de-France stands under the French national framework: identity documents, anti-discrimination law, criminal law, care access and marriage are set nationally and apply uniformly across the region, and no separate regional regime governs transgender visitors. What is specific to the region is where recorded anti-LGBT+ offending falls and how the Paris agglomeration's LGBT venues and events are policed.

The Interior Ministry's statistics service (SSMSI), in Infraction rapide n°53 of May 2025, records 4,800 anti-LGBT+ offences across France in 2024, up 5% on 2023, with crimes and délits rising 14% per year since 2016. Only about 4% of victims file complaints, so the recorded figure understates incidence. Acts concentrate in urban units of over 200,000 inhabitants, notably Paris, whose rate is 22 per 100,000 against a national rate of 7; the note attributes part of Paris's elevated rate to non-resident victims and commuters. Recorded victims are more than 70% men, so the statistics do not isolate trans victims.

Large LGBT events in the Paris agglomeration now carry a documented far-right counter-presence and a heavy security response. The Paris Pride march (Marche des Fiertés) of 28 June 2025 was classed a sensitive event by the Interior Ministry, and CRS police reinforcements were deployed after a far-right homo-patriotes group announced it would join the march; police were framed as separating the opposing groups, with extremists described as the enemy.

Paris holds France's densest LGBTQ infrastructure, including France's only officially organised gaybourhoods and the annual Paris Pride parade. As of 2004 the city had 140 LGBT bars, clubs, hotels, restaurants and shops. The city also carries a targeted-violence history: Bertrand Delanoë, who became France's first openly gay mayor of Paris in 2002, was stabbed that same year during the Nuit Blanche festival by an assailant who told police he hated politicians, the Socialist Party and homosexuals. This is the most recent documented anti-LGBT political assault in this record; no later instance is documented here.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in France - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia (LGBTQ rights in France), the national framework a traveller in Île-de-France stands under: France introduced same-sex civil partnerships (PACS) in 1999 and became the thirteenth country to legalise same-sex marriage in 2013, with anti-discrimination protections on grounds of sexual orientation (1985) and gender identity (2012). Since 2017 transgender people may change their legal gender without surgery or any medical diagnosis, and in 2010 France was the first country in the world to declassify gender dysphoria as a mental illness.
