82085004B21656044714531.name: New South Wales
82085004B21656044714531.summary:
New South Wales issues its own birth certificates and driver licences and runs its own anti-discrimination, conversion-practices and corrections regimes. Marriage and passports are national matters and are carried at the national level.

Discrimination on the basis of transgender status has been prohibited in New South Wales since 1996 under the Anti-Discrimination Act 1977, which reaches employment, public education, goods and services, banking, health care, property and nightclubs. Section 16 of the Mental Health Act 2007 states expressly that sexual orientation and gender identity are not mental illnesses.

The Act's exemptions remain significant for a trans visitor. Sport and broadly based religious exemptions in non-public schools permit exclusion on sex and gender grounds, including barring transgender people from female sports categories, and religiously run adoption agencies may refuse same-sex couples.

Sex designations on New South Wales birth certificates changed on 1 July 2025. Until 30 June 2025 a person had to undergo sexual reassignment surgery and pay $153 to change the sex recorded on a birth certificate; since 1 July 2025 no surgery is required, and the process is an application form, a $73 fee, and a good-faith witness who is an unrelated adult known to the applicant for a year. There is no cap on the number of sex changes, unlike name changes, which are limited to once every 12 months and three in a lifetime; 766 sex changes had been recorded by September 2025. The new certificate does not disclose that a change occurred.

Non-binary and unspecified markers are available. In April 2014 the High Court of Australia held that the law permits registration of a change of sex to a non-specific designation, in the case brought by Norrie May-Welby, and since March 2022 rainbow birth certificates listing no gender or sex have been available to people born or adopted in New South Wales.

Conversion practices have been a criminal offence in New South Wales since 4 April 2025 under the Conversion Practices Ban Act 2024, passed unamended on 22 March 2024. Practices causing substantial mental or physical harm carry up to five years' imprisonment, and taking a person out of New South Wales for conversion therapy carries up to three years. Anti-Discrimination NSW can investigate complaints from 4 April 2025 with civil referral pathways. The Act carries limited religious and parental exemptions, including an exception for religious sermons.

Publicly threatening or inciting violence has been an offence since 13 August 2018 under the Crimes Amendment (Publicly Threatening and Inciting Violence) Act 2018, passed unanimously by both houses in June 2018, with a penalty of up to three years' imprisonment.

Documented fatal violence against a trans woman traveller in the state is the 2021 killing of Mhelody Bruno, a 25-year-old transgender woman from the Philippines visiting Australia, in Wagga Wagga. The perpetrator's guilty plea to manslaughter drew a 22-month term. The most recent documented case of this kind in this record is from 2021; no later instance is documented.

Corrections practice is governed by New South Wales prisoner protocols and guidelines in place since 1996, which permit transgender people who have had sexual reassignment surgery to be housed in female prisons for protection. An undisclosed New South Wales government settlement was granted to a transgender individual held in a male prison in November 2024.

Facilities: Sydney City Council implemented a gender-neutral bathrooms policy in April 2023.

82085004B93533858076668.name: Western Australia
82085004B93533858076668.summary:
Western Australia's Equal Opportunity Act 1984 protects one attribute relevant to trans people: "gender history", defined in the statute and in state government guidance as living, or seeking to live, as a member of the opposite sex. Guidance published by the state government and updated on 12 February 2026 states that direct and indirect discrimination on this ground are unlawful, and that treating a person as their former sex is a form of direct discrimination. The attribute is not framed as gender identity, so the state's protection is worded more narrowly than the gender-identity grounds used in several other Australian jurisdictions.

Eligibility to complain is tied to legal recognition. Gender history is established through a recognition certificate or a recorded change of sex or gender under the births, deaths and marriages framework, which means a trans person who has not amended Western Australian identity documents may sit outside the complaint mechanism even where the treatment described is discriminatory. The Equal Opportunity Commission's fact sheet records that the 2024 recognition reforms amend section 4(1) of the Act to delete the "gender reassigned person" definition and insert one keyed to certificates or registration, that the amendment does not operate retrospectively, and that complaints will have to satisfy the new registration requirements once it commences.

The Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Act 2024 was assented to on 26 September 2024 and took effect on 30 May 2025. It repeals the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 and abolishes the Gender Reassignment Board, which the Premier and Attorney-General described at introduction on 16 April 2024 as the last body of its kind in the country. Medical and surgical reassignment are no longer prerequisites; a statement from a medical practitioner or psychologist certifying appropriate clinical treatment, which may include counselling, replaces the board process. Male, female, indeterminate/intersex and non-binary descriptors are available, a change may be made once a year, the fee is A$195 and non-refundable, and processing takes up to four weeks. Applicants under 18 need parental consent or the permission of the Family Court of Western Australia. The Act carries a statutory review clause after three years.

The removal of surgical prerequisites has a longer history in the state. Sterilisation was required before 2012, until the High Court held on 6 October 2011 in AB v Western Australia that two trans men who had undergone bilateral mastectomies and androgen therapy were entitled to male recognition certificates without hysterectomy, oophorectomy or genital reconstructive surgery. The requirement that an applicant be unmarried was repealed by legislation that passed both chambers in early 2019 and commenced on 19 March 2019.

Complaints go to the state Commissioner of Equal Opportunity, with a 12-month lodgement window, acknowledgment of receipt within one week and a free conciliation conference as the next step. A complainant may instead use the federal route to the Australian Human Rights Commission under national sex discrimination law within 24 months, or 12 months for employment matters, but only one route may be chosen. TransFolk of WA and the Freedom Centre, the latter for people under 26, provide trans-specific support in the state.

Prison policy reported in November 2020 allows transgender prisoners to be housed according to their gender identity for health and safety reasons, provided their criminal record carries no sexual offences. Placement turns on that record check rather than operating as an unconditional entitlement.

No law in Western Australia prohibits conversion practices. The government said a bill would be introduced only after the March 2025 state election; as of September 2026 Western Australia and Tasmania were the only Australian jurisdictions without an explicit criminal prohibition, leaving Western Australia the only mainland state where the practices remain lawful. A Public Order Bill that would criminally ban harassment on grounds of sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics passed the lower house but had not passed the upper house. Announced reforms to the Equal Opportunity Act would add gender identity and sex characteristics as protected attributes and repeal the exemption allowing religious schools to discriminate; neither change had been enacted.

In October 2021 the Western Australia Supreme Court removed a transgender child from parental custody entirely over continuing abuse, the first order of its kind in the country, following the April 2021 death of a 15-year-old trans teenager in Perth that prompted calls to reform the birth-certificate law.

82085004B93533858076668.blindSummary:
This division's equal opportunity statute of 1984 protects one attribute relevant to trans people: "gender history", defined in the statute and in division-level government guidance as living, or seeking to live, as a member of the opposite sex. Guidance published by the division-level government and updated on 12 February 2026 states that direct and indirect discrimination on this ground are unlawful, and that treating a person as their former sex is a form of direct discrimination. The attribute is not framed as gender identity, so this division's protection is worded more narrowly than the gender-identity grounds used in several other divisions of this country.

Eligibility to complain is tied to legal recognition. Gender history is established through a recognition certificate or a recorded change of sex or gender under the births, deaths and marriages framework, which means a trans person who has not amended this division's identity documents may sit outside the complaint mechanism even where the treatment described is discriminatory. The divisional equal opportunity commission's fact sheet records that the 2024 recognition reforms amend section 4(1) of the statute to delete the "gender reassigned person" definition and insert one keyed to certificates or registration, that the amendment does not operate retrospectively, and that complaints will have to satisfy the new registration requirements once it commences.

The registration amendment statute of 2024 dealing with changes of sex or gender was assented to on 26 September 2024 and took effect on 30 May 2025. It repeals the gender reassignment statute of 2000 and abolishes the gender reassignment board, which the head of government and the chief legal officer described at introduction on 16 April 2024 as the last body of its kind in this country. Medical and surgical reassignment are no longer prerequisites; a statement from a medical practitioner or psychologist certifying appropriate clinical treatment, which may include counselling, replaces the board process. Male, female, indeterminate/intersex and non-binary descriptors are available, a change may be made once a year, the fee is 195 in local currency units and non-refundable, and processing takes up to four weeks. Applicants under 18 need parental consent or the permission of the division's family court. The statute carries a statutory review clause after three years.

The removal of surgical prerequisites has a longer history in this division. Sterilisation was required before 2012, until the highest national court held on 6 October 2011 in a case involving two trans men who had undergone bilateral mastectomies and androgen therapy that they were entitled to male recognition certificates without hysterectomy, oophorectomy or genital reconstructive surgery. The requirement that an applicant be unmarried was repealed by legislation that passed both chambers of the legislature in early 2019 and commenced on 19 March 2019.

Complaints go to this division's commissioner for equal opportunity, with a 12-month lodgement window, acknowledgment of receipt within one week and a free conciliation conference as the next step. A complainant may instead use the federal route to the national human rights commission under national sex discrimination law within 24 months, or 12 months for employment matters, but only one route may be chosen. Two local organisations provide trans-specific support in this division, one of them for people under 26.

Prison policy reported in November 2020 allows transgender prisoners to be housed according to their gender identity for health and safety reasons, provided their criminal record carries no sexual offences. Placement turns on that record check rather than operating as an unconditional entitlement.

No law in this division prohibits conversion practices. The division-level government said a bill would be introduced only after the division-level election in March 2025; as of September 2026 this division and one other division within this country were the only divisions of this country without an explicit criminal prohibition, leaving this division the only division on the mainland where the practices remain lawful. A public order bill that would criminally ban harassment on grounds of sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics passed the lower house of the legislature but had not passed the upper house. Announced reforms to the equal opportunity statute would add gender identity and sex characteristics as protected attributes and repeal the exemption allowing religious schools to discriminate; neither change had been enacted.

In October 2021 the supreme court of this division removed a transgender child from parental custody entirely over continuing abuse, the first order of its kind in this country, following the April 2021 death of a 15-year-old trans teenager in a major city within this division that prompted calls to reform the birth-certificate law.

82085004B40257551482390.name: Australian Capital Territory
82085004B40257551482390.summary:
The Human Rights Act 2004 is in force in the Australian Capital Territory and is the statutory rights framework the territory's public authorities must operate within. Courts may issue declarations of inconsistency, and section 31 provides that interpreters may consider international law and the judgments of foreign and international courts and tribunals relevant to a human right. A visitor who encounters discriminatory conduct by an ACT police officer, public servant or public facility therefore has a review mechanism written into territory law. The ACT Legislation Register also records uncommenced amendments made by the Human Rights (Housing) Amendment Act 2025.

The ACT operates an explicit self-identification policy for housing trans and gender-diverse prisoners. Strip-searching inside ACT prisons is documented in a 2026 Human Rights Law Centre report produced with the trans-community groups Flat Out and FIGJAM, which records the disproportionate harms of the practice for trans, gender-diverse and Indigenous prisoners.

Conversion practices are a criminal and civil offence in the territory. The Sexuality and Gender Identity Conversion Practices Bill passed the ACT Legislative Assembly on 27 August 2020 and applied from early 2021, carrying up to 12 months' imprisonment or a $24,000 fine, alongside civil penalties that give the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal power to issue orders and order redress. Practices supporting someone undergoing or considering a gender transition are explicitly not banned. The bill was amended before passage after the Association of Christian Schools and the ACT Law Society argued that the definition of conversion practice was too broad and vague.

Gender-affirming care in the ACT is constrained by capacity rather than by prohibition. The ACT government's LGBTIQ+ Health Scoping Study, reported on 16 April 2022, found serious barriers for transgender and gender-diverse Canberrans: a shortage of primary-care professionals including GPs, mental-health supports and paediatric specialists with LGBTIQ+ health understanding, producing excessive wait times, delays from referrals and high costs associated with interstate and international travel. The study called the ACT the only jurisdiction in the country without a comprehensive gender-focused health service, in private practice or through a publicly-funded gender clinic.

25490228B8471183517505.summary:
Castilla y León operates under Spain's national legal framework on gender recognition and anti-discrimination. Its own regional protection layer has been the subject of legislative activity rather than settled law: in December 2024 the PSOE parliamentary group registered a bill for the real and effective equality of LGBTI+ people in Castilla y León, one of three bills the group tabled that week. The bill's stated purpose includes ending the out-migration of LGBTI people from the region, and the group's leader, Tudanca, called for the fastest possible processing.

On 11 June 2025 the Cortes de Castilla y León voted to take the PSOE-sponsored LGTBI+ bill into consideration. The text runs to 76 articles and answers long-standing demands of the region's LGBTI+ collectives. The motion carried; the Partido Popular abstained and Vox voted against. Taking the bill into consideration opens debate, and LGBTI advocates have said they fear the process could stall in committee, which would leave the initiative without effect.

No regional LGBTI equality statute in force in Castilla y León appears in the material reviewed, and no region-specific rules on identity documents, facility access, health care or hate-crime enforcement were identified for the region. A trans visitor to Castilla y León encounters no documented regional-layer rule that departs from the national framework; the open question is whether the pending bill becomes law.

25490228B48808997991554.name: Ciudad Autónoma de Ceuta
25490228B48808997991554.summary:
Ceuta is an autonomous city of Spain with no LGTBI or gender-identity statute of its own. It stands under the national framework of Ley 4/2023 and central-government policy, and no regional ordinance supplements them, so a trans visitor deals directly with Spanish law and Spanish institutions rather than with any local statute.

FELGTBI+'s September 2025 radiography of LGTBI+ public policy, prepared with the Universidad de Salamanca, names Asturias, Castilla y León, Ceuta and Melilla as the only Spanish territories still without a specific law on the promotion of LGTBI+ rights. The report records legislative progress in Castilla y León and Asturias in June 2025 and no equivalent step for Ceuta or Melilla.

The gap is not new. A 2020 precedent study cited in the same body of work placed Ceuta and Melilla at the tail of rankings for the recognition and protection of trans students.

Protection questions in Ceuta also run through migration. Europa Press reported on 17 September 2026 that the LGTBI+ association Arcópoli wrote to the Secretary of State for Migration, Pilar Cancela, demanding the urgent transfer to the peninsula of LGTBI+ migrants remaining in Ceuta after thousands entered irregularly on 30 and 31 July. Arcópoli described transfer as the only effective measure to guarantee their protection and inclusion, cited the extreme vulnerability of people fleeing criminalisation and persecution in countries including Morocco, and launched a free remote social, psychological and legal support service for those in Ceuta.

For a visitor, the practical consequence is that no regional layer of LGTBI+ policy exists to consult or appeal to: recognition, anti-discrimination and criminal-law protection operate through the national framework, and the documented deficit is one of regional legislation and regional-level provision rather than of a hostile local statute.

25490228B18225280299410.name: Ciudad Autónoma de Melilla
25490228B18225280299410.summary:
Ciudad Autónoma de Melilla has no autonomous LGTBI or gender-identity statute. An index of Spain's regional LGTBI legislation states expressly that Melilla and Ceuta have no laws of this kind and rely instead on the national framework and on central-government equality policies. The city therefore stands entirely under Spanish national law for legal gender recognition, anti-discrimination protection, criminal aggravating circumstances and access to facilities, and no city-level rule either adds to or subtracts from those guarantees.

The only city-level instrument touching partnership recognition is a registry for unmarried couples, created in Melilla in 2008. Comparable registries exist in Ceuta and across the mainland communities, and the benefits they confer on unmarried couples are regarded as mainly symbolic. The Melilla registry is not an LGTBI or gender-identity statute and does not modify the national rules on marriage or adoption, so a trans visitor's recognition as a partner or spouse rests on the national framework rather than on anything the city has enacted.

sources.summary: Melilla has no autonomous LGTBI or gender-identity statute, so the national framework governs there. A registry for unmarried same-sex couples was created in the autonomous city of Melilla in 2008, alongside Ceuta in 1998 and all 17 mainland communities, granting unmarried couples benefits regarded as mainly symbolic; this is not an LGTBI or gender-identity statute. The national framework applying in Melilla provides same-sex marriage and adoption nationwide since July 2005, bans hate speech on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity since 1995 with crime-law penalty enhancements for such motives, and has allowed legal-gender self-determination on documents without surgery or sterilisation since the trans law approved 16 February 2023 (vote 191-60 with 91 abstentions, applying to people over 16). National criminal and equality law and the state police govern in Melilla.

15666254B53975248776023.name: Kelantan
15666254B53975248776023.summary:
Kelantan is a state of Malaysia, and its Syariah criminal jurisdiction operates within the national legal framework; the provisions set out below are specific to Kelantan. The state assembly passed the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kelantan) Bill 2026 on 13 August 2026, legislating decency, the covering of aurat, and gender change as matters of Islamic criminal law. The enactment replaces 16 provisions of the Kelantan Syariah Criminal Code Enactment 2019 that the Federal Court struck down in February 2024, so the state's regulation of dress, modesty and gender presentation has been rebuilt on a new statutory basis rather than withdrawn. Clause 15 requires Muslims to safeguard the sanctity and modesty of their private parts in accordance with Islamic law.

The state legislature has placed gender change expressly inside the criminal jurisdiction of Islamic law, and the new decency and gender-change provisions are in force and being applied by the Syariah courts from 2026. For a trans visitor in Kelantan, a presentation or a document that raises a gender-change question therefore falls under provisions drafted for that subject, with the operative boundaries set by the state's religious courts rather than by anything the Federal Court's 2024 ruling settled.

A February 2026 case, decided before the bill was tabled, was the first Kelantan Syariah Court matter involving gender change. Judicial practice on the question was already running in the state in the months before the replacement enactment came into force.

15666254B71460903090065.name: Terengganu
15666254B71460903090065.summary:
Terengganu is a state of Malaysia and stands under the national framework; the federal Penal Code and the national rules on identity documents, entry and enforcement apply here as they do elsewhere in the country. The findings below are specific to Terengganu.

Official state-level hostility toward LGBTQ people is stated openly. In May 2025 a Terengganu state executive councillor confirmed that warning signboards against homosexual practices, installed at strategic locations in the state, are intended to instil hatred of those acts, and said the state wants people to regard them as "dirty, wrong, and to be avoided". The statement is an endorsement of hostility by a serving member of the state government rather than a remark by a private individual, and it sets the posture a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor moves through in the state.

The signboards drew a public challenge. In May 2025 thirteen civil-society organisations, among them Justice for Sisters, called on the Kuala Terengganu City Council to take the signboards down, describing them as discriminatory and as a violation of international human rights law, and criticising the executive councillor's defence of them as incitement to hatred and discrimination against LGBTQ people. The appeal was directed at the municipal authority associated with the signboards' placement.

Terengganu's own Sharia enactment carries a longer institutional-rehabilitation term than the six months recorded in some other states. A 2022 amendment extended to one year the period for which a person convicted under the state enactment may be ordered into counselling or rehabilitation at a religious institution, a custodial and institutional alternative to imprisonment available to the state's Sharia courts.

15666254B71428205180864.name: Kedah
15666254B71428205180864.summary:
Kedah's own criminal law is set out in the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kedah Darul Aman) Enactment 2014 (En.18/2014). Sections 23 and 24 criminalise liwat and musahaqah, punishable by a fine of up to RM5,000, up to three years' imprisonment, up to six strokes of whipping, or any combination of those penalties. Section 26 criminalises a male posing as a woman in public, carrying a fine of up to RM1,000 or up to one year's imprisonment. Female cross-dressing is not an offence under the enactment, so the state's public-presentation offence falls asymmetrically on trans women and on anyone read as male presenting as a woman. Section 52 allows a woman convicted of musahaqah to be committed to an approved home for up to six months in addition to the sentence imposed.

Enforcement in Kedah has reached private gatherings. In October 2020 a private birthday party was raided and 30 trans women were singled out and arrested, while the event organiser was placed under investigation for "encouraging vice". A coalition of Malaysian human-rights groups publicly objected to the probe, describing a pattern in which organisers and allies of transgender people are pursued alongside those who attend.

65028918B28366581005022.summary:
West Java stands under the national framework of Indonesia; the findings below are those specific to the province.

On 22 June 2025 the West Java Regional Police detained 75 people at a privately rented villa in the Puncak area of Bogor Regency, acting on a tip from local residents. Police described the gathering as an LGBT "family gathering" held "to avoid detection".

Amnesty International condemned the arrests on 24 June 2025 as a discriminatory raid and "a blatant violation of human rights and privacy", stated that the gathering violated no law, and demanded the release of those held and accountability for the operation.

In August 2026 men doused a trans woman with what appeared to be urine on a street in Bogor, one of a wave of attacks on trans women in the province.

Activists link that violence to a 2025 presidential regulation classifying the spread of LGBTQ culture as a non-military threat and to discriminatory regional regulations, arguing that official language of this kind legitimises violence against trans women.

A trans woman quoted in the reporting said that people who previously appeared in public now live in fear.

65028918B6690755070061.name: Bali
65028918B6690755070061.summary:
Bali stands under Indonesia's national framework, and that framework is where the legal risk sits. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted anywhere in Indonesia, that provision reaches consensual relations involving a trans visitor that would be locally classed as same-sex; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Same-sex marriage remains unrecognised for visitors and residents alike.

Bali's own social environment differs from the national legal picture. Peer-reviewed ethnographic fieldwork published in 2025, drawing on four case studies in Bali, documents a visible transpuan (trans feminine) community living with precarity, discrimination and informal resistance, challenging narratives of pure victimhood while confirming real material insecurity.

Traveller-facing guidance rates Bali 6.3 out of 10 overall but gives it a legal score of 2.0, warning that LGBTQ+ travellers face legal risk under Indonesian law and advising visitors to keep affection quiet despite the island's tolerant reputation. A March 2026 guide describes Bali as broadly welcoming on a 'live and let live' basis, while noting that the new Criminal Code in effect from January 2026 adds complexity to the legal backdrop. Same-sex relationships are not separately criminalised under a Bali-specific provision; the exposure runs through the national code.

Same-sex marriage is not legally recognised anywhere in Indonesia. Seminyak (Eat Street and Batu Belig), Canggu and Ubud are named as the most consistently LGBTQ+-friendly areas with active venues, and public displays of affection warrant discretion across the island.

65028918B16658067687714.name: Papua
65028918B16658067687714.summary:
Papua is a province of Indonesia and stands under the national legal framework. The sources identify no Papua-specific criminal provision on same-sex conduct, and no Papua-specific enforcement of the national morality provisions is documented.

Documented state violence in the province is severe and largely unpunished. A July 2025 briefing by the advocacy group TAPOL records 138 acts of torture or ill-treatment in detention by police and military personnel in Maybrat and the Central Highlands between September 2021 and the first quarter of 2025, with almost no consequences for those responsible. Arrests were largely for alleged links to armed groups or for participation in demonstrations, and deaths during torture were documented in operation areas. The incidents are catalogued on the Papuans Behind Bars database.

A quarterly monitoring report covering the third quarter of 2025, published on 31 October 2025, records killings, arbitrary detentions, torture, arrests of protesters and the failure of accountability mechanisms as security forces expand across the region, alongside a healthcare crisis under scrutiny. That report carries no trans or LGBTI findings.

For a trans visitor the practical exposure is the generalised impunity of the security forces rather than documented targeting: the abuses on record arise from counter-insurgency operations and protest policing, not from enforcement against trans or gender-nonconforming people. A visitor detained in the province would enter the custody environment those findings describe. No trans-specific violence, hate-crime data or protection measure for Papua appears in the sources.

sources.summary: Since June 2021 Indonesia's Ministry of Home Affairs has run an outreach programme issuing transgender Indonesians identification papers (KTP). Papua is among the provinces where trans residents have received them, alongside Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi and Lampung. Only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised, and the birth gender is printed unless a court order was already obtained. The same national legal framework applies in Papua: the 2022 penal-code amendment criminalising sexual activity outside marriage, carrying up to one year in prison, takes effect on 2 January 2026; same-sex marriage is not recognised; and customary laws may apply. Trans people in Papua may therefore obtain identity documents through the national outreach programme while remaining subject to that framework.

65028918B17554737605304.name: South Sulawesi
65028918B17554737605304.summary:
South Sulawesi is a province of Indonesia and stands under the national legal framework, which applies here in full.

OutRight Action International's 2022 report Creeping Criminalisation, by Katjasungkana and Wieringa, lists South Sulawesi among the eight Indonesian provinces it covers and records that provincial and city bylaws in these jurisdictions criminalise same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity, adopted under the regional-autonomy powers that let local legislatures pass their own regulations.

In Makassar, the mayor reaffirmed in April 2025 a commitment to push an anti-LGBT regional regulation (Perda) after a same-sex act at a night-entertainment venue circulated online. The deputy chair of the city legislature's law-drafting body (Bapemperda) backed the move, saying the regulation was needed to preserve moral and religious norms.

The proposal is not new. It entered the 2023 local legislative programme (prolegda) as a priority for discussion, and two city legislature members, including Azwar ST of the PKS faction, said it was modelled on regulations already passed elsewhere, such as Bogor. As of April 2026 the Makassar rule remained a draft (Ranperda) rather than an enacted regulation.

65028918B9551391119865.summary:
South Sumatra is one of two Indonesian provinces that criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside the national morality provisions; the Human Dignity Trust country profile records the provincial offence. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship faces a provincial criminal exposure that does not exist across most of the country.

The Palembang city government is preparing a regulation rejecting LGBT people. Mayor Ratu Dewa announced the move on 19 July 2026 in the Grand Mosque courtyard, presenting it as local follow-through on the national defence policy that lists the spread of LGBTQ culture among non-military threats. The regulation is in preparation; no penalty has been specified and no enforcement has been documented.

OutRight Action International's mapping of discriminatory regional regulations across eight Indonesian provinces includes South Sumatra, placing the province inside the regional bylaw belt that drafts such as Palembang's extend.

31927357B17004778023462.name: Aguascalientes
31927357B17004778023462.summary:
Aguascalientes stands under Mexico's national framework, and legal gender recognition in Mexico is settled state by state. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state survey of 11 March 2025 records that Aguascalientes 'has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people'; its reporting of 31 March 2025 places the state among those that have not legislated such a procedure. The state therefore operates no administrative mechanism of its own for changing name or gender markers on official records.

The March 2024 Human Rights Watch report on the cost of absent recognition names Aguascalientes among the non-reforming states whose trans residents have no lawful marker procedure. Its documented consequence is that trans people carry documents contradicting their lived identity, which amplifies discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police.

A court-ordered route now exists. Infobae reported on 9 April 2026 that the Supreme Court, in Amparo en Revisión 430/2025 on a draft by Minister Giovanni Figueroa Mejía, held that the state Civil Code's requirements for changing the gender on a birth certificate, namely judicial or ministerial intervention, civil trials, probative proof of identity and marginal annotations, are discriminatory and violate privacy. The Court ordered the Civil Registry to grant recognition through a simple, confidential administrative procedure honouring self-perception, issuing a new birth certificate with no marginal note revealing a prior gender. The immediate effect is confined to the persons represented by the civil association that brought the case, so the ruling establishes a recognition route in the absence of legislative reform without yet establishing one for the state's trans population generally.

No trans-specific homicide offence covers the state. The Guardian reported on 24 July 2024 that Mexico City criminalised transfemicide; Aguascalientes is among the states that have adopted no comparable reform.

Violence and coercive practice persist according to local accounts. La Jornada Aguascalientes reported on 23 August 2026 that activists Alicia Cruz, Kevin Cruz and Hened Musalem of Diversx Laboratorio Cultural Disidente say conversion-therapy operations continue in the state under the guise of addiction-treatment annexes despite the legal prohibition, and that a person who escaped one such space reached the group the previous year. The same activists state that trans women continue to suffer prejudice-motivated aggression.

31927357B33389180120223.name: Baja California Sur
31927357B33389180120223.summary:
Baja California Sur does not criminalise trans people or their presence. The state's elected congress created an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition through a 2021 reform to the state Civil Code, and after the Supreme Court of Mexico ruled in June 2023 that excluding children and adolescents from that procedure was unconstitutional, the congress passed a further Civil Code reform in 2024 extending recognition to children, adolescents and non-binary people.

Human Rights Watch's state-by-state tracker of legal gender recognition in Mexico, dated March 2025, records Baja California Sur among the states that have legislated an administrative procedure, and records the 2024 reform as the one that expanded access to minors and non-binary people following the Supreme Court's June 2023 ruling.

El Financiero reported on 27 June 2024 that the reform approved by the Baja California Sur congress allows minors to change their gender and chosen name on birth certificates, and that the administrative processes are described as rapid, free and free of prejudice for trans and non-binary children. The XVI Legislature worked the dictamen on the order of the Supreme Court's June 2023 ruling, which had struck down the adult-only limit.

For contrast, Human Rights Watch's report of 6 March 2024 on Tabasco, a state with no recognition procedure, documents what the absence of such a procedure produces: institutional mistreatment, the unsolved August 2023 killing of activist Karina Gómez, hate-motivation provisions absent from Tabasco's criminal code, and healthcare staff routinely outting patients by calling legal names. That pattern describes Tabasco, not Baja California Sur, but it indicates what a non-reforming state's trans residents face.

National impunity conditions bear on any visitor's expectation of protection. The Guardian reported on 24 July 2024 that over 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022, and that Mexico City approved the Paola Buenrostro law on 18 July 2024 making transfemicide a crime with sentences up to 70 years, in one of Latin America's deadliest settings for trans people. That law applies to Mexico City, not to Baja California Sur.

Global Affairs Canada advises travellers to exercise a high degree of caution across Mexico because of high levels of criminal activity and kidnapping, with an avoid non-essential travel advisory covering Baja California Sur and the northwestern mainland coast. This is a general-country advisory rather than a trans-specific one.

31927357B65177449444732.name: Chiapas
31927357B65177449444732.summary:
Chiapas is a state of Mexico and sits under the national framework that governs identity documents and criminal law. Its legislature has not created a legal gender recognition procedure. As of March 2025, no administrative route existed in the state for changing the name or gender marker recorded on identity documents, and Human Rights Watch's state-by-state assessment places Chiapas among the states that have not reformed their legislation on this point.

Recognition therefore runs through the courts alone. A trans person in Chiapas who needs documents matching their identity must bring an individual petition before a judge, with no administrative application to file and no published standard governing the result; the documents stay as issued until a ruling is handed down. Human Rights Watch describes the position of residents as mismatched documents combined with case-by-case judicial recourse. A visitor cannot obtain corrected documents from Chiapas either, since the state operates no such procedure; the papers a visitor carries are the papers presented.

Human Rights Watch has urged the states that lack a recognition procedure to adopt one, and promotes a simple self-identification mechanism as the remedy. No such mechanism has been adopted in Chiapas.

31927357B32124965101143.name: Coahuila de Zaragoza
31927357B32124965101143.summary:
Coahuila de Zaragoza, one of Mexico's states, runs its own administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. The congress of Coahuila passed the Ley del Registro Civil del Estado de Coahuila in 2018; articles 124 to 128 of that law establish the administrative procedure by which a person's self-identified gender identity is recognised. Human Rights Watch's March 2025 tracker of legal gender recognition across Mexico's states records Coahuila among those that have legislated such a procedure and links the official gazette text of the reform at articles 124 to 128.

The law defines the concept it administers. Article 2, fraction XI, of the Civil Registry law defines gender identity as a personal and internal conviction. The 2018 reform also amended article 133 of the Ley para la Familia de Coahuila de Zaragoza, so the change reached the state's family law alongside the registry.

Use of the procedure is documented. The director of Coahuila's Civil Registry, Ricardo Malacara, said that between early 2019 and March 2023 around 1,500 people in the state completed the legal gender-identity change before the registry, in both directions, male to female and female to male.

sources.summary: The 2018 Law on the Civil Registry of the State of Coahuila (arts. 124-128) established an administrative procedure for recognition of self-identified gender identity. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state tracker on legal gender recognition in Mexico (March 2025) records this among the 32 states that have legislated such a procedure, alongside the Supreme Court rulings that drove the expansion.

Human Rights Watch report 'I Just Want to Contribute to Society' (6 March 2024) on Tabasco, cited as a baseline for how a state without a legal gender-recognition procedure behaves: no administrative procedure exists there, the August 2023 killing of activist Karina Gomez remained unsolved, hate-motivation provisions are absent from Tabasco's criminal code, and healthcare staff out patients by calling legal names.

Tangential to Coahuila: Mexico City made transfemicide a crime on 18 July 2024, with sentences up to 70 years under the Paola Buenrostro law, in one of Latin America's deadliest settings for trans people, the Guardian reported on 24 July 2024. More than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022.

31927357B12556965236767.name: Hidalgo
31927357B12556965236767.summary: Hidalgo falls under Mexico's national regime in full, including the state's own administrative gender-recognition procedure of April 2019, with no local exception to the country-level picture. The state is largely rural, conservative and socially traditional, with substantial indigenous and small-town populations; trans visibility tends to attract scrutiny in smaller municipios rather than organised targeting, and local reporting on trans-specific incidents, police conduct and remedies is thin — a gap to be read as uncertainty, not reassurance. Pachuca, the state capital, is the most visible and institutionally equipped centre and sits close to the Mexico City metropolitan area and its tourism economy, but Hidalgo has little queer-venue or travel infrastructure by national comparison, and support networks are thinner than in the capital. Friction for a trans visitor is most likely in ordinary encounters — hotels, clinics, banks and routine police checks — where foreign documents that do not match presentation invite questions, and where recourse in outlying areas is limited and official response uneven. No Hidalgo-specific restriction on trans travellers' entry, facilities, custody or care is on record, but neither is there local evidence of reliable protection. For minors, no statewide exclusion is documented, though local schools and health facilities may still misgender or exclude.

31927357B65869129959700.name: Jalisco
31927357B65869129959700.summary: Jalisco is subject to Mexico's national legal framework in full, with no local exception. Guadalajara and the Puerto Vallarta resort corridor have long-established LGBTQ tourism, visible community institutions and large annual Pride events, with tolerance concentrated in urban and tourist-facing districts such as Guadalajara's Americana and Chapultepec areas; an outed trans visitor there would likely meet more acceptance than in many other parts of the country. The state also operates its own administrative route for gender-marker changes, though this is a resident-facing signal rather than a protection for foreign visitors. Outside these enclaves the picture is more conservative: Jalisco is a strongly Catholic, machismo-shaped society, rural parts of the state appear less tolerant and are less documented, and family or workplace exposure can escalate. Documented local exposures include Guadalajara police harassment and extortion of trans people, particularly street-based trans women, and reported transfemicides in the metropolitan area, alongside weak enforcement of anti-discrimination and anti-transfemicide protections. Organised criminal violence across parts of the state further weakens police protection and recourse, and local response varies heavily by municipality. Trans-specific violence has been reported here, but available information does not establish its rate relative to the general violence baseline or show that foreign trans visitors are targeted as such. No Jalisco-specific visitor restriction or specialised visitor protection is on record, and its absence is not evidence of safety; resort-area tolerance is a practical buffer rather than an enforceable one, and encounters with officials still carry real exposure.

31927357B41082348713023.name: Mexico
31927357B41082348713023.summary:
Mexico has no single national procedure for legal gender recognition; the process is set state by state. As of March 2025, 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more operated one in practice without legislative enactment, and six state legislatures had enacted none. Only seven states extend recognition to children. In 2022 the Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. A trans visitor's document position therefore depends on which state they are in.

Several states legislated recognition in their own right. Mexico City's Civil Code amendments allowing transgender people to change gender and name on birth certificates took effect on 13 March 2004. In late August 2008 the Legislative Assembly passed, by 37 to 17, a law formalising the procedure for changing names and obtaining revised birth certificates, replacing a prior process with no specific rules that could take years in court; on 13 November 2014 the Assembly approved a gender identity law making the process much quicker and simpler. The Michoacán Congress approved a gender identity law on 13 July 2017, Nayarit on 20 July 2017, Coahuila on 13 November 2018, Hidalgo on 25 April 2019, and San Luis Potosí began authorizing legal gender changes on 17 May 2019. The Supreme Court held on 17 October 2018 that a transgender person may change name and gender marker on official documents through a simple administrative process based solely on their own declaration of gender identity.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Mexico (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: On 13 March 2004 amendments to the Mexico City Civil Code took effect allowing transgender people to change gender and name on their birth certificates. In September 2008 the Mexico City Legislative Assembly passed a law making it easier for transgender people to change their gender on birth certificates. On 13 November 2014 the Legislative Assembly of Mexico City approved a gender identity law making the process for transgender people to change gender much quicker and simpler. On 13 July 2017 the Michoacan Congress approved a gender identity law and on 20 July 2017 a gender identity law was approved in Nayarit. On 17 October 2018 the Supreme Court held that a transgender person could change name and gender marker on official documents through a simple administrative process based solely on their own declaration of gender identity. On 13 November 2018 Coahuila passed a gender identity bill allowing transgender individuals easier access to birth certificates reflecting their new legal gender. On 25 April 2019 the Hidalgo Congress approved a gender identity law and on 17 May 2019 San Luis Potosi began authorizing legal gender changes for transgender people. Private same-sex sexual conduct between adults ceased to be a criminal matter in 1871 through adoption of the Napoleonic Code. On 2 September 1999 Mexico City passed an ordinance banning discrimination based on sexual orientation, the first of its kind in the country. A federal anti-discrimination law took effect on 11 June 2003 creating a national council to enforce it. Article 1 of the Federal Constitution was amended in 2001 to prohibit discrimination under the term preferences and in June 2011 the more precise term sexual orientation was inserted. Mexico City passed same-sex marriage on 21 December 2009 with effect on 4 March 2010 and the Supreme Court upheld its constitutionality on 5 August 2010 by 9 to 2. On 3 June 2015 the Supreme Court released a jurisprudential thesis deeming laws restricting marriage to a man and a woman unconstitutional and requiring every judge to validate same-sex unions through amparo, with a nationwide adoption jurisprudence finalized on 23 September 2016. By 31 December 2022 every state had legalized same-sex marriage by legislation, executive order or judicial ruling though only twenty allowed those couples to adopt children. Civil unions for same-sex and opposite-sex couples are performed in Campeche, Coahuila, Mexico City, Michoacan, Sinaloa, Tlaxcala and Veracruz. Acceptance of transgender identities has been documented among Isthmus Zapotecs and Yucatan Mayas, with Zapotecs recognizing a traditional third gender known as muxe intermediate between male and female. Muxes are assigned male at birth but typically act and behave like women and do both women and men's work, and having a muxe in the family is perceived as good luck and a blessing. The article states: "Although they are perceived to be different from the general heterosexual male population, they are neither devalued nor discriminated against in their communities." It further states: "Mestizos, especially mestizo police, occasionally harass and even persecute muxe boys, but Zapotec parents, especially mothers and other women, are quick to defend them and their rights to \"be themselves\", because, as they put it, \"God made them that way.\"" It adds: "I have never heard an Isthmus Zapotec suggest that a muxe chose to become a muxe." Visible and well-attended LGBTQ marches and pride parades have occurred in Mexico City since 1979, in Guadalajara since 1996, and in Monterrey since 2001.

31927357B22618747134228.name: San Luis Potosi
31927357B22618747134228.summary:
San Luis Potosí sets its own rules on gender recognition, marriage and hate-crime aggravators within Mexico's national framework; the national layer is carried by the Mexico record. The state began authorising legal gender changes for transgender people on 17 May 2019, and is counted among the states that enacted a gender-identity law that year.

Partner recognition is settled at state level. The state Congress voted 14-12 on 16 May 2019 to approve same-sex marriage, which took effect on 21 May 2019, and joint adoption by same-sex couples became legal in the state in the same month. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can therefore marry and be treated as a spouse here, and such couples can adopt jointly.

The state's hate-crime statute treats motivation by gender and sexual preference as an aggravating factor. On the source's wording the provision names gender and sexual preference rather than gender identity.

The state's anti-discrimination law bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender, but not gender identity. Gender-identity discrimination therefore falls outside the state's own prohibition even though the hate-crime statute reaches gender-based motivation.

31927357B30231562725156.name: Sinaloa
31927357B30231562725156.summary:
Sinaloa stands under Mexico's national framework on legal gender recognition; national passport and marker rules, federal enforcement and national statistics are carried by the national record. The state's own position is unresolved. Human Rights Watch's count of 31 March 2025 places Sinaloa outside the group of Mexican states that had legislated a gender-recognition procedure by that date. Wikipedia's Mexico-wide LGBT rights article lists Sinaloa among the states that enacted such a law, dated there to 2022. The two accounts cannot both be correct, and the Sinaloa state code has not been consulted. A trans visitor cannot rely on an administrative route to corrected state documents, and cannot rule one out.

Marriage recognition in Sinaloa rests on a court order and a later statute. The Mexican Supreme Court ordered the state to legalise same-sex marriage within 90 days on 15 May 2018, and the Sinaloa Congress passed a marriage law for same-sex couples on 15 June 2021. Civil unions are performed in the state for both same-sex and opposite-sex couples. For a trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status, the 2021 marriage law is the operative recognition route in the state.

Sinaloa's local law bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, and the state has hate-crime statutes covering gender and sexual preference.

31927357B37261891092938.name: Sonora
31927357B37261891092938.summary:
Sonora is a state of Mexico and stands under the national framework of Mexico, which carries the country-level legal and enforcement picture; the findings below are those of the state itself.

Sonora's Congress approved the Ley de Identidad de Género on 1 October 2020, the Hermosillo daily El Sol de Hermosillo reported at the time, creating a state procedure for people who identify with the opposite gender to modify their official documentation. Wikipedia's LGBT rights in Mexico page lists Sonora among 25 Mexican states with a gender identity law dated to 2020 and describes the statute as giving trans people a statutory route to rectify gender on civil documents.

The state's protections extend past documents. On 6 December 2022 Sonora's Congress banned conversion therapies (ECOSIG). Sonora's hate-crime legislation recognises motivation by gender and sexual preference as an aggravating factor, and the state ratified the 2011 constitutional amendment prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation.

Marriage between partners of the same legal sex is available in Sonora; by 31 December 2022 every Mexican state, Sonora included, had legalised it by legislation, executive order or judicial ruling. A trans visitor whose relationship would be locally classed as same-sex falls under the same recognition.

No source in the inventory records how these provisions are enforced in Sonora, and no trans-specific violence or incident data for the state was identified. The formal protections exist on the statute book; the state-level enforcement record is undocumented in these sources.

31927357B81008000569871.name: Tabasco
31927357B81008000569871.summary:
Tabasco is a state of Mexico. It has not reformed its legislation and operates no legal gender recognition procedure; Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that the state is one of eight in Mexico with no such procedure.

Without a procedure, a trans person's identity documents never match their gender. Mismatched documents invite police stops and institutional mistreatment.

Human Rights Watch's Tabasco-dedicated report, published on 6 March 2024 and produced with a local community centre for inclusion, documents that the documentary mismatch curtails rights across four socio-economic areas.

The report sets those findings against the August 2023 murder of Karina Gómez, a trans woman killed in Tabasco.

31927357B88239390016047.name: Tamaulipas
31927357B88239390016047.summary:
Tamaulipas has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people, according to Human Rights Watch's state-by-state table dated 31 March 2025. The table places the state among eight Mexican states with no procedure at all. A trans person whose identity documents are issued in Tamaulipas therefore has no administrative route to change those documents to match their gender identity. Tamaulipas stands under Mexico's national framework, which governs passports, entry and federal enforcement.

On 18 June 2025 the Tamaulipas Congress unanimously approved reforms to the state Penal Code adding a chapter on crimes against sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression. The reforms explicitly ban conversion therapies, with prison terms of two to six years and fines of up to 2,000 UMA. Penalties rise by half where victims are minors, disabled or elderly, or where the offence occurs in a subordinate setting such as the family, a medical context or the workplace. The state's criminal law thus protects gender identity even though no administrative gender-recognition procedure exists.

On 4 February 2026 deputies of Tamaulipas's 66th legislature and LGBT+ civil-society groups agreed a joint agenda to press for a Gender Identity Law and for anti-discrimination and health reforms. The initiatives have been pending since June 2025. The absent law continues to limit trans people's access to health care, education and employment. As of early 2026 no legal gender-recognition procedure exists in Tamaulipas and the Gender Identity Law remains unpassed.

31927357B22008724034476.name: Tlaxcala
31927357B22008724034476.summary:
Tlaxcala stands under Mexico's national framework and adds its own state statute on top of it. The state congress's 2019 reform of the Civil Code (Decree D.113, dated 1 October 2019) created an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, and the decree text is published on the state congress's own site. The procedure requires no court proceeding, which is the legal basis a trans visitor would rely on to update identity documents in Tlaxcala.

The state's civil-union law took effect on 12 January 2017, giving Tlaxcala a state-level partnership status that rests on a separate instrument from the 2019 recognition decree.

31927357B35199150741361.name: Yucatan
31927357B35199150741361.summary:
Yucatán is one of Mexico's 32 states and stands under the national framework; the federal layer of law and enforcement is carried by the national record. The rules that govern a visitor's documents, marriage and access to conversion therapy inside the state are the state's own.

Legal gender recognition in Yucatán is administrative. In 2024 the state congress passed a reform to the Civil Registry Law creating a procedure through which transgender people can update the legal gender recorded on their documents without a court order. The reform was published in the state's official gazette, the Diario Oficial, on 26 April 2024. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state rundown of 11 March 2025 carries Yucatán on that basis. The operative fact for a visitor is that a Mexican identity document issued through Yucatán's registry can be corrected by application rather than litigation.

Marriage is open to same-sex couples in Yucatán, first through the courts and then by statute. On 1 July 2013 the Third District Court of the State of Yucatán ruled that two petitioners could marry, and the first same-sex marriage in the state was registered on 8 August 2013. The Yucatán Constitutional Court dismissed a challenge to the Civil Code's marriage provisions on 2 March 2015, and the federal Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 31 May 2015. The Congress of Yucatán passed a constitutional amendment allowing same-sex marriage on 7 September 2021 and amended secondary legislation to permit it on 1 March 2022. A trans visitor whose relationship would be classed as same-sex under local law can marry here.

Yucatán enacted a conversion-therapy (ECOSIG) ban on 25 August 2021, making the practice unlawful for those who carry it out in the state.

The Congress of Yucatán passed a constitutional amendment allowing same-sex marriage on 7 September 2021 and amended secondary legislation to permit it on 1 March 2022. Yucatán is listed as enacting a conversion-therapy (ECOSIG) ban on 25 August 2021, in effect alongside the state bans from Mexico City (31 July 2020) and other states. 31927357B22408340646138.name: Zacatecas
31927357B22408340646138.summary:
Zacatecas is a state of Mexico and stands under the national framework for passports, federal identity documents and federal criminal jurisdiction. The findings below are those specific to the state.

Zacatecas has a legislated administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. Deputies of the state's 64th Legislature approved a reform of the Family Code on gender identity on 23 December 2022 by 14 votes in favour to 7 against, after the Justice Committee issued a positive opinion on the measure. The reform establishes the possibility of issuing a new birth certificate recognising an applicant's gender identity, principally for the trans community. Zacatecas is not among the states identified as having no legislated gender-recognition procedure.

Implementation followed at the administrative level. In 2023 the director of the state Civil Registry issued guidelines giving effect to the law. Human Rights Watch's March 2025 state-by-state feature on legal gender recognition records both the 2022 Family Code reform and the 2023 Civil Registry guidelines for Zacatecas.

The state's criminal law carries its own protections. On 25 August 2021 the Congress of Zacatecas approved a prohibition and sanction on conversion therapies, known locally as ECOSIG, by adding fraction VI to article 182 Bis of the state Penal Code. Anyone who incites hatred or violence on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or who promotes such practices, faces one to three years' imprisonment or up to 300 days of community work. The same session typified hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity in the state Penal Code.

Recognition came later than those protections. A gender-identity initiative debated in the same 2021 session, alongside a constitutional and family-code reform, failed to obtain enough votes and remained pending; the gender-identity reform passed in December 2022.

82249235B96958463903898.name: Newfoundland and Labrador
82249235B96958463903898.summary:
Newfoundland and Labrador stands under Canada's national framework on gender identity and gender expression; that national layer is carried on the country's own record and is not restated here. The findings below concern provincial documents, provincial services and enforcement of provincial responsibility.

Provincial law has not required sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing the gender marker on a birth or marriage registration since an amendment to the Vital Statistics Act, 2009 received Royal Assent on 13 April 2016. The amendment brought the statute into compliance with an order of a Board of Inquiry under the provincial Human Rights Commission, issued in December 2015 on complaints brought by two trans women.

Since 23 June 2021, when further amendments to the same act received Royal Assent, a person born outside Newfoundland and Labrador who has lived in the province for at least three months has been able to obtain a change of sex designation there. The change certificate costs $25, counts as official provincial identification, and is described by the government as a document that can be leveraged to update records in other jurisdictions. The amendments align with the earlier addition of a non-binary option on provincial birth certificates; the bill received second reading on 17 June 2021.

Under the current application rules, applicants must be 16 or older, or be represented by a parent or legal guardian, with the consent of the other parent or guardian and the written consent of applicants aged 12 to 15. Applicants must be born in the province or have resided there at least three months. The application itself carries no fee; charges apply only to official copies of the updated documents, at $35 for a new birth certificate or $30 online.

The province states that it cannot guarantee a birth certificate bearing an 'X' gender marker will be accepted by authorities in other organisations. That is the documented cross-border caveat for carrying provincial records outside Newfoundland and Labrador.

Police-reported hate crime in the province was recorded at 5.3 per 100,000 for 2024, the joint-lowest provincial rate in Canada alongside Manitoba. The figure rests on 29 incidents, up from 19 in 2023, which makes the 51 per cent rise statistically fragile at that volume. Police counts capture only incidents reported to and recorded by police. Statistics Canada published the data on 30 March 2026.

sources.summary: Statistics Canada (30 Mar 2026, police-reported hate crime 2024): 4,882 hate crimes reported nationally (+1% on 2023, after a +34% jump in 2023); national rate 12.1 per 100,000. Newfoundland and Labrador had the joint-lowest provincial rate at 5.3 per 100,000 (with Manitoba), while Ontario recorded the highest (16.0); the province's +51% rise reflects only 19 incidents in 2023 to 29 in 2024 — very small absolute numbers, so the rate change is statistically fragile. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply uniformly; police figures capture only reported incidents.

Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report examines national police-reported hate-crime data, including offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity. Egale Canada is an LGBTIQ+ organisation.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Newfoundland and Labrador (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Gender identity is explicitly included as a prohibited ground of discrimination in human rights acts in all provinces and territories and by the federal government as of 2017, prohibiting discrimination in employment, housing and public and private accommodations. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. The concepts of sex under section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms have been interpreted to include transsexuality, providing equality protection applicable to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities. In Saskatchewan, The Education (Parents’ Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoked the notwithstanding clause to require schools to obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity. In Alberta, the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024, and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act were met with legal challenges, after which Bill 9: Protecting Alberta’s Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 invoked the notwithstanding clause. British Columbia, Ontario and Saskatchewan grant parental status to three or more intentional parents, allowing for a wider range of queer and trans families. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 by the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968–69, with the general age of consent for all sexual activities 16 since June 2019, or 18 where there is a relationship of trust, authority or dependency. Section 159 of the Criminal Code on anal intercourse was declared unconstitutional by courts in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Alberta, with repeal pursued through Bill C-32 incorporated into Bill C-75 receiving royal assent on June 21, 2019. The Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act received royal assent on June 21, 2018, allowing the RCMP and federal departments or agencies to destroy or remove any judicial record of conviction for homosexual acts prior to being lawful in 1969 or anal intercourse under section 159. Sexual orientation was held constitutionally protected under section 15 in Egan v Canada in 1995, and failure to include it in human rights law was held a violation in Vriend v Alberta in 1998. Same-sex marriage was legalized nationwide on July 20, 2005 by the federal Civil Marriage Act, making Canada the fourth country in the world and first in the Americas to do so. Same-sex adoption was legalized in Newfoundland and Labrador in 2002, with joint adoption legalized in all provinces and territories by 2011, and conversion therapy was statutorily banned nationwide for minors and adults in 2022 and made a crime under the Criminal Code. A 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office found that 87.6% said they would be "comfortable" if a neighbour was a transgender person. The same poll separately measured sexuality tolerance, finding 91.8% said they would be "comfortable" if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual, preserving a distinct result for transgender acceptance. Historical record states many transgender people in traditional Indigenous roles were in positions of reverence, where they acted as caretakers of children who had lost their families, spiritual healers and warriors in battle, with terms including Cree napêw iskwêwisêhot, Ktunaxa titqattek, Blackfoot aakíí'skassi, and Ojibwe ikwekaazo and ininiikaazo. Following colonisation and spread of Christianity by missionaries many traditions died out and transgender individuals were forced and assimilated, with Indigenous groups in the early 1990s reclaiming customs and proposing "two-spirit" to refer to a traditional and cultural "third gender," with LGBT2S or LGBTQ2S increasingly used. Formal state apologies acknowledged past harm, with the Prime Minister on November 28, 2017 apologizing "For the oppression of the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and two-spirit communities," and the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police in December 2020 apologizing for harm to Two-spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, and Queer Communities and stating "We must stand together against homophobia, transphobia, and any other kind of marginalization."

sources.summary: Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations is now prohibited by all provinces and territories as well as the federal government, with explicit inclusion as prohibited grounds in human rights acts as of 2017. The concepts of sex and physical disability in section 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms have been interpreted to include transsexuality, extending equal protection guidance for interpreting human rights laws, although the Charter applies to laws and government institutions including law enforcement and not directly against the private sector. Transgender people are now able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. Saskatchewan's Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 requires schools to obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, enacted while invoking the section 33 notwithstanding clause. Alberta in 2024 passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024, and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges in Alberta courts, followed by Bill 9: Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 which used the notwithstanding clause to prevent those challenges. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, Trans and Queer communities, stated police must stand against transphobia and marginalization, and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 when the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 (Bill C-150) took effect upon royal assent, after an era when sex between men was a capital crime and gross indecency was enforced. Section 159 of the Criminal Code criminalizing anal intercourse was declared unconstitutional by courts in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Alberta, and was repealed on June 21, 2019 through Bill C-75, setting the age of consent for anal intercourse at 16, matching the general age of consent of 16 since June 2019 and 18 where a relationship of trust, authority or dependency exists. In Egan v Canada in 1995 the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under the section 15 equality clause as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta in 1998 held failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law violated section 15. Parliament enacted the Civil Marriage Act on July 20, 2005 making Canada the fourth country in the world and first in the Americas to legalize same-sex marriage nationwide without a residency requirement, following court rulings from 2002 to 2005 and a Supreme Court reference in December 2004, while same-sex adoption was legalized province by province culminating with Nunavut in 2011 after Prince Edward Island allowed joint adoption in 2009. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, housing and public and private accommodations is now prohibited by all provinces and territories and the federal government, with explicit inclusion in human rights acts as of 2017. In 2022 Canada became the third country in the world and first in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults and make subjecting anyone to it a crime as defined in the Criminal Code. Nova Scotia stands under the Canadian national framework, which the parent record carries. Within provincial competence, the province operates no restrictive trans-specific legislation and instead maintains an explicit inclusion framework.

The Government of Nova Scotia released the province's first 2SLGBTQIA+ Action Plan on 8 January 2026, developed under the Dismantling Racism and Hate Act passed in 2022, described by the province as the first Canadian law of its kind to explicitly acknowledge 2SLGBTQIA+ people. The plan was informed by more than 600 community members through surveys, virtual meetings and consultations, and maps actions to improve programs and policies supporting full inclusion of 2SLGBTQIA+ people.

On 10 June 2026 the province announced more than $176,000 through the first round of its 2SLGBTQIA+ Community Impact Grant program, including $12,067 to SeaHorse Sexual Health Centre for queer and trans outreach on the Eastern Shore, $25,000 to LakeCity Works' Queer Careers program in Dartmouth, $25,000 to Pictou County Pride, and $50,000 to Truro Pride to host the province's first provincial 2SLGBTQIA+ conference. Per-project grants are capped at $25,000 from the 2025-26 fiscal year.

Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and accommodation is prohibited in Nova Scotia as in all Canadian provinces, territories and the federal government; as of 2017 all Canadian jurisdictions explicitly include gender identity as a prohibited ground in their human rights acts. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in Nova Scotia under provincial rules.

The documented Nova Scotia correctional case concerns a transgender woman from the Halifax region held in a men's prison while serving a two-year robbery sentence. On 18 March 2025 a federal judge granted her more time to file her application for judicial review of that placement, citing a lack of transparency and clear, timely communication in the institutional decision-making and systemic barriers restricting her access to her lawyer. No later instance of this case is documented in the record.

Statistics Canada reported on 30 March 2026 that 4,882 police-reported hate crimes were recorded nationally in 2024, a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000, down 2% in 2024 and up 142% since 2018; eight provinces recorded stable or declining rates.
