14911670B1613159902410.name: Rondonia
14911670B1613159902410.summary:
Rondônia is a state of Brazil and stands under the national framework; the state has no statute of its own prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, so protection for trans visitors and residents rests on national law rather than on state legislation.

An ordinance signed on 28 August 2025 by appellate judge Daniel Ribeiro Lagos guarantees transgender people the use of their social name and the use of bathrooms and locker rooms in accordance with gender identity. It is the clearest region-specific rule on gendered facilities in the state.

In 2022 Hanier Miranda became the first person in Rondônia to obtain a birth certificate carrying an X sex marker. The civil registry had refused the entry for lack of a regulated third-gender procedure, and the marker was secured through a year-long lawsuit brought by the Center for Legal Practices, Research and Extensions at the Catholic Faculty of Porto Velho.

On 5 May 2025 the state prosecution service, the federal prosecution service, the labour prosecution service, the federal public defender's office and the state public defender's office jointly recommended that the state security secretariat and the state justice secretariat provide regular training for military police, civil police, firefighters, penitentiary and socio-educational agents on respect for LGBTQIA+ rights and improved service. The recommendation set a response deadline of 20 business days and required a training plan within 60 days covering 2025 and later years. It also requires gender identity, sexual orientation and social name to be recorded in police occurrence reports and prison records, with data protection and privacy safeguards, so that violence against transsexual women and travestis, including domestic and family violence, can be monitored.

Police records in the state logged 240 occurrences of anti-LGBTQIA+ violence across 2020 and 2021.

sources.summary: Same-sex marriage is legal nationwide under the CNJ Resolution of 14 May 2013 (14-1 vote), with adoption permitted since 2010 and full rights since 2015. Gender-marker change requires no surgery, hormones or diagnosis under the STF ruling of 1 March 2018. On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. No third-gender option exists nationwide, but civil-registry 'non-binary/unspecified' entries have been possible since 2020, and a 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. The first transgender federal legislators, Salabert and Hilton, were elected in 2022.

Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances are significant but face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. The country retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination, and trans voters may register under lived name and identity even before documents are updated. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections, evidencing local political visibility.

Brazil has among the most progressive LGBTQ+ protections in Latin America: same-sex marriage (CNJ Resolution 175/2013), joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and homophobia and transphobia criminalised as equivalent to racism (ADO 26 and MI 4733, 13 June 2019, imprisonment of 1-5 years). Enforcement is uneven in practice. Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasilia, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba and Florianopolis are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure. Smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Rondonia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Rondonia has no state law prohibiting discrimination based on gender identity, but since 2019 such discrimination is criminalized nationally by a Supreme Federal Court ruling equating it with the crime of racism. On 1 March 2018 the Supreme Federal Court ruled that a transgender person has the right to change official name and sex by self-declaration of psychosocial identity without surgery or professional evaluation. In July 2022 Hanier Miranda became the first person in the state to obtain a birth certificate with sex marker X after initial denial at the registry for lack of a regulated third-gender procedure and a year-long lawsuit by the Center for Legal Practices, Research and Extensions at the Catholic Faculty of Porto Velho. On 28 August 2025 an ordinance signed by Appellate Judge Daniel Ribeiro Lagos guarantees transgender people the use of their social name and the use of bathrooms and locker rooms in accordance with gender identity. Between 2017 and 2021 there were 12 murders of transgender people in the state, with Rondonia ranked as the 3rd state with the highest homicide rate in the North Region of Brazil. In 2025 federal and state prosecution and defender bodies recommended training on gender identity for police officers and firefighters and inclusion of LGBTQ population data in official reports. State Law no. 5123 banning gender-neutral language in schools, approved in October 2021 and signed on the 19th by Governor Marcos Rocha, was blocked in November 2021 by preliminary injunction and struck down on 10 February 2023, while a law passed on 10 July 2026 requiring parental authorization for classes on gender identity was struck down on 17 August by the Court of Justice of Rondonia. Homosexuality has been legal in Rondonia and throughout Brazil since 1830 when the Imperial Penal Code removed all references to sodomy. On 26 April 2013 the General Inspectorate of Justice published Provision 008/2013-CG providing for direct same-sex marriage and conversion of stable union into marriage in civil registration records. In 2025 federal and state prosecution and defender bodies recommended training on sexual orientation for police officers and firefighters and inclusion of LGBTQ population data in official reports. A law passed on 10 July 2026 requiring parental authorization for students to attend classes on sexual orientation, sexual diversity and gender equality, enacted by Assembly President Alex Redano after Governor Marcos Rocha neither vetoed nor signed, was struck down on 17 August by the Court of Justice of Rondonia. Between 2020 and 2021 there were 240 police reports of violence against LGBTQ people recorded in the state. sources.title: Brazilian Supreme Federal Court (STF) 2019 ruling on homophobia/transphobia
sources.summary: On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court criminalized transphobia throughout Brazil including Rondônia by applying Law 7.716/1989 Article 20 to anti-LGBTI discrimination and offenses, punishable by 1 to 3 years' imprisonment as a non-bailable and imprescriptible crime.

sources.title: 2025 Joint Recommendation - MPF, MPRO, MPT, DPU, DPE-RO

14911670B86532577506919.summary:
Sergipe's own constitutional layer is older than most in Brazil: in 1989 the state, alongside Mato Grosso do Sul, was among the first to write a ban on sexual-orientation discrimination into its constitution. On 17 December 2025 Constitutional Amendment No. 59, proposed by state deputy Linda Brasil (PSOL), amended article 3(II) of the State Constitution to guarantee protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, with violators subject to punishment by law, effective on promulgation. Sergipe is the first Brazilian state to write gender-identity protection into its constitution.

The state judiciary has its own marriage provision. On 5 July 2012 the State Judiciary Power issued Provimento nº 06/2012, which regulated same-sex marriage throughout Sergipe. Since 2025 the state has allowed individuals to change their gender marker on documents to non-binary.

Court facilities in the state capital are explicitly gender-neutral. From 28 August 2025 the Court of Justice of Sergipe provides operating gender-neutral bathrooms on the ground, first and eighth floors of the Palácio da Justiça in Aracaju, usable by any person regardless of gender identity. The same measure directs that in all Sergipe judiciary units male and female bathrooms be used respecting each person's gender identity, under human-rights and non-discrimination principles, and requires that all new constructions and renovations be planned with gender-equity demands.

14911670B72497658138655.name: Tocantins
14911670B72497658138655.summary:
Tocantins has no state law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, a gap recorded by the state's own Public Defender's Office. A trans visitor in Palmas or in the interior depends on Brazil's national framework, which applies here without state-level variation, and on national enforcement machinery rather than any state statute.

The state bodies that have acted on trans documentation are the Public Defender's Office of Tocantins (Defensoria Pública do Estado do Tocantins) and the state judicial inspectorate, the Corregedoria-Geral da Justiça. On 29 January 2026 the Public Defender's Office published an article explaining how trans people change names and gender markers on documents.

Rectification in Tocantins is administrative and rests on self-declaration. A trans man, trans woman, travesti, non-binary or queer person may apply at the civil registry where the birth was recorded, with effect on the birth certificate and on all official documents, without medical or psychological reports and without proof of surgery or hormone treatment. The service is free where the applicant proves inability to pay, and a court is involved only if the registry refuses the request.

The exception is a change to a non-binary or unspecified marker, which the Public Defender's Office states requires a judicial decision. In August 2022 that office asked the Corregedoria-Geral da Justiça to allow "non-binary" entries in civil registry records, and in 2023 the inspectorate published a resolution authorising non-binary individuals to change their documents to include a third gender option. Whether an administrative route to a non-binary marker is open in practice is unresolved.

sources.summary: Same-sex marriage legal nationwide via CNJ Resolution of 14 May 2013 (14-1 vote), adoption since 2010 (full rights 2015), and gender-marker change without surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the STF ruling of 1 March 2018. On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. No third-gender option nationwide, but civil-registry 'non-binary/unspecified' entries have been possible since 2020 and a 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. First transgender federal legislators (Salabert, Hilton) were elected in 2022.

OutRight International country report of 12 March 2026: Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances are significant but face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination, and trans voters may register under a lived name and identity even before documents are updated. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections, evidencing local political visibility.

Brazilian law-firm guide for expatriates (OAB/SP, April 2026): Brazil has among the most progressive LGBTQ+ protections in Latin America on paper: same-sex marriage (CNJ Resolution 175/2013), joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and homophobia and transphobia criminalised as equivalent to racism (ADO 26 and MI 4733, 13 June 2019, imprisonment of 1 to 5 years). Enforcement is uneven in practice. The guide contrasts major urban centers, broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, against smaller cities and rural areas, where identical legal rights may still meet more social friction.

14911670B28216513632935.name: Espirito Santo
14911670B28216513632935.summary:
Espirito Santo sits within Brazil's national framework for LGBTI rights; the national record carries the marriage, identity-marker and hate-crime provisions that apply here, and what follows is the state's own layer of law, institutions and enforcement.

Facilities are contested at municipal level. On 6 June 2022 the Vitoria City Council approved a bill banning the installation of unisex restrooms in the city. The source records the council vote but not whether the mayor signed or vetoed the measure, so its current legal force is unresolved.

On 14 April 2024 the Legislative Assembly of Espirito Santo approved a bill restricting athletes' participation in competitions according to biological sex. Governor Renato Casagrande vetoed it on 28 April 2024.

On 21 June 2025 the Legislative Assembly approved a law allowing parents to prohibit their children from participating in classes dealing with LGBTQ topics. LGBTQ rights organisations challenged it at the Supreme Federal Court, which began hearing the case on 21 November 2025 and struck the law down in May 2026 by 8 votes to 2; Justice Carmen Lucia stated that it violated the Brazilian Constitution.

Partner recognition was addressed in Espirito Santo before the national framework was settled. On 3 August 2012 a judge in Colatina authorised registration of the marriage of Ediana Calixto and Kamila Roccon, the first same-sex marriage recognised in the state. The State Public Prosecutor's Office appealed and the recognition was revoked on 15 August; on 20 September the state Court of Justice reversed that decision and authorised recognition. On 15 August 2012 the General Inspectorate of Justice issued a Circular Letter requiring all civil registries to treat same-sex marriages on the same terms as opposite-sex couples, making Espirito Santo the third Brazilian state to address the question statewide.

State institutions have also acted on document recognition. On 22 January 2025 the Public Defender's Office of Espirito Santo filed suit to secure name and gender rectification for a non-binary person from Vitoria, and the court granted the request and authorised the rectification. On 27 June 2025 the Legislative Assembly and the Public Defender's Office held a free event to help trans, non-binary and travesti people change their name and gender on official documents.

14911670B30315977547221.name: Parana
14911670B30315977547221.summary:
Paraná is a state of Brazil and stands under the national framework carried by the parent record; the findings below are specific to the state and its municipalities.

Access to sex-separated facilities has been contested in Paraná's own legislature and in municipal councils. In 2021 state representative Mara Lima introduced a bill prohibiting unisex bathrooms statewide and requiring separate male and female facilities. On 16 November 2021 the Curitiba City Council approved a municipal bill of the same kind, introduced by councilman Ezequias Barros. The inventory does not record whether either measure was enacted.

On 4 October 2023 the Curitiba City Council approved, by symbolic vote, a motion of protest against Resolution 2/2023 of the federal Ministry of Human Rights and Citizenship, issued on 19 September 2023, which provided that educational institutions must guarantee use of bathrooms, changing rooms and other gender-segregated spaces according to each student's gender identity and expression, while recommending additional individual-use bathrooms in public spaces. The Ministry stated that the resolution has no binding effect and that no school is obliged to adopt it. The Curitiba motion was to be converted into an official letter to the federal government.

Gender markers on documents issued in the state are governed by the Court of Justice of the State of Paraná. In 2023 that court published a provision guaranteeing inclusion of a non-binary option in the Civil Registry gender marker, then revoked it in November 2023, limiting administrative replacement of first name and sex to male and female only. In 2025 the Court of Justice of the State of Paraná authorized a third gender option on documents.

Trans participation in sport has produced conflicting rulings between a municipality and the national courts. On 26 April 2024 Londrina enacted a law banning transgender people from competing in sports according to gender identity, with a R$10,000 fine for non-compliance. On 26 February 2026 the Londrina City Council approved a motion to bar transgender athlete Tiffanny Abreu from the Brazilian Women's Volleyball Cup; the Brazilian Volleyball Confederation filed suit in the Supreme Federal Court and Justice Cármen Lúcia issued a preliminary injunction the same day allowing her to compete. In March 2026 LGBTQ rights organizations filed suit against the Londrina law in the Supreme Federal Court, and on 7 August 2026 rapporteur Justice Cristiano Zanin voted to strike the law down. The inventory does not record a final judgment.

Relationship recognition in Paraná was established before the national rule took effect. On 26 March 2013 the General Inspector of Justice of Paraná ruled that same-sex marriage and the conversion of stable unions to marriage must use normal marriage procedures, and same-sex civil marriage was authorized in all cartórios statewide under the same procedure and documentation as heterosexual marriage, with conversion of a stable union into marriage permitted without judicial authorization. In 2004 Curitiba recorded the first recognition of a same-sex union in Brazil: common-law marriage status, previously limited to opposite-sex couples, for an English-Brazilian couple who had cohabited fourteen years.

State courts have granted adoption to same-sex couples. On 14 May 2009 the 2nd Court of Childhood, Youth and Adoption granted the first gay-couple adoption in Paraná to a Curitiba couple, finding a stable and affectionate union able to raise a child in a healthy environment. On 27 October 2010 Judge Sergio Luiz Kreuz in Cascavel authorized irreversible adoption of an eight-year-old child with cerebral palsy by a gay couple together twelve years, under Superior Court of Justice precedent. On 16 September 2011 Maringá justice authorized adoption of two children by a lesbian couple.

14911670B68448774564157.name: Rio Grande do Sul
14911670B68448774564157.summary:
On 27 January 2020 the Rio Grande do Sul government installed signage in the women's restrooms of state government offices stating that use follows gender identity, and installed unisex restrooms.

State Law No. 14,896, enacted by the Legislative Assembly on 19 December 2002, prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation. The statute does not name gender identity as a protected ground.

Enforcement of anti-discrimination rules in commercial venues is unsettled. On 28 September 2025 a Porto Alegre court ordered a bar to pay 10,000 reais in compensation for denying a trans man access to the men's restroom. On 28 May 2026 an appellate court overturned that decision, acquitting the nightclub of the transfobia allegation on the ground that the evidence did not show the man had been barred from the restroom.

sources.summary: As of 5 Apr 2026, same-sex marriage is available nationwide (binding CNJ Resolution 175/2013), with spousal-visa equality, joint adoption, and name and gender-marker changes without surgery. The 13 Jun 2019 ADO 26 ruling makes homophobia and transphobia crimes equivalent to racism. Larger cities have legal infrastructure, and smaller cities and rural areas carry more social friction.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Rio Grande do Sul (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2019, discrimination based on gender identity has been prohibited nationwide in Brazil through a Supreme Federal Court decision. On 1 March 2018, the Supreme Federal Court ruled that a transgender person may change official name and sex by self-declaration of psychosocial identity without surgery or professional evaluation. On 27 January 2020, the Rio Grande do Sul government installed signs in women's restrooms of state government offices stating use in accordance with gender identity and installed unisex restrooms. In August 2021, Special Secretary of Culture Mário Frias criticized those restroom measures as posing risks to children. On 22 April 2022, Rio Grande do Sul Justice allowed non-binary people to change first name and sex in the birth record to include 'non-binary' upon request to a notary without judicial authorization, but in December 2023 the Court of Justice revoked that provision. On 28 September 2025, a Porto Alegre court ordered a bar to pay 10,000 reais compensation for denying a trans man access to the men's restroom, and on 28 May 2026 an appellate court overturned that decision. Homosexuality is legal in Rio Grande do Sul. On 19 December 2002, the Legislative Assembly enacted State Law No. 14,896 prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation. On 29 May 2012, four of six notaries in Porto Alegre agreed to convert civil unions into marriages. On 11 November 2005, a Bagé judge permitted adoption of two brothers by a lesbian couple in a seven-year stable union, described as Brazil's first LGBTQ adoption. On 6 April 2006, same-sex couples in committed relationships were allowed to register at any notary office with rights to jointly own property, establish custody of children, and claim pensions and property on a partner's death. On 27 April 2010, the Superior Court of Justice recognized shared adoption of two sons by Bagé lesbian couple Lídia Brignol Guterres and Luciana Reis Maidana to secure pension, separation and inheritance rights. On 3 June 2011, Pelotas justice authorized adoption of a four-year-old by a gay couple with the biological mother's consent.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court - 2019 nationwide gender identity discrimination ban
sources.summary: On 24 May 2019 a majority of Brazil's Supreme Federal Court (6 of 11 justices) voted to criminalize transphobia and homophobia as equivalent to racism, punishable under Brazil's racism law until Congress enacts specific LGBT-protection legislation.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court ruling of 1 March 2018 on name and sex change
sources.summary: On 1 March 2018 in ADI 4275 the Federal Supreme Court held that the right to equality without discrimination encompasses gender identity and expression as a manifestation of personality that the State must recognize, and therefore authorized change of name and gender on the civil registry without sex-reassignment surgery or judicial authorization.

sources.title: Statement by Special Secretary of Culture Mario Frias - August 2021
sources.summary: In August 2021, Rio Grande do Sul's Secretariat of Culture maintained a women's bathroom designated as inclusive of trans women and travestis, which federal Special Secretary of Culture Mario Frias publicly criticized.

1811400B81659894240990.name: Puducherry
1811400B81659894240990.summary: Puducherry is subject to India's national framework in full, with no local exception of its own. What distinguishes the region is its character: a small, urbanised coastal union territory built around Pondicherry town, a former French enclave whose cafes, guesthouses and Auroville-area traffic draw steady international visitors, with a generally more liberal social atmosphere than conservative rural South India. Tamil culture has a longstanding, visible aravani community, and the territory runs its own transgender welfare board. The region also sits within the Madras High Court's jurisdiction, so its 2021 directions on police conduct toward LGBT+ people formally bind local officers. In the seafront and tourist quarters, visible gender nonconformity tends to draw curiosity, staring and misgendering rather than confrontation, and routine policing is generally less overtly hostile than in some conservative districts of the interior, with courts reachable if needed. Document and presentation mismatches still produce awkward bureaucracy at hotels, transport, clinics and police contact, including placement by documented sex in hospital wards. Conservative attitudes persist in outlying and rural pockets, where friction is more likely than on the seafront, and transgender-specific infrastructure beyond the welfare board is thin. No local campaign targeting trans visitors, territory-specific facility restrictions, or documented local remedy has been recorded — that gap reflects an absence of reporting rather than demonstrated safety, and how consistently local police and facilities apply the protections on paper to a visitor is genuinely uncertain.

1811400B74762431478096.name: Nāgāland
1811400B74762431478096.summary: Nāgāland falls under India's national transgender regime in full, with no local carve-out. What distinguishes the state is social and administrative rather than legal. It is a small, predominantly Baptist and largely rural society in which Naga customary law — insulated by Article 371A — and church bodies shape public morality, and where there is no local hijra or third-gender tradition to signal acceptance. Binary gender norms are strong, gender diversity is unfamiliar, and community or support infrastructure outside Kohima and Dimapur is very thin, as is gender-affirming care. In close-knit towns and villages anonymity is limited, so a visitor read as gender-nonconforming can become highly visible quickly; the responses most often described are curiosity, disapproval and moral pressure rather than physical violence. No trans-specific violence or targeting by police is documented in the state, but reporting is thin, so that silence should not be read as assurance. Administratively, foreigners require an Inner Line or Protected Area Permit, and permit and identity checks are routine at Dimapur airport and railway station and along state highways; parts of the state also fall under the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, adding checkpoints where papers are examined. Document mismatches are therefore more likely to be questioned here — by police, hotel staff or community leaders — than in most of India, and social anonymity does not extend to official encounters. Tourist-facing settings such as the Hornbill Festival and hotels in Kohima and Dimapur may be more tolerant in practice, and the Gauhati High Court's Kohima bench offers formal recourse, though local legal-aid services are limited.

1811400B55669546485086.name: Lakshadweep
1811400B55669546485086.summary: Lakshadweep is a small Union Territory of India of roughly 65,000 people, overwhelmingly Muslim, socially conservative and socially insular, with close-knit communities that leave almost no anonymity — a visitor's presence and any outing can spread quickly. Tourism is restricted and heavily administered, entry generally requires a permit, and identity documents are scrutinised at the permit and ferry or flight stage, adding a document-mismatch exposure specific to the territory. There is no documented transgender community infrastructure, no visible queer venues, and no record of local sensitisation programmes or enforcement of protective guidelines, while medical and legal services are thin, with serious incidents or care usually handled through Kavaratti or referred to Kochi; local police capacity and the handling of complaints are not well documented, and police responses may reflect local conservatism. No territory-specific hostile legislation, organised targeting, trans-specific violence or criminal prosecution, or local regime of imprisonment or execution for being transgender is documented — but neither are local protections or specialised recourse, and absence of such records is not evidence of safety. India's national framework still applies: same-sex conduct is decriminalised, constitutional anti-discrimination protection covers gender identity, courts function, and Supreme Court rulings against harassment stand, alongside 2021 Madras High Court police and conversion-therapy guidelines and expanded healthcare coverage. Offsetting these, a 2026 change narrows formal legal recognition to hijra, kinner and intersex people, excluding many trans men, trans women and non-binary people (that domestic pathway does not govern a visitor's home-issued documents), gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences have been removed, and document and security frictions are documented — passport medical-examination demands, invasive questioning at airports and stations, security stops of openly trans travellers, and reported police groping. For a trans visitor who is outed, or visibly gender-nonconforming, these combine: high visibility in a small population with limited privacy raises the likelihood of discovery, and local disapproval may translate into staring, intrusive questioning, harassment, refusal of services, social confrontation, pressure to leave, coercive policing or hospital ward-placement problems — resolved slowly and informally against thin, distant recourse, with national constitutional protections still formally operating.

1811400B49281905528064.name: Mizoram
1811400B49281905528064.summary: Mizoram is subject to India's national legal framework in full, with no local exception. The state is small, predominantly Christian and socially conservative: church bodies have publicly condemned homosexuality, the legislature formally opposed same-sex marriage, and there is no entrenched third-gender social tradition of the kind found in parts of mainland India, so unfamiliar gender expression tends to be read as a community matter rather than a private one. With limited urban anonymity, low inbound tourism and minimal queer visibility, an out or gender-nonconforming visitor can expect persistent curiosity, misgendering, intrusive questioning by staff, police or healthcare workers, service hesitation or refusal of lodging, gossip, and pressure from family, church or Mizo Local Councils, which have enforced customary community morality against perceived immorality. Villages and small towns carry more of this than better-known visitor settings. Inner Line Permit and Protected Area Permit checks add repeated identity-document scrutiny, and complaints may be handled unevenly. Legal recourse exists on paper but is thin locally, through low awareness and few specialist support services for visitors. On the other hand, Mizoram is a peaceful, low-crime state with functioning courts, and there is no known pattern of organized state targeting, raids or trans-specific violence against travellers in the state — but local data on the issue is thin, so this silence is an absence of evidence rather than a guarantee of safety.

A news organisation (26 March 2026) records that the nation’s legislature passed an amendment to the 2019 trans-rights law replacing self-identification with recognition based on biological or physical traits plus traditional identities, with medical boards and district authorities required to certify gender-affirming surgery; the government says the narrower definition targets welfare benefits and anti-trafficking protection while critics warn it excludes many trans men, trans women and non-binary people; a supreme court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw the amendment, calling removal of self-identification a setback against the 2014 ruling, and presidential assent remained pending; the national transgender population is estimated in the millions.

1811400B16134215155042.summary: Arunāchal Pradesh is subject to India's national legal framework in full, with no local exception. What distinguishes the state is the paperwork: foreign visitors need a Protected Area Permit and most entrants need an Inner Line Permit, with identity documents checked repeatedly at district and police checkpoints, so a mismatch between documents and presentation is examined more often here than in most of India. The state is remote, sparsely populated and overwhelmingly rural, with policing capacity, hospitals and legal-aid services thin and concentrated in Itanagar; there are almost no trans-specific services, sensitised clinics or community organisations outside the capital. Social attitudes vary across tribal, Christian and urban communities, with mission-influenced conservatism growing in some districts alongside village councils and limited LGBTQ visibility, though some tribal traditions retain recognised gender-diverse roles. Parts of the state have been covered by the Armed Forces Special Powers Act, and elevated police-abuse risk in conservative rural areas describes much of this state. No region-specific documentation of trans-targeted enforcement, facility bans or organised hostility was identified, and no distinct local trans-protective regime exists to offset the national picture; such thin local evidence, policing and record-keeping should not be read as safety.

1811400B28404458933503.name: Meghālaya
1811400B28404458933503.summary: Meghalaya is subject to India's national law in full, with no local exception. What distinguishes the state is its social setting: Khasi, Jaintia and Garo matrilineal custom, a Christian-majority hill society, and a tourism-facing economy centred on Shillong, with heavy visitor traffic to Sohra and Umiam. Shillong has a visible queer community and public Pride and advocacy activity, a functioning local administration and comparatively open public life, and everyday discovery there is less likely to escalate than in many Indian cities. Specialist care and practical recourse are concentrated in Shillong; outside it, trans-specific community and healthcare infrastructure is thin, and remote areas bring more staring, gossip and service friction. Matrilineal inheritance does not by itself signal acceptance of gender diversity — conservative Christian institutions and rural conservatism make gender nonconformity an object of social disapproval, and rural policing, complaint-handling and clinic refusal are the main local risks. Unsympathetic police handling and service refusal are more plausible in conservative rural districts than in tourist areas, where outsiders are routine and reported harassment is lower than in some neighbouring states. National remedies exist but are slower and less accessible from the state. Visitors should also note that most travel to the state routes through Guwahati, in neighbouring Assam. No documented pattern of trans-specific raids, organised violence or harsher local detention rules is on record for Meghalaya, and no state enforcement regime targeting gender expression is known — but this reflects the limits of what has been documented rather than evidence of safety, and documentary friction remains a live concern wherever identity becomes visible.

1811400B97532436596698.name: Manipur
1811400B97532436596698.summary: Manipur is subject to India's national law in full, with no local statutory exception of its own. Local conditions, however, differ from the national picture in both directions. The state has one of India's most visible indigenous gender-diverse communities — the Nupi Maanbi among the Meitei, alongside a recognised hijra presence in Imphal and a historic Maibi priestess tradition — with organized advocacy, a state transgender welfare board, and everyday familiarity in the capital that is uncommon elsewhere; specialist care, though, is concentrated in Imphal. Against this, both the Meitei valley and the tribal hill districts are strongly gender-binary and conservative, and the largely Christian hill areas are socially less familiar with gender diversity. Since May 2023 severe ethnic conflict has left the state militarised: armed barricades, security-force and insurgent-group checkpoints and curfews on most roads, identity documents checked by military, paramilitary, civil-defence and armed-group actors, and large-scale displacement. Police are stretched thin and divided along community lines, state authority is contested in hill areas, and documented mass sexual violence has gone largely unaccounted for — so a visitor who is outed, detained or harmed may find remedy unreliable, particularly outside Imphal and while in custody. Travel also requires Inner Line or Protected Area permits, adding further document scrutiny. No Manipur-specific statute targeting transgender visitors is known, and no Manipur-specific incidents of anti-trans targeting are documented here; the conflict itself is not evidence of such targeting, but the absence of records cannot be read as safety.

1811400B56841107211215.name: Karnātaka
1811400B56841107211215.summary: Karnātaka is subject to India's national law in full, with no local exception. Bengaluru is the centre of gravity for a trans visitor: a large technology and university city with one of India's most visible trans and hijra communities, an annual Namma Pride march, established queer venues, and a dense network of NGOs and activist organisations, including Bengaluru-based advocates. The state runs a transgender welfare board along with third-gender employment and welfare measures, and urban institutions and the hospitality sector are broadly accustomed to gender diversity — though these provisions are principally resident-facing and do not by themselves give a visiting trans person a remedy. Everyday exposure is lower in Bengaluru and other large urban centres; rural and smaller-town districts are markedly more conservative, with weaker recourse and a greater risk of humiliation or extortion at police hands, and the coastal belt is also described as markedly conservative. Police conduct in Bengaluru is inconsistent despite periodic sensitisation work, but the state has no documented record of targeted enforcement against trans people at the level seen in more conservative regions, and no documented record of organised targeting or custody abuse of visitors. Identity checks remain the practical friction point: passport or ID mismatches at Kempegowda International Airport, hotel or station checks, and hospital ward or custody placement can all turn on documents, and state-level protections are not tested against that practice. Where official encounters go poorly, the Karnataka High Court is an available forum. The thinness of local reporting on mistreatment of trans visitors should not be read as evidence of its absence.

1811400B51283975314925.name: Dādra and Nagar Haveli and Damān and Diu
1811400B51283975314925.summary: The region is subject to India's national law in full, with no local exception. Dādra and Nagar Haveli and Damān and Diu is a small union territory run directly by a centrally appointed Administrator, with judicial matters going to the Bombay High Court; it has no separate territorial equality law, hate-crime provision or trans-specific welfare scheme, and no local anti-trans statute or documented policing campaign against gender-nonconforming people is known. The territory is really two different pieces: inland Dadra and Nagar Haveli is largely rural and Adivasi, with Silvassa — a small, conservative industrial town — as its administrative centre, while Daman and Diu are coastal enclaves ringed by Gujarat, with a Catholic minority and a Portuguese-derived civil code governing family matters. Daman and Diu run a beach- and weekend-tourism economy with foreign visitors, and those tourist belts feel noticeably more relaxed than the rural and tribal interiors, which tend to be more conservative. Local attitudes are conservative but not organised against gender diversity; what a visitor is more likely to meet is misgendering, discomfort in binary-marked washrooms, invasive questioning and uneven police sensitivity. Small size works against anonymity: in these towns a gender-nonconforming visitor will be noticed. There is no local trans community to speak of and no gender-affirming care available on the territory — Mumbai, Surat and Ahmedabad are the nearest centres — so healthcare or peer support means travelling off-territory. The police force is small and general crime is low, but local records are thin: no trans-specific incidents are documented here, and that silence should be read as absence of evidence rather than as safety.

1811400B6111924962807.name: Goa
1811400B6111924962807.summary:
Goa is a state of India and stands under the national framework on transgender recognition, identity documents and criminal law. No Goan statute diverging from that national position is on file.

Marriage and partnership recognition in Goa is set by the Goa Civil Code, a state-level instrument that defines marriage as between a man and a woman and gives no legal recognition to same-sex marriage or civil union. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status cannot have that relationship recognised in Goa, and the code applies in this state rather than the personal-law system used elsewhere in India.

Goa has no state-level anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation. Protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity in Goa rests on the national Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, which applies in the state.

On 7 May 2025 the state government constituted a 14-member Model Transgender Welfare Board, chaired by the Chief Secretary, under the 2019 Act and the 2020 Rules, with a mandate covering implementation of welfare schemes and safeguarding transgender persons' rights in healthcare, education, employment and housing.

Administrative recognition in Goa lags the resident population. The 2011 census recorded 398 transgender people in Goa; by 2024 only 12 transgender people were registered on the state's electoral rolls, the first registrations having taken place in 2022. sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Goa (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Federal law has recognized transgender identity since NALSA v. Union of India in 2014. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 prohibits discrimination based on gender identity. In 2025 Goa formed the Model Transgender Welfare Board under the provisions of that Act to facilitate welfare schemes for transgender people. The 2011 census counted 398 transgender people in Goa, but as of 2024 only 12 transgender people were registered in electoral rolls, with the first registrations occurring in 2022. A 2018 Goa Livelihoods Forum study found 87% of transgender respondents had dropped out of school due to harassment. Same-sex activity was decriminalized at federal level in 2018 by Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India. In 16th century Goa, the Goa Inquisition criminalized same-sex activity with death penalty by burning to ashes and confiscation of property to the Crown, as applied in 1528 to a Muslim man and later to 16-year-old Portuguese army soldier Alberto Homem. Under the 1568 Constitutions of the Archbishopric of Goa, same-sex activity was classified as a serious sin punishable by deposition from office and lifelong penance in a religious institution for a clergyman and excommunication until repentance and required penance for a layman. In 1644 the Tribunal of Goa sought clarification on female same-sex acts and the majority concluded such acts generally did not constitute sodomy but sexual immorality rather than the crime of sodomy. Goa applies the Goa Civil Code defining marriage as between a man and a woman with no legal recognition for same-sex marriages or civil unions, though in 2023 the Supreme Court noted same-sex couples have the right to cohabit and enjoy some protections under law. Following the Supreme Court's 2023 decision not to legalize same-sex marriage, activists in Goa urged legislative steps but no bills have been introduced. There are currently no state-level anti-discrimination laws protecting sexual orientation in Goa.

Custody placement remains the sharpest documented exposure. Baden-Württemberg's own prison law retains the unrevised 1970s-era placement rules, which operate on a binary men and women housing model. A Verfassungsblog analysis of 18 March 2026 reports that placement rules in most Länder have stood unchanged since the 1970s and are now being revised: since 1 March 2026 a new Art. 17 of Rhineland-Palatinate's prison law is in force, and Bavarian, Saxon and Hamburg rules have also recently entered into force, giving a majority of Länder revised rules. The same analysis argues that no constitutional duty exists to anchor placement to the registered gender entry, since a prisoner self-declaration would intrude less on the right to gender self-determination. Only Bremen's law explicitly references the gender entry; other Länder, implicitly or not at all, do so.

How placement is applied in practice has gone both ways. A July 2026 report concerns a convicted far-right extremist holding a legally recognised female gender entry who was transferred from a women's prison to a men's prison after public outcry. The transfer indicates that placement follows the civil-registry entry and that exceptions permitting placement contrary to that entry are invoked inconsistently.

10402087B44391416804171.name: Bremen
10402087B44391416804171.summary:
Bremen, as a German city-state, stands under the national framework set by the Self-Determination Act (Selbstbestimmungsgesetz). It has enacted no trans-specific statute of its own and no prison-placement rule of its own. Prison administration and the civil-registry offices are competences of the city-state, so the layer a trans person actually deals with in Bremen is run by Bremen authorities, applying the federal framework without local amendment.

Under the Self-Determination Act the legal gender entered in the civil registry is the reference point for prison placement in every Land, and § 6(1) SBGG permits Land law to override that entry. Bremen has not passed such an override. The placement of a trans person held in a Bremen facility therefore turns on the registered entry rather than on a Bremen exception clause; how intake review is conducted in Bremen's prisons is not documented in the available sources.

Legal gender changes for Bremen residents are processed through the city-state's own registry offices. Bremen maintains no separate rule on bathrooms, changing or leisure facilities, or identity documents of its own, so a visitor meets the national framework rather than a local variant.

sources.summary: A 16 July 2026 France24/wire report covers the neo-Nazi prisoner in the 'Liebich' case, placed in a men's prison despite a legal gender change. The case drove Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia to launch a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act. The issue is framework-level for every Land, since prison administration and registry offices are Land competences.

Framework analysis (Verfassungsblog, 18 Mar 2026) of German state prison-placement rules under the Self-Determination Act: all Länder tie placement to the prisoner's legal gender; § 6(1) SBGG lets state law override the entry, and many Länder have enacted exception clauses — some abstract (all inmates), some criticised as trans-targeted. Bremen has no placement statute of its own, so this national framework is the operative standard for inmate-placement questions.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Germany - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Germany's federal Self-Determination Act, the framework a trans visitor to Bremen stands under, passed parliament by 374-251 and took effect on 1 November 2024: adults over 18 can change their legal gender by self-determination, and the change is entered in the civil registry, i.e. handled through offices including Bremen's own. The article records that years of self-identification apply to adults without requiring the previous medical/court pathway, and that same-sex marriage has been legal since 1 October 2017. It confirms no Bremen-specific deviation: the city-state operates the unchanged federal act as of the article's coverage.

The overview also documents the federal criminal-law history in which Bremen's current status sits, including the Nazi-era tightening of Section 175a with penitentiary terms of up to ten years and the persecution of men including forced castration in prisons. No Bremen-specific statute or enforcement appears in the overview. Bremen relies on the federal framework.

10402087B45896528657515.summary:
Prison administration in Germany is a competence of the individual states, and Hamburg is a state as well as a city. Placement decisions for transgender people held in Hamburg's correctional facilities therefore rest with the Hamburg justice administration rather than with a federal authority. No case file, official guidance or enforcement account concerning a transgender prisoner in Hamburg appears in the sources reviewed for this assessment; the longer contest over how a legal gender entry interacts with prison housing is documented nationally and in other German states, and belongs to the parent country assessment.

Documentary matters for a trans visitor or resident in Hamburg stand under the national framework of Germany. Legal gender and first-name changes are made by self-declaration at Hamburg's registry offices under the Self-Determination Act, in force since 1 November 2024, with three months' notice and without a psychological evaluation or a court order. Hamburg's own procedural handling of those declarations is not documented in the sources reviewed.

Hamburg has a long-established gay commercial quarter in the St. Georg district, where bars, cafés and clubs operate in the streets adjoining the Reeperbahn entertainment area; German-language reference material describes the city as the principal centre of the gay scene in the north of the country. That material records no Hamburg-specific dispute over trans access to those venues.

10402087B86022102756745.name: Nordrhein-Westfalen
10402087B86022102756745.summary:
North Rhine-Westphalia has enacted no trans-specific legislation of its own. A trans visitor's legal position in the state is set by the German national framework, and the state's correctional law contains no trans-specific placement provision, so a detained trans person in a North Rhine-Westphalia prison is placed under the national default rule that the legal gender entry governs, with no state exception clause to override it.

The closest thing to a regional assessment of trans people's situation is the study "Queer durch NRW – Lebenslagen und Erfahrungen von LSBTIQ*", published on 25 April 2025, the first comprehensive dataset on the living situations of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, inter, queer and non-binary people in the state. It combined quantitative online surveys of more than 5,000 LSBTIQ* respondents, 775 relatives and over 5,000 professionals with qualitative focus groups and expert interviews. Three thematic areas structure it: discrimination, violence and safety; health, care and ageing; and integration, migration and flight.

The study was commissioned under a Landtag resolution, Drucksache 18/6360, to give the state's "Aktionsplan für Vielfalt und gegen Homo- und Transfeindlichkeit" a broader data basis. The action plan is a policy programme of the state government rather than a statute, and it creates no rights a visitor can invoke. That discrimination, violence and safety are among the domains the state government measures indicates a recognised problem, but the figures for trans respondents are not in the reviewed sources, so no risk magnitude can be stated for the state.

10402087B42728698084544.name: Rheinland-Pfalz
10402087B42728698084544.summary:
Prison placement for people held in Rheinland-Pfalz is set by the state rather than the federal government: prison administration is a competence of the German Länder, so the placement rule for Rheinland-Pfalz prisoners sits in the state's own correctional act, while legal gender recognition and anti-discrimination law sit in the federal framework. Section 17 of the Landesjustizvollzugsgesetz Rheinland-Pfalz took effect on 1 March 2026 and anchors inmate placement to the legally recorded gender entry. The accompanying exception clause is drafted in general and abstract terms and is available to all prisoners; it is not written specifically for transgender prisoners. A trans visitor detained in Rheinland-Pfalz therefore has the placement decision taken at intake against the gender entry on their legal record, with the exception clause as the only route away from it.

A constitutional-law analysis published on 18 March 2026 reads the Rheinland-Pfalz drafting as the model preferable to the alternative used in other states, where exception clauses are written to target transgender prisoners specifically, and raises constitutional doubts about that alternative approach. 10402087B83775792336645.name: Saarland
10402087B83775792336645.summary:
Saarland has no trans-specific statute of its own. Its state constitution was amended in 2011 so that its anti-discrimination provisions explicitly include sexual orientation and gender identity, one of five Länder constitutions to carry such a clause. The consequence for a visitor is that transphobic hate speech is prohibited under Saarland's constitution, while hate speech on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned nationwide.

Prison placement in Saarland is governed by the national framework because the state has enacted no placement statute of its own; the legal gender entry is the default basis for placement unless a state law provides otherwise. A constitutional-law analysis published on 18 March 2026 cites Saarland's single-cell accommodation with en-suite shower as a positive practice model for trans inmates. The same analysis records that constitutional law does not oblige authorities to follow the legal gender entry, so the default in Saarland is a practice rather than an enforceable guarantee.

sources.summary: The page records that Saarland's state constitution was amended in 2011 so that its anti-discrimination provisions explicitly include sexual orientation and gender identity, one of only five Lander constitutions to carry such a clause (Berlin since 1995, Brandenburg since 1992, Bremen since 2001, Saarland since 2011, Thuringia since 1993; Saxony-Anhalt in the public sector since 1997). It further records that Saarland, with Hesse, Berlin, Bremen and Schleswig-Holstein, tabled a joint Bundesrat motion for a ban on conversion therapy, presented in plenary on 12 April 2019, with Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia agreeing and Bavaria offering modified support. Gives the state-constitutional protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity that a trans visitor stands under within Saarland.

sources.title: Transgender rights in Germany (Wikipedia)

For Saarland this is a jurisdiction-specific enforcement difference: transphobic hate speech is prohibited under the state constitution, unlike in most of Germany, and the federal General Act on Equal Treatment (in force since 18 August 2006) bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in employment, education, health services and the provision of goods and services.

25490228B56567998760255.summary:
The Basque Country's own legal layer is a 2013 law passed by the Basque Parliament against discrimination on grounds of gender identity and recognising the rights of trans people. The region's instruments sit under Spain's national framework, which carries legal gender recognition and the bias-motive aggravator in criminal law; the regional layer adds to that framework rather than displacing it.

Institutional markers predating it include the first Basque Pride march in Bilbao in 1978, the legalisation of the activist collective EHGAM in 1983, and the creation of Emakunde, the Basque Women's Institute, in 1988. A 2017 survey by the Basque Youth Observatory reported that 9 in 10 Basque young people favour same-sex marriage and legal change of sex. Osakidetza, the Basque health service, provided assisted reproduction regardless of sexual orientation and reaffirmed that position in 2013. The Basque Country operates its own non-discrimination legal instruments and equality institutions, including Emakunde, within the national framework.

25490228B27950689864224.name: Región de Murcia
25490228B27950689864224.summary:
Región de Murcia stands under Spain's national framework. The region's own layer is Ley 8/2016 of 27 May 2016 (BOE-A-2016-6170), which prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, and sex characteristics across public and private activity in the region. Within its scope the statute bars any requirement that a person prove a declared gender identity by psychological or medical report, so a regional service, clinic or venue cannot demand documentation of a visitor's gender as a condition of service.

Article 5 creates the Observatorio regional contra la discriminación por orientación sexual e identidad de género, a participation and consultation body on which LGTBI entities are represented.

Title IV sets the sanctioning ladder. Minor breaches draw a warning or a fine of up to EUR 3,000. Serious breaches run EUR 3,001 to EUR 20,000 and cover degrading remarks or incitement to violence against LGBTI people or their families in the provision of services. Very serious breaches run EUR 20,001 to EUR 45,000, with accessory penalties that include exclusion from regional public aid for up to one year. Multiple discrimination raises the grade of the infraction.

Murcia was among eight autonomous regions that approved LGBTI and trans equality laws in the 2010s, and Ley 8/2016 remains the operative regional instrument. Implementation of the national trans-equality law falls to the regional government.

25490228B94236519555378.summary:
Galicia is an autonomous community of Spain, and the national framework set by Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, the organic law on real and effective equality for trans persons and the guarantee of LGBTI rights, governs legal gender recognition and protection against LGBTIphobic discrimination in the region as it does in the rest of the country.

The statute assigns implementation of its education-facing and administrative provisions to the autonomous communities. The Xunta de Galicia is one of the regional governments charged with carrying them out, and public authorities in Galicia act within their own competences when they do so. How the region's schools, administrative services and public bodies apply those provisions determines what trans residents and visitors meet in practice, and the sources reviewed do not describe Galicia's implementation record.

Galicia's courts have produced the first application of the discrimination aggravating circumstance for transfobia recorded in the country. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo fined the author of WhatsApp messages that threatened a trans woman EUR 300. The conviction was a misdemeanour, and it is the only documented regional enforcement of that aggravating circumstance in the sources reviewed.

Nothing in the sources reviewed documents region-specific legislation or practice in Galicia that restricts trans visitors. Recognition, document markers, facility access and healthcare access are governed by the national law, and no Galicia-level measure narrowing them appears.

The law mandates measures across administrative, workplace, health and education fields, with public authorities acting within their competences; the education-facing and administrative provisions are implemented by the autonomous communities, this region's government among them.

Human Rights Watch, 16 February 2023, reporting the Spanish Congress of Deputies' passage of the comprehensive LGBTI law known as the 'Trans Law': legal gender recognition by self-identification through a simple administrative process, replacing the prior requirements of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment aligned to the sought marker. The law strengthens sexuality education, bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before their consent, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples and prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing; children from age 12 may obtain recognition under certain conditions, a provision that provoked political conflict. HRW assesses the reform as upholding European and international standards against abusive, disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition.

25490228B80227492032103.name: Cataluña/Catalunya
25490228B80227492032103.summary:
Catalunya stands under the national framework of Spain; the region-specific layer is set by Ley 11/2014 of 10 October 2014, published in the Diari Oficial de la Generalitat de Catalunya (DOGC núm. 6730) on 17 October 2014.

Ley 11/2014 defines direct discrimination, indirect discrimination and discrimination by association on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics.

The statute obliges Catalan public administrations to establish mechanisms so that administrative documentation reflects a person's gender identity.

Its protections extend across education, health, employment and sport, and it broadens the mandate of the Observatori Català de l'Esport to act against violence and discrimination in sport.

On partnership, the statute guarantees participation in death procedures, specifically identification of the body, burial and the handling of personal effects, to a surviving partner whose relationship is classed as same-sex under the law.

Article 35 sanctions minor breaches by reference to the indicador de renda de suficiència de Catalunya, at between seven days' and three months' worth of that indicator. Article 38 places the sanctioning regime under the department competent for LGBTI non-discrimination, and the Síndic de Greuges may instigate proceedings.

Implementation of the national framework in the region falls to the Generalitat de Catalunya.

The one Córdoba-specific enforcement fact in the inventory concerns a cluster of deaths. 19177384B45303095947895.name: Formosa
19177384B45303095947895.summary: Formosa is subject to Argentina's national law in full, with no local exception, and no Formosa-specific rule barring trans visitors from facilities, entry, care or documents is known, nor is there evidence of organised state targeting. What distinguishes the province is its local conditions: a small, relatively poor and economically peripheral northeastern territory on the Paraguayan border, more rural and socially conservative than Buenos Aires or Rosario, with denser community scrutiny, less anonymity, and fewer visible trans organisations, specialist services and legal-aid resources. Officials in police, health and lodging settings are likely less trained, and distance from Buenos Aires institutions lengthens any practical recourse. Provincial governance has been dominated by a single long-serving administration, and oversight of police and institutions is considered less independent than in the capital. For a trans visitor, the realistic exposure is therefore everyday friction rather than legal jeopardy: curiosity, social disapproval, misgendering, intrusive questioning and uneven official handling once identified, with thin and slow recourse if something goes wrong. Being outed in a rural or Chaco-area community carries more social cost than the legal rules would suggest, and the practical privacy that a larger city offers is limited here. Local police and service responses remain uncertain, and the absence of documented hostility should not be read as assurance: there has been no Formosa-specific study or pattern of targeting recorded either way.

19177384B99972609216724.name: La Pampa
19177384B99972609216724.summary: La Pampa is subject to Argentina's national gender-identity framework in full, with no local exception. It is a sparsely populated, largely agricultural province of dry pampas and small farming settlements, with Santa Rosa as its capital. No province-specific anti-discrimination ordinance, facility restriction or documented local hostility toward trans visitors is on record, nor is there a province-level protective enforcement machinery beyond the national framework; what distinguishes La Pampa is social and geographic rather than legal. A visibly trans visitor is conspicuous in Santa Rosa and especially in smaller towns, where provincial social conservatism, thinner institutional density and slow practical recourse shape everyday encounters. Trans-specific health and support services and community organisations are concentrated in the capital and scarce elsewhere, and police and service staff outside it are less trained in gender-identity procedures than their Buenos Aires counterparts. Provincial authorities have adopted a trans employment quota and maintain diversity offices, a sign of institutional commitment sitting alongside that conservatism. In practice, outing is more likely to bring friction than official action: intrusive questioning, misgendering or refusal of service in lodging, clinics or contacts with police remain possible, and remedies are slower to reach than in the capital. Identity documents are checked normally in ordinary travel institutions and discovery alone is not a crime, but a traveller should expect uneven understanding rather than consistent application of protections, with weak local anti-discrimination recourse and complaint handling that moves slowly. Risk here sits above provinces where presentation itself is criminalised and below more urban, institutionally responsive parts of Argentina.

19177384B7010788354129.name: Tierra del Fuego
19177384B7010788354129.summary: Tierra del Fuego is subject to Argentina's national law in full, with no local exception. The province has a distinctly rights-forward institutional record: it was the first Argentine province to allow a legal sex-marker change on identity documents before the national law took effect, and Ushuaia hosted the country's first same-sex wedding in 2010. Provincial public-sector inclusion measures are also cited locally as a positive social-climate signal. Ushuaia's cruise-and-tourism economy brings a steady flow of international visitors and a generally open public environment, with comparatively liberal local attitudes. Río Grande, more industrial and socially conventional, and the smaller remote settlements are less accustomed to visible difference, with thinner advocacy, legal-aid and hospital infrastructure. Distance is the practical constraint: a small police force, limited specialist medical services, and legal or consular support that is harder to reach quickly. Where a trans visitor is outed locally, the likely exposure is curiosity, administrative questioning and service friction, plus practical difficulty in detention, emergency care or continuity of care, rather than targeted state action; federal policy decisions apply regardless of local attitudes, and local authorities cannot by themselves offset them. No province-specific hostile enforcement, trans-specific targeting, border friction or facility restrictions are documented — but in a province this small and this far from major centres, an absence of reported incidents is not evidence of safety, and remedies are thinner than in Buenos Aires.

sources.summary: Case report (Association for Legal Intervention, 13 Mar 2024): a Polish regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman, on hormone therapy since 2018, in a guarded centre for male foreigners. The Border Guard refused to move or release her although Polish law bars placement where a stay would threaten life or health or where the person shows signs of having suffered violence. After the association applied to the Border Guard Post commander, she was released (page updated 28 Mar 2024). The case sets the framework applied to trans foreigners in Polish immigration detention and bears on any trans visitor detained in this voivodeship.

ECtHR ruling coverage (TGEU, 16 Jul 2024): on 11 Jul 2024 the European Court of Human Rights held that Polish prison authorities violated a trans woman's right to private and family life (Article 8 ECHR) by denying her hormone-replacement therapy in Siedlce prison, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages. The Court left the alleged breaches of Articles 3 and 14 undecided but held that the refusal had no reasonable legal grounds and was disproportionate. The judgment binds Poland and governs trans people's healthcare in Polish prisons and detention in every voivodeship, including this one.

17162690B77437931625010.name: Pomeranian Voivodeship
17162690B77437931625010.summary: Pomeranian Voivodeship is subject to Poland's national law in full, with no local exception. The voivodeship's Tricity — Gdańsk, Gdynia and Sopot — is a Baltic university and tourism centre and one of the country's most socially liberal, internationally exposed urban areas. Gdańsk hosts regular Equality Marches that have not drawn the large-scale counter-protest violence seen elsewhere in Poland, operates a municipal anti-discrimination resolution covering gender identity and sexual orientation, and the region has no anti-LGBT resolutions among the handful still in force nationally. The coastal tourism economy serves large numbers of foreign visitors, and Tricity policing, services, NGOs and administrative courts are comparatively cosmopolitan and used to rights claims, so a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor there has better odds of neutral, routine treatment than in most of the country. That local climate is social rather than legal: it does not change border, police or detention rules, and it stops largely at the Tricity. Rural and smaller-town Pomerania is more conservative and may produce staring, questioning or local hostility, and resort areas outside the main cities do not reliably carry the Tricity's atmosphere. Mismatched documents can still prompt secondary inspection at Gdańsk airport. No region-specific pattern of anti-trans enforcement, violence or official mistreatment has been documented in the voivodeship, and no local rules exclude trans visitors — but nor is there region-specific evidence on how trans travellers are treated at borders, in hospitals or in custody, so the absence of documented local harm should not be read as a guarantee.

17162690B34878575347312.name: West Pomeranian Voivodeship
17162690B34878575347312.summary: West Pomeranian Voivodeship is subject to Poland's national law in full, with no local legal exception. What distinguishes the region is its social geography. Szczecin is a mid-sized western university and port city with a visible LGBTQ civic presence, recurring equality marches and a comparatively secular, outward-facing culture; the voivodeship is not among the areas where county- or commune-level anti-LGBT resolutions and Family Rights Charters are known to remain in force, and administrative-court practice against such acts has been locally supportive. The Baltic coast around Świnoujście and Kołobrzeg is tourist-facing and generally accustomed to visitors. Against this, smaller towns and rural parts of the province remain more conservative, and public attitudes are more mixed away from Szczecin and the main coastal resorts. Practically, local services and transport behave ordinarily, and there is no known West Pomeranian visitor-facing trans restriction or documented pattern of official targeting — though local violence and harassment rates are not established, so the absence of recorded incidents should not be read as a guarantee. Discovery at borders, hotels or during document checks can still prompt bureaucratic questions and awkward or hostile reactions; these encounters follow national procedures rather than any local rule. Risk is more a matter of setting than of law: tolerance is variable in conservative venues and late-night settings, while the everyday environment in Szczecin and the coastal resorts is modestly more accommodating than in Poland's deep conservative regions. Any hostility or bureaucratic difficulty a trans visitor meets here reflects national conditions, locally softened rather than replaced.

17162690B16879770934003.name: Silesian Voivodeship
17162690B16879770934003.summary: The region is subject to Polish national law in full, with no separate Silesian regime for trans visitors. Locally, the dense Katowice conurbation — a highly urbanised, university- and business-facing conurbation with transport hubs, a long multicultural and secular tradition, recurring equality marches and visible LGBT civil society — is comparatively socially liberal and anonymous, which reduces everyday scrutiny and tends to produce more ordinary police responses. Katowice and Bielsko-Biała have visible queer organising and tourism life. Conditions shift sharply outside it: smaller towns, mining communities, rural communes and the Beskid districts remain more strongly Catholic and conservative, and some Silesian municipalities have kept family-rights declarations or anti-LGBT statements in force, so gender-nonconforming visitors may meet harsher reactions there. No Silesian rule or documented local pattern of police targeting, detention practice or enforcement distinguishes the region from the national picture; remedies remain the national ones. For a trans visitor whose status becomes known, the locally reported harms are misgendering, refusal of service, bureaucratic friction and public harassment; serious violence is possible but is not a documented regional campaign. Local tolerance is best described as moderate rather than protective, and equality marches and community organisations exist as infrastructure rather than as a guarantee of acceptance or of effective protection.

27671186B81745654473385.name: Cross River
27671186B81745654473385.summary:
Cross River stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 and the Criminal Code apply within the state as they do nationwide, and Cross River is not among the twelve northern states where Shari'a provisions carry a death-penalty maximum for same-sex conduct (Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara).

A trans visitor to Cross River therefore does not face the capital exposure available in those twelve states. The offences, penalties and enforcement risk that apply are those of the national statutes.

sources.summary: Report (August 2026) on the latest UK travel advice for this country: warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation; up to 14 years for same-sex sexual activity; some northern states' religious law can prescribe the death penalty; the 2014 Act also punishes assisting, attending or promoting same-sex relationships and LGBTQ+ organisations; separately warns of short-notice curfews and vehicle-movement restrictions, mobile-network shutdowns with little notice, and political rallies and communal violence.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria — Wikipedia
sources.summary: Cross River falls under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 makes same-sex marriage or civil union, and registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or publicly showing same-sex affection, punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment nationwide. The Criminal Code separately criminalises sex between men (14 years) and gross indecency between men (3 years). The twelve northern states under Shari'a law carry up to a death-penalty maximum: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. Cross River is not among them. The source documents the nationwide 'kito' entrapment-and-blackmail scheme targeting gay men and trans women, police profiling and extortion of people perceived as gay, and mass arrests (42 men in Lagos, August 2017; 53 charged in Kaduna, April 2017; 100+ detained after a Delta hotel raid, June 2018; 67 in Warri, August 2023; 76 in Gombe, October 2023). No anti-discrimination protections exist for LGBTQ people.

sources.title: "Everyone's on the Game": Corruption and Human Rights Abuses by the Nigeria Police Force (Human Rights Watch)
sources.summary: Human Rights Watch's 17 August 2010 report on the Nigeria Police Force documents arbitrary arrests, mass 'raid' arrests, prolonged unlawful detention used as a 'cash cow', and extortion using threats and acts of physical abuse, with bribery the standard price of release. 27671186B56513237316251.name: Oyo
27671186B56513237316251.summary:
Oyo stands under Nigeria's national framework, including the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, which applies in the state as it does elsewhere in the country.

Oyo is a southern state outside the Shari'a regime. The death-penalty exposure for male same-sex conduct that applies in twelve northern states does not reach Oyo. The criminal code in force in the state is the Criminal Code, which criminalises sex between men with up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency with up to 3 years.

No anti-discrimination protection exists for LGBTI people in Oyo.

Dating applications carry an entrapment risk that is not confined to any one city. Criminal gangs pose as potential dates on popular apps, lure men to meetings, film them and then extort, beat or kidnap them; one investigative report interviewed 21 people about being targeted this way. The documented cases and the underground scene described are based in Lagos, and the sources extend the same risk to gay and transgender app users in Oyo. Victims seldom report to the police, because making a report carries its own risk of arrest or assault.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria — Wikipedia
sources.summary: Oyo is a southern state outside the Shari'a regime. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 punishes same-sex marriage or civil union, and the registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or public show of same-sex affection, with up to 14 years' imprisonment. The Criminal Code criminalises sex between men (up to 14 years) and gross indecency (up to 3 years). Twelve states apply Shari'a law: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara, where male same-sex conduct carries a maximum of death. Police profile, entrap and extort people perceived as gay ('kito'), and mass arrests recur: 42 men arrested in Lagos in August 2017, 53 charged in Kaduna in April 2017, more than 100 detained after a Delta hotel raid in June 2018, 67 in Warri and 76 in Gombe in 2023. No anti-discrimination protections exist. The 2014 statute reaches LGBTI organisations, and LGBTI people face arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation under a framework that applies in full to Oyo.
