sources.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's overview of LGBT rights in Nigeria records that same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across the country since 1916. The Same Sex Marriage Prohibition Act was passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014. It criminalises all forms of same-sex unions and renders any marriage or civil union entered into between persons of the same sex invalid and void. The maximum penalty under federal law is up to 14 years' imprisonment, with the death penalty confined to the twelve northern states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes. In the southern portion of the country, which includes Akwa Ibom, the maximum punishment for same-sex sexual activity is 14 years' imprisonment. The page also records no legal recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protections and no recognition of same-sex relationships.

sources.summary: The UK Home Office's June 2025 country policy and information note on Nigeria documents the national criminal framework on sexual orientation and gender identity that applies across all states, including the 2014 statute punishing same-sex unions, and records countrywide harm patterns of arrests, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people. The twelve northern states' Shari'a penal codes remain in force, with penalties for same-sex conduct ranging from lashes or caning up to death by stoning. A Shari'a court in Bauchi sentenced three men to death by stoning in 2022, a sentence that could not be carried out until ratified by the state governor. A further death-by-stoning sentence was reported from Bauchi in May 2024, and in January 2014 a mob stormed a Bauchi court demanding death during a sodomy trial. The death-penalty risk layer is confined to the northern Shari'a states and does not extend to southern states such as Akwa Ibom, which stands under the secular national framework of up to 14 years' imprisonment. No state-specific enforcement divergence is documented.

27671186B47021609715037.name: Bayelsa
27671186B47021609715037.summary:
Bayelsa State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 was passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014. It criminalises all forms of same-sex unions and renders any marriage or civil union entered into between persons of the same sex invalid and void. Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across Nigeria since 1916.

The maximum penalty a visitor faces in Bayelsa is 14 years' imprisonment. That is the ceiling in the southern portion of the country, which includes Bayelsa, and it covers same-sex sexual activity and same-sex unions alike under the 2014 statute.

The death penalty does not reach Bayelsa. It is confined to the twelve northern states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes, where penalties for same-sex conduct run from lashes or caning up to death by stoning; those provisions have no application in Bayelsa, which stands under the secular national 14-year framework.

The framework governing Bayelsa recognises no gender identity, provides no anti-discrimination protections and recognises no same-sex relationships. A trans visitor therefore has no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation in the state, and any union they enter is void under the 2014 Act.

No state-specific enforcement divergence is documented for Bayelsa. The UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 records countrywide harm patterns of arrests, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people across all states, including the 2014 statute's reach, without identifying any Bayelsa-specific arrest, prosecution or incident.

27671186B41407594687181.name: Ondo
27671186B41407594687181.summary:
Ondo is a state in south-western Nigeria and stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 and the secular criminal provisions covering same-sex conduct extend to Ondo in full. The sources record no Ondo statute, protective measure or enforcement divergence of the state's own, and Wikipedia's overview of LGBT rights in Nigeria does not name Ondo at all.

The Shari'a penalty layer does not reach Ondo. The twelve northern states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes, where male sodomy can carry death by stoning, are separate jurisdictions; as a southern state Ondo stands under the secular framework, where the maximum penalty recorded is a life sentence.

Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across the country since 1916. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act was passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, criminalising all forms of same-sex unions with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 quotes Section 217 of the Criminal Code, under which any male who commits or procures an act of gross indecency with another male, in public or in private, is guilty of a felony liable to three years' imprisonment. That offence applies in southern states such as Ondo. Victor Oluwasina Ayeni, senior lecturer in law at Adekunle Ajasin University in Ondo state, observed in a January 2017 book chapter that the Code fails to define what constitutes an act of gross indecency.

The same Home Office note documents the national criminal framework applying across all states, including the 2014 statute, and records countrywide harm patterns of arrests, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people. It confirms that the twelve northern states' Shari'a penal codes, with penalties up to death by stoning, remain in force, so that penalty layer does not extend to Ondo.

Wikipedia records no legal recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protections and no recognition of same-sex relationships anywhere in the country, and Ondo supplies none of these itself.

27671186B69086015704361.name: Delta
27671186B69086015704361.summary:
Delta State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies in the state, as does section 217 of the Criminal Code, which makes male gross indecency a felony carrying three years' imprisonment; the maximum exposure under the 2014 Act is 14 years' imprisonment. Delta has enacted no protective statute of its own. The death penalty attached to same-sex conduct under Shari'a provisions operates only in the twelve northern states and has no application in Delta.

Enforcement in Delta has taken the form of raids on private hotel gatherings. In June 2018 police in Asaba arrested more than 100 people attending a party at a hotel on charges that they were gay and lesbian, and by July 2018 the group was facing homosexuality-related charges in court.

The Warri raid of 27 August 2023 is the most detailed Delta incident in this inventory. At around 9 pm, officers from the Ekpan Division of the Delta State Police Command raided Teebolus Hotel on Refinery Road, Ekpan, in Uvwie Local Government Area and arrested 67 people at what police described as a same-sex wedding between a 22-year-old groom and a 20-year-old bride. The command spokesman, DSP Bright Edafe, said the operation followed a confession by a male cross-dresser that he belonged to a gay club travelling to a marriage ceremony, that the suspects fled on the officers' arrival, that 67 were chased and arrested, and that drugs and 'gay marriage ceremonial dresses' were recovered. The 67, publicly known as the 'Warri 67', were charged to court, and the spokesman said efforts continued to arrest those who fled.

Accounts of that night differ. The USSD 2023 human rights report records that police raided a 'white party' organised by the LGBTQI+ community in Delta State on 27 August 2023 and detained more than 200 individuals, that police alleged the event was a same-sex wedding, and that some civil society representatives disputed that description. 27671186B95832466049157.summary:
Rivers State has no statute, policy or enforcement practice of its own on same-sex conduct or gender expression in the sources reviewed. The state stands under Nigeria's national framework, which applies nationwide; its provisions and penalties are set out in the national assessment. The layer that varies by geography is the criminal code in force across southern Nigeria, and it applies in Rivers: sex between men carries up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency up to 3 years. Rivers is not among the northern states where Sharia provisions apply, so the death-penalty exposure those states attach to same-sex conduct does not arise for a visitor to Port Harcourt or elsewhere in the state.

The sources place one documented incident inside Rivers. In January 2015 a 21-year-old man from Lagos travelled to Port Harcourt to meet a person he had contacted on Facebook and was attacked and sexually abused there. He did not report the attack to the police. The sources record no arrest, charge or official response in connection with it.

Beyond that case, the sources identify no Rivers prosecution, arrest, police operation or state-government statement on same-sex conduct or gender expression, and no enforcement pattern specific to the state. No Rivers institution appears in the sources as either hostile or protective, and no trans-specific incident, facility rule or care restriction particular to Rivers is recorded.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria - Wikipedia
sources.summary: The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, signed by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, makes same-sex marriage and civil unions invalid and illegal and criminalises registering, operating or supporting gay organisations. The Nigerian Criminal Code in the south criminalises sex between men with penalties up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency up to 3 years. In 2022 a group of Nigerian human rights organisations and activists sued over Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Act, and the court ruled them unconstitutional and unenforceable nationwide, removing those provisions as a basis for prosecuting LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals. No legal protections exist for LGBTQ people, and sharia-based states apply penalties from lashing up to death. None of these provisions names Rivers or Port Harcourt; the federal framework applies nationwide and covers a visitor to Rivers State.

sources.title: Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe: The Impact of Nigeria's Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act | Human Rights Watch
sources.summary: Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report on the SSMPA, passed in January 2014, records that the law imposes 10 to 14 years' imprisonment on anyone who registers, operates, participates in or supports gay clubs, societies or organisations, and bans same-sex cohabitation and any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship. It documents that arbitrary arrest and extortion by police became commonplace after the Act, including eight of the 21 young men arrested, but never charged, at a birthday party in Ibadan. It also records the case of Daniel, a 21-year-old gay man from Lagos who in January 2015 travelled to Port Harcourt to meet someone he had contacted on Facebook and was attacked and sexually abused there, saying he did not report it to the police. The Port Harcourt incident and the nationwide abuse pattern substantiate the enforcement climate a same-sex couple or trans visitor faces in Rivers.

27671186B96047513549152.name: Kogi
27671186B96047513549152.summary:
Kogi State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2013 and the Criminal Code provisions on sexual conduct apply in full on its territory, and the ceiling on a visitor's exposure is the national 14-year maximum rather than any Kogi-specific statute.

Kogi is not one of the twelve Nigerian states that administer Shari'a criminal law. The death-penalty Zina provisions applied to same-sex acts in Kano and Katsina do not operate here, so the exposure in Kogi is imprisonment under secular provisions, not corporal or capital punishment.

The 2013 act, passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, makes entering a same-sex marriage or civil union liable to 14 years' imprisonment, and makes registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or making a public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, liable to 10 years. The Criminal Code separately criminalises sex between men with up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency with up to 3 years.

In 2022 a coalition of Nigerian human rights organisations won a court ruling that Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 act breached the Constitution and could not be enforced anywhere in the country. Those provisions therefore do not operate in Kogi either, and the ruling effectively allows LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals to exist and organise there. The same source records no comparable ruling for the conduct provisions or the marriage-prohibition provisions, which remain the operative exposure in Kogi.

BBC News reported on 9 August 2024 that mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people take place across Nigeria, including in Kogi, and are especially frequent in northern states.

Mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common across Nigeria, including in Kogi, and are especially frequent in northern states.

Plateau State is not recorded as showing the concentration of arrests and communal tension attributed to the North Central zone.

Nigeria has no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and violence against them is documented as frequent.

27671186B76680224160916.name: Anambra

Anambra is a state in south-eastern Nigeria, capital Awka, formed in 1976 and Igbo-majority in population. It sits outside the twelve northern Nigerian states that apply Shari'a criminal law, so the death-penalty provisions those states provide for male sodomy do not reach Anambra; the federal statutory penalties apply here in full.

Same-sex sexual activity in Anambra carries the secular statutory maximum of up to 14 years' imprisonment under Nigeria's national framework, which governs the state. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act extends criminalisation to attempted same-sex marriages.

LGBTQ+ people in Anambra have no legal protections under Nigerian law and face violence; the national record documents police torture, arbitrary arrests, mass arrests at private gatherings and hotels, and unprosecuted killings of transgender women.

27671186B37873222803025.name: Osun
27671186B37873222803025.summary:
No Osun-specific law, enforcement action, incident or institution appears in the source inventory. The one sub-national distinction the material draws is jurisdictional: the death-penalty exposure that foreign travel advice attaches to Sharia penal codes applies to the twelve northern states and not to Osun, which is not among them. The federal penalties and the arrest, blackmail and intimidation warnings in that advice apply in Osun in full. What a trans visitor should expect in the state is therefore set by Nigeria's national framework rather than by anything specific to Osun.

UK Foreign Office travel advice dated 19 August 2026 warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, stating that same-sex sexual activity is illegal and can attract up to 14 years' imprisonment, with the law also reaching wedding arrangers and organisers and anyone involved with gay groups. The advisory's Sharia death-penalty warning applies only to northern states and does not apply in Osun; the imprisonment exposure and the warnings about arrest and blackmail apply in Osun in full.

BBC reporting of 9 August 2024 on the killing of the 33-year-old Nigerian transgender TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama records that her beaten body was found on the Katampe–Mabushi expressway in Abuja, roughly a year after she had said she feared for her life, and that an investigation was announced. The same report notes that despite constitutional guarantees of non-discrimination and private and family life, mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common, especially in northern states. This is national-climate evidence bearing on Osun.

27671186B90910891533368.name: Enugu
27671186B90910891533368.summary:
Enugu State stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies in full across the state. Enugu-specific documentation comes from Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report, which records the statute's effects through testimony gathered in the state.

An Enugu-based activist told Human Rights Watch that there are no clinics in Enugu State where gay men and men who have sex with men can obtain services without fear of harassment. For a trans visitor who needs medical care while in the state, that leaves no documented service point where disclosure of gender or sexual identity is not itself a risk.

Human Rights Watch also records the account of Sharon, a bisexual woman from Enugu State, who married a male friend from high school in July 2015 under family and social pressure and said, "For as long as I am in Nigeria, I will stay married." The account documents the law operating as social pressure toward heterosexual marriage in the state.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Indonesia – Wikipedia
sources.summary: The national-framework article on LGBTQ rights in Indonesia, which applies throughout the country including this province, records that since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach issuing transgender Indonesians identification papers (KTP), with only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors recognised and birth-gender printed unless a court order was already obtained, and that electronic ID cards were issued to transgender people in nine provinces. It records that the 2022 penal-code amendment criminalising sexual activity outside marriage is set to take effect on 2 January 2026, with unmarried partners facing up to one year in prison, and that because same-sex marriage is not legally recognised, all sexual activity between same-sex couples falls under that outside-marriage restriction. It further notes that transgender identity (waria) has long been part of Indonesian culture, alongside documented repressive incidents including raids on transgender women by the Jakarta Social Agency and the January 2021 flogging of two men in Aceh province (BBC/Reuters). A visitor in this province therefore stands under Indonesia's national position: no criminalisation of gender identity itself, no X-marker, and no legal recognition of same-sex marriage.

The article notes that the code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex relationships, but because Indonesia does not recognise same-sex marriage, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls within the outside-marriage restriction. It also records international criticism, including from the United Nations, for failing to accommodate protections and rights for LGBT individuals and domestic partnerships. This national statutory framework, effective from 2 January 2026, governs a visitor in this province.

65028918B10722647473585.name: Bangka-Belitung Islands
65028918B10722647473585.summary:
Bangka-Belitung Islands stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is assessed as a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to one year's imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The provision applies in Bangka-Belitung Islands as throughout Indonesia.

No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and Indonesia has no anti-discrimination or hate-crime provisions for LGBT people. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are unrecognised, so no same-sex relationship carries legal recognition anywhere in the country.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, a process that shapes what documents a trans visitor or resident can present at airports, hotels and police checks.

Physical risk is rising across Indonesia. Reporting by The Diplomat in August 2026 describes a transgender community facing growing repression, with vigilante mobs attacking trans people as the government moves to codify anti-LGBT provisions. Reporting in the same period ties the surge in attacks to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism, placing them inside national defence policy.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; in Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. A visitor travelling onward from Bangka-Belitung Islands to either province carries the national exposure plus that provincial layer.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Social and institutional hostility is documented at national level. A 2025 Pew figure found 93% of Indonesians rating homosexuality 'morally unacceptable'. The Constitutional Court rejected a petition to criminalise gay sex on 14 December 2017 by 5-4, and Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025. No deviation from this national position has been documented in Bangka-Belitung Islands.

15666254B97003483933575.name: Kuala Lumpur
15666254B97003483933575.summary:
Kuala Lumpur is a federal territory of Malaysia. It stands under the national framework: Malaysia's Penal Code applies directly in the territory, with Sections 377A and 377B punishing "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" by up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping and Section 377D covering "gross indecency" with up to two years, and the Federal Territories Sharia criminal enactment operates alongside it. The Sharia offences bind Muslims only; non-Muslim visitors are exposed to the Penal Code alone.

Enforcement in Kuala Lumpur is carried out jointly. On 28 November 2025 an operation by the Kuala Lumpur police, Kuala Lumpur City Hall and the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) arrested over 200 people at an all-male health centre in the territory. The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Malaysia, last updated 16 December 2025, records that enforcement since the 2018 election has included arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment, and that the Federal Court has struck down some state Sharia criminal-code provisions as beyond state power.

Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters, reporting on 10 August 2022, interviewed 73 LGBT people between 2018 and 2021, including people living in Kuala Lumpur, and documented state-sponsored discrimination against them. The report states that each state and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintain Sharia codes that typically criminalise same-sex conduct, quotes a Kuala Lumpur activist describing regression as a conservative strand of Islam gains ground, and calls on lawmakers to decriminalise same-sex conduct and gender diversity. The sample was LGBT people broadly rather than trans people specifically, and the interview window closed in 2021.

15666254B60207109163985.name: Negeri Sembilan
15666254B60207109163985.summary:
Negeri Sembilan stands under the national framework of Malaysia, which carries the federal Penal Code offences, the identity-document rules and the entry position; those apply here as they do nationwide and are set out in the national record. The state's own layer is its Sharia criminal law.

In November 2014 the Court of Appeal declared section 66 of the Syariah Criminal Enactment 1992 (Negeri Sembilan), which criminalised cross-dressing, unconstitutional for breaching rights guaranteed by the Federal Constitution. The Federal Court has more recently struck down Sharia criminal-code provisions in Selangor and Kelantan on the ground that state legislatures lack criminal-law power; those rulings concern other states, not Negeri Sembilan's section 66.

Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters, reporting on 10 August 2022, documented state-sponsored discrimination and criminalisation of LGBT people in Malaysia through interviews with 73 people conducted between 2018 and 2021, including people living in Negeri Sembilan. The report states that every state and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintain Sharia codes that typically criminalise same-sex conduct, and calls on lawmakers to decriminalise same-sex conduct and gender diversity and to abandon 'rehabilitation' programs and rhetoric.

Enforcement against trans and gender-nonconforming people in Negeri Sembilan is carried out by the state Islamic religious department under Sharia provisions that apply to Muslims. The Human Dignity Trust profile of Malaysia, last updated 16 December 2025, records a national crackdown involving arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment since the 2018 election, alongside the persistence of federal criminalisation under Sections 377A and 377B of the Penal Code 1936, which carry up to 20 years' imprisonment with whipping.

28173009B80457268982215.name: Altai Krai
28173009B80457268982215.summary:
No law, enforcement action or incident specific to Altai Krai appears in the sources. The national framework of Russia applies in full, and the national assessment of risk to a trans visitor carries over to this region without regional deviation.

No case under the propaganda statutes or the extremism provisions is documented in Altai Krai. The sources covering the region, among them the US State Department travel advisory and the UK Home Office country policy and information note, are national in scope and do not disaggregate enforcement by region.

sources.summary: UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity (June 2025, assessment updated 11 Jun 2025): same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited, trans people cannot adopt or foster, trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, and no legislation prohibits SOGI-based discrimination in housing, healthcare or employment. Publicly 'promoting' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is an administrative offence (fines or detention up to 15 days; repeat offences can become criminal, up to 4 years), the 2023 'extremist' designation of the international LGBT+ movement criminalises support/activity, and at least 139 people were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws 2022-2024. Assesses LGB people generally face no real risk of state persecution on orientation alone, except in the North Caucasus — a zone that does not include Altai Krai; this is the national baseline the record stands assessed at.

US State Department travel advisory for Russia, which covers Altai Krai: foreigners found guilty of violating the 'propaganda' law may be arrested and detained for up to 15 days and then deported, displaying certain symbols including the rainbow flag is a crime, and the advisory advises against all travel to Russia.

Human Rights Watch (30 Jun 2025): Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions over alleged participation in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols, about 98 of them administrative. Since January 2024, 81 people in 98 court cases were found guilty of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying symbols such as the rainbow flag. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges for alleged participation; one died by suicide in pretrial detention, two were sentenced to prison, and 17 cases remain pending or unknown. On 15 May 2025, investigators charged three staff of two publishing houses under article 282.2 with running an 'extremist organisation' over selling fiction exploring LGBT themes; they face up to 12 years in prison. These national figures apply equally in Altai Krai, where no specific case is documented.

28173009B92397886288731.name: Sverdlovsk Oblast
28173009B92397886288731.summary:
Sverdlovsk Oblast has no legislation of its own on gender identity or sexual orientation and stands under the national framework of Russia, which applies in full; the oblast administration has added no protections of its own. What is documented at regional level is enforcement pressure and violence in Yekaterinburg, the oblast capital.

Reporting dated 21 October 2024 records that a gay man in Yekaterinburg was beaten and robbed after being lured into a fake date, and that a Yekaterinburg LGBTQ+ support group shut down after pressure. Together they show targeting in the oblast operating through private violence and through pressure on the organisations that would otherwise provide support.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Khakassia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender, and gender-affirming care is banned. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition which prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, after April-May 2023 proposals to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents and to ban reassignment without surgery. The propaganda law as expanded in 2022 applies to anyone regardless of age group and prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and single-person foreign adoption is allowed only where the country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor allows gender transition. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on gender identity. In a 30 September 2022 speech President Putin said teaching children about other genders and offering sex-change surgeries is unacceptable, linking opposition to transgender rights to willingness to use all means against Ukraine. Officials cited protection of family values and draft evasion, claiming about 2,700 recent legal-gender changes and that many young men turned to private clinics for sex change to avoid conscription in connection with the special operation. Consensual sexual activity between adults of the same sex is legal after 1993 re-legalisation removing Article 121 from the RSFSR Penal Code, which had punished consensual sex between men with three to five years imprisonment under Article 154-a and later Article 121, with age of consent at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, with a July 2020 constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage, and same-sex couples are ineligible for legal protections available to opposite-sex couples with no legal recognition offered despite the 2021 Fedotova and Others v. Russia ruling. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation, and refuses to register LGBTQ organisations. A 2013 federal law criminalised distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors, expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age group. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols a criminal offense punishable by prison time. Enforcement includes arrests of gay bar owners, fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag, a 2010 European Court of Human Rights fine for systemic refusal of pride parade permits and an August 2012 Moscow City Court decision upholding a ban on Moscow Pride through 2012, and Chechnya detentions, torture and killings targeting persons based on perceived sexual orientation since February 2017 with over 100 men detained and OSCE confirmation in December 2018. Adoption is limited domestically to single persons regardless of sexual orientation and jointly only to married heterosexual couples, with foreign single-person adoption barred where the country recognises same-sex marriage.

28173009B68474107072963.name: Astrakhan Oblast
28173009B68474107072963.summary:
Astrakhan Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, which applies in full across all the country's regions. Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the position has hardened since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" statute criminalises public expression that, explicitly, "justifies" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and national government warnings state this directly to LGBT travellers.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025, assessment section updated 11 June 2025) records that same-sex activity is not criminalised in Russia, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. No discrimination legislation based on sexual orientation or gender identity covers housing, healthcare or employment.

Penalties applicable in Astrakhan Oblast are substantial. 'Gay propaganda' offences carry fines up to 400,000 roubles (about £3,600) for individuals or up to 15 days' detention, and repeat offences can bring criminal prosecution with up to four years in prison. The November 2023 Supreme Court 'extremist' designation of the international LGBT+ movement makes participation punishable by two to six years and organising by six to ten years.

Enforcement volume is documented. Between December 2022 and March 2024 at least 139 people were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions tied to the International Public LGBT Movement designation, approximately 98 administrative and three criminal. The Home Office assessment finds that trans people, publicly active LGBT+ advocates and those in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, and affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.

Two foreign-government advisories bear on visitor exposure. The US State Department rates Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers, and states that official support is 'very limited' in parts of the country.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Mari El (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender, and gender-affirming care is banned. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition which prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, following April-May 2023 State Duma proposals to prevent trans women from changing legal gender from male to female without surgery and to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents. The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law applies to anyone regardless of age group and prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and foreign single-person adoption is permitted only where the country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. The article links legal gender change to conscription avoidance, stating that many young men have turned to private clinics to provide a sex change to avoid conscription in connection with the special operation and that Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin claimed 2,700 such decisions in recent times. On 30 September 2022 President Putin stated "Do we want them to be taught that instead of men and women, there are supposedly some other genders and to be offered sex-change surgeries? This is unacceptable to us." while invoking transgender rights in justification for action against Ukraine and willingness to use all means at disposal. Consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is legal after re-legalisation in 1993 removing Article 121, which had previously punished consensual sex between men with three to five years imprisonment under 1934 Article 154-a and up to five years under 1961 Article 121, with age of consent at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, voters approved a constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage in July 2020, no legal recognition is offered despite the 2021 Fedotova and Others v. Russia ruling finding a human rights violation, and only married heterosexual couples may adopt jointly though single persons regardless of sexual orientation may adopt domestically. The 2013 federal law criminalised distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors and was expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols a criminal offense punishable by prison time. Enforcement includes arrests of gay bar owners, fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag including earrings, at least one death in custody as of April 2025, and between March and May 2026 city courts outlawing nine organisations including Centre T, Coming Out, Russian LGBT Network and others with convictions of founders for leading an extremist organisation. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation and gender identity and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community, with estimates of 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 with 365 fatalities, annual crimes tripling from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015, and group-organised hunting via dating apps including Occupy Pedophilia active in 40 regions. In Chechnya, authorities targeted persons based on perceived sexual orientation with forced disappearances, secret abductions, imprisonment, torture and extrajudicial killing, with over 100 men detained and tortured and at least three dead from February 2017 and around 40 detained and two killed from December 2018, confirmed by a December 2018 OSCE report and followed by March 2021 EU sanctions on two officials.

28173009B3082792446388.name: Nenets Autonomous Okrug
28173009B3082792446388.summary: Nenets Autonomous Okrug is subject to Russia's national regime in full, with no local exception. The okrug is a sparsely populated Arctic district of roughly 44,000 people centred on Naryan-Mar, reachable mainly by air, with oil and gas settlements and traditional Nenets hunting and reindeer-herding communities scattered across a vast territory. It has no LGBTQ venues, no community organisations and no trans-specific legal aid, and local healthcare and police services are limited. Social attitudes in these small, close-knit communities are conservative, and a visibly transgender outsider stands out sharply: small settlements reduce anonymity rather than provide it, and unlike Moscow or St. Petersburg there is no urban crowd to disappear into. Federal police and courts operate directly in the okrug, so local discovery routes into national enforcement with no local mitigation. No documented local protection, sanctuary or complaint mechanism is available, and remote placement offers no independent remedy — expect the national picture to apply here unchanged, with less community support and fewer routes to help if something goes wrong.

28173009B27844369294009.name: Novosibirsk Oblast
28173009B27844369294009.summary:
Novosibirsk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia. The federal ban on legal gender recognition, the expanded propaganda statutes and the November 2023 extremism designation of the "international LGBT movement" are carried by the national record; what follows is what is documented in the oblast itself.

A court in Novosibirsk fined the Elton John Bar 500,000 rubles (about £4,598) for "promoting LGBTI propaganda" through a rainbow flag. The case followed the venue's appearance in a video by the LGBT+ activist blogger Karen Shainyan. The fine shows the propaganda statutes reaching a commercial venue in the oblast, a step beyond enforcement against individuals posting online.

Coercive conversion practice has been documented in the oblast. A transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a centre near Novosibirsk and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour. She escaped only after police responded to a phone she had found.

A priest in a village in the Novosibirsk region told The Moscow Times that religion can correct "deviations", indicating that local religious authority frames gender variance as a defect to be corrected.

Human Rights Watch's tally of 101 extremism-related convictions nationally since the November 2023 designation records no case specific to Novosibirsk Oblast. The absence of a documented oblast case does not establish that none has been brought.

sources.title: Vitaly Milonov - Wikipedia

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Russia - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's country overview of LGBTQ rights in Russia supplies the federal framework Saint Petersburg is assessed under: a 2013 law criminalises distributing 'propaganda' of 'non-traditional sexual relationships' among minors, with fines up to 5,000 roubles for citizens, 50,000 for officials, and 1 million roubles plus up to 90 days' suspension for organisations, while foreigners face up to 15 days' detention, a fine up to 100,000 roubles and deportation. sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Sakha Republic (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender and gender-affirming care is banned. In 2022 the 'propaganda' law was expanded to apply to anyone regardless of age group and to prohibit distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition which prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, following April-May 2023 State Duma proposals to 'rule out the possibility of changing a person's gender purely by changing the documents' and to ban reassignment without surgery on 'family values' grounds. In 2024 Russia passed a law banning adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions; inside Russia single persons regardless of sexual orientation can adopt but a couple can adopt jointly only if a married heterosexual couple, and a foreign single adopter must live in a country that neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. In the draft-evasion context, authorities claimed many young men turned to private clinics for sex change to avoid conscription in connection with the special operation, with the Duma Speaker claiming some '2,700' such decisions, and Russian men were described as considering changing legal gender to avoid being drafted. On 30 September 2022 President Vladimir Putin said teaching children that 'instead of men and women, there are supposedly some other genders and to be offered sex-change surgeries' is 'unacceptable to us' while stating Russia would use 'all means at our disposal' against Ukraine. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on gender identity, and authorities refuse to register LGBTQ organisations while pro-LGBTQ advocacy groups have been declared extremist and prohibited from operating. Consensual sexual activity between adults of the same sex is legal after re-legalisation in 1993 removing Article 121, which under Stalin from March 1934 as Article 154-a and from 1961 as Article 121 punished consensual sex between men with three to five years' imprisonment with a maximum of five years, with an estimated 800 to 1000 men imprisoned per year in the Soviet era; the age of consent is 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation, and homosexuality was removed from the mental-illness list in 1999 with ICD-10 but new laws on 1 July 2023 effectively reinstated classification as mental illness. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, the 2020 constitutional amendment bans same-sex marriage, marriage is defined as between a man and a woman, same-sex couples are ineligible for legal protections available to opposite-sex couples, and Russia did not implement the 2021 European Court of Human Rights Fedotova ruling requiring legal recognition after leaving the court in 2022. The 2013 federal law criminalised distribution of 'propaganda' promoting 'non-traditional sexual relationships' among minors and was expanded in 2022 to anyone regardless of age; in November 2023 the Supreme Court designated 'the international LGBT public movement' as extremist, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations, where leading, participating in, financially supporting or repeatedly displaying symbols is a criminal offense punishable by prison time, leading to arrests of gay bar owners with at least one dying in custody as of April 2025 and fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag including earrings. Enforcement includes refusal to register LGBTQ organisations, prohibition of advocacy groups as extremist and 'foreign agents,' systemic refusal of pride parade permits with Moscow never approving a request and Moscow City Court upholding a yearly ban through 2012 despite a 2010 European Court fine for discrimination, and Defence Ministry guidance recommending asking recruits about sexual history and examining genital or buttocks tattoos allegedly indicating homosexual orientation while openly gay men are formally not excluded from service but warned not to reveal orientation to avoid beating. Violence and custody include Chechen forced disappearances, secret abductions, imprisonment, torture and extrajudicial killings targeting perceived sexual orientation, with over 100 men detained and tortured since February 2017 and at least three dead, a December 2018 OSCE report confirming persecution ignored by authorities, another purge from December 2018 with around 40 detained and two killed, and March 2021 EU economic sanctions on two Chechen officials; nationally the government does not officially record hate crimes, with an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 including 365 fatalities, annual crimes tripling from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015, increased premeditated group attacks in 2017-2019 using dating apps to 'hunt' homosexuals, and 205 cases by homophobic hate groups including Occupy Pedophilia active in 40 regions. Protection machinery is absent with no anti-discrimination protections based on sexual orientation and no hate-crime designation, illustrated by the January 2013 firing of television anchor Anton Krasovsky after announcing he was gay and the September 2013 firing of Khabarovsk teacher Alexander Yermoshkin after attack by neo-Nazi group 'Shtolz Khabarovsk' amid a campaign by 'Movement against the propaganda of sexual perversions.'

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Tuva (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender, and gender-affirming care is banned. In 2022 the propaganda law was expanded to apply to anyone regardless of age group and to prohibit distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. In April and May 2023 the State Duma considered laws to prevent trans women from changing legal gender from male to female without surgery to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents, amid claims that men sought gender change to avoid conscription with Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin citing 2,700 such decisions. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition which prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright. In 2024 Russia passed a law banning adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and single persons living abroad may adopt Russian children only if that country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. On 30 September 2022 President Vladimir Putin said teaching children that instead of men and women there are supposedly other genders and offering sex-change surgeries is unacceptable to Russia. Consensual sexual activity between adults of the same sex is legal after re-legalisation in 1993 removing Article 121 from the RSFSR Penal Code, which had punished consensual sex between men with three to five years imprisonment under Article 154-a from 1934 and Article 121 from 1961 with an estimated 800 to 1000 men imprisoned per year, with age of consent at 16 since 2003 regardless of orientation and homosexuality removed from mental illness list in 1999 under ICD-10 though new laws on 1 July 2023 effectively reinstated the classification. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, with a July 2020 constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage, same-sex couples ineligible for protections available to opposite-sex couples, couples allowed to adopt only if married heterosexual, and no anti-discrimination protections or hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation and gender identity. In 2013 Russia passed a federal law criminalising distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors, expanded in 2022 to anyone regardless of age. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations, where leading, participating in, financially supporting or repeatedly displaying symbols is a criminal offense punishable by prison time, leading to arrests of gay bar owners and fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag including earrings, and between March and May 2026 city courts outlawed nine LGBTQ organisations as extremist. Authorities in Moscow have never approved a gay pride rally, and in 2010 the European Court of Human Rights fined Russia for discriminating by refusing permits, while in 2012 the Moscow City Court upheld blocking permits yearly through 2012 citing public disorder. In Chechnya since February 2017 over 100 men were detained and tortured with at least three dead in extrajudicial killings in what witnesses called concentration camps, confirmed by a December 2018 Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe report as ignored by authorities, with another purge reported in December 2018 with around 40 detained and two killed, and European Union sanctions imposed in March 2021 on two officials. The government does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community, with an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 with 365 fatalities, annual crimes tripling from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015 with increased premeditated group-organised crimes using dating apps to hunt homosexuals between 2017 and 2019, including 205 cases by homophobic hate groups such as Occupy Pedophilia present in 40 regions.

28173009B63182593849600.name: Tver Oblast
28173009B63182593849600.summary: Tver Oblast offers no exception to Russia's national regime. There is no legal gender recognition, and a 2023 law bars gender-reassignment surgery and changes to gender markers, so a visitor's foreign documents remain as issued and any mismatch may surface during checks. The 'international LGBT movement' extremist designation exposes anyone displaying symbols or attending LGBTQ venues to administrative or criminal charges, with documented arrests, raids — including searches and photographing of patrons — and extremism prosecutions; the expanded propaganda statutes on 'non-traditional relationships' and material affecting minors reach everyday expression, enforced through fines and criminal charges. There is no anti-discrimination protection, hate-crime aggravation, or working legal recourse, pretrial detention has proved lethal in extremism cases, national polling indicates deep public hostility, and the US State Department advises against travel to Russia. In the oblast itself there is no local statute, court practice, police protocol, or service provision creating a protective exception, no trans-specific advocacy or refuge, and little anonymous queer infrastructure outside limited urban venues; federal security services and courts operate uniformly and local authorities follow rather than mitigate federal enforcement. Accounts describe the oblast variously as a conservative Volga-region oblast and as a central Russian province on the Moscow–Petersburg corridor; either way, its smaller cities, heavy transit character, heritage-tourism areas, and conservative climate can heighten social visibility, document checks, street confrontation, and discretionary police questioning, while adding no distinct formal penalty — though a smaller visible scene than Moscow's may also mean somewhat less everyday exposure, which is not documented. No region-specific information establishes separate border treatment, facilities, policing, detention conditions, access to care, venue-raid record, or a local enforcement pattern, so Tver cannot be characterised as either more protective or more punitive than the national picture. For a trans visitor whose identity is discovered or who is outed, the principal danger remains state detention and prosecution under this inherited federal framework, compounded by social hostility and the absence of documented local recourse or a safe haven.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Kalmykia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender, and gender-affirming care is banned. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition that prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, after April-May 2023 proposals to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents and to ban reassignment without surgery. The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions and applies to anyone regardless of age group. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and a single person living abroad may adopt only if their country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor allows gender transition. A 1 July 2003 military medical expertise statute provided that people "who have problems with their identity and sexual preferences" can only be drafted during war times, while Major-General Valery Kulikov stated the statute does not forbid people of non-standard sexual orientation from serving. Amid draft-avoidance claims, Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin claimed some "2,700" gender-change decisions had been made in recent times, with reports that young men turned to private clinics for sex changes to avoid conscription in connection with the special operation. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on gender identity. Sexual activity between consenting adults of the same sex is legal, after re-legalisation in 1993 removing Article 121; prior law punished consensual sex between men with three to five years imprisonment under 1934 Article 154-a and up to five years under 1961 Article 121, and the age of consent stands at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are ineligible for legal protections available to opposite-sex couples, and July 2020 voters approved a constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage after the 2021 Fedotova ruling found failure to offer any recognition violated human rights, though Russia left the court in 2022. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation, and authorities refuse to register LGBTQ organisations while pro-LGBTQ advocacy groups have been declared extremist and prohibited. A 2013 law criminalised distribution of "propaganda" promoting "non-traditional sexual relationships" among minors, expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age group. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated "the international LGBT public movement" as extremist, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations and persons, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying symbols a criminal offense punishable by prison time. Enforcement has included arrests of gay bar owners, fines or jailing for displaying the rainbow flag designated as the movement's symbol, at least one death in custody as of April 2025, and between March and May 2026 city courts outlawing nine LGBTQ organisations as extremist including Centre T, Coming Out, LGBT Resource Centre, Irida, Kallisto movement, Moscow Community Center for LGBT+ Initiatives, Parni Plus, Russian LGBT Network and T9 NSK with founders convicted for leading an extremist organisation. Authorities have never approved Moscow pride requests, and in 2010 the European Court of Human Rights fined Russia for discriminating by refusing permits, while in August 2012 Moscow City Court upheld blocking yearly permits through 2012 citing public disorder. Documented violence includes Chechnya detentions since February 2017 of over 100 men with torture and at least three extrajudicial killings, a further purge from December 2018 with around 40 detained and two killed, and an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 with 365 fatalities rising from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015, including 205 cases by homophobic hate groups such as Occupy Pedophilia using dating apps to hunt homosexuals.

Khabarovsk Krai is a krai within the Russian Federation and has no regional law or institution of its own on gender identity or expression. The national framework applies in full, and the national assessment of visitor risk governs here.

The region's documented enforcement event concerns a biology and chemistry teacher in Khabarovsk who was forced to resign in September after video of him dancing in high heels surfaced amid public controversy. sources.summary: The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity for Russia (June 2025) sets out the national position: consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. Public expression 'promoting' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the 'gay propaganda' law by fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023.

Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025) reports that Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for participating in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation, with sentences of up to 12 years in prison. HRW also documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences (article 20.3) for displaying banned symbols, mostly on social media, and 257 'gay propaganda' penalties imposed in 2023-24 versus 22 in 2021-22.

28173009B46831765844996.name: Primorsky Krai
28173009B46831765844996.summary: Primorsky Krai is subject to Russia's national law in full, with no local exception. Locally, the krai is a militarised Far Eastern border region, and its security-sensitive character is felt most sharply in Vladivostok, a major Pacific port with historic cross-border tourism. The city's tourist core is somewhat more cosmopolitan than the interior and supports a small underground queer scene, but queer infrastructure across the krai is limited, and no sanctuary provision, identity-respecting facility or protective police practice has been documented. Compared with Moscow and St Petersburg, Vladivostok and its surroundings are less likely to offer visible trans support or consistent institutional recourse. Ports, checkpoints, hotel registration and police stops all add occasions where documents and presentation may be compared, raising the chance of discovery for a visitor whose papers do not match how they are seen. Police oversight in the Far East is reported to be weaker than in the European centres, and there is a recorded pattern of nationalist violence against gender-nonconforming people. Local authorities are conservative and social attitudes remain broadly hostile, with nothing in local practice softening the national framework for a trans visitor who is discovered. The thinness of local reporting should not be read as evidence of lighter enforcement.

28173009B30250450380208.name: Bashkortostan
28173009B30250450380208.summary:
The Republic of Bashkortostan stands under Russia's national legal framework. No source in this inventory contains information specific to Bashkortostan, so a trans visitor should expect the national regime to apply unchanged.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (version 2.0, June 2025; page updated 12 August 2026) is the assessment framework for this division. It records that same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned. Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023.

Under the 'gay propaganda' law, public expression 'promising' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition, including displaying rainbow symbols, is punishable by fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) for individuals or detention of up to 15 days. A repeated offence can bring up to four years' imprisonment.

The Supreme Court designated the international LGBT+ movement an 'extremist' organisation in November 2023. Between 2022 and 2024, at least 139 individuals were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for participating in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols since that designation, with penalties of up to 12 years in prison. HRW also identified 81 people in 98 cases found guilty since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. The 2013 'gay propaganda' law already made any positive or neutral depiction of non-heterosexual relations an administrative offence.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia advises against all travel regardless of personal characteristics. It warns that foreigners found guilty under the 'propaganda' law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and deported, and that displaying certain symbols including the rainbow flag is a crime.

76434192B57942368908249.name: Free State
76434192B57942368908249.summary:
Gender-affirming care in South Africa is concentrated in the major metropolitan centres, and the Free State has no documented concentration of its own. A trans visitor who needs hormone therapy or surgery while in the province should expect to travel outside it, paying private prices in the hundreds of thousands of rands or waiting on a long public list. No Free State-specific provider, waiting-time or funding data was identified.

No Free State-specific statute, provincial enforcement record, prosecution or documented incident involving a transgender person was identified. Policing, provincial hospitals, municipal facilities and the province's correctional centres operate under the national framework carried by the South Africa record, and for those matters the national assessment is the one a visitor should rely on.

sources.summary: Court record (High Court of South Africa, Gauteng Local Division sitting as an Equality Court, case 2024/070075, judgment 10 November 2025) in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (Medium B): the landmark ruling for a trans inmate against the Department of Correctional Services - refusal of gender expression (feminine attire, she/her pronouns), inadequate accommodation and denial of state-funded gender-affirming hormone therapy held to be unfair discrimination; hormone therapy recognised as part of the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment under section 35(2)(e).

Human-rights commission / National Preventive Mechanism media statement (14 November 2025): welcomes the 10 November 2025 High Court ruling in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075); describes the OPCAT monitoring mandate over places of deprivation of liberty, the inmate's account (initially allowed to express her gender, later restricted from feminine clothing and make-up, misgendered, denied prescribed hormone therapy, DCS arguing it was cosmetic), and the court's finding that gender-affirming healthcare forms part of adequate medical treatment under section 35(2)(e) of the Constitution.

sources.title: LGBT rights in South Africa - Wikipedia
sources.summary: National framework applicable in the Free State: the 1996 Constitution was the world's first to expressly bar sexual-orientation discrimination, and the Constitutional Court's December 2005 judgment compelled Parliament to legalise same-sex marriage (Civil Union Act, National Assembly vote 229-41, November 2006). The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act 2003 allows a person to change sex status in the population registry, and therefore on identity documents and passports, on proof of medical treatment such as hormone therapy, without requiring surgery. Gender-affirming care is concentrated in the main cities, so transgender people in provinces like the Free State must travel long distances to reach it; private treatment costs hundreds of thousands of rands and public waiting lists are long. The Justice Department's National Task Team (2011) and 2014 National Intervention Strategy for LGBTI Communities address hate crimes against LGBT people.

19338628B5758982491638.name: Centre-Val de Loire
19338628B5758982491638.summary: Centre-Val de Loire is subject to French national law in full, with no local exception, and no region-specific legislation, protection or restriction governing transgender visitors has been identified here. What distinguishes the region is its scale and social texture: a largely rural area of mid-sized, socially centre-right cities — Orléans, Tours, Blois, Chartres and Bourges — set among the château country of the Loire Valley, markedly less cosmopolitan than Paris and Île-de-France. Day-to-day exposure in small towns and the countryside tends to be ordinary staring-level curiosity rather than organised hostility, and the tourist-facing hospitality of the Loire Valley modestly softens that friction. Trans community infrastructure and trans-affirming clinicians are thin outside Tours, so a visitor needing specialist services, correct name or gender handling, or institutional support may find fewer options than in the capital; provincial settings can also mean more visible misgendering and administrative scrutiny, with anonymity harder to come by than in a large city. Police, courts and oversight bodies operate on the national system, and no local police sweeps, border practices or facility-specific rules differing from the national pattern are documented. Practical exposure therefore runs close to the countrywide picture, shaped mainly by a quieter, less anonymous and less well-served environment.

19338628B74392602121343.name: Grand Est
19338628B74392602121343.summary: The region is subject to French national law in full, with no local exception. Grand Est adds no trans-specific restrictions of its own, and what shapes a trans visitor's experience here is geography and social texture rather than any local rule. Strasbourg hosts the Council of Europe and the European Court of Human Rights alongside a substantial urban LGBT infrastructure — associations, Pride events and daily cross-border life with Germany — which makes official and service-provider encounters there comparatively routine. Metz, Nancy and Reims are similarly larger, university cities with visible LGBTQ communities, and the region's visitor economy (the Alsace Christmas markets, Colmar, Reims) is habituated to an international, mixed clientele. Away from those centres, the rural Vosges, Ardennes and parts of Champagne and Alsace are more socially conservative, with a thinner LGBTQ presence; Alsace-Moselle also retains its own local legal tradition within a practising Catholic milieu. Strasbourg's international character partly offsets that conservatism, leaving the difference from the national picture one of degree rather than kind. Because the region sits on Schengen borders — crossings into Germany, Luxembourg, Belgium and Switzerland, including Mulhouse–Basel — identity documents may be checked more often here than inland, and periodic security and immigration controls add to that routine scrutiny. No organised targeting specific to the region is documented.

19338628B73800214047876.name: Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes
19338628B73800214047876.summary:
Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes stands under the French national framework. No region-specific signal was identified: the region's own page carries no trans-specific content, and no regional deviation from the national position was located in the source inventory.

Prison placement follows no statutory rule. Article D248 of the criminal procedure code assigns detainees according to the sex inscribed on their identity documents, and each facility improvises around that rule. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018, 'The Plight Of Trans Women In Prison', reports first-person accounts of placement in all-male facilities, including a three-day stay in Lille's men's prison in 2014 marked by detainee and staff hostility, and the story of an Argentinian trans woman's incarceration. The feature also covers the well-publicised case of a US trans woman detained in poor conditions after a 2016 Paris protest case.

The controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty states that transgender detainees are the group that suffers the most in prison.

The CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021, issued by the Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté, examines the treatment of transgender persons in all places of deprivation of liberty. It rests on about forty referrals received since 2010, interviews with trans associations and European experts, and five on-site inspections covering Fleury-Mérogis men's and women's prisons, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse-Seysses and the Toulouse central police station, where eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed. The opinion finds persistent serious violations of the fundamental rights of trans detainees, including isolation and overcrowding risks, and recommends that the 2016 depathologising law, which removed the surgery requirement for civil-status change, be translated into prison regulations. Its scope explicitly extends to intersex and non-binary people.

For partner recognition, France legalised same-sex marriage and full adoption in 2013, and civil solidarity pacts have existed since 1999. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore encounters a recognised legal baseline.

Penal Code article 225-1 has covered gender identity since an 18 November 2016 amendment that replaced 'sexual identity', protected since 2012. Homophobic hate speech has carried penalties of up to EUR 45,000 and/or one year's imprisonment since a 31 December 2004 amendment.

On legal gender recognition, a bill approved by the Senate on 6 November 2015 and by the National Assembly on 24 May 2016 was signed into law on 18 November 2016 and took effect on 1 January 2017. It abolished the sex-reassignment-surgery and forced-sterilisation requirements, rejected a Senate amendment that would have demanded proof of medical treatment, and requires going before a court rather than any medical intervention.

Transsexualism is classed under long-term-illness ALD 31, so gender-affirming treatment is funded by the Sécurité Sociale.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed feature (Rozenn Le Carboulec) on trans women in French prisons: Article D248 of the Criminal Procedure Code mandates separate establishments for men and women, so placement follows the sex on identity documents and trans women are typically held in men's facilities - as of 1 Nov 2016 there were 13 transgender detainees held across eight establishments, most at Fleury-Mérogis. Profiles Paola, an Argentine trans woman transferred to a men's facility in 2014 and met with shouts of 'We don't want any women here', despite a passport listing her as female, because French law does not recognise her Argentine legal gender for placement purposes. Documents inconsistent access to treatment and a 2,000-euro symbolic damages award over detention conditions, with the justice minister pressed to amend D248.

Opinion of the Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté (CGLPL), France's national preventive mechanism, dated 25 May 2021, on the care of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: building on referrals received since 2010 and a 2010 opinion on transsexual prisoners, it covers all places of deprivation of liberty. Inspections cited include Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station, with evidence from eight transgender women; it documents discrimination, stigmatisation and health and social-care blind spots and recommends policies to combat the discrimination and exclusion they face, referencing law n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016 on justice modernisation and prison transfers and the 'racism, antisemitism, LGBT and discrimination' referents appointed since 2018. The CGLPL reports persistent serious violations of trans detainees' rights across the prisons it inspected.

36201628B45254163682963.summary: No Mimaropa-specific signal was identified in the sources consulted; the region stands under the national framework of the Philippines, and the national assessment applies in full.

sources.summary: Outright International (IGLHRC) Philippines country overview (updated 2025): same-sex relations are legal and acceptance indices rank the country among the most accepting in Asia, but trans people cannot access legal gender recognition - the 2001 Clerical Error Law (RA 9048) blocks gender-marker correction - and national non-discrimination bills filed since 1999 remain unenacted, with two civil-union bills filed since 2022 facing religious-conservative opposition; non-discrimination ordinances exist at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels. A 2018 SWS survey found only 22% of Filipinos supported same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets. The Safe Spaces Act criminalises homophobic and transphobic slurs; the Anti-Bullying Act and the Gender-Responsive Basic Education Policy (reiterated 2022, June designated Pride Month) cover sexual orientation and gender identity in schools; Executive Orders No. 100 (2019) and No. 51 (2023) creating the national Diversity and Inclusion Program remain unimplemented as of 2025.

Bulatlat (26 Jun 2025): 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol, a Cagayan State University business-management student, was found dead in a Cagayan province river on 23 June 2025, days after being reported missing, with signs of physical assault. A criminology student who admitted driving her surrendered to police while denying involvement. On the same day, trans woman and former activist-journalist Ali Macalintal was shot by an unidentified gunman inside an acupuncture clinic in General Santos. Bahaghari and other groups cite the cases in calling for passage of the SOGIESC Equality Bill, stuck in Congress for 25 years (latest version Senate Bill 1600), which would prohibit admission denial, denial of public and health services, and infliction of physical harm or verbal abuse based on SOGIE.
