36201628B90061603712355.name: Davao Region
36201628B90061603712355.summary:
Davao Region has no regional statute or regional ordinance of its own governing sexual orientation or gender identity. A trans visitor to the region stands under the national framework of the Philippines, together with the municipal law of the particular city or municipality visited.

Davao City, the region's administrative center, is recorded among the Philippine localities that have a non-discrimination ordinance. Its council passed the measure in December 2012, banning discrimination against gays (LGBT people), minorities and differently-abled persons. Within Davao City, that ordinance is the only documented local layer of protection available beyond the national position.

Custody practice specific to the region is documented. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology in Davao moves LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex, holding them alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens as a stated measure to prevent abuse. Placement of trans detainees in Davao thus takes the form of administrative segregation rather than gender-matched accommodation.

sources.summary: Korea Times (22 July 2024): the Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a 3 million won claim, ruling that police advice to a person transitioning from male to female, who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights. The appellate court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 NHRCK survey of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink and 36% forwent restroom use. A 2021 Daegu District Court (Pohang branch) award of 7 million won against a beauty academy that prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom forms part of the national standard applied in Gangwon, where no specific incident is documented.

Yonhap wire (8 May 2024): a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that court guidelines requiring surgery are now only reference, not criteria. The court said every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity. The ruling removed the surgical prerequisite for registered-sex change and is the standard applied in Gangwon, where no province-specific case is documented.

Ulsan stands under the national framework of South Korea. No ordinance, municipal directive, police practice, court decision or documented incident specific to transgender people in Ulsan appeared in the available sources.

Two decisions are final and apply in Ulsan. An appellate court finalised an award of 300,000 won against the state, on a claim of 3 million won, over police advice given to a woman who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020 telling her to avoid women's public restrooms; the court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. The advice the court condemned is a general police practice rather than an incident confined to one city, so the ruling reaches officers in Ulsan, though no comparable Ulsan complaint has been documented.

In May 2024 a regional court approved a registered-sex change from male to female for five transgender applicants who had not undergone sex-reassignment surgery. It held that gender change cannot be determined by surgery, that court guidelines requiring surgery are reference material rather than criteria, and that every person has the right to live according to their gender identity. Applications in Ulsan proceed on that footing; the sources record no Ulsan applicant and no Ulsan court ruling on the question.

1875124B91024374055933.name: La Libertad
1875124B91024374055933.summary:
La Libertad stands under Peru's national framework, which governs identity documents, facility access and discrimination law; this assessment covers only what is specific to the region. Two documents carry the region-specific record: a national prosecution study that disaggregates homicides of LGTB people by prosecution district, and a 2024 regional ordinance on labour inclusion. Neither establishes a regional anti-discrimination enforcement mechanism, and no region-specific data on policing, restroom-law enforcement or service access appears in the sources.

The Public Prosecutor's Office published a study of intentional deaths of LGTB people between 2012 and 2021, drawn from 84 criminal complaints covering 88 victims and 72 identified suspects. Six fiscal districts accounted for 58% of the deaths. La Libertad recorded 10, second only to Lima's 12 and level with Lima Norte, ahead of Lima Este (7), Lima Sur (6) and Callao (6). The ranking is by raw count. La Libertad is one of Peru's more populous regions, and the study supplies no per-capita denominator, so the figure does not by itself show that a trans visitor faces higher risk in La Libertad than in a smaller district. The study was produced with the Justice Ministry's human-rights office and the Cayetano Heredia University LGTB-rights observatory with UNDP support.

Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR, approved in Trujillo on 6 September 2024 and published in El Peruano on 7 November 2024, promotes the labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender people in La Libertad. It declares their right to formal, dignified and productive work in equitable and satisfactory conditions without discrimination on grounds of gender identity or its expression, and recognises the trans community as a group in a situation of vulnerability in the region. It is a positive-action measure addressed to employment, not a protection a visitor can invoke against police, service providers or private venues, and it specifies no penalty or enforcement body.

The ordinance recommends that local governments issue municipal ordinances recognising gender identity and fundamental rights, and orders a working group (mesa de trabajo) to be convened. It cites constitutional equality guarantees and article 323 of the Penal Code on discrimination, and recalls a 2014 regional-council session that set a framework against discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity. Whether any La Libertad municipality has acted on the recommendation is not documented in the sources.

1875124B58976419670313.name: Tacna
1875124B58976419670313.summary:
Tacna stands under Peru's national framework; national law on criminalisation, anti-discrimination protection, identity documents and public-facility access applies here as it does across the country and is set out under Peru.

On 19 April 2025 Marcia Paucara Cora, a 48-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a room of the Los 5 Titos hostel on Arias y Aragüez street in central Tacna. The autopsy recorded death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the airways. She had entered the hostel with a man who registered under a false identity and who left alone roughly two hours later carrying a white bag. Staff found the body when the rental time expired.

Tacna authorities are investigating the death as a possible hate crime, an offence motivated by prejudice and discrimination on grounds of the victim's sexual orientation or gender identity. No suspect had been identified in the reporting of 21 and 27 May 2025. The victim was initially processed as an unidentified body and was named through the hostel's cameras; police were analysing surveillance footage from inside and outside the premises to trace the suspect's escape route.

Family members and local LGTBIQ+ collectives held a vigil on Friday 23 May 2025 demanding justice, describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence that silences trans lives. Relatives publicly denounced the killing and pressed for police action.

13589884B77991835419453.name: Atlántico
13589884B77991835419453.summary:
Atlántico department stands under Colombia's national framework. The department's own signal comes from the 2025 report "Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia", published by the regional LGBTI+ rights organisation Caribe Afirmativo and covered by Publimetro Colombia.

For Atlántico the report counts 54 cases of intrafamily violence, 41 sexual offences, 69 threats, 12 discrimination cases, 8 cases of digital violence, 8 cases of lethal violence, and 2 killings of LGBTIQ+ human-rights defenders during 2025. These are raw departmental totals; the report supplies no population or per-capita denominator, so they cannot be read as a ranking against other Colombian departments and no conclusion about relative danger follows from the counts alone.

The report designates Barranquilla and Soledad as territories carrying a "high" threat level for this population. Violence is described as expanding into territories with illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence, with the state response judged insufficient.

Threat cases recorded in the report show near-total impunity: 99.8% never advance past the investigation stage. Whether that percentage is calculated for the department or for the country as a whole is not stated in the material available here.

The department's development plan and Barranquilla's development plan commit the local authorities to coordinated action with the prosecutor's office, the police and the judiciary to strengthen reporting, investigation and prosecution of violence against LGBTIQ+ people.

For the Atlántico department it documents 54 intrafamily-violence cases, 41 sexual offences, 12 discrimination cases, 8 digital-violence cases, 69 threats, 2 killings of LGBTIQ+ human-rights defenders and 8 lethal-violence cases, and designates Barranquilla and Soledad as territories with 'high' threat levels for this population; it recalls the department's and Barranquilla's development plans commit coordinated action with the prosecutor's office, police and judiciary to strengthen reporting, investigation and prosecution of violence against LGBTIQ+ people. It also reports threats show near-total impunity, with 99.8% of cases never advancing past the investigation stage.

Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report 'Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia' records that in 2025 one LGBTIQ+ person was killed every 32 hours, and describes violence as a continuum running from discrimination through intrafamily violence (1,531 cases), sexual violence (628 cases) and threats (1,184 victims) to homicide and impunity. It documents territorial expansion of the violence, including into territories with illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence, and criticises the insufficient state response.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Amazonas (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2006 Amazonas state policies include discrimination based on gender identity, and since 2019 transphobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to racism. Since the March 2018 unanimous Supreme Federal Court ruling, transgender people may change legal gender at a registry post without surgery, hormonal therapy, judicial authorization or medical report, with registry-office gender changes reported up 59% by 2024. Amazonas has no specific law recognizing non-binary gender; in 2022 Álex Souza de Sá became the first non-binary person recognized, requiring rectification in Rio de Janeiro and six months of insistence plus intervention by the Public Defender's Office to obtain recognition in Manaus where the registry lacked a gender-neutral marker. For facilities, on 18 October 2022 the mayor of Manaus signed a law banning unisex restrooms in the city. For care, in November 2023 the State Public Defender's Office opened monitoring of public health services for transgender and travesti people including hormones and surgeries, in August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended the state formally enable outpatient and hospital transsexualization services including sexual reassignment surgeries with deadlines for submission to the Ministry of Health, and on 10 June 2025 Governor Wilson Lima signed Law No. 7,552 banning gender-affirming care for minors under 18. For protection machinery, in 2021 the State Public Defender's Office created the Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship Working Group focused on human rights violations and training security agents, and in August 2024 the State Court of Justice released the booklet Home is a Right! for LGBTQ youth expelled from homes stating conversion therapies are "prohibited and ineffective." Cases of violence against LGBTQ people in the state are described as underreported, with 43 cases registered according to Brazilian Public Security Forum data cited in research. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1830 when the Imperial Penal Code removed all references to sodomy. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Amazonas since 2013 via National Council of Justice decision following the 2011 Supreme Federal Court decision, with a 328% increase between 2020 and 2025, 287 unions registered in 2024 and 98 in the first five months of 2025. Same-sex adoption was first authorized in Amazonas in November 2012 by a state court judge, with nationwide legalization by the Supreme Federal Court in 2015. Since 2006 state policies include discrimination based on sexual orientation, and since 2019 homophobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to racism. Assembly and expression restrictions include State Law 6,469/2023 prohibiting participation of children and adolescents in pride parades with fines up to R$10,000, and the 17 October 2024 law prohibiting reproduction of digital media using children linked to homosexuality, amended on 13 December 2025 to remove the term homosexuality and prohibit reproduction of sexual content linked to children in cultural and artistic media. On 5 July 2025 Fernando Vilaça de Souza was beaten and killed in Manaus after reacting to homophobic insults, with prior bullying reported by area residents.

sources.title: Brazilian Supreme Federal Court ruling, March 2018 - legal gender change
sources.summary: In March 2018 Brazil's Supreme Federal Court ruled that transgender people may change their legal name and gender marker on civil records without sex-reassignment surgery, hormonal treatment, or judicial authorization.

sources.title: Manaus municipal law banning unisex restrooms - 18 October 2022
sources.summary: On 18 October 2022 Manaus sanctioned a municipal law prohibiting multigender/unisex restrooms.

sources.title: Federal Public Prosecutor's Office (MPF) Recommendation - August 2024
sources.summary: In August 2024, the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended that the state of Amazonas guarantee integral health care to the LGBTQIAPN+ population, including trans people.

sources.title: Amazonas Public Defender's Office (DPE-AM) monitoring process - November 2023
sources.summary: In Amazonas as of 1 November 2023 the State Public Defender's health unit opened a collective procedure to audit SUS care for trans people covering access to hormonization, outpatient services, and lack of accreditation for gender-affirming surgeries including sexual reassignment, and in October 2023 the Manaus Municipal Health Secretariat committed to dispense standardized medications to trans people on prescription from the Codajás Outpatient Clinic that handles hormonization and to designate reference UBS primary-care units in each city zone, while the State Health Secretariat was ordered to report on equitable integral care including remedying hormoniotherapy gaps guaranteed under Federal Council of Medicine Resolution No. 2,265 of 2019.

sources.title: Amazonas State Law No. 6,463/2023 - gender-neutral language ban in schools
sources.summary: On 10 October 2023 Amazonas State Law No. 6,463 expressly prohibited use of neutral language, non-binary dialect, or any expression departing from standard Portuguese in curricula and teaching materials of public and private educational institutions and in official documents of schools and public agencies statewide.

sources.title: Amazonas State Court of Justice (TJAM) booklet Lar e Direito! / Home is a Right! - August 2024
sources.summary: In Amazonas as of August 2024, LGBTQIAPN+ adolescents facing family discrimination and expulsion are guaranteed under ECA Article 17 physical, psychological and moral integrity including identity and autonomy and under Constitution/ECA duties of family, society and State to ensure health, food, education and protection from negligence and discrimination with equal treatment of children regardless of sexual orientation, with bullying criminalized under Law 14.811/2024 by fine to 4 years' imprisonment, homophobia criminalized per 2019 STF ruling as imprescriptible and non-bailable, conversion/"gay cure" therapy prohibited as illegal and ineffective, and legal support available through the Defensoria Especializada em Direitos Humanos.

sources.title: DPE-AM Working Group on Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship - 2021
sources.summary: On 28 June 2021 the Amazonas Public Defender's Office created the permanent Working Group on Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship to identify LGBTQIA+ human-rights violations in public security, train public-security agents for service to LGBTQIA+ people, and issue recommendations and extrajudicial measures, while LGBTQIA+ victims in Manaus can obtain assistance via Disk 129 Monday-Friday 8am-2pm through the Specialized Human Rights unit, in a context where Amazonas led North and Central-West states with 4.66 LGBTQIA+ persons murdered per million inhabitants in 2018.

sources.title: Nationwide criminalization of homophobia and transphobia - 2019
sources.summary: On 23 May 2019 a majority of Brazil's Supreme Federal Tribunal (6 of 11 justices) voted to criminalize transphobia under Brazil's 1989 racism law punishable by up to five years' imprisonment until Congress enacts specific LGBT-discrimination legislation, to take effect after all justices voted on 5 June 2019.

sources.title: Brazilian Public Security Forum / Brazilian Journal of Public Security data + Fernando Vilaca de Souza homicide 5 July 2025
sources.summary: In Amazonas during 2021-2022, crimes involving transsexual persons formed part of only 0.36% of total reported crimes in the capital and interior, police occurrence reports did not identify transfobia or gender, sexuality, race and intersectionality markers, trans victim data were few and badly structured with victims not infrequently inverted to accused through faulty BOs, and unprepared public agents and defective registration mechanisms left trans subjects invisibilized and without protection.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Colombia
sources.summary: Colombia decriminalised homosexuality in 1981, and in 2011 Congress passed a law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation. The Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in a 6-3 ruling of 28 April 2016, with the first wedding in Cali on 24 May 2016. Three rulings between February 2007 and April 2008 had granted same-sex couples property, social-security and pension rights, and a November 2015 ruling granted full adoption rights with dual-parent birth registration. Since August 2023 passports issued within Colombia offer three gender options: male, female and X. Adults can change legal gender before a notary without surgery, with a free simultaneous name change on first request. Gays, lesbians and bisexuals have served openly in the armed forces since a 1999 court ruling. Casanare adds no separate legal regime, so these national provisions define the formal legal exposure of a trans visitor to the department.

13589884B16144547040567.name: Caquetá
13589884B16144547040567.summary:
Caquetá is a department of Colombia and stands under the national framework: legal gender recognition, identification markers, entry rules, marriage and partner recognition, and the national protection machinery are carried by the national record and are not restated here. The department-specific signal concerns organised armed-group targeting rather than statute.

Reporting dated 30 July 2024 documented armed groups in Caquetá running a 'social cleansing' campaign, distributing flyers on the streets and through WhatsApp that named 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets.

The campaign has produced displacement. A trans woman who was a local election candidate was told by three armed men that she had one week to leave town; she hid for a week and then fled at night. A second trans woman in the department said a friend had been killed.

For a trans visitor, the exposure in Caquetá is not the statute book but the presence of armed groups that have publicly designated trans people as targets and have acted on that designation by driving residents out. The campaign's categories are social rather than documentary: the flyers name people by perceived sexual orientation and gender expression, not by any official record.

sources.summary: EL PAÍS English, 14 April 2025, reports the killing of Sara Millerey, a trans woman, in Bello, Antioquia: she was attacked in broad daylight on 4 April 2025, the assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April, and she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents, but no one was arrested even after the president ordered an urgent investigation. The article reports 13 trans people killed by hate in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, and cites earlier killings of gay men and the stabbing death of a trans rough-sleeper. The incident occurred outside Caquetá; it evidences the national pattern of lethal anti-trans violence that a visitor faces.

Police interrogated local residents, and no one had been arrested even after the president ordered an urgent investigation. EL PAÍS English (14 April 2025) reports 13 trans people killed by hate in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, alongside earlier killings of gay men and the stabbing death of a trans rough-sleeper. Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina has no recorded incident, law or enforcement finding on this point. What bears on a visitor to the islands is the national pattern of lethal anti-trans violence.

The Guardian (30 July 2024) documented armed groups in Caquetá department running a 'social cleansing' campaign: flyers on the streets and via WhatsApp named 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets. Three armed men told a trans woman and local election candidate she had one week to leave town; she hid for a week, then fled at night. A second trans woman said a friend was killed. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work. Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina has no specific finding here; the national kill figures and the armed-group 'social-cleansing' pattern are what bear on a visitor.

1875124B3772980127380.name: Puno
1875124B3772980127380.summary:
No region-specific finding on trans visitor safety was identified for the department of Puno. The sources record no Puno ordinance, exemption, enforcement practice or regional institution of its own on trans matters.

The national framework that governs Puno includes a public-restroom restriction. On 2 April 2025 the Peruvian congressional Plenary approved, exempt from a second vote, a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', with narrow listed exceptions; IDEHPUCP's legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of 15 April 2025 states this violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors argue the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

An earlier committee-stage measure of the same family, reported by Infobae Perú on 20 February 2025, was approved unanimously by the congressional Women and Family Commission as a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, where medical attention is required, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over the Jorge Chávez airport's gendered restroom labels. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho called the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and noted there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. As national law this binds Puno.

1875124B82769317880582.name: Tumbes
1875124B82769317880582.summary:
Tumbes stands under Peru's national framework. No region-specific signal was identified: the sources addressing this department do so only through national legislation and national legal analysis, and none records a Tumbes ordinance, enforcement action, incident or institution. The national assessment applies.

Under the national framework binding Tumbes, Law 32331 of 13 May 2025 restricts trans people's use of public restrooms. The congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, required medical attention, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho called the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and noting there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for narrow listed exceptions. IDEHPUCP legal analysts Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte argue this violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. They state that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

Separately, the April 2025 'Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents' mandates that public-restroom entry be restricted by 'biological sex', barring trans people including trans youth from facilities matching their identity; its vague child-protection articles enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational content, and the obscenity minimum sentence rises from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states child protection is a pretext for repression and trans scapegoating. The IDEHPUCP states the restriction openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing trans people as harassment risks; the institute cites Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, under which gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

1875124B82769317880582.localsOnly:
Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November 2016, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem to cover trans healthcare; after protests, in June 2024 the Ministry of Health (MINSA) revised the term to 'gender discordance' for health-insurance classification purposes. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities also removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases. Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, a protection with specific relevance to trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices.

The 2016 national education curriculum includes information on sexual orientation, sex and gender issues, describing sexual orientation as the result of complex biological, cognitive and environmental circumstances and not a voluntary choice. Pride marches have been held annually since 2002, with the oldest recorded march in 1984.

sources.summary: Infobae Perú (20 Feb 2025) reports that the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex. The framework governs Piura as national law.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Amazonas (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2006 Amazonas state policies prohibit discrimination based on gender identity, and since 2019 transphobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to the crime of racism. In 2021 the Amazonas State Public Defender's Office created the Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship Working Group to address human rights violations and train security agents, and in November 2023 it opened a process to monitor public health services for transgender and travesti people including provision of hormones and surgeries. In March 2018 the Supreme Federal Court unanimously ruled transgender people may change legal gender at a registry post without surgery, hormonal therapy, judicial document or medical report, with registry gender changes reported up 59% by 2024. On 18 October 2022 the mayor of Manaus signed a law banning unisex restrooms in the city. In August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended Amazonas formally enable outpatient and hospital services for the transsexualization process including sexual reassignment surgeries, with deadlines for approval and presentation to the Ministry of Health. On 10 June 2025 Governor Wilson Lima signed Law No. 7,552 banning gender-affirming care for minors under age 18. Amazonas has no specific law recognizing non-binary gender, and in 2022 Alex Souza de Sa became the first non-binary person recognized in the state after rectification in Rio de Janeiro and intervention by the Public Defender's Office to secure recognition in Manaus after six months when the local notary lacked a gender-neutral marker. Homosexuality has been legal in Amazonas and Brazil since 1830 when the Imperial Penal Code removed all references to sodomy. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 via National Council of Justice decision following the 2011 Supreme Federal Court decision, and same-sex adoption was first allowed in Amazonas in November 2012 by an Amazonas Court of Justice judge before nationwide legalization by the Supreme Federal Court in 2015. Since 2006 Amazonas state policies prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation, and since 2019 homophobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to the crime of racism. The August 2024 Amazonas Court of Justice booklet Home is a Right! for LGBTQ youth expelled from homes states that conversion therapies are "prohibited and ineffective." Research from the Brazilian Journal of Public Security states that cases of violence against LGBTQ people in Amazonas are underreported. Data from the Brazilian Public Security Forum indicates cases of violence against LGBTQ people have increased, with 43 cases registered. On 5 July 2025 Fernando Vilaca de Souza was beaten and killed in Manaus after reacting to homophobic insults, and residents reported he had previously been bullied by other young people in the region. The Ministry of Human Rights and Citizenship, the Order of Attorneys of Brazil and federal deputy Erika Hilton expressed regret over the incident. The article provides no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically so no such quote can be reproduced, and the above violence figures refer to LGBTQ people generally not to transgender people specifically.

sources.title: Federal Public Prosecutor's Office (MPF) recommendation - August 2024
sources.summary: In August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended that the state of Amazonas guarantee comprehensive health care for the LGBTQIAPN+ population, including trans people.

sources.title: Public Defender's Office of the State of Amazonas (DPE-AM) monitoring process - November 2023
sources.summary: In Amazonas in October-November 2023, trans access to SUS was under enforcement review for primary care, outpatient services, hormonization, and lack of local authorization for transexualizing surgeries including sexual reassignment, with the municipal health authority committing to dispense standardized hormone medications on Ambulatório Codajás prescriptions and to designate a reference UBS in each city zone and the state health authority required to report on equitable integral care and hormoniotherapy gaps guaranteed under CFM Resolution No. 2.265/2019.

sources.title: Manaus municipal law banning unisex restrooms - 18 October 2022
sources.summary: On 18 October 2022 the municipality of Manaus sanctioned a law prohibiting multigender/unisex bathrooms.

sources.title: Amazonas State Law No. 6,463/2023 on gender-neutral language ban
sources.summary: On 10 October 2023 Amazonas Law No. 6,463 prohibited the use of gender-neutral language, non-binary dialect, or any expression deviating from standard Portuguese in the curricula and teaching materials of public and private educational institutions and in official documents of educational institutions and public offices throughout the state of Amazonas.

sources.title: Amazonas State Court of Justice (TJAM) booklet Lar e Direito! / Home is a Right! - August 2024
sources.summary: In Amazonas since August 2024, LGBTQIAPN+ adolescents facing family discrimination and expulsion from home are affirmed as protected by ECA Article 17 guaranteeing physical, psychological and moral integrity including identity, autonomy and beliefs, by Constitutional/ECA duties of family, society and State to ensure health, food, education and protection against negligence and discrimination with equal treatment of all children regardless of sexual orientation, by Law No. 14.811/2024 criminalizing bullying with penalties ranging from fine to 4 years' imprisonment, by the 2019 STF recognition of homophobia as an imprescriptible and unbailable crime, and by the prohibition of conversion/"cura gay" therapies as illegal and ineffective, with legal support available from the Defensoria Especializada em Direitos Humanos.

sources.title: Amazonas State Public Defender's Office (DPE-AM) Working Group - 2021
sources.summary: On 28 June 2021 the Amazonas Public Defender's Office (DPE-AM) created the permanent Working Group "Diversidade Sexual, Identidade de Gênero e Cidadania" to defend LGBTQIA+ rights and identify human rights violations in the area of public security. Its mandate includes training public security agents for service to LGBTQIA+ persons and issuing recommendations and other extrajudicial referrals. Victims of LGBTphobia are served by the Specialized Human Rights Defensoria via Disk 129 in Manaus Monday to Friday 8h-14h, in a context where Amazonas led North and Center-West states with an average of 4.66 LGBTQIA+ persons murdered per million inhabitants in 2018.

sources.title: Brazilian Public Security Forum / Brazilian Journal of Public Security + 5 July 2025 homicide case
sources.summary: In Amazonas during 2021-2022 trans persons faced persistent diverse violence intensifying each year while only 0.36% of crimes reported in the capital and interior involved homosexual, lesbian, bisexual and transsexual victims, police occurrence reports did not identify homophobia and transfobia motives or gender, sexuality, race and intersectionality markers, victim data were few and poorly structured with victims at times inverted to accused through faulty reports, and unprepared public agents and defective registration mechanisms produced invisibilization and lack of protection for trans victims.

25984515B39003465173278.name: Ağrı
25984515B39003465173278.summary:
Ağrı stands under the national legal framework of Türkiye; the source inventory records no province-specific statute, ordinance, enforcement pattern or incident series applying to the province. What a trans visitor encounters in Ağrı is Turkish national law and national police practice as described in the parent record.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft of Türkiye's omnibus 11th Judicial Package would open the way to criminal charges against LGBT people, described there as one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades. Conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', including its so-called 'promotion', would carry up to three years in prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to four years; same-sex marriage is not legal in Türkiye, so such ceremonies are by definition symbolic. The package would also restrict gender-affirming care: raising the surgery age from 18 to 25, making permanent infertility mandatory, exposing medical professionals to fines or up to seven years' imprisonment, and imprisoning transgender patients for up to three years for care outside the new limits, which would push treatment into underground settings. The package contains no Ağrı-specific provision, and whether it has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources.

Kaos GL's report on 2025, 'A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy', documents six right-to-life violations, three recorded as hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected. These counts are drawn from media and civil-society reports because the state keeps no official hate-crime statistics. The report also records 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the previous year, mostly linked to peaceful assembly, alongside 336 assembly violations and 313 liberty violations — a roughly 2.5-fold rise in liberty violations, consisting mostly of detentions — together with event-specific bans and violent police attacks on peaceful gatherings. Hostility is presented as institutionalised under 'Year of the Family' instructions to public institutions, with hate speech from senior officials, censored broadcasts and cancelled artistic events. The report describes national practice rather than provincial choice, and no Ağrı-specific finding appears in it.

25984515B97476213604692.name: Antalya
25984515B97476213604692.summary: Antalya is subject to Turkey's national law in full, with no local exception, and no local rule adds protection for trans visitors. Antalya is a Mediterranean tourism province centred on Antalya city, Alanya, Side and Kaş, with a large foreign-visitor economy and a service culture accustomed to diverse guests; Kaş in particular has a long-established gay-friendly community. Resort districts generally treat foreign guests with pragmatic indifference, and street-level policing of gender nonconformity is visibly lighter than in Istanbul's Beyoğlu, with police priorities leaning toward tourist security. This produces less everyday friction for a trans visitor rather than any legal or custodial safeguard: local authorities and businesses have an economic incentive to avoid public scandal involving foreign guests, but hotel registration and document checks remain routine, and a check is still the point at which a visitor can be outed, questioned or detained. Outside hotel and beach enclaves, attitudes are more conservative, and trans-specific community infrastructure and venues are thin compared with Istanbul. Provincial authorities have banned LGBTI+ events in the past, and local enforcement follows national policy; there is no record of local prosecutions, lethal violence or raids targeting trans visitors, but that reflects the limits of documentation rather than demonstrated safety. Anyone needing continuing medication should plan for private provision, as trans-specific support services and advocacy locally are sparse.

25984515B1602304411378.name: Artvin
25984515B1602304411378.summary: Artvin is subject to Turkey's national regime in full, with no local exception. Artvin is a small, mountainous, predominantly conservative Black Sea province on the Georgian border, built around small towns with limited tourist infrastructure rather than large-city anonymity. No local LGBT or trans organisations, pride events, recorded local protections, or region-specific incidents involving foreign visitors are documented; the province's small size, ethnic homogeneity and close-knit communities mean that being outed tends to become known locally rather than passing unnoticed. Distance from the legal-aid, advocacy and support networks concentrated in Istanbul and Ankara, along with limited specialised healthcare, leaves a trans visitor dependent on local police discretion and private arrangements if something goes wrong. Any police, hospital or official encounter would occur far from modest recourse networks, and no organised local anti-trans campaign is documented — but neither is there any local remedy, shield or protective practice to offset the national picture. The absence of local reports does not demonstrate safety or effective local recourse. Social exposure and stigma in this rural conservative setting appear stronger than in the western metropolitan centres where most documented incidents occur, making the inherited national exposure harder to manage.

25984515B63739470532168.name: Aydın
25984515B63739470532168.summary: Aydın is a western Aegean province centred on the city of Aydın and the coastal resort towns of Kuşadası and Didim, with a university city and an economy built on tourism; the region is subject to Turkey's national legal framework in full, with no local exception. Public life here is comparatively secular and accustomed to foreign visitors, so a trans traveller generally encounters less everyday social friction than in Istanbul or inland Anatolia, and visible foreignness in hotels, beaches and promenades tends to go unremarked in visitor-facing settings. That tolerance is informal and uneven rather than a legal protection. Conservative sentiment persists, identity checks in the province's holiday districts are an active local route into police contact, and centralized police practice means a visitor who is outed has no local remedy and remains exposed to questioning, detention and privacy harm. No local ordinance and no documented pattern of region-specific anti-trans targeting is known in Aydın, and absence of such evidence is not a guarantee of safety. Some rights infrastructure does exist — the Aydın branch of the Human Rights Association joined demands for an independent investigation into prison practices — but that represents local advocacy rather than recourse available to an individual visitor.

25984515B55384476443375.name: Balıkesir
25984515B55384476443375.summary: Balıkesir is a province in western Turkey centred on its eponymous city, with Aegean coast resorts around Ayvalık, Burhaniye and Edremit and the Kaz Dağları hills that draw mainly domestic tourists alongside some foreign visitors. Coast and interior differ: the seaside towns are somewhat more accustomed to outside visitors, while the province's interior is socially conservative and rural districts fall under the gendarmerie rather than city police. No region-specific protection, hostility or distinct legal rule for trans visitors has been recorded here — there is no local anti-discrimination ordinance, no pride or community infrastructure, and no documented pattern of region-specific police action against trans people. What a visitor finds instead is thin local support: little visible LGBT infrastructure, no dedicated legal aid or advocacy presence, and few trans-friendly health providers, so a trans visitor is more conspicuous, with less anonymity and fewer avenues of recourse than in Istanbul or İzmir. 25984515B73855241915553.summary:
Elazığ stands under the national framework of Turkey. The province's own documented signal is a state-facilitated anti-LGBT mobilisation staged in its central public space: on 19 December 2022 a rally was held at Cumhuriyet (Republic) Square under a banner reading "LGBT sapkınlıktır" ("LGBT is perversion"), and Nazif Bilginoğlu, a deputy mayor from the ruling AKP, took part.

The rally statement denounced consensual same-sex relationships and "homosexual marriage" as a "revolting loss of reason" attributed to Western states, used the terms "perverse" and "degenerate mentality", and tied gender and sexual themes to Turkey's denunciation of the Istanbul Convention. The gathering was organised rather than spontaneous and carried official participation. For a visibly LGBTQ visitor, the documented exposure in Elazığ is public-space hostility that has been staged in a central square with a municipal officeholder present.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's national 'LGBT rights in Turkey' page is the framework every Turkish province, Kırıkkale included, stands under: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the military: the armed forces' health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual' illness making members unfit for service, and conscripts who declare their homosexuality have to provide photographic proof. Same-sex marriage is not recognised; a 2012 constitutional-writing request to include it was rejected by both the AKP and the MHP. Authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years and police have used tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans; on 14 June 2019 the 7th Izmir Pride, the 3rd Antalya Pride and the 27th Istanbul Pride were banned by the cities' governors. The page also records a February 2026 newspaper report that the government was considering a law criminalising publicly encouraging 'behavior contrary to biological sex', with a sentence of one to three years in prison.

sources.title: Türkiye - Amnesty International country report (Report 2025/26)
sources.summary: Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26) applies in any province, Kırıkkale included. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained. In November a court overturned a ban in Istanbul governorate as 'disproportionate' and 'unlawful', though prosecutions involving 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December 2025 an Izmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had engaged in activities outside its stated purpose and shared 'obscene' images incompatible with the law. Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, an unprecedented assault that would criminalise any expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible. They were ultimately not submitted to parliament.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Muş province stands under the national legal framework of Türkiye; no Muş-specific ordinance, incident or court decision is documented for the province. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but no comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTI people are barred from military service: conscripts who declare their homosexuality are classified under a definition of homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', must provide photographic proof, and risk their 'unfit report' being leaked publicly. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, and since 2015 local authorities have repeatedly banned and forcibly dispersed Pride marches; police used water cannon and tear gas on the 2015 and 2016 Istanbul parades. Press reports in early 2026 stated that the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', a provision ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package.

sources.title: Türkiye - Amnesty International country report (Report 2025/26)
sources.summary: Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26) documents the national LGBTI climate under which Muş province sits: in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. Amnesty also records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025 - an unprecedented assault that would criminalize expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible - but they were ultimately not submitted to parliament.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's 'LGBT rights in Turkey' page sets out the national position that applies in Osmaniye. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but no comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service: conscripts who declare their homosexuality are classed under a definition of homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', must provide photographic proof, and risk their 'unfit report' leaking publicly. Same-sex marriage is not recognised. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied bans. In 2026 the draft judicial package's LGBTI-discriminatory provisions were removed. A February 2026 press report described a proposed law criminalizing publicly encouraging 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison; it was not included in the 2026 omnibus bill (the 12th judicial package).

Anyone outed here therefore has fewer sympathetic institutions, fewer community supports and a lower likelihood of local documentation than the national picture alone would suggest. Tourist activity around Lake Van and Akdamar Island brings some outsider tolerance and may moderate day-to-day friction in hospitality settings, but nothing in local conditions is documented as a trans-specific protection. 25984515B19658467647683.summary: Yozgat is a small, socially conservative and largely rural province and city in central Anatolian Turkey, with little foreign tourism and no tourism-facing economy. What distinguishes Yozgat is not a different legal regime but the near-total absence of the infrastructure that softens it in the big cities: no documented LGBTQ+ venues, organisations, legal-aid networks or community support, and little independent monitoring or tourist-facing anonymity. Practical recourse for a trans visitor who is outed or detained sits far away in Ankara, Istanbul or Izmir, leaving local police as effectively the only authority and point of contact. Small-city visibility works against a visitor's anonymity — a visibly trans or outed visitor is likely to be noticed, remembered and reported, and tight-knit networks raise the chance of being outed. Traditional and religious social norms are strong, so social disapproval, curiosity, harassment or refusal of service are realistic everyday exposures, while any custody would fall to local facilities unfamiliar with such cases. Sparse local documentation reflects limited monitoring and reporting rather than safety: no Yozgat-specific incident, enforcement pattern, protective measure or local tolerance has been identified, and the absence of local evidence should not be read as evidence of safety.

19177384B49506124846693.name: Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires
19177384B49506124846693.summary:
Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires stands under Argentina's national framework on legal gender recognition, gender markers, health care and hate-crime law. The sources assembled for the City record no municipal statute of its own on those matters and no city-level enforcement figure.

Activists based in Buenos Aires told the Washington Blade, in reporting published on 10 April 2025, that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers in the city has become more common since the current national government took office, and that harassment and hate speech have risen. The account supplies no incident counts and no dates for individual cases, and no later City-specific instance is documented in these sources.

Emergency decree DNU 61/2025, published in February 2025, re-regulates the housing of transgender people deprived of liberty and invites the provinces and the City of Buenos Aires to adhere. It prohibits people who have legally changed gender from being housed in women's prisons when they are detained for sexual offences or violence against women. FALGBT and legal experts describe the decree as illegal and unconstitutional and are seeking judicial intervention. The sources do not record whether the City has adhered or how its prisons have applied the rule.

sources.summary: The national administration eliminated the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry, closed the National Institute Against Discrimination, Xenophobia and Racism (INADI), dismissed trans people hired under the Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserved at least 1% of public-sector jobs, and has moved to restrict the 12-year-old Gender Identity Law. Buenos Aires-based activists told the Washington Blade on April 10, 2025 that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has become more common since the current government took office, with harassment and hate speech rising nationally.

Argentina recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, up 62% year-on-year, a ten-year record of one crime every 38 hours. According to Agencia Presentes data published on 19 March 2026, 32% of the crimes occurred in police stations and penal facilities, security-force violence multiplied from 17 cases (2024) to 64 (2025), and trans women and travestis concentrated 62.5% of victims (142 cases). Most perpetrators were security personnel and unknown assailants.

Via emergency decrees published in February 2025, DNU 62/2025 modified Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law (Law 26743) to prohibit gender-affirming interventions for persons under 18, and DNU 61/2025 re-regulates the housing of transgender people deprived of liberty, inviting the provinces and the City of Buenos Aires to adhere. The latter decree prohibits those who legally changed gender from being housed in women's prisons if detained for sexual offences or violence against women. FALGBT and legal experts call the decrees illegal and unconstitutional and are seeking judicial intervention.

14911670B90188072957077.name: Santa Catarina
14911670B90188072957077.summary:
Santa Catarina stands under Brazil's national framework, and its own record shows a state legislature moving against trans and LGBTIQ people while the courts have narrowed the state's own protections.

The state constitution carries an anti-discrimination clause dating to 2002 that lists sexual orientation among the protected grounds, but as of 2019 it does not address discrimination against transgender people. Two state statutes that did cover gender identity have been stripped back: State Law No. 12,534 of 4 April 2003 was repealed on 8 October 2015 by Complementary Law No. 656, and Complementary Law No. 527 of 28 December 2010 was partially overturned on 11 October 2018 after a 2015 Supreme Federal Court challenge on labour-law grounds. What remains of Complementary Law No. 527 penalises private entities and, where applicable, state public servants who promote, permit or tolerate discriminatory acts based on gender or sexual orientation, covering violent, coercive or vexatious acts, refusal of entry to places of free public access, denial or surcharging of lodging and property transactions, and prohibition of affectionate expression permitted to others, punishable by a R$2,500 fine rising to R$5,000 on repeat, a 30-day licence suspension or revocation, and up to 30 days' suspension for state servants; complaints go to the State Secretariat of Public Security and Defense of the Citizen, with fines paid into the State Civil Police Improvement Fund. In ADI 5307 on 29 October 2018 the Supreme Federal Court unanimously declared Article 2, items VI and VII of that law formally unconstitutional.

Legislative hostility is documented in volume. From January 2019 to June 2025, state deputies introduced 19 anti-LGBTQIA+ bills against 4 pro-LGBTQIA+ bills, including proposals to prohibit neutral language in official government communications and to bar minors from hormone therapy, surgical interventions and other gender-transition care; 4 of the anti-LGBTQIA+ bills were archived and none were enacted. As of 2025 the Legislative Assembly had 19 anti-LGBTQ bills on record with 11 authored by the Liberal Party. A 2026 count recorded 271 unconstitutional laws processed since 2015 against women's or LGBTQ rights, about 70% involving the trans and travesti community and 41% ruled unconstitutional by the Supreme Federal Court. A separate report covering January 2015 to October 2025 found the Legislative Assembly and its 295 municipal chambers approved or advanced at least 271 laws, bills and normative acts already declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Federal Court, 41% attacking gender and sexuality with particular focus on LGBTIA+ people, 36% already in force and only 11% judicially annulled, concentrated in the Vale do Itajaí and accelerating in the last five years.

Restroom access is contested. On 21 January 2026 Governor Jorginho Mello signed State Law No. 19,686/2026 requiring all public and private educational institutions from preschool through higher and vocational education to maintain strictly separate male and female restrooms and changing rooms; from 18 June 2026 the Federal University of Santa Catarina installed signs indicating restrooms may be used in accordance with gender identity. In a 2014 Florianópolis shopping-mall case where a trans woman was denied access to the women's restroom, a lower court ordered R$15,000 in compensation for pain and suffering, the Court of Justice of Santa Catarina overturned it, and on 6 June 2024 the Supreme Federal Court dismissed her appeal pending since 2014 by an 8-3 vote, withdrawing its recognized general repercussion on procedural grounds that the original claim pleaded only consumer-law damages rather than constitutional provisions, thereby issuing no binding constitutional ruling on trans bathroom access; in August 2025 an extraordinary appeal was filed with the Inter-American Court of Human Rights against both courts.

Education policy has also been restricted. A decree of Governor Carlos Moises on 15 June 2021 banned gender-neutral language in state schools until it was overturned on 6 May 2025 by the Supreme Federal Court, and a Joinville law of 20 December 2021 banned it in public office until struck down on 3 August 2022 by the Court of Justice. On 15 October 2025 the Supreme Federal Court struck down a 2015 Tubarão law that had prohibited teaching of gender and sexual orientation in schools. On 1 April 2026 Governor Jorginho Mello signed a law published 6 April allowing parents to prohibit children from participating in classes on LGBTQ topics. In December 2023 the Constitution and Justice Committee of the Legislative Assembly approved a bill prohibiting transgender women from participating in women's sports, still under review as of 18 August 2026.

Document and registry practice in the state runs through the courts rather than a state statute. Since 2020 people in Santa Catarina have obtained documents recording non-binary gender through the courts or notarial offices, although no specific state law prescribes this; in 2021 Idris Kawabe became the first person in Santa Catarina to judicially change documents to reflect a neutral gender, and judicial actions are still required because no state law recognizes the marker, with legal sex still required on birth certificates. The Army provides that any person in the draft cohort expressing a gender identity other than male who holds a final, unappealable court ruling or civil registry amendment is treated as non-binary in the same manner as intersex individuals and considered exempt from mandatory military service for not meeting Federal Constitution, Military Service Law, implementing regulations and the 2024 General Conscription Plan requirements.

Violence and hostility figures for the state are recorded. In 2024 three murders of trans people were recorded in Santa Catarina. The 2024 Brazilian Public Security Yearbook reported 85 cases of intentional bodily injury against LGBTQ individuals in the state, with low rates attributed to underreporting. On 3 September 2026 the Court of Justice ordered the parents of a gay teenager in Jaguaruna to pay R$100,000 in compensation after kicking him out and exposing his sexual orientation on social media.

Florianópolis carries some protective signals. A legal guide updated 5 April 2026 names it among Brazil's broadly welcoming major cities, with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages, adoptions and name or gender-marker changes, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction even though legal rights are identical nationwide. In a Florianópolis case, judge M. C. F. Ribeiro da Silva of the 1st Civil Court blocked immigration authorities from deporting an Italian citizen who had lived over ten years in a stable relationship with a lesbian Brazilian. On 29 April 2013 the Corregedoria-Geral da Justiça of Santa Catarina authorized notarial and civil-registry offices to process marriage habilitations regardless of the sex of the spouses, allowing same-sex couples where both partners reside in Santa Catarina to formalize civil marriage and expanding Article 629 of the CGJ Code of Norms beyond the stable union recognized since 2011.

Nationally, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 under CNJ Resolution 175/2013, and a 2019 Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling made discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989.

Constitutional guarantees and federal criminal provisions adopted after the 2019 Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling prohibit discrimination and hate crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity. A deeply conservative Congress has nonetheless generated a surge of anti-LGBTIQ proposals, including efforts to repeal the marriage equality recognised by the Supreme Court in 2013. These guarantees apply nationwide and cover visitors in Santa Catarina. In September 2025 the government reinstated the National LGBTI+ Health Technical Committee, a participatory mechanism dissolved in 2019, for shaping and monitoring inclusive public-health policy. The Superior Court of Justice ruled that nonbinary people may amend their civil registry to reflect their gender identity.

A legal guide updated 5 April 2026 names Florianópolis among Brazil's broadly welcoming major cities, with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages, adoptions and name or gender-marker changes. Smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction, though legal rights are identical nationwide. Foreign same-sex spouses and partners are treated identically for visa and residence categories, including the spousal residence permit, and foreign same-sex marriages are recognised for immigration purposes. Joint and second-parent adoption are confirmed by STF RE 846.102 (2015). Gender-marker changes proceed without surgery. ADO 26 (2019) criminalises homophobia and transphobia as equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989.

82249235B24619009834807.summary:
British Columbia stands under the national framework of Canada. No statute of the province restricts trans people's access to restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, to gender-affirming care, or to gender-related name use in schools, and the province has enacted no hostile legislation of its own in these areas.

British Columbia's human rights legislation lists gender identity and gender expression as prohibited grounds across employment, housing, and public and private accommodations. Complaints against private businesses proceed under that statute, since Charter equality guarantees do not bind the private sector directly.

Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms applies in British Columbia. The Supreme Court of Canada has interpreted the concepts of sex and physical disability in section 15 to include transsexuality, and section 15 reaches all laws and government institutions in the province, including law enforcement authorities. Those guarantees remain subject to reasonable limits under section 1 and to the notwithstanding clause in section 33.

Vital statistics, including birth certificates and other identity documents, fall under British Columbia's provincial jurisdiction, so a gender-marker change on a provincial birth certificate is governed by the province rather than by Ottawa.

sources.summary: Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms applies in British Columbia and protects LGBTQ people from discrimination based on sexual orientation. Sexual orientation has been covered federally since 1996, and the Criminal Code's hate-propaganda and anti-discrimination provisions protect gender identity and gender expression. A 2021 Criminal Code amendment, in force since 2022, made Canada the first country in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults. Transgender people may change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. British Columbia has no hostile provincial legislation, and the national baseline near the top of its index rests on Charter equality protection, nationwide conversion-therapy criminalisation, and legal gender change in every province including BC.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in British Columbia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Federal, provincial and territorial law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations, and as of 2017 all provinces, territories and the federal government explicitly list gender identity as a prohibited ground in their human rights acts. The Supreme Court has interpreted the concepts of sex and physical disability in Charter section 15 to include transsexuality, with section 15 applying to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities, while complaints against private businesses proceed under the applicable federal or provincial human rights statute. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules, with vital statistics including identity documents such as birth certificates falling under provincial jurisdiction. In 2023 Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoking the notwithstanding clause to require schools to obtain parental consent for students under 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, prompting calls for repeal and legal action. In 2024 Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024 and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges blocked when the government passed Bill 9: Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 using the notwithstanding clause. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans, Transgender and Queer communities, stated police must stand together against transphobia, and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 when the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 received royal assent, and the anal-intercourse provision in section 159 of the Criminal Code was repealed on June 21, 2019 by Bill C-75, setting the age of consent at 16 for all sexual activities, 18 where there is a relationship of trust, authority or dependency, with close-in-age exceptions for ages 12 through 15. In Egan v Canada in 1995 the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under Charter section 15 as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta in 1998 it held failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law violated section 15, with all provinces, territories and the federal government explicitly prohibiting sexual orientation discrimination as of 2017. Charter equality protections apply to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement but not directly against the private sector, are subject to reasonable limits under section 1 under the Oakes Test and to section 33's notwithstanding clause, which has never been used by the federal Parliament. Canada legalized same-sex marriage nationwide on July 20, 2005 through the federal Civil Marriage Act, becoming the fourth country in the world and first in the Americas to do so, after court rulings between 2002 and 2005 struck down the opposite-sex common-law definition. Same-sex adoption is legal in all provinces and territories, beginning with British Columbia in 1996 and ending with Nunavut in 2011, and British Columbia, Ontario and Saskatchewan grant parental status to three or more intentional parents. In 2022 Canada became the third country in the world and first in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for minors and adults, making it a crime under the Criminal Code to subject anyone to it as defined by statute. On June 21, 2018 royal assent was granted to the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act allowing RCMP, federal departments, and notified provincial, municipal police and courts to destroy or remove judicial records for pre-1969 homosexual acts and section 159 convictions for living and deceased persons, distinct from a pardon or record suspension. Canada was ranked first in Asher & Lyric's LGBTQ+ Danger Index in 2023 indicating least dangerous, first in the Gay Travel Index in 2024, and ninth in the Equaldex Equality Index in 2024. The 2020 Pew Research showed 85% of Canada's general population, including 92% among Canadians aged 18 to 29, favoured social acceptance of homosexuality, up from 80% in 2013. June 2013 polls showed a vast majority blessed same-sex marriage available throughout Canada since 2005, with 70% agreeing same-sex couples should have the same rights to adopt as heterosexual couples and 76% agreeing they are just as likely to successfully raise children. A 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office found 91.8% of those surveyed said they would be "comfortable" if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual. The same poll documented transgender-specific tolerance, finding that "87.6% said they would be 'comfortable' if a neighbour was a transgender person."

Región de Valparaíso stands under the national framework of Chile: the legal regime, document rules, entry provisions and protection machinery are those set out in the national record. What is specific to the region is the distribution of recorded anti-LGBTI discrimination cases and a municipal diversity-office structure.

Movilh's XXIV annual human rights report, published in March 2026 and covering 2025, records that Valparaíso concentrated 51.32% of the anti-LGBTI discrimination cases recorded nationally in 2024, an increase of 80.93% on 2023. That is a share of recorded cases, not a per-capita rate, and no population denominator accompanies it; recorded cases reflect where monitoring organisations operate and where victims report, as well as where incidents occur.

In 2025 recorded cases fell in Valparaíso and in the Región Metropolitana while every other region rose. Movilh reads the pattern as hostility moving toward regions where LGBTIQ issues have less visibility.

sources.summary: Outright International country page (12 March 2026): same-sex marriage and adoption have been legal since March 2022; since 2012 Chile's hate-crime law has included sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances; same-sex civil unions have been recognised since 2015. A 2019 comprehensive legal gender-recognition law is based on self-determination, and a third sex option has been available for intersex children on birth certificates since 2006. No legal ban exists on medically unnecessary interventions on minors, though the Health Minister published non-binding intersex-affirming guidance in 2023. A 2020 family-court decision recognised two women as parents of a child born through assisted reproduction, and a 2025 criminal court issued the country's first conviction in the field.

Movilh XXIV Annual Human Rights Report on sexual and gender diversity in Chile (published March 2026, covering 2025): Valparaíso concentrated 51.32% of national recorded anti-LGBTI discrimination cases in 2024, up 80.93% over 2023; in 2025 cases fell only in Valparaíso and Metropolitana while all other regions rose - Movilh reads this as the decentralisation of hate toward territories where LGBTIQ themes have less visibility; full per-region and per-commune series 2002-2025.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Chile - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's Chile country overview is the national framework a visitor to Región de Valparaíso stands under: the 2012 Zamudio anti-discrimination law protects sexual orientation and gender identity, civil unions have been recognised since 2015, and same-sex marriage with full adoption rights has been legal since March 2022. Gender Identity Law 21.120 (introduced 2013, enacted 2018) has since 2019 let transgender people aged 14 and over change their name and gender on all official documents without surgery, and the armed forces admit LGBT personnel. Until 2022 Article 365 of the Penal Code set a higher age of consent of 18 for male homosexual acts; the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in a 5-5 vote in August 2018, and it was abolished by Law 21,483 in August 2022, equalising the age of consent.

San Antonio, in Región de Valparaíso, was among the founding comunas of the Red de Municipalidades por la Diversidad, Inclusión y No Discriminación (Red Diversa), created in 2014 as a network of municipalities with LGBTIQA+ offices or programmes and grown beyond 60 municipalities by 2024. In April 2016 the first Carabinero contracted a civil union with a same-sex partner, and in 2020 the Chilean Army formally incorporated its first transgender member. The national framework under which these sit comprises Ley Zamudio (2012) against discrimination, same-sex marriage under Ley 21.400 (promulgated 9 December 2021, in force 10 March 2022), and Ley 21.430 (2022) banning discrimination based on sex characteristics for children and adolescents.

13589884B3780741375954.name: Antioquia
13589884B3780741375954.summary:
Antioquia stands under Colombia's national framework: the national rules on identity documents, recognition of marriages performed abroad, access to public and commercial premises, and the treatment of detainees apply in the department as elsewhere in the country, and the inventory identifies no Antioquia-specific statute, departmental decree or court ruling of its own.

The region-specific record is a killing in Bello, in the metropolitan corridor around Medellín. On 5 April 2025 a video circulated showing Sara Millerey González Borja, a 32-year-old trans woman, beaten and thrown into a waterway in daylight while onlookers filmed; her legs, arms and hands were fractured, she could not swim, and she died of cardiac arrest the following afternoon.

She was the third LGBTQ person killed in Bello during 2025, the two earlier victims being gay men. A clinic reportedly declined to treat her as an emergency, on the stated ground that she had not been shot. Bello city hall drew criticism for referring to her by her pre-transition name. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and protests followed in several cities.
