She was the third LGBTQ person killed in Bello in 2025 (the first two victims were gay men); a clinic reportedly did not treat her as an emergency 'because she didn't get shot', and she died of cardiac arrest the following afternoon. The article records 13 trans people killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025 alone and notes city hall was criticised for using her pre-transition name.

The Guardian (30 July 2024), reporting from Caquetá: 41 transgender women were killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight more between February and April 2024, national figures that also cover Antioquia. Armed groups in Caquetá, where ex-rebel structures persist despite the 2016 peace agreement, distributed flyers on streets and WhatsApp announcing a 'social cleansing' plan naming 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets, and trans women there fled after death threats. No Antioquia-specific source covers these national 2023-24 kill tallies or the southern-department flyers.

25490228B43154843394848.name: Comunidad de Madrid
25490228B43154843394848.summary:
Madrid stands under Spain's national framework for legal gender recognition, with the Comunidad de Madrid's own statute as a layer beneath it. Madrid is one of Europe's principal LGBT urban centres, and the region was among the first in Spain to pass a gender-identity law, adopting its statute in 2016 alongside the Islas Baleares and the Región de Murcia and after Extremadura in 2015. That regional statute was later amended by Ley 17/2023. Regional law must comply with Spain's Ley 4/2023, which sets the statutory floor that a trans visitor's recognition and protection claims in the region rest on.

What the region has withdrawn since then matters to anyone relying on local antidiscrimination machinery. After the 2023 regional election, the new government of the Comunidad de Madrid repealed the region's non-discrimination law, repealed the regional ban on conversion therapy as it applies to trans people, removed the penalties that attached to conversion therapy, and repealed several trans legal recognitions. These measures act on the region's own guarantees and leave the national framework in place.

The safety picture the region's own sources report does not follow from the legal position. Homophobic and transphobic discrimination and violence are described as significant problems in Madrid, and trans people and migrants are reported to face additional barriers within the city's LGBT population.

The community is concentrated and long established. The Chueca district is the centre of the city's LGBT life, and MADO, held annually in late June or early July, is among the largest Pride events in the world and draws millions of attendees. COGAM, founded in 1986, is the city's most influential LGBT organisation; the city government maintains an Oficina de Atención a la Diversidad Sexual y de Género; and Arcopoli works against discrimination and violence.

sources.summary: Official text (BOE) of Ley 4/2023 (28 February 2023), "for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of the rights of LGTBI people": establishes self-ID legal gender recognition (16+, no diagnosis), broad anti-discrimination guarantees, employment and health measures, and an LGTBI equality strategy. National framework that Madrid's 2023 amendments sit beside.

Human Rights Watch (Feb 2023): "Victory in Fight for Gender Recognition in Spain" - hails Spain's self-ID gender-recognition law as a hard-won victory after years of activism. National framework context.

Spanish criminal-law firm analysis (June 2026): disentangles three statutes - what Law 4/2023 does and does not do; the discrimination aggravating factor of Article 22.4 of the Penal Code (gender identity/expression motives); and the hate offences of Article 510 CP extended to trans/LGBTI people. National framework context.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2005; Madrid Pride (MADO), held annually in late June or early July, is among the largest Pride events in the world and draws millions of attendees; the Chueca district is the epicentre of the community. Local institutions recorded are COGAM, founded 1986 and the city's most influential LGBT organisation, the city government's Oficina de Atencion a la Diversidad Sexual y de Genero, and Arcopoli, which works against discrimination and violence. The safety finding it reports is that homophobic and transphobic discrimination and violence remain significant problems in Madrid, and that marginalised LGBT groups such as migrants and trans people face additional barriers.

19338628B36302232233914.name: Hauts-de-France
19338628B36302232233914.summary:
Hauts-de-France legislates nothing of its own on detention, identity documents or anti-discrimination. The region stands under the national framework of France: custodial placement, gender markers and discrimination protections are set nationally. No regional statute, regional court ruling or regional administrative instruction on transgender detainees or visitors appears in the sources.

The single documented case in the region is Paola, a trans woman whose identity documents record her as male, transferred in 2014 to the correctional facility at Lille and held in a men's establishment. Detainees there shouted "We don't want any women here!"; a fellow inmate tried to attack her with a knife; she spent two days in solitary confinement. The account was published in a BuzzFeed News investigation of 12 January 2018.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed investigation posted 12 January 2018: under Article D248 of the criminal-procedure code men and women must be held in separate establishments, but placement follows the legal gender on identity documents, so trans women still recorded as male are held in all-male facilities - the group that, per controller-general Adeline Hazan, 'suffers the most' in prison. Region-relevant case: Paola, transferred in 2014 to Lille's northern correctional facility, was met by detainees shouting 'We don't want any women here!', a fellow inmate tried to attack her with a knife and she spent two days in solitary confinement; Kara B. was held under conditions described as worrying after her 2016 Paris protest trial; the Ministry of Justice counted 13 transgender detainees across eight facilities as of 1 November 2016.

National detention-oversight opinion of 25 May 2021 (covering every place of deprivation of liberty; prepared from referrals received since 2010 concerning transgender detainees): assignment to establishments or wards (male or female) is based exclusively on civil status, so the vast majority of transgender people are held in institutions or wards that do not correspond to their gender identity, and search procedures for persons whose civil-status sex does not match their identity add constraints such as isolation. It recommends guaranteeing every transgender detainee the possibility of choosing the sex of searching officers and of their ward, bars identity-based isolation, requires continuity of medical and hormone care with free choice of doctor, urges research funding, and faults the administration for not translating the 2016 justice-modernisation law (n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016) into prison rules.

19338628B57683459369229.name: Occitanie
19338628B57683459369229.summary:
Occitanie stands under the national legal framework of France. The region-specific record in the sources is the opinion issued on 25 May 2021 by the CGLPL, the national inspectorate of places of deprivation of liberty, whose visits covered two facilities in Toulouse: Toulouse-Seysses prison and the Toulouse central police station.

The opinion concerns eight transgender women held in those Toulouse facilities. It documents isolation imposed on detainees because of their trans status, and staff who had received no training on trans issues. It further finds that the depathologisation law of 18 November 2016 (n° 2016-1547) was never written into prison rules or into healthcare guidance, so the statutory change of status had no operational effect on how trans detainees were held or treated.

The inspectorate's recommendations bearing on the region call for financed research, policies against discrimination, and suitable procedures for searching and for assigning detainees whose civil-status sex does not match the identity they present. For a trans visitor, the operative exposure in Occitanie is custody: police custody at a central station and detention at a prison are the settings where the documented failures occur, and the placement and search practices described apply regardless of how a person presents in ordinary daily life.

65028918B14696209246677.name: Jakarta Special Capital Region
65028918B14696209246677.summary:
Jakarta stands under Indonesia's national framework, which the national record carries; what is specific to the Special Capital Region is a police practice of raiding private LGBT gatherings under pornography and morality provisions rather than under any Jakarta statute naming LGBT people.

The raid series runs back a decade. In May 2017 police arrested 141 people at what was described as a gay sex party in Jakarta. On 21 May 2017 officers detained 144 people at the Atlantis Gym sauna, ten of whom were charged. In October 2017 police arrested 51 people at a sauna in Central Jakarta, of whom six were charged. All of these cases were pursued under the pornography law.

The pattern continued in 2025. On 1 February 2025 police detained 56 people at a hotel in South Jakarta, described in reporting as a gay party. On 24 May 2025 nine people were detained after a raid on a different hotel in South Jakarta. Offences of this kind can carry up to 15 years' imprisonment.

City government, not only the police, has acted against transgender residents. In March 2018 the Jakarta Social Agency declared transgender waria 'socially dysfunctional' and held trans women in city-run rehabilitation centres unless they signed statements promising not to repeat their offence.

For a trans visitor the operative exposure in Jakarta is attendance at a private gathering: a hotel party, a sauna, a rented venue. The charges that follow are laid under broad pornography and morality provisions with long sentences available, and the sources record no Jakarta statute creating offences specific to LGBT people.

sources.summary: An October 2025 presidential decree named 'the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture' a non-military national security threat alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction. Journalists report a constant chilling effect, with editors killing LGBTQ+ stories fearing state reprisal or religious backlash. Civil-society and independent media space has contracted since 2024-25, documented amid student-led anti-government protests.

More recently it records 56 people detained at a hotel in South Jakarta on 1 February 2025, nine detained at another South Jakarta hotel on 24 May 2025, and 75 arrested at a private villa near the capital on 22 June 2025 — offences there can carry up to 15 years' imprisonment. In March 2018 the Jakarta Social Agency declared transgender waria 'socially dysfunctional' and detained trans women in city-run 'rehabilitation' centres unless they signed statements promising not to repeat their 'offence'. Transgender people may change legal gender only after surgery and a judge's approval, and there is no general anti-discrimination law, so police action in Jakarta operates on pornography and morality provisions rather than any LGBT-specific statute.

Amnesty International Indonesia's deputy director called the villa raid 'a blatant violation of human rights and privacy' that 'exemplifies the hostile environment for LGBTI people in Indonesia', and demanded the release of those arrested. The release notes that police made the arrests without naming detainees or conducting judicial proceedings, and that those detained risk up to 15 years' imprisonment under Indonesia's broadly worded Pornography Law.

68945753B55100681051852.summary:
Seoul stands under the national framework of South Korea. National rules on criminal law, identity documents, military service and legal gender recognition are carried by the country record; what follows is specific to Seoul.

On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court, with presiding judge Chung In-jae, dismissed the government's appeal in a damages action brought by a transgender plaintiff identified as A, and the judgment became final when neither side appealed further. The court awarded 300,000 won (about $240) of the 3 million won claimed. It held that a police officer's advice to an LGBT person in the middle of legal transition to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, and that the right to use restrooms comfortably is a fundamental and universal human right.

The ruling addresses police conduct rather than venue policy. It establishes that advice of this kind from an officer is unlawful in Seoul. It does not by itself require any particular venue, school or business to admit a trans person to a given restroom.

31927357B30293642818187.name: Quintana Roo
31927357B30293642818187.summary:
Quintana Roo stands under the national framework of Mexico. The state's own law governs legal gender recognition, marriage, adoption, hate-crime liability and the prohibition of conversion practices.

Quintana Roo enacted legal gender recognition in 2020.

On 15 December 2023 the state congress banned conversion practices, following Morelos. The reform prohibits and sanctions efforts to correct sexual orientation and gender identity, commonly called conversion therapies, with penalties of two to six years in prison and fines of 1,000 to 2,000 times the daily UMA value. It applies across the state, including the tourist corridors of Cancún and the Riviera Maya.

The state penal code treats crimes motivated by sexual orientation or gender as hate crimes, and the state ratified the 2011 federal constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination.

Marriage in Quintana Roo has been open to couples without regard to gender since 2012. Two marriages were performed in Kantunilkín in November 2011, annulled by the governor in April 2012, and reinstated on 3 May 2012 after the state conceded that its Civil Code sets no gender requirement. That silence in the Civil Code is the operative basis on which a trans visitor's marriage would be recognised in the state.

The state congress legalised adoption by same-sex couples in August 2022.

31927357B30293642818187.displaySummary: Quintana Roo stands under the national framework of Mexico; the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail. The state's own law governs legal gender recognition, marriage, adoption, hate-crime liability and the prohibition of conversion practices. Quintana Roo enacted legal gender recognition in 2020. On 15 December 2023 the state congress banned conversion practices, following Morelos. The reform prohibits and sanctions efforts to correct sexual orientation and gender identity, commonly called conversion therapies, with penalties of two to six years in prison and fines of 1,000 to 2,000 times the daily UMA value. It applies across the state, including the tourist corridors of Cancún and the Riviera Maya. The state penal code treats crimes motivated by sexual orientation or gender as hate crimes, and the state ratified the 2011 federal constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination. Marriage in Quintana Roo has been open to couples without regard to gender since 2012. Two marriages were performed in Kantunilkín in November 2011, annulled by the governor in April 2012, and reinstated on 3 May 2012 after the state conceded that its Civil Code sets no gender requirement. That silence in the Civil Code is the operative basis on which a trans visitor's marriage would be recognised in the state. The state congress legalised adoption by same-sex couples in August 2022.

15666254B89722251658211.name: Selangor
15666254B89722251658211.summary:
Selangor stands under Malaysia's national framework: the federal Penal Code, the national rules on identity documents and the entry provisions recorded in Malaysia's own dossier apply to visitors here as elsewhere in the country. Two further layers operate inside the state. The Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 binds Muslims, and Selangor's Islamic religious department polices appearance and public conduct under it.

In February 2021 the Federal Court struck down provisions of the Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 as exceeding the state's legislative power. The ruling did not decriminalise anything under the federal Penal Code, which continues to apply in Selangor as elsewhere.

Selangor's Sharia court has imposed custodial sentences with corporal punishment on same-sex conduct: five men received six to seven months' imprisonment with six strokes of the cane in a case documented by the Human Dignity Trust profile updated 16 December 2025.

State authorities in Selangor issued an arrest warrant for a trans businesswoman, Nur Sajat, who failed to appear in court in 2021 to answer charges of "insulting Islam" based on her attire, and announced the deployment of 122 religious-affairs officers to locate her. She subsequently fled to Thailand, was permitted to remain under UNHCR protection, and later settled in Australia. The deployment was cited by Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters, in a report released 10 August 2022, as evidence of how far authorities go to enforce rigid gender norms.

At least 1,733 people had attended state "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021, under a crackdown on the LGBT community that the Human Dignity Trust records as ongoing since the 2018 election. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters found that these state programmes internalise discrimination and foster self-hatred.

Investigations into LGBT people documented by Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters covered Selangor alongside Kuala Lumpur, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah.

Penal Code sections 377A-377D criminalise same-sex intimacy and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment with whipping; the provisions have been enforced in recent years, apply to both men and women, and are usable against trans people. Sharia state enactments criminalise cross-dressing and "males posing as females". In Selangor, the Federal Court struck down provisions of the Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 as exceeding state power (2021). State authorities issued an arrest warrant for a trans businesswoman who failed to appear in court and announced the deployment of 122 religious-affairs officers (the Sajat case). A Selangor Sharia court sentenced five men to six to seven months' imprisonment with six strokes of the cane. At least 1,733 people had attended state "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021, under a crackdown on the LGBT community ongoing since the 2018 election.

HRW/Justice for Sisters report release (10 August 2022) documenting Malaysia's state-backed discrimination. In 2021 Nur Sajat, a transgender woman and cosmetics entrepreneur, failed to appear in court in Selangor to answer criminal charges for "insulting Islam" based on her attire. The state's religious department issued a warrant for her arrest and announced it had mobilised 122 religious-affairs officers to hunt her down, then sought her extradition from Thailand. HRW/JFS cite the deployment as showing how far authorities go to enforce rigid gender norms. She was permitted to stay under UNHCR protection and later settled in Australia. National framework context: the federal penal code punishes oral and anal sex with up to 20 years in prison; Sharia codes in the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya criminalise same-sex activity and gender nonconformity; investigations covered Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah; state "rehabilitation" programmes were found to internalise discrimination and foment self-hatred.

15666254B42356713390762.name: Johor
15666254B42356713390762.summary:
Johor is one of thirteen Malaysian state jurisdictions and stands under the national framework: the federal Penal Code applies in full within its borders, and Johor maintains its own Sharia enactment binding on Muslims. The substance of both layers is set out in the national assessment.

In November 2023 the Johor state government announced plans to establish conversion-therapy centres to "rehabilitate" LGBT people. The announcement is a formal statement of policy by the state administration rather than a criminal provision, and it is the clearest documented expression of official hostility from this state's government in the record.

The conversion-therapy announcement sits within a national pattern of state-conducted "rehabilitation" programmes: at least 1,733 people had attended such programmes as of June 2021, under a crackdown running since the 2018 election. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters' state-conducted investigations, published 10 August 2022, covered Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah; Johor was not among the states investigated in that reporting, so no Johor-specific enforcement incident is documented in this record.

sources.summary: National-framework source (applies country-wide, including the state of Malacca): the Human Dignity Trust Malaysia country profile (last updated 2024) reports the Federal Penal Code 1936 ss.377A/377B criminalise same-sex sexual activity with a maximum penalty of twenty years’ imprisonment and whipping, and s.377D “outrages on decency” criminalises gross indecency in terms that can be used to target transgender people; state Sharia enactments additionally criminalise “cross-dressing” for Muslims. It records evidence of the law being enforced in recent years, a crackdown on the LGBT community since the 2018 election, a high-profile 2021 case of a prominent transgender woman fleeing the country following threats of arrest, and consistent reports of discrimination and violence with transgender people particularly vulnerable to physical and verbal abuse.

National-framework source (applies country-wide; no Malacca-specific breakdown): An HRW report published 10 Aug 2022 with Justice for Sisters documents government-sponsored discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia. It cites the federal penal code punishing oral and anal sex with up to 20 years in prison and Sharia law codes in the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya that typically criminalise same-sex activity and gender nonconformity. It details conversion and rehabilitation programs, officials shutting down events, and the 2021 prosecution of transgender woman Nur Sajat in western Selangor, and concludes that pervasive antipathy toward sexual and gender diversity influences law enforcement, judicial outcomes, family behavior, and public discourse.

27671186B76269877687363.summary:
Abuja Federal Capital Territory stands under Nigeria's national framework, and no territorial variation from it was identified in this inventory: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 and the criminal provisions it reinforces apply in the capital as they do elsewhere, and the national layer is carried by the parent record.

1875124B65618634887963.name: Lima
1875124B65618634887963.summary:
Lima stands under the national framework of Peru, and the national assessment carried by the parent record applies here. No separate departmental or municipal regime modifying that framework was identified in the sources.

Jorge Chávez international airport in Lima had installed signage reading "for all persons with female identity" and "male identity". The national norm approved in Congress on 2 April 2025 bars such "ambiguous" signage, and article 5 of the fused bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR prohibits entry to and use of public sanitary facilities by any person whose biological sex does not match the sex for which the facility is designated, subject to listed exceptions. The inclusive signs at Lima's international gateway fall inside that prohibition, so a trans visitor should expect facilities across the department to be designated by birth sex rather than by identity.

Enforcement of the restriction, as described by LGBTIQ activist Gianna Camacho, would reduce to security staff judging for themselves whether a woman entering a facility is trans and demanding her national identity card (DNI). The sources document no guidance, oversight or complaint route governing that judgement.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in Lima, reported on 15 April 2025 in an analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte that the plenary approved the fused bills on Wednesday 2 April 2025, exempt from a second vote. The authors call article 5 direct legislation conditioning basic rights on a "biological sex", a violation of the equality and non-discrimination principle, and note that trans people, though framed as aggressors by the rule, are more often the victims of violence and discrimination.

On 12 February 2023 Rubí Torres Silvano, a 31-year-old trans woman and sex worker, was kidnapped from jirón Chancay in central Lima by the "Los Gallegos" extortion gang and killed with roughly 30 gunshots. The most recent documented killing of a trans woman in Lima in this record is that case of 12 February 2023; no later instance is documented.

The Agencia Presentes report of 22 July 2024 records state inaction that bears on accountability for that case: no official system records victims' sexual orientation, and hate crimes go unsanctioned. The sources record no outcome in the Rubí Torres Silvano case.

1875124B43998217738279.summary:
Lima stands under Peru's national framework: Congress and national agencies set the rules on gender identity, access to public facilities, identity documents and hate-crime protection, and no municipal ordinance of the city's own on these matters appears in the reporting reviewed. What is specific to the capital is where those national rules land, at the airport that serves it, in its public buildings and commercial venues, and in the violence documented in its central streets.

The bathroom bill approved unanimously by the Congressional Women and Family Commission on 20 February 2025 obliges the removal of "ambiguous" signage, and the text names the signage installed at Jorge Chávez International Airport, which reads "for all persons with female identity" and "male identity". The airport serving Lima is the first site where that removal obligation would apply, and the signs in question are the ones that currently direct arriving trans passengers to a facility.

Gianna Camacho, a trans human-rights defender, warns that enforcement will take the form of identity-document checks by security staff deciding who may enter a bathroom, a practice she describes as discriminatory and grounded in prejudice. In the capital that discretion would sit with staff at municipal buildings, transport terminals and private venues rather than with any single agency.

On 12 February 2023 the gang known as Los Gallegos kidnapped Rubí Torres Silvano, a 31-year-old trans sex worker, from jirón Chancay in the central city and killed her with roughly 30 gunshots. The Observatory report on hate crimes cites the case as an example of the pattern in Lima.

What is specific to this division is where those national rules land, at the airport that serves it, in its public buildings and commercial venues, and in the violence documented in its central streets.

The bathroom bill approved unanimously by a standing legislative committee dealing with women and family affairs on 20 February 2025 obliges the removal of "ambiguous" signage, and the text names the signage installed at the international airport serving this division, which reads "for all persons with female identity" and "male identity". The airport serving this division is the first site where that removal obligation would apply, and the signs in question are the ones that currently direct arriving trans passengers to a facility.

A trans human-rights defender warns that enforcement will take the form of identity-document checks by security staff deciding who may enter a bathroom, a practice she describes as discriminatory and grounded in prejudice. In this division that discretion would sit with staff at municipal buildings, transport terminals and private venues rather than with any single agency.

Violence in this division is documented in the same reporting. On 12 February 2023 a gang kidnapped a 31-year-old trans sex worker from a street in the central part of the city and killed her with roughly 30 gunshots. The hate-crime monitoring report cites the case as an example of the pattern in this division.

25984515B47806653651907.name: Ankara
25984515B47806653651907.summary:
Ankara stands under Turkey's national framework: the sources record no Ankara-level law or municipal measure, and the city's distinct exposure is institutional, since the presidency, the Ministry of Family and the drafting machinery for national legislation sit there. The penal-code package reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 is drafted, and would be enforced, through institutions operating in Ankara.

The leaked draft, known as the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct treated as contrary to biological sex and general morality, punishable by up to three years in prison, and to punish participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, surgery included, from 18 to 25, attach mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals, expose health professionals performing such interventions to fines and up to seven years in prison and trans people receiving care the authorities deem illegal to up to three years, and allow courts to order pretrial detention. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, which had not been enacted as of the reporting date.

Kaos GL's 2025 annual report concludes that hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy, centred on the presidency and implemented through the Ministry of Family, both of them Ankara institutions. It records censored broadcasts, artistic events cancelled or banned, and an LGBTI+ association closed for the first time in years, with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members.

The same report counts six violations of the right to life over the year, three of them recorded as hate-motivated, with trans people the most affected group, alongside a rise in torture and ill-treatment violations to 89 from 51 the previous year. Turkey compiles no official hate-crime statistics, so these figures rest on the organisation's own monitoring; with no general homicide or violence denominator in the sources, the six deaths cannot be expressed as a rate or compared with the risk borne by the general population.

25984515B12971548112787.name: Eskişehir
25984515B12971548112787.summary:
Eskişehir stands under Turkey's national framework; no Eskişehir-specific statute, municipal ordinance or local protection body appears in the source inventory, so the national assessment governs here. The region-specific record concerns public assembly.

In June 2021 police blocked Eskişehir's first Pride parade. Officers reached the area hours before the scheduled meeting time and carried out identity checks. Organisers were not permitted to hold a press meeting or conduct the parade, and police detained 20 people on the grounds of violating the ban on the march.

The ban is the clearest local signal that even in a university city, local authorities have suppressed the local Pride event. For a trans visitor, the documented exposure in Eskişehir is assembly and identity checks at LGBT-related gatherings rather than any city-level criminal provision.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (29 Oct 2025): a leaked '11th Judicial Package' would amend the penal and civil codes with articles threatening LGBT people — behaviour 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' and its 'promotion' (up to three years' prison, amending the indecent-acts provision); sharp restrictions on gender-affirming care (minimum age 25, onerous eligibility); potential charges against trans people, care providers, civil-society organisations and journalists; justified as protecting 'the family and public morals'.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's country page on LGBT rights in Turkey is the framework under which Eskişehir stands, and it names the province directly: in June 2021 police blocked the first Eskişehir pride parade, showing that even in this university city local authorities have suppressed the local Pride event. On the national frame, homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858 and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988 (with surgery, medical examination and court permission), but there is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law and same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in most years, and participants have faced police attacks; in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries. In early 2026 Turkish media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', a provision that was ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package. It also records that Kadir Has University surveys saw public support for equal rights for LGBTQ people rise from 33% in 2016 to 45% in 2020.

İstanbul stands under the national framework in force across Turkey; country-level law, detention conditions and healthcare are covered in the national assessment. What is specific to the city is the assembly ban and the policing of trans women on its streets.

The Governorship of İstanbul has denied permission for and locally banned Pride parades since 2015 on security and public-order grounds, with the 2016 to 2018 bans stated explicitly; one source dates the ban to 2014. Water cannon were used against marchers on 29 June 2015. The 2014 march drew more than 100,000 participants, the largest LGBT event recorded in Turkey.

Suppression escalated after the ban. In 2021 police blockaded the route and used tear gas, arresting 25 people. On 26 June 2022 riot police dispersed the march at Taksim Square, blockaded streets in the adjacent Cihangir neighbourhood, shut down public transport to the square and detained 373 people, among them the photojournalist Bülent Kılıç; those held were released after a night in custody. The district governor's offices of Kadıköy and Beyoğlu had banned all Pride Week events for seven days. Arrests continued at 113 in 2023 and 11 in 2024, three of them minors, after organisers moved Pride out of Taksim Square into other public spaces and issued false meeting calls to evade police.

Policing extends to trans women going about ordinary business. On 31 July 2025 İstanbul police stopped around 20 trans women in Beyoğlu for identity checks, recorded their names and filmed them; the report describes the operation as profiling.

66186276B86072070009793.name: Puerto Rico
66186276B86072070009793.summary:
Puerto Rico is a United States territory and stands under the United States federal framework for entry, documents, federally funded care and federal custody; the findings below are the territory's own law, its own enforcement and its own institutions.

Ley Núm. 63 de 2025, the Law for the Protection of the Health and Wellbeing of Minors, was enacted in July 2025. It bars gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, withdraws public funding for that care, and penalises violations with a fixed 15-year prison term, a $50,000 fine per violation for legal persons, and permanent loss of medical licences for professionals. Article 4, the operative prohibition, is directed at medical institutions and health professionals: none may perform surgical interventions or medication treatments that alter sex biology under the pretext of gender transition or as part of gender-dysphoria treatment.

Article 3 defines the banned chemical and surgical practice more broadly than the operative clause. It expressly names the use of puberty blockers and sex hormones, including androgen blockers, oestrogen, progesterone or testosterone, when used to treat gender dysphoria, and it sets the protected class at anyone under 21. Article 6 penalises any person who violates the law's provisions.

The gap between a definition framed around patient use and an operative clause that restricts only providers leaves an unresolved question. Under ordinary criminal-law principles a successful prosecution of a visiting under-21 trans person for using their own lawfully prescribed hormones, or of a parent accompanying them, would almost certainly fail, and no test case had resolved the question at the time of writing. For an under-21 trans traveller the practical reading is that carrying and using prescribed hormone treatment on the island sits inside the law's literal definition of a banned practice, and that enforcement risk is harassment-shaped rather than conviction-shaped: questioning, detention or investigation by hostile officials, with the answer arriving only after the fact. The law's protected class is anyone under 21 and does not on its face reach patients 21 or older.

The law was pushed through non-public hearings and is written with deliberate vagueness, so doctors and affirming parents who facilitate hormone treatment or top surgery risk prosecution, a reach that extends to the accompanying parents of a travelling trans teenager. It mandates campaigns by the Education and Health departments on the risks of trans-affirming care. Health Secretary Víctor Ramos Parés proposed amendments that would have allowed puberty blockers and the continuation of existing hormone treatment; the text as enacted stands as the most restrictive care law in any United States jurisdiction according to the report documenting it. The Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court.

The ACLU of Puerto Rico urged Governor Jenniffer González Colón to veto Senate Bill 350, which it said criminalizes doctors and parents and creates two distinct categories of children divided by whether identity aligns with sex assigned at birth. Policy Counsel Lolimar Escudero Rodríguez stated that the bill allows parents to authorise treatment where a child's identity aligns with the sex assigned at birth and prohibits them the same right where it does not. Executive Director Annette Martínez Orabona said the measure discriminates against transgender people and denies the existence of trans children and youth. The bill was authored by Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz and Senator Joanne Rodríguez Veve, passed both chambers in April, was returned for amendments suggested by Health Secretary Ramos Parés that the ACLU warned did not remedy the rights violations, and was re-approved and returned to the Governor on 28 June. Opposition was registered by the Puerto Rico College of Physicians and Surgeons, the Puerto Rico Psychology Association, the College of Social Work Professionals, the Puerto Rican Association of Professional Counseling, the Puerto Rico Bar Association and the LGBTQ+ Federation of Puerto Rico.

Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics. The first hate crime charges in the territory's history were brought in 2020, after Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged in the murder of two transgender women on 22 April 2020; Bonilla confessed to the killings. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island.

Anti-discrimination coverage is partial. The 2013 law that passed, Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013, was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities, housing, transit and business transactions are not covered. An earlier bill, House Bill 1725, passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 with wider coverage, but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved.

Marriage recognition for same-sex couples was won through federal court rather than local statute. The challenge was filed in March 2014 in the Ada Conde Vidal case, with intervention from Lambda Legal and Puerto Rico Para Todas, and in June 2014 four couples joined as plaintiffs, among them a former National Guard member and two couples already married in Canada in 2007 and in New York in 2012.

Consensual private sexual activity between adults is not criminalised. The Puerto Rico Supreme Court upheld the territory's sodomy ban in 2002; after the United States Supreme Court's 2003 ruling invalidated state and territorial sodomy statutes covering consensual private acts, Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute.

sources.title: Ley Núm. 63 de 2025 (LexJuris de Puerto Rico) — primary legal text
sources.summary: Ley Núm. 63 de 2025, 'Ley para la protección de la salud y el bienestar de los menores de edad en Puerto Rico' (primary legal text, LexJuris). Article 4 — the operative prohibition — is directed at medical institutions and health professionals: none may perform surgical interventions or medication treatments altering the sex biology of a minor 'bajo el pretexto de una transición de género o como parte de un tratamiento de disforia de género'. The Article 3 definition of banned 'chemical and surgical mutilation' is drafted broader than the prohibition: it expressly includes 'el uso de bloqueadores de pubertad y hormonas sexuales (incluyendo bloqueadores androgénicos, estrógenos, progesterona o testosterona) utilizados con el propósito de tratar la disforia de género' — the USE itself of puberty blockers and sex hormones for gender-dysphoria treatment — and defines 'niño o menor de edad' as any person under 21. Article 6 then penalises 'toda persona que viole las disposiciones de esta Ley' with a fixed 15-year term, plus permanent licence loss for professionals and a $50,000 per-violation fine for juridical persons. Legal analysis of this drafting notes a structural tension: the definition speaks of patient 'use' while the operative clause restricts only providers, and the penalty catch-all says 'any person'. Under standard criminal doctrines (definitions create no offence by themselves; a protected class cannot be prosecuted as the perpetrator of its own victimisation; the principle of legality bars analogy; and travel with lawfully prescribed personal medication), a successful prosecution of a visiting under-21 trans person for using their own prescribed hormones — or of their parents for enabling it — would almost certainly fail, and the statute is a textbook void-for-vagueness candidate. But the textual ambiguity is precisely what legal advocates flag as its chilling effect: it leaves interpretive room for hostile officials to question, detain or investigate trans youth and their families on the ground, with the answer coming only after the fact. For a travelling under-21 trans person the practical reading is: carrying and using prescribed HRT in Puerto Rico sits inside the law's literal definition of banned practice, enforcement risk is harassment-shaped rather than conviction-shaped, and no test case had resolved the question at the time of writing. The ACLU of Puerto Rico had urged a veto before signature, stating the bill 'criminalizes doctors and parents' and creates 'two distinct categories of children' divided by sex-assigned-at-birth identity, and the island's College of Physicians and Surgeons, Psychology Association, College of Social Work Professionals, Bar Association and LGBTQ+ Federation all registered opposition.

Washington Blade (26 Apr 2019): Gov. Rossello announced SB1253 ('clarify religious freedom principles') and SB1254 (conversion-therapy ban with pastoral exemption); LGBT council president Johanne Velez Garcia and allies said the pair would open discrimination doors, criticizing the religious-freedom carve-out as license to refuse service on orientation/gender-identity grounds.

Washington Blade (25 Jun 2014): four same-sex couples joined the federal marriage lawsuit in PR (filed March; Ada Conde Vidal case), with Lambda Legal and PR Para Todas intervening - one couple married in Canada 2007, another in New York 2012; former National Guard member among plaintiffs. Road to marriage equality in PR ran through federal court.

Washington Blade (18 Mar 2019): the pro-statehood NPP caucus in the PR House blocked a floor vote on SB1000, which would have banned conversion therapy for minors; Sen. Zoe Laboy (co-sponsor) dissented publicly. Conversion-therapy ban died in the House despite Senate passage and governor support.

Washington Blade (13 Jun 2019): Gov. Rossello asked lawmakers to withdraw SB1253/SB1254 amid sustained opposition; his April announcement had included a pastoral-capacity exemption for clergy in the conversion-therapy ban. Record of LGBT advocates defeating the religious-freedom bill pairing.

Erin in the Morning (2025): PR enacted a trans youth care ban pushed through non-public hearings; law is deliberately vague so doctors and affirming parents facilitating HRT or top surgery risk prosecution; mandates Education/Health department campaigns on 'risks' of trans-affirming care; Health Secretary Ramos Otero proposed amendments allowing puberty blockers and continuation of existing HRT, but the enacted text is the most extreme care restriction in US jurisdictions per the report. For a trans visitor the ban closes off all gender-affirming care on the island for anyone under 21, and the deliberately vague facilitation language reaches the accompanying parents of a travelling trans teenager.

sources.title: Executive Order 14168 ("Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government") - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Executive Order 14168 (signed 20 January 2025) directs US federal agencies, including the Bureau of Prisons, to recognize only two sexes, and federal practice has followed by placing transgender inmates in facilities congruent with their sex assigned at birth rather than their asserted gender identity. The ACLU said it had received reports that transgender women were being transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender people it holds. Advocates say the order violates the Prison Rape Elimination Act's requirement that trans inmates' housing be decided on an individual safety assessment. Federal custody rules apply in Puerto Rico as a US territory. No separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections trans-inmate housing policy, special unit, or ruling was located.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Puerto Rico's sodomy ban was upheld by the Puerto Rico Supreme Court in 2002, but after the U.S. Supreme Court's Lawrence v. Texas ruling in 2003 struck down all state and territorial sodomy statutes for consensual private acts, Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute. In July 2025 Puerto Rico banned gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, barred public funding for it, and threatened doctors who violate the ban with up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine, and permanent loss of their licenses; the Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court. An anti-discrimination bill (House Bill 1725) passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 and would have barred discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, public transportation and public facilities, business transactions and housing, but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved. The 2013 law that did pass (Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013) was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities remain uncovered. A 2017 religious freedom bill that would have let public businesses legally discriminate against LGBTQ people was vetoed by Governor Ricardo Rosselló in February 2018, and a similar 2019 bill was withdrawn by Rosselló on 13 June 2019 after House approval amid protests. Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics, and the territory is also covered by the U.S. federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. 2020 was the first year anyone in Puerto Rico was charged with a hate crime: Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged after Bonilla confessed that he and Díaz de León murdered two transgender women on 22 April 2020. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island. In 2013 the legislature passed House Bill 488 (signed 29 May 2013) extending domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity.

sources.title: ACLU of Puerto Rico Urges Governor to Veto Senate Bill 350 (ACLU-PR press release)
sources.summary: The ACLU of Puerto Rico called on Governor Jenniffer González Colón to veto Senate Bill 350, 'which criminalizes doctors and parents and aims to prohibit gender-affirming medical treatments for individuals under the age of 21'. Policy Counsel Lolimar Escudero Rodríguez stated the bill 'creates two distinct categories of children: one that allows parents to access and authorize treatments if the child's identity aligns with the sex assigned at birth, and another that prohibits parents the same right if their child's identity is different'. The release records that the bill was authored by Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz and Senator Joanne Rodríguez Veve, passed both chambers in April, was returned for amendments suggested by Health Secretary Víctor Ramos Parés that the ACLU warned 'do not remedy the violation of fundamental constitutional, civil, and human rights', and was re-approved and returned to the Governor on 28 June. It states the bill's 'text is clearly and exclusively aimed at minors whose identity does not correspond to the sex assigned to them at birth' and that it disregards the specialist consultation process that precedes parents authorising puberty blockers or hormonal treatments, 'and instead, criminalizes them'. Executive Director Annette Martínez Orabona: the measure 'directly discriminates against transgender people and denies the existence of trans children and youth, whose very lives may be at risk'. The release lists local opposition from the Puerto Rico College of Physicians and Surgeons, the Puerto Rico Psychology Association, the College of Social Work Professionals, the Puerto Rican Association of Professional Counseling, the Puerto Rico Bar Association and the LGBTQ+ Federation of Puerto Rico.

sources.title: Senate Bill 350 — ACLU of Puerto Rico legislation page
sources.summary: The ACLU of Puerto Rico opposed Senate Bill 350 'because of its direct impact on access to gender-affirming care for trans people, particularly trans youth and trans children, as well as on the rights of families and minors. The measure bans gender-affirming medical treatments for people under 21 years of age.'

sources.title: Puerto Rico bans hormone therapy and gender surgery for transgender youth (AP News)
sources.summary: AP reported that Puerto Rico's governor signed a bill prohibiting hormone therapy or gender-affirming surgeries for transgender youth, a move that 'has drawn sharp criticism from activists in the largely conservative U.S. territory'. The law applies to those younger than 21 and calls for 15 years in prison for violators, a $50,000 penalty, and revocation of the licences and permits of medical staff.

sources.title: Human rights in Puerto Rico — Amnesty International report
sources.summary: Amnesty International's Puerto Rico reporting records that 'In July, the government signed Law 63-2025, prohibiting gender-affirming health care for people under the age of 21.'

sources.title: LGBTQ+ advocacy group criticizes Puerto Rico law criminalizing gender-affirming care (JURIST)
sources.summary: JURIST reported that Puerto Rico's LGBTQ+ Federation denounced the Law for the Protection of the Health and Wellbeing of Minors in Puerto Rico, which 'prohibits the use of puberty blockers, hormone treatment, and gender-affirming surgeries for anybody under the age of 21' and 'imposes a sentence of up to 15 years and a $50,000 fine on offenders'.

This division is a territory of this country and stands under this country's federal framework for entry, documents, federally funded care and federal custody; the findings below are the division's own law, its own enforcement and its own institutions.

A statute enacted in July 2025, the Law for the Protection of the Health and Wellbeing of Minors, bars gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, withdraws public funding for that care, and penalises violations with a fixed 15-year prison term, a $50,000 fine per violation for legal persons, and permanent loss of medical licences for professionals. Article 4, the operative prohibition, is directed at medical institutions and health professionals: none may perform surgical interventions or medication treatments that alter sex biology under the pretext of gender transition or as part of gender-dysphoria treatment.

Article 3 defines the banned chemical and surgical practice more broadly than the operative clause. It expressly names the use of puberty blockers and sex hormones, including androgen blockers, oestrogen, progesterone or testosterone, when used to treat gender dysphoria, and it sets the protected class at anyone under 21. Article 6 penalises any person who violates the law's provisions.

The gap between a definition framed around patient use and an operative clause that restricts only providers leaves an unresolved question. Under ordinary criminal-law principles a successful prosecution of a visiting under-21 trans person for using their own lawfully prescribed hormones, or of a parent accompanying them, would almost certainly fail, and no test case had resolved the question at the time of writing. For an under-21 trans traveller the practical reading is that carrying and using prescribed hormone treatment in this division sits inside the law's literal definition of a banned practice, and that enforcement risk is harassment-shaped rather than conviction-shaped: questioning, detention or investigation by hostile officials, with the answer arriving only after the fact. The law's protected class is anyone under 21 and does not on its face reach patients 21 or older.

The law was pushed through non-public hearings and is written with deliberate vagueness, so doctors and affirming parents who facilitate hormone treatment or top surgery risk prosecution, a reach that extends to the accompanying parents of a travelling trans teenager. It mandates campaigns by the education and health departments on the risks of trans-affirming care. A senior health official proposed amendments that would have allowed puberty blockers and the continuation of existing hormone treatment; the text as enacted stands as the most restrictive care law in any jurisdiction of this country according to the report documenting it. A territory-wide LGBTQ+ federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court.

A territory-level civil liberties organisation urged the governor to veto a bill in the upper chamber, which it said criminalises doctors and parents and creates two distinct categories of children divided by whether identity aligns with sex assigned at birth. A policy counsel at that organisation stated that the bill allows parents to authorise treatment where a child's identity aligns with the sex assigned at birth and prohibits them the same right where it does not. Its executive director said the measure discriminates against transgender people and denies the existence of trans children and youth. The bill was authored by the presiding officer of the upper chamber and one of its members, passed both chambers in April, was returned for amendments suggested by the senior health official that the civil liberties organisation warned did not remedy the rights violations, and was re-approved and returned to the governor on 28 June. Opposition was registered by the division's college of physicians and surgeons, its psychology association, its college of social work professionals, its association of professional counsellors, its bar association and the territory-wide LGBTQ+ federation.

This division amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics. The first hate crime charges in the division's history were brought in 2020, after two named defendants were charged in the murder of two transgender women on 22 April 2020; one of the defendants confessed to the killings. In January 2021 the governor declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals in this division.

Anti-discrimination coverage is partial. The 2013 law that passed, signed 29 May 2013, was amended in the lower chamber to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities, housing, transit and business transactions are not covered. An earlier bill passed the lower chamber 43-6 in November 2009 with wider coverage, but the upper chamber held no hearings and took no action after its presiding officer said it would not be approved.

Marriage recognition for same-sex couples was won through federal court rather than local statute. The challenge was filed in March 2014 in a named case, with intervention from two advocacy organisations, and in June 2014 four couples joined as plaintiffs, among them a former member of the territory's reserve force and two couples already married in a neighbouring jurisdiction in 2007 and in another jurisdiction of this country in 2012.

Consensual private sexual activity between adults is not criminalised. The division's highest civil court upheld its sodomy ban in 2002; after the highest court of this country issued a 2003 ruling invalidating state and territorial sodomy statutes covering consensual private acts, this division amended its penal code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute.

SYN-ASM.name: American Samoa
SYN-ASM.summary:
American Samoa's own criminal code does not punish consensual sodomy. The first sodomy statute, enacted in 1963, covered male homosexual and heterosexual conduct and did not address lesbian conduct; the Fono's 1979 revision, effective in 1980, retained prohibition only for public acts, prostitution, conduct involving minors and conduct with persons unable to consent. The age of consent is 16, regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Same-sex marriage is not licensed. On 20 March 2003 the Senate rejected a bill introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster that would have outlawed it, after the House Judiciary Committee recommended the bill be killed; at the committee hearing fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that fa'afafine do not seek marriage with men, describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech and citing Christian upbringing. In July 2015 Attorney General Talauega Eleasalo Ale was reviewing whether the United States Supreme Court's 2015 marriage-equality ruling reached the territory and said he did not know, while the Governor stated that it did not apply, citing the territory's preamble, its constitution, Christian values and its unorganised and unincorporated political status. No same-sex couple had filed an application at that point, and a 2026 law-review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa records that none has applied since.

In January 2016 the Senate unanimously confirmed former Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as a District Court judge after he told confirming senators, including retired High Court associate judge Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, that he had not read the 2015 ruling, that the district court does not deal with it, and that he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws change.

In July 2024 an on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, tested whether the territory's ban would survive a challenge under the Fourteenth Amendment. As of mid-2024 the ban is treated locally as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question. The 2026 article reaches the opposite conclusion on the law, holding that the 2015 ruling does apply despite those official statements and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied; it sets out a litigation path through the High Court of American Samoa first, with the Territorial Registrar as defendant, then the United States Department of the Interior. Since 13 December 2022 the territory has been obliged to recognise, though not perform, same-sex marriages performed legally in another jurisdiction, with equal treatment for same-sex and opposite-sex couples.

The territory's marriage code does not specify the sex of the parties. It refers to the age of 'the male' and 'the female' on a form in which parties identify as 'son' and as 'daughter'.

Gender markers on local documents are changeable within limits. The High Court of American Samoa has held that birth certificates may be altered only to correct information that was erroneous at the time of recordation or to reflect a name change due to adoption, and the Office of Vital Statistics reads that ruling as covering applications from transgender people: it changes the name on a birth certificate when presented with a name change order, and may change the gender marker with medical documentation of the sex change.

Documented trans-specific legal matters in the territory concern employment and criminal proceedings. In June 2023 a federal civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity, and in September 2023 the United States Justice Department secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teenager; that charge is the most recent documented instance of violence against a trans person in this record, no later instance is documented, and no outcome for the charge is stated.

Public climate combines cultural recognition with religious conservatism. Fa'afafine, defined as people born male who embody both male and female traits, are described in Samoan scholarship as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, and the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa, formed in 2010, campaigns for the community and runs annual events; the first Pride festival was held in August 2016 in Utulei, and beauty pageants among the fa'afafine community draw family support. Society is nonetheless highly religious, conservative attitudes on gender and sexuality dominate, and open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend. A 2009 travel column described reserved public behaviour as expected of people of all orientations in the territory.

sources.summary: The UH Manoa libraries research guide on Pacific gender identities, last updated 2026-07-23, states that the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS) was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, explicitly re-anchored to cultural pride: 'we are fa'afafine Samoa'. It defines fa'afafine as born male but embodying both male and female traits, 'a recognized and integral part of traditional Samoan culture', and frames colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of Pacific gender identities.

Out Traveler 'Ask the Expert' column (Ed Salvato, 2009-07-01) answering a honeymoon question about American Samoa: the two Samoan nations share the fa'amatai chiefly system; ASM's ~57,000 residents across seven islands/atolls; 'Samoan culture tends toward traditionalism, and reserved behavior by people of all orientations is expected', yet 'unlike the homophobia rampant in Fiji, homosexuality is a widely accepted part of Samoan culture', with Western gay men reportedly courted by fa'afafine transgender locals and by officially straight men; local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin calls the Samoan islands 'the homeland of fa'afafine culture'; ASM hotels skew business-travel (Tradewinds, Pago Pago).

The Independent (2015-07-10): American Samoa was then the only US territory unsure whether the 2015 federal marriage ruling applied — its AG said applicability was 'still being reviewed... I don't know' while Puerto Rico, USVI, Guam and CNMI moved to apply it; no licence applications had been made.

sources.title: American Samoa Senate rejects bill outlawing same sex marriages (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: American Samoa's Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended the bill be killed. The bill was introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster, who wanted to preempt the kind of marriage lawsuits then unfolding in US states. At the committee hearing, fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine 'don't believe in marriages with other men', describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech who do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing. The territory therefore deliberately declined a formal marriage ban before Obergefell, and the hearing records contemporaneous local fa'afafine views on the question.

sources.title: American Samoa judge objects to same sex marriage (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: In January 2016 the American Samoa Senate unanimously confirmed former territory Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as District Court judge, filling the seat left by Judge John Ward II's retirement. At his confirmation hearing Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, a retired associate judge of the High Court of American Samoa, asked whether Sunia had read Obergefell; Sunia replied he had not read the US Supreme Court decision and that the district court 'doesn't deal with this ruling', and said he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws are changed. The exchange shows that eighteen months after Obergefell the territory's judiciary was operating on the premise that the ruling did not automatically apply.

sources.title: The Ambiguity that Isn't: Why Same-Sex Marriage Is Legal in American Samoa (Harootunian & Lawrence, American University JGSPL vol 33 iss 2 (2026) pp 163-207)
sources.summary: 2026 law review article by two attorneys practicing in American Samoa (American Samoa Legal Aid, with Freedom From Religion Foundation) concluding that Obergefell DOES apply in the territory despite local officials' statements, and that American Samoa would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. It records that to date no same-sex couple has applied for a marriage license in the territory, and lays out the litigation roadmap: the High Court of American Samoa first (defendant the Territorial Registrar), then the US Department of the Interior. The article is the most recent dated authority on whether the 2015 ruling is operative in American Samoa, and it separates the law as written from the practical reality.

sources.title: Survey conducted on-island focuses on local same sex marriage ban (Samoa News, Asi Andrew Fa'asau, Pago Pago)
sources.summary: Samoa News reported in July 2024 an on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, testing whether American Samoa's same-sex marriage ban would survive a challenge under the 14th Amendment. The survey also probes cultural dimensions bearing on the question (collectivistic vs individualistic orientation; linear vs polychronic time). As of mid-2024, nine years after Obergefell and more than a year after the Respect for Marriage Act obliged recognition of outside marriages (Dec 13 2022), the local ban is treated on-island as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question.

USA TODAY (7 Mar 2025): Trump executive order requires all US identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; ACLU sued the State Department for seven plaintiffs; trans/nonbinary travelers report passports confiscated or blocked, leaving some stranded abroad.

Lambda Legal's FAQ sets out passport and identity-document rules for TGNCNBI people under the current federal policy change: which documents to consider, how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the current status of document updates.

HRC (updated 2025): since Jan 2025 executive order, new/renewed US passports show sex assigned at birth regardless of gender identity or name change; the 'X' marker (available since 2022) eliminated; policy challenged in federal courts -- current passport posture for trans US travelers.

Condé Nast Traveler (Feb 2025) reports that the State Department stopped processing X-marker passports and markers not matching sex assigned at birth; existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiration; new applications are processed only as M or F per supporting documents.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in American Samoa (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The High Court of American Samoa has held that birth certificates should only be altered to correct information that was erroneous at the time of recordation or to reflect a name change due to adoption. The Office of Vital Statistics has interpreted this ruling to cover applications from transgender individuals. The Office will change the name on a birth certificate when presented with a name change order. The Office may change the gender marker on a birth certificate with medical documentation of the sex change. The first criminal law against sodomy was enacted in 1963 and made male homosexual and heterosexual sodomy illegal, but did not address lesbian sex. In 1979 the Fono revised criminal law so that consensual sodomy was no longer illegal unless it involved public acts, prostitution, minors or people unable to give consent due to mental illness, with the law taking effect in 1980. The age of consent is set at 16 years, regardless of gender and/or sexual orientation. The American Samoa Code does not specify the sex of the parties to a marriage but refers to the age of "the male" and "the female" and prescribes a form in which parties identify as "son" and as "daughter," and a 2003 bill to ban same-sex marriage was voted against by the House Judiciary Committee and then the full Senate. Same-sex marriages are currently not licensed in American Samoa, with the Attorney General in July 2015 reviewing applicability of Obergefell v. Hodges and the Governor stating the ruling does not apply due to preamble, constitution, Christian values and unorganized and unincorporated political status. Under the Respect for Marriage Act passed by the 117th United States Congress and signed by President Joe Biden in 2022, all territories including American Samoa are required to recognize, though not perform, same-sex marriages performed legally in another jurisdiction, with equal treatment for same-sex and opposite-sex couples. The article states American Samoa remains the only part of the United States along with select Native American tribal jurisdictions to enforce a ban on same-sex couples marrying, while same-sex couples married legally in other jurisdictions are recognized and must be treated equally under US federal law since 13 December 2022. The article states "American Samoa, like the neighboring country of Samoa, tends to be tolerant and accepting of transgender people and identities." It notes a long-standing tradition of raising some boys as girls to play an important domestic role in Samoan communal life, with such individuals known as the fa'afafine. It states nevertheless American Samoan society is highly religious and conservative attitudes regarding gender and sexuality tend to dominate. It states open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend. The main LGBTQ organization is the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (S.O.F.I.A.S.) which annually organizes events and festivals and campaigns for the betterment of the fa'afafine community. The first Pride festival was held in August 2016 in Utulei with pageant, song, dance and poetry choral competitions, beauty pageants among the fa'afafine community are quite popular, and families generally turn up en masse to support candidates.

sources.title: 2003 Same-Sex Marriage Ban Bill by Rep. Sua Carl Schuster
sources.summary: On 20 March 2003 the American Samoa Senate rejected Representative Sua Carl Schuster's bill to outlaw same-sex marriage after the House judiciary committee recommended it be killed, with fa'afine witness Tiffany Poutasi testifying that fa'afine are men who express femininity through dress and speech and oppose marriage with other men as against Christian upbringing.

sources.title: Attorney General Talauega Eleasalo Ale - July 2015 Review Statement
sources.summary: As of July 10, 2015, American Samoa had not authorized same-sex marriage and no same-sex marriage license applications had been filed while Attorney General Talauega Eleasalo Ale reviewed the U.S. Supreme Court marriage-equality ruling for applicability to the territory, which maintained a tradition of embracing faafafine — males raised as females taking on feminine traits — alongside dominant conservative Christian churches.

SYN-ASM.tangentialFactors:

That comparison is dated 10 July 2015 and describes the position at that time.

This division's own criminal code does not punish consensual sodomy. The first sodomy statute, enacted in 1963, covered male homosexual and heterosexual conduct and did not address lesbian conduct; the legislature's 1979 revision, effective in 1980, retained prohibition only for public acts, prostitution, conduct involving minors and conduct with persons unable to consent. The age of consent is 16, regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Same-sex marriage is not licensed. On 20 March 2003 the senate rejected a bill introduced by a representative that would have outlawed it, after a legislative judiciary committee recommended the bill be killed; at the committee hearing a resident of a locally recognised third-gender identity testified that members of that identity do not seek marriage with men, describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech and citing Christian upbringing. In July 2015 the attorney general of this division was reviewing whether this country's highest court's 2015 marriage-equality ruling reached the division and said he did not know, while the governor stated that it did not apply, citing the division's preamble, its constitution, Christian values and its unorganised and unincorporated political status. No same-sex couple had filed an application at that point, and a 2026 law-review article by two attorneys practising in this division records that none has applied since.

In January 2016 the senate unanimously confirmed a former attorney general as a district court judge after he told confirming senators, including a retired associate judge of the highest civil court serving as a senator, that he had not read the 2015 ruling, that the district court does not deal with it, and that he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws change.

In July 2024 an on-island survey by an academic teaching constitutional and comparative law at a university in this country tested whether the division's ban would survive a challenge under this country's constitutional equal-protection guarantee. As of mid-2024 the ban is treated locally as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question. The 2026 article reaches the opposite conclusion on the law, holding that the 2015 ruling does apply despite those official statements and that the division would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied; it sets out a litigation path through the highest civil court of this division first, with the territorial registrar as defendant, then this country's interior department. Since 13 December 2022 the division has been obliged to recognise, though not perform, same-sex marriages performed legally in a neighbouring jurisdiction, with equal treatment for same-sex and opposite-sex couples.

The division's marriage code does not specify the sex of the parties. It refers to the age of 'the male' and 'the female' on a form in which parties identify as 'son' and as 'daughter'.

In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teenager; that charge is the most recent documented instance of violence against a trans person in this record, no later instance is documented, and no outcome for the charge is stated.

Public climate combines cultural recognition with religious conservatism. A locally recognised third-gender identity, defined as people born male who embody both male and female traits, is described in local scholarship as a recognised and integral part of traditional culture, and a community organisation for that identity, formed in 2010, campaigns for the community and runs annual events; the first Pride festival was held in August 2016 in a local town, and beauty pageants among members of that identity draw family support. Society is nonetheless highly religious, conservative attitudes on gender and sexuality dominate, and open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend. A 2009 travel column described reserved public behaviour as expected of people of all orientations in the division.
